archetype.justification: His outgoing manner, emotionally charged words, and strong follow through fit an outgoing, spirited member.

Aaron Bean.bottom_line: Lead with the stakes, then give him a clean next step to own. Pressure from outside carries real weight with him, so line up supporters before you ask.
do: Give him room to speak, since he is outgoing
Let him pause and gather his points before you reply
Bring a dated plan, since he sees bills through
dont: Fill every pause he leaves with your own argument
Expect a quiet room to mean he has no stake
Aaron Bean.warning_sign: By default he is outgoing, so lively energy is normal. In hearings a sudden drop in that energy signals he is wary, so ease off and ask which point matters most to him.
Aaron Bean.follow_up: Within a week, mail his office a single page recap listing the people helped and the dated plan he can own.
Aaron Bean.personality: Bean is an outgoing member who is fairly curious and holds details less carefully than most. Words carry a lot of emotional charge, well beyond typical colleagues, and his description of work includes a fair amount of exact detail. Bills and votes rank near the top of the House. He draws little notice for his role, and his bills span a narrower mix than typical.
Aaron Bean.speaks: Emotional charge runs through what he says, and word choice carries feeling into every topic. His talk covers a narrow range of issues in speech, so remarks stay with a few themes. Feeling sits at the center of his argument rather than in any single phrase. A few themes recur in each exchange, and the emotion keeps them vivid. The charge in his words is easy to hear from the first sentence.
Aaron Bean.decides: He judges a request by its practical feasibility, and a clear dated plan with named steps earns his trust. Public pressure carries heavy weight with him, so a campaign of outside voices can shift his stance. His visibility runs far below his role, so a commitment from him needs a named colleague who follows the next steps closely and early.

archetype.justification: His public words about the work are more detailed than nearly anyone's, his bills cover few issues, and he follows through on bills more reliably than most.

Abraham Hamadeh.bottom_line: Lead with a plain, outcome-first case and keep it short. He follows through on bills, so ask for one dated next step.
do: Start with what the policy changes, in plain words
Bring the figures on the program's results, with the sources listed
Cite the bills he has seen through to a vote
Close by confirming the one bill milestone he should check next
dont: Stage a combative hearing-style challenge at a formal hearing
Plan a press event to raise his public visibility
Drop the ask early, since outside voices move him a little more than most
Abraham Hamadeh.warning_sign: Hearings find him less combative than most members, so a change is easy to see. If he turns pointed and presses witnesses harder than usual, he is not convinced yet. Answer only the question he raised, and leave the rest for later.
Abraham Hamadeh.follow_up: Send his office a brief written note within two days, with one dated step and its owner named.
Abraham Hamadeh.personality: Hamadeh is detailed in public talk, more so than nearly any member of the House, and his public words stay narrow in range. His bills cover few issues. Few members are less visible than he is, and in hearings he is less combative than most. Bills he takes on get carried through more reliably than most.
Abraham Hamadeh.speaks: His public words stay narrow and detailed, and his hearing manner runs milder than most members. Specifics are how he describes his work, so a short written note suits the detail he brings. Keep formal asks plain.
Abraham Hamadeh.decides: Outside voices sway him only a little more than most members, and a clear request that is repeated can pay off. He sees bills through more reliably than most. Give him time with the figures before the next meeting. Close by asking which program figure he wants refreshed first.

archetype.justification: He works a few issues in depth, with bills reaching fewer areas than nearly any other House member's and unusually careful, exact language about his work.

Adam Gray.bottom_line: Bring him one specific ask, back it with people he listens to, and leave with a concrete next step.
do: Bring district voices or groups who back the ask
Agree on a next step and its owner before you leave
Check in with his staff as the bill moves
In a hearing, expect civil questions and answer them directly
dont: Assume a commitment will carry itself through without follow-up
Treat an early no as final when outside support can still shift
Adam Gray.warning_sign: He is usually far milder than most members in hearings. If he presses a witness hard on your issue, he has a real objection. Find out what it is before you meet.
Adam Gray.follow_up: Within a day, send his staff a short note with the ask, the agreed next step and its owner, and the groups in his district who support it.
Adam Gray.personality: Gray, from California, is a specialist. His bills reach into fewer issue areas than nearly any other House member's, and his public remarks are careful and exact. In hearings he is much milder than most members. His record of casting votes and finishing bills is a little below average.
Adam Gray.speaks: Most of his talk stays within a handful of topics and rarely ranges past them. When he talks about them he goes into specifics, choosing his words with care and getting the details right. In hearings his tone stays even and mild, and he questions rather than spars.
Adam Gray.decides: For him, outside backers count for more than they do with the typical member, so who supports an ask matters. He works in few issue areas, so an ask that fits them gets more of his attention. Carrying bills forward comes somewhat slowly for him, so commitments stick only when a named step is set.

archetype.justification: He is quite skeptical, his words lean heavily toward action, and outside pressure moves him less than most members.

Adam Schiff.bottom_line: Make one clear ask and let him test the facts himself. Outside voices sway him a little less than most, so argue from the record.
do: Send a short written case with the facts up front
Let him take the floor and finish his argument
Give him a clear next step he can check himself
dont: Push a crowded room to decide on the spot
Read his skepticism as a final no to the request
Adam Schiff.warning_sign: He usually keeps an even tone and talks at length. If he starts defending his points harder than usual, he is on guard. Let him finish, then restate the one point he cares about most.
Adam Schiff.follow_up: Once the session wraps, follow up in writing with the agreed action, the person accountable for it, and a deadline.
Adam Schiff.personality: Schiff remains very careful and inquisitive, and he grows quite doubtful of tidy answers. His words are heavy on action, and he keeps company more through work than through social ties. He is highly visible in the Senate, and he is fairly outgoing. Broadly, he reads his own record, often leads talk a bit more than most, and holds a position under challenge.
Adam Schiff.speaks: His pace runs a bit quicker than most, with shorter gaps between phrases. Replies run longer than usual, and length varies more than most. His words sit low on emotional charge. Challenged, he defends his point more than most, and his manner in hearings is somewhat more combative. His pitch also rises more than most, which gives his replies lift.
Adam Schiff.decides: Before backing anything, he checks whether the facts survive and whether he can verify them personally. Outside voices sway him a little less than most, and he reaches across the aisle a bit more than most. His follow through on bills trails most colleagues a little, and he takes charge of the agenda more than most. So an ask earns his support when it is documented and he can own the next step.

archetype.justification: Very curious and fairly careful, with answers longer than almost anyone's, and few members are more visible for their role.

Adam Smith.bottom_line: Plan for a long meeting, since his answers run long. Ask for the decision only after his full point is on the table.
do: Bring the policy's results and facts on one page
Open with a short summary, since his replies run long
Let his longest answers reach their end before you jump in
Close by naming one next step and a date
dont: Answer his upbeat wording with a louder, faster delivery of your own
Assume his forceful wording shows a closed mind
Let him steer the meeting away from your ask
Adam Smith.warning_sign: He usually fills his answers with heavy filler, and his pitch swings widely. If his voice goes flat and the filler fades, he has moved on from your point. Cut your remaining points to one sentence each.
Adam Smith.follow_up: Send a short written note to his legislative director by Friday, with the main outcomes in plain words.
Adam Smith.personality: Smith is markedly curious and fairly careful, and he likes to explore ideas. He builds with the other party more than nearly any member of the House, while his bills touch a wider spread of issues than most. He follows through on votes and bills somewhat less than most. For the role he holds, few members are more visible in the House, and his public words carry much more emotion than most.
Adam Smith.speaks: In interviews he gives one of the longest answers in the House, while his longest ones stretch past almost anyone's. Filler runs thick through them, more than nearly any other member. Pace is a little slower than most, and pauses between phrases stretch longer than almost anyone's. His volume stays much more even than most, while his pitch swings widely. Wait through the pauses rather than filling them with your own points.
Adam Smith.decides: A plain account of what the policy does fits him best. Few members work across party lines as much as he does. His follow-through is somewhat less reliable than most, so note his commitments in your own record. Pick out the plain sentence he lands on after his filler, and read it back before you leave. End by asking which part of the plan he would change first.

archetype.justification: Very outgoing and very dependable at carrying bills forward, and he handles details more loosely than most.

Addison McDowell.bottom_line: Put the policy results first in a short, direct case, then lock in one dated step before you leave.
do: Lead with the results the policy will deliver in plain terms
Keep the ask to a few steps he can track
Speak evenly and leave room between points
dont: Open with a sweeping vision instead of concrete results
Addison McDowell.warning_sign: By default hearings draw less fight from him than from most members, and he speaks with long pauses. If he turns sharper in a hearing, he feels pressed, so answer each point with results and give him space to reply.
Addison McDowell.follow_up: Mail him a short page with every step, who owns it, and when it is due, and copy his staff.
Addison McDowell.personality: McDowell comes across as very open, and his voting record is more dependable than most. His outlook leans away from the practical, and he handles details more loosely than most colleagues. When he describes his own work, he gives more detail than most. His legislation touches a narrower set of topics than most. In hearings, his combativeness runs lower than most members.
Addison McDowell.speaks: His pace ranks among the lowest of all members, and his pauses between phrases are among the longest. Volume varies widely, and pitch shifts more than most. His recorded speech comes from the House floor, so read the delivery as floor style. These traits make him sound deliberate rather than quick, and he tends to pause before each point, so his delivery stays unhurried.
Addison McDowell.decides: Before backing anything he asks if it can actually get done, since his bills tend to follow through more reliably than most. Results and facts carry him further than broad vision does. Pressure from outside lands on him far less than on most members. A push from others does not easily settle his view, so a decision needs a dated plan to stick.

archetype.justification: Her skepticism, forceful wording and habit of defending her position set her apart from most colleagues.

Adelita Grijalva.bottom_line: Lead with one specific ask and let her test it before she commits. She digs in when a case feels pushed, so show who benefits rather than pressing harder.
do: Bring the one ask with a clear reason tied to people helped
Let her question the ask before you answer any part
Agree a dated next step before the meeting ends
dont: Assume her skepticism will fade once the ask is repeated
Trade sharp words back when her wording turns pointed
Adelita Grijalva.warning_sign: She usually answers in brisk, back and forth turns, and digs in on her view once pushed. If she suddenly keeps defending the same point and pushes back harder, she is losing patience, so pause and ask what she needs.
Adelita Grijalva.follow_up: Within two days, email her staff a single page recap of the request that names the upcoming step and who owns it.
Adelita Grijalva.personality: Grijalva is a skeptical member who gets worked up easily and handles details less tightly than most colleagues. Her doubt shows up early, and she defends her position once challenged, so she tests a premise before she accepts it. Forceful public wording comes with little interest in fine print. She is also much more oriented toward action in her public words than most colleagues. The result is a member who moves quickly from doubt to pushback, and who can skip the detail that holds a plan together.
Adelita Grijalva.speaks: Her speech arrives in quick exchanges, carries more filler than nearly any colleague, while she drops off far less than most of them. Forceful, emotionally charged words run through her talk, and her pitch and volume rise and fall more than most colleagues do. Her answers run a shade shorter than most colleagues. When challenged she holds her position and restates it, so the exchange gets quicker and more pointed instead of softer.
Adelita Grijalva.decides: She weighs an ask against her own doubts, and an early yes does not settle it. Outside voices move her a bit more than most colleagues do, and people an ask helps carry weight with her. She is quick to defend a position, so an ask pressed hard tends to harden her. Seeing bills through is a point where she ranks among the least dependable, so a choice can fade after the session. Any commitment holds only once someone owns the next step by name.

archetype.justification: Among the most reserved members, he is very careful in his work and among the least eager to take charge.

Adrian Smith.bottom_line: Keep talk short and let him fill quiet moments, since he is as unhurried about leading as almost anyone.
do: Open with one question, since his answers run among the shortest
Wait through his long pauses before you add anything
dont: Read a quick run of short replies as a refusal
Fill his silences with more points before he answers
Adrian Smith.warning_sign: By default he leaves much longer pauses between phrases than most. If the pauses shorten and his answers run on, he has moved from weighing the point to settling it, so give him a next step to confirm.
Adrian Smith.follow_up: Once the session ends, email him a brief written recap of the point he accepted and the revisit date within two days.
Adrian Smith.personality: Smith is as reserved as almost anyone in the House and very careful in his work. He is among the least easily flustered members and somewhat agreeable, so tense exchanges do not unsettle him. His words are as action focused as almost any House member. They are also much flatter than most. Cross party work is something he does less than nearly any member. A little less visible than most, he keeps his attention on the bill in front of him.
Adrian Smith.speaks: In interviews his answers run among the shortest in the House, and his longest answers are shorter than nearly anyone's. Short replies come in quick runs much more than most. Gaps between his phrases run far longer than most, and his loudness holds far more level than most. In his delivery his pitch stays a little flatter than most, and his speech runs somewhat slower than most.
Adrian Smith.decides: Each ask gets weighed at his own pace. A yes from him holds once the follow up is set, since he is somewhat dependable in carrying bills across the line. Pressure from outside can tip him, though only a little more than it tips most members. He is among the least eager to take charge, so a decision with him comes after he has had the case in writing.

archetype.justification: Curiosity sets him apart, and he is very visible, yet his interview replies come out much briefer than most.

Adriano Espaillat.bottom_line: Open with the people your plan reaches, and keep each reply brief, since he trades quick, short turns.
do: Prepare a one-page case built around the families it helps
Open with one new idea and a direct question about who it helps
Keep each reply short enough to match his quick turns
Clear any public mention of the meeting with his office, since he is very visible
dont: Return to the same request each week without new facts
Match his gentle tone with sharp attacks
Rush to fill his long pauses with more of your own talk
Adriano Espaillat.warning_sign: In hearings he usually asks a little sharper questions than most members do. If those questions turn mild, he has stopped testing your case. After the hearing, ask him which point he plans to raise next time.
Adriano Espaillat.follow_up: Within a day, send his office a summary of each next step, with an owner and a date beside each one.
Adriano Espaillat.personality: Espaillat stands out for his curiosity, which runs well ahead of most House members. He is also very visible. Hearings bring out a bit more edge in him than in most members. His public tone is much softer than most, and his legislation spans somewhat more ground than most. He is a touch less reliable than most at seeing bills through, and he holds the floor much less than most.
Adriano Espaillat.speaks: Across interviews, his answers come out much briefer than most, and he replies in quick runs. Expect him to hand the floor back early, and do not wait for a long monologue. His pace is as slow as anyone's in the House, and he leaves long pauses between phrases, so let the silences sit. Give him a moment to ask his own question next, and let the pace stay unhurried.
Adriano Espaillat.decides: He moves toward cases that show who is helped, and people-first framing fits him. Outside pressure sways him slightly less than most members. He is very easy to work with, so a friendly, direct request suits him. Let a decision wait one meeting if he is still weighing it, since he responds a touch less to outside pushing than most. Give him a clear yes-or-no question at that point, so the answer is easy to give.

archetype.justification: Lynx fits: he is not easily rattled, and his wording stays low in emotional heat.

Al Green.bottom_line: Lead with who the policy helps, since pressure from outside groups carries less weight with him.
do: Let him take his time, since his answers run long
Bring data he can examine, since he is curious
Match his slow pace and leave room between points
dont: Expect outside pressure alone to settle his vote
Plan for a low temperature in a hearing, though he ranks among the least combative
Al Green.warning_sign: He usually talks slowly, with pauses between phrases and a volume that rises and falls. When his pitch flattens and fillers creep into his pauses, caution has set in, so ease off and leave him room.
Al Green.follow_up: Email his legislative aide a short list of who the policy helps by Friday and ask him for a written reply.
Al Green.personality: Green is an unusually curious member with a very outgoing streak, a careful, organized temperament and a fairly agreeable manner. He is not easily flustered, and his public words run warm. Coverage of issues is wide, bills span many areas, and conversations often follow his lead somewhat more than others. Visibility is high for his role. Answers tend to run much longer than others.
Al Green.speaks: Speech comes slowly to him, with lengthy gaps between phrases, and his loudness swings widely, rising and falling from phrase to phrase. Pitch stays flat, and wording carries little emotional heat. Topics range across a wide set of issues, and longest answers run notably long. Little filler appears, and he seldom trails off. His manner is unhurried, and his public language reads as one of the warmest in the House.
Al Green.decides: He sizes up a request by the people it benefits, and he takes in many issues before he decides. Outside pressure sways him less than others, so the case has to stand alone. He leads conversations somewhat more than others and gives long answers, so a rushed ask gets less of a hearing. Crossing the aisle comes somewhat less readily to him, and his support holds only when the stakes for people are clear.

archetype.justification: Among the most reserved and least visible members of his chamber, careful and organized, and his words carry among the least emotional charge.

Alan Armstrong.bottom_line: Bring a written, technical case and let the facts carry the ask. Outside pressure works much less on him than on most colleagues, so do not count on it.
do: Send a written, technical summary before the meeting
If he runs long, let him finish before your next point
Offer a private briefing, since he is seldom visible in public debate
Let him speak first and wait out any silence before you fill it
dont: Rely on outside pressure to carry the ask
Alan Armstrong.warning_sign: By default he speaks at length and often trails off before finishing a sentence. If he starts trailing off more than usual, he is still working through the point, so pause and let him finish rather than pressing ahead.
Alan Armstrong.follow_up: The day after, mail his office a brief written recap of the request and the evidence behind it, with one named next step.
Alan Armstrong.personality: Armstrong ranks with the most reserved members in his chamber, among the least seen, and much less easily rattled than the typical member. He is among the most careful and organized, and his language is much gentler than the typical member's and carries among the least emotional charge. He covers among the narrowest range of issues and takes charge of conversations somewhat less than the typical member. Yet his answers run among the longest and often trail off unfinished. He is a quiet specialist from Oklahoma and is also a little skeptical.
Alan Armstrong.speaks: His account of his own work is somewhat more precise and thorough than the typical member, and his public talk reaches somewhat fewer issues. His tone is much gentler than the typical member's and carries among the least emotional charge. In conversation his answers run among the longest. He trails away mid thought much more often than colleagues, and his speech carries somewhat more filler than the typical speaker.
Alan Armstrong.decides: He weighs an ask on written, technical grounds and on whether it fits the issues he already works on. His bills touch among the fewest issues, so he tends to act where his own record already reaches. Outside pressure works much less on him than on most colleagues. He leans a little skeptical toward new claims, so he wants a step with a clear owner before he commits.

archetype.justification: Few senators build across party lines more than he does, and he is fairly agreeable, with a wide spread of bills.

Alex Padilla.bottom_line: Put results and facts first, and point to his cross-party record. He digs in when pressed, so bring the proof before he commits.
do: State the ask in one sentence at the start of the meeting
Open by showing where the plan already has backers in both parties
Set the agenda yourself, since he holds the floor much less than most
Borrow his unusually warm wording for the issue, not policy jargon
dont: Give up a firm point just to keep the talk friendly
Argue back each time he holds a point firmly
Press him for a yes in a public hearing
Alex Padilla.warning_sign: He usually lets you steer the talk. If he takes over and stops asking you questions, he has set your case aside. Stop and ask one open question.
Alex Padilla.follow_up: By Thursday, email his office a written memo with the results and a reply to each open point.
Alex Padilla.personality: Padilla builds across party lines more than almost any senator, and his bills reach somewhat wider than most. He is a very careful, organized person, and he is very dependable on votes and bills. He has spoken about a photo of John Lewis in his office, which he says inspires him. Once he takes a stance, he holds it more than most. He is fairly agreeable, and he holds the floor much less than most.
Alex Padilla.speaks: His answers in interviews run far longer than most, and his very longest stretches run well past most, so let him finish a long reply before you respond. He holds his ground more than most when challenged, so ask one clear question rather than arguing back. Delivery-wise he speaks at a clearly quicker pace than most, and his pitch swings up and down far more than nearly any senator. His pauses between phrases stretch much longer than most, so let each pause sit before you reply.
Alex Padilla.decides: He commits on results, and his votes and bills follow through reliably. Once challenged, he firmly defends his view, and he holds that view firmly once it is set. Pushing from outside sways him more than most senators do. Check every figure you leave behind before it goes out to anyone outside your office, since facts and figures fit him best.

archetype.justification: One of the most outgoing and visible members, she carries much of her work in public settings and conversation.

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.bottom_line: Give her a public role and a short case about who is helped, then one concrete next step. Keep the pitch short, since her answers run brief.
do: Lead with the people who benefit, since she is outgoing and curious
Keep answers brief and tie each point to one concrete outcome
Hold her to a named commitment when she takes the floor
In a hearing, expect fast, combative questioning and stay on your facts
dont: Press for dense technical detail, since her replies rank among the briefest in the chamber
Back down at the first challenge, since she defends her position
Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.warning_sign: When challenged, she usually defends her position a bit more firmly than most members do. Watch for that shift, then slow the exchange and ask for one specific commitment.
Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.follow_up: Afterward, put the affected people and one dated step into a brief memo for her office.
Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.personality: Ocasio-Cortez ranks among the most outgoing members in the chamber, and among the most visible. Her public language reads as much more social than most and somewhat more upbeat and action focused. Strong feelings come fast for her, much more than most, and when challenged she holds her ground somewhat more than most. Her replies rank among the briefest in the chamber, and she keeps her work described in broad strokes.
Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.speaks: Her talk spans much wider ground than most, and her words run among the most charged in the chamber. Delivery runs much faster than most, while her pitch stays somewhat flatter. Her replies rank among the briefest in the chamber, and her longest replies still fall well short of most. In a hearing she turns far more combative than a typical colleague, and she holds her ground when challenged.
Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.decides: Her calculus on any request turns on whether affected people get a front seat and a visible platform. Across the aisle, she works somewhat less than most, so a cross-party pitch alone will not win her. She holds the floor somewhat more than most, so she needs a clear role in any joint effort. A yes from her holds only with a dated next step attached.

archetype.justification: Her very warm public words and her focus on who a policy helps fit the Bear.

Alma Adams.bottom_line: Lead with the people the policy helps, and keep your ask short and direct so she can take it on.
do: Open with a story about one family the bill would help
Give her the bottom line in the first sentence
Let her take charge of the conversation, then confirm the next step
dont: Stack extra background before the ask
Talk over her when her voice rises mid point
Alma Adams.warning_sign: She usually finishes every point she starts. If she starts trailing off mid point and her pitch climbs, she is getting heated and wants to be heard, so let her finish.
Alma Adams.follow_up: Send a one page recap of the next step to her staff within two days, naming the owner.
Alma Adams.personality: Adams stays very inquisitive yet friendly in public remarks, and her legislation spans a much broader range of topics than most. Conversation brings out brief answers, but her words are forceful and she often leads the room. Visibility sits somewhat below what her role would suggest. She represents North Carolina, and her language runs flatter in tone than nearly any colleague's.
Alma Adams.speaks: She speaks in short turns and finishes her points, so her answers stay tight. Loudness varies more across a sentence than is typical, and pitch moves through a wide range with brief pauses between phrases. Words come across as warm and forceful at once, and public talk covers a wide range of topics. Replies are briefer than almost every peer's, and wording carries little excitement.
Alma Adams.decides: Who a bill helps, and how well it matches the broad issues she already handles, are what she weighs first. Her attention to community impact means a clear story about families moves her more than a stack of data. Pressure from outside carries less sway over her than over most peers, so a choice holds once she has personally settled the action.

archetype.justification: Very careful and organized, and his interview answers run long and even.

Ami Bera.bottom_line: Make one precise ask, then give his long answers the room they need. Expect him to take a full stretch to reach his point before you respond.
do: Send written technical detail to his office before the meeting
Open with a single technical question so his long answer has a clear target
Keep the tone friendly, since his words run much more social than most
Hold to the request, since he moves more under outside pressure than most
dont: Argue each point head on the moment he defends his view
Frame the ask as a contest between the two parties
Take the ask to the press before the first meeting
Ami Bera.warning_sign: Filler is usually part of how he talks, so its absence is the signal. If his answers lose the filler and turn formal, he is giving you his settled answer. Drop the point for now and come back to it later.
Ami Bera.follow_up: Send his legislative staff a numbered list of answers to each question he raised, within two days, with each next step paired with an owner.
Ami Bera.personality: Bera is very precise and well organized, and he is very easy to work with. Hard to fluster, he is much more so than most. Bills span a bit more ground for him than most. He is very active across party lines, more than most members. Yet his public profile is very high for the role he holds, and his hearing manner runs somewhat more combative than most members.
Ami Bera.speaks: Interview answers from him come out much longer than most, though their length changes less than almost anyone's. He speaks at a clearly quicker pace than most, while his pitch changes less than almost any other House member's. Few House members use more filler than he does, and his public words are a bit gentler than most. Pushed on a point, he defends his view, across different shows. Hold your reply until he has finished the thought, then answer exactly what he said.
Ami Bera.decides: A case that fits him is one with the written technical detail laid out step by step, since that is the type of case he weighs. Once he settles on a view, he defends it when challenged, so make your case while his view is still open. Pressure from outside shifts his position more than it shifts most members, so a firm, restated ask keeps its weight. Close by asking which point still needs an answer, and answer that one first.

archetype.justification: She is very outgoing, with warm, forceful public language and high visibility in the Senate.

Amy Klobuchar.bottom_line: Open outgoing and end with one clear next step. She works across the aisle much less than most, so tie the ask to her own lane.
do: Speak warmly and keep the tone upbeat, since her public language runs warm
Let her hold the conversation for a while, since she takes charge
Give her room to finish, since she trails off somewhat more than most
dont: Treat a hearing as a low-stakes exchange, since she is much more combative there
Pitch your ask flatly, since her language runs high in energy
Amy Klobuchar.warning_sign: By default she holds firm on each point and takes charge of the discussion. If she stops contesting points and gives quick, unfinished answers, she is losing interest, so cut to the one next step.
Amy Klobuchar.follow_up: Follow up with a written recap listing each step, who owns it, and a date you can verify.
Amy Klobuchar.personality: Klobuchar comes across as very outgoing and ranks among the most agreeable members in the Senate. She is much warmer and much more upbeat in her public language than most, and much more forceful, with a focus on action that most colleagues lack. She leads conversations and holds the floor more than most, yet works across the aisle much less than most. Legislation from her reaches more topics than nearly any senator's, and she is very visible. Before entering politics she practiced corporate law, and Minnesota is her home base.
Amy Klobuchar.speaks: Her pitch holds much flatter than most, and her tempo runs somewhat quicker than most. Pauses come somewhat shorter than most, and volume varies less than most. Warmth and upbeat wording mark her public language, which runs much warmer than most. How long her answers run swings more than nearly anyone's in the Senate, and answers trail off somewhat more than most. At hearings she grows much more combative than most members.
Amy Klobuchar.decides: Before backing it she checks whether she can take charge of it, since she holds the floor more than most. Public campaigns sway her slightly more than most colleagues, so a visible push can help her decide. She works across the aisle much less than most, so an ask that is only bipartisan on paper will not hold. Any choice holds only when a written next step has a named person behind it.

archetype.justification: Among the most outgoing colleagues and very curious, she keeps her public talk to a small range of topics, and she is loose with details.

Analilia Mejia.bottom_line: Bring one narrow ask inside her issues and let her carry it. Outside pushes carry a little less weight with her, so an invitation beats pressure.
do: Bring one specific question, since she is very curious
Offer her a joint announcement she can front with a colleague
dont: Count on outside pressure to settle her position quickly
Analilia Mejia.warning_sign: A general meeting won't tell you how she responds when an ask stalls. So ask her office how it wants setbacks raised before you press again.
Analilia Mejia.follow_up: Write her office a short note naming the shared role and the narrow ask, with a date for her reply.
Analilia Mejia.personality: Mejia ranks with the most outgoing House colleagues and is very curious about the work in front of her. Her details arrive loosely, and her public talk centers on a handful of subjects. Seldom visible for her role, she keeps an outgoing manner all the same. Her New Jersey seat and House Small Business work give her a clear lane to build from.
Analilia Mejia.speaks: She keeps her public talk on a narrow range of issues and returns to the same few areas. Those areas recur across what she says, so the subjects she raises are easy to predict. Her manner is that of a legislator who stays in her own lane rather than ranging across the chamber's debates. She speaks about what she already works on, not about everything at once.
Analilia Mejia.decides: She is among the most outgoing colleagues, so a visible role suits her. Her test for any request is whether it hands her a shared role she can own. Because she is seldom visible, a clear part in the announcement gives her a reason to commit. A push from others counts for less with her than a clear role does. So an ask needs a named role for her to hold.

archetype.justification: Reserved, narrow in what she covers, careful in detail, and rarely visible, with short pauses between phrases.

Andrea Salinas.bottom_line: Lead with a shared role or announcement she can take, and keep the case direct. Outside voices shift her well past what colleagues feel, so bring a visible backer.
do: Offer a visible shared role she can lead or announce
Give her a clear, specific ask with a named next step
Name a joint partner early, and keep your points brisk
dont: Expect a slow, reserved yes when she is pressed in the room
Count on outside pressure alone to move her decision
Andrea Salinas.warning_sign: Usually she stays reserved and sticks to a tight range of topics, so a shift stands out. If she talks more or presses past the detail, that signals guardedness, so ask what she needs to see before she commits.
Andrea Salinas.follow_up: Email a brief note that same day listing the agreed step, who owns it, and the deadline.
Andrea Salinas.personality: Salinas is reserved and narrow in what she covers, though careful and detailed when she describes her own work. Her style runs less practical than most colleagues, and she reaches across the aisle a bit more than peers. Her public language is a little more emotionally loaded than most, and she gets worked up a little more easily. Outside voices sway her well beyond what colleagues feel, so a visible backer matters.
Andrea Salinas.speaks: She talks faster than most and leaves very short pauses between phrases. Her volume stays fairly even, so her delivery sounds level rather than swelling. Public words from her carry a little extra emotional charge, and she describes the work in careful, detailed terms. In a hearing she is a touch less combative than peers. Her delivery reads as engaged rather than heated, which fits how she frames each point.
Andrea Salinas.decides: She assesses a request by whether it hands her a visible role and a backer with clout. Outside voices shift her clearly further than colleagues, so a request with community support will hold. She works with the opposite camp more than most, so a partner from there helps the request land. Her follow-through is somewhat less dependable, so a written next step with an owner gives the commitment a place to land.

archetype.justification: He ranks among the most skeptical members, his answers run short, and detail is loose for him, so results-first brevity suits him.

Andrew Clyde.bottom_line: Open with the result in a short, direct case, and do not oversell it, since results-first framing fits him best.
do: Send a short note on the outcome, ahead of the meeting
Keep your opening to one sentence, since his replies stay short
Ask him to restate each short answer in his own words before you reply
Stop at the time set for the ask, before a second point crowds it out
dont: Assume an easy yes because the ask is well meant
Press with sharp words, because his own words are gentler than most
Wait for him to name the next step, since he takes charge less than most
Andrew Clyde.warning_sign: His sentences usually end cleanly, since he leaves fewer thoughts hanging than nearly any colleague. If they start breaking off mid-thought, he has stopped working the point with you. Leave the point open, and say plainly which part is still unsettled.
Andrew Clyde.follow_up: Send his staff a short letter within the week, naming each next step, its owner, and the day it falls due.
Andrew Clyde.personality: Clyde is skeptical to a degree few colleagues match, and practical to an unusual degree. Details are much looser for him than for most colleagues. Seeing bills through is a fairly dependable habit for him. In hearings he is much less combative than most members. He gets worked up quickly, much more than most. For his role, he is very visible.
Andrew Clyde.speaks: In interviews his replies are shorter than almost any House member's, and his longest ones stay short too. Pauses between his phrases stretch a bit longer than most. Filler turns up in his speech more than nearly anyone's. His pitch stays flat in a way few members match. Give his short answers room to finish the point before you reply. Plan on brief replies and let them close the point.
Andrew Clyde.decides: He drives a conversation less than most, so bring the decision to him rather than waiting for him to raise it. Lead with the decision itself, and let the reasons follow once he has the question in view. Frame the ask as one step he can accept or refuse, and close on a specific yes or no he can answer on the spot.

archetype.justification: His public manner is about as reserved as they come, and he keeps a low profile while his bills range widely.

Andrew Garbarino.bottom_line: Bring results and facts up front, and keep the ask short. A brief, plainly stated case suits him better than a long pitch.
do: Put the key results on a single page for him to keep
Ask his office which format it prefers for the next meeting
Keep the ask off the public stage, with no role for him to front
Stay on the facts if the setting turns formal, since his tone there runs sharper
dont: Mistake his quiet manner for a lack of interest
Count on outside groups to sway him
Write him off for his lighter cross-party work
Andrew Garbarino.warning_sign: Usually, in hearings, his manner runs somewhat more combative than most members. If he turns even sharper than usual, he is going no further with the ask. Set the rest of the ask aside, and keep the one piece he can still accept.
Andrew Garbarino.follow_up: Give his staff a short results sheet by Friday, with one next step and its date.
Andrew Garbarino.personality: Garbarino keeps a very low profile, even for his role. Reserve is a defining trait, since few colleagues are quieter in public. He leans somewhat more curious than most. Few members have bills that span as many issues as his. Cross-party work is somewhat lighter for him.
Andrew Garbarino.speaks: His language carries little emotional lift. In hearings his tone runs somewhat more combative than most colleagues. His public talk ranges across more issues than nearly any colleague's. Give the detail in writing, and keep your own voice even.
Andrew Garbarino.decides: Outside pressure carries somewhat less sway with him than it does with most. A plain account of what the policy delivers carries the most weight. End by asking what result he would want to see first in writing.

archetype.justification: His wide issue range, loose detail work and brisk bursts of brief turns fit a busy, loose style.

Andrew Ogles.bottom_line: Bring a short, direct case on what the bill delivers, with a named owner for each step. He rarely joins deals across the aisle, and threads slip without an owner.
do: Open with a short, direct case on what the bill delivers
Put each step and its owner in a written list before leaving
dont: Assume a quick yes from him will hold across the next meeting
Let a long, wide ranging answer replace a clear decision
Andrew Ogles.warning_sign: He usually talks in brisk bursts and his answers vary in length more than almost anyone's. If he suddenly slows down and stops pressing the point, he is losing the thread, so pause and restate the ask.
Andrew Ogles.follow_up: Send him a short written recap of the step, its owner and its date within two days.
Andrew Ogles.personality: Ogles is a reserved member who is fairly curious and a little skeptical, with a wide spread of issues. He handles details much more loosely than most colleagues, and he rarely works across the aisle. Getting worked up comes a bit more easily than most, though his public wording runs warmer than almost anyone's. His work touches many bills, but he ranks among the least reliable at carrying them through.
Andrew Ogles.speaks: His talk comes in brisk bursts of brief turns, with answer length that shifts sharply from one turn to the next. The longest answers he gives run longer than most, yet he trails off less than almost anyone. His tone is flat with little upbeat energy, and his words lean toward action more than almost anyone's. Warmth comes through in how he words things, more than nearly any colleague.
Andrew Ogles.decides: Requests are judged by whether they fit the wide set of bills he already carries. He rarely works across the aisle, so a shared deal is a long shot with him. In hearings he is a bit less combative than most, so prepare for a looser exchange. He moves through bills unevenly, so a choice sticks only once an accountable person and a deadline are set.

archetype.justification: His pace runs well below the usual level, and his account of his work is very careful and detailed.

André Carson.bottom_line: Give him time to finish, and bring a careful, detailed ask in writing. Outside pressure moves him much less than most, so do not expect a quick shift.
do: Let him finish each turn, since his pace runs slow and his turn lengths vary
Keep points few and clear, since he is quite reserved and gives shorter answers
Expect milder questions in a hearing, and answer them one at a time
Ask one direct question and wait, since he gives few quick short replies
dont: Rush him to a yes, since his pace is slow and his turn lengths vary
André Carson.warning_sign: He usually finishes his sentences more often than almost anyone does. If he begins leaving them unfinished, he is irritated or losing interest. Pause, ask one clear question, and let him finish.
André Carson.follow_up: Afterward, put the next step, a date, and a shared role for each colleague into a brief written summary.
André Carson.personality: Carson comes across as quite reserved, with a very careful and detailed way of describing his work. He is a touch skeptical, and less easily rattled than most. Those traits show most when a conversation turns to contested points, and they shape how he takes in a request. In conversation his replies come in slightly briefer form than most. Hearings bring out a lower combative edge, a little under the usual level.
André Carson.speaks: His pace runs well below the usual level, with longer pauses between phrases. Once he starts a sentence, he finishes it more reliably than almost anyone. Pitch shifts somewhat more widely than most. His longest replies run slightly shorter than usual, while his turn lengths vary far more from one to the next. In hearings he keeps a lower combative edge, a little under the usual level.
André Carson.decides: An ask lands with him when it leaves time to test the detail. Outside pressure moves him much less than most, so private argument carries real weight. His replies come in slightly briefer form than most, so he needs room to finish before deciding. A yes from him only holds when the next step carries a named owner and a firm date attached.

archetype.justification: Few House members cover as much ground in their bills as he does, and he is a bit skeptical, yet fairly dependable on votes and bills.

Andy Barr.bottom_line: Build the brief around what the policy delivers, in a short, direct form. He is somewhat skeptical, and a clear result carries the weight with him.
do: Send a short written brief on the results, with the facts in the first lines
Expect doubt at first, and answer it without pressing him
Make your full case at once, since outside pressure counts for little with him
Close by naming one step and its date
dont: Build the ask on a cross-party coalition, since he rarely works across the aisle
Ask him to work across the aisle in the first meeting
Turn a private meeting into a hearing-style challenge
Andy Barr.warning_sign: In hearings he usually questions witnesses a little harder than most. If he drops the substance and asks only about timing, he has moved to another question. Ask which point still needs settling, and let him name it.
Andy Barr.follow_up: By Friday, call his office to confirm who attends the next meeting, since he follows through fairly reliably.
Andy Barr.personality: Barr is somewhat skeptical, and his bills reach across more issues than nearly every colleague. He runs looser on specifics than most, though his votes and bills are fairly dependable. Across party lines, he builds less than nearly every colleague. He is fairly curious and a little reserved. Under questioning in hearings, he runs a little sharper than most colleagues.
Andy Barr.speaks: His talk ranges across a wider field of issues than nearly any member, and his own account of his work runs more detailed than nearly any colleague's. Delivery-wise, he speaks faster than most and leaves shorter pauses than nearly anyone. Match his quick delivery with tight points, since he leaves almost no gap between phrases. His volume stays even, and his pitch runs somewhat flatter than most.
Andy Barr.decides: Few members work across party lines less, so name the members of his own party who have already looked at the plan. Ask his staff which of them he would most want to hear from, and ask that member to join the next talk. Keep those names near the top of the written case, so he sees them before anything else.

archetype.justification: He takes charge of conversations, defends his position very firmly when challenged, and his answers run far briefer than most.

Andy Biggs.bottom_line: Let him take the floor, then answer with written evidence he can check. Outside pressure moves him less than nearly any member, so the written case must stand alone.
do: Let him hold the floor first, then respond to each point
Put the technical evidence in writing before you meet
Name the next vote and who owns the follow through
dont: Read his skepticism as a closed door on the whole idea
Argue each point head on, since he digs in harder than nearly anyone
Andy Biggs.warning_sign: By default he takes charge, holds the floor, and defends his position hard when challenged. If he drops that defense and gives short, flat answers, he is losing interest, so stop pressing and give him the one next step.
Andy Biggs.follow_up: Send a written summary of the next vote and name the person who will check the bill.
Andy Biggs.personality: Biggs shows a very outgoing manner, few colleagues are more skeptical, and he gets worked up faster than nearly anyone in the House. His details run much looser than most, and he takes charge of conversations much more than most colleagues. He builds bipartisan deals somewhat less than most. Few colleagues are more visible for their role, and he digs in hard when challenged. Arizona shapes his base, and his stance tends to harden under challenge.
Andy Biggs.speaks: Answers come back briefer than most, and their length stays much more even from one to the next. His words sound much flatter than most, and they carry much less force, so the tone stays level. Short replies rarely come in rapid bursts, so each answer tends to stand alone. Filler words creep in a little more often than in others' speech, and he defends his points hard when pressed.
Andy Biggs.decides: He tests a request by how it holds up under pressure, so a case that answers his challenge on the facts gets a hearing. Outside pressure moves him less than nearly any member, so calls and crowds do not decide it. Few colleagues stand out more for their role. A decision with him needs a written next step and a date to stick.

archetype.justification: He is quite skeptical and reliable at seeing bills through, which fits the Bull's dependable style.

Andy Harris.bottom_line: Bring written, technical evidence early and record each agreed step. Outside backing moves him less than it moves most lawmakers, so let the paper trail do the persuading.
do: Share the written technical evidence ahead of the meeting
Confirm each agreed step in writing the same day
dont: Bank on outside pressure to settle the question
Send him loose claims without the written detail
Andy Harris.warning_sign: A sit down gathering will not reveal whether he needs the record in writing before he commits. Ask early which written point he needs, then send exactly that before you leave the room.
Andy Harris.follow_up: Email his legislative staff a written list of agreed steps and owners by the next morning.
Andy Harris.personality: Harris is reserved in public and practical in outlook, and quite skeptical. His grip on exact details is looser than most colleagues, though he explains his work with precise, thorough language. Legislation from him spans fewer areas than nearly anyone's, yet it is seen through reliably. Heating up comes somewhat faster than for colleagues, and the language is far less charged than colleagues'.
Andy Harris.speaks: Tempo is quick, and pitch moves up and down much more than most. Volume stays somewhat more even than colleagues' volumes. Pauses are brief between phrases. A narrow set of issues gets most of the talk, and the work is explained with precise, thorough language. Language is far less charged than most, so the delivery sounds businesslike even at speed.
Andy Harris.decides: Whether the written detail holds up is how he judges an ask, since he is quite skeptical of claims that arrive without it. He works in a narrow set of issues, so an ask outside them gets little traction. Lobbying from outside groups tugs on him less than on the usual member, and once he agrees to something, he sees it through. So a decision from him sticks only when the written record shows what he agreed to and when the next step falls due.

archetype.justification: He speaks warmly, gives long answers, and his delivery fits the Bear's expansive style.

Andy Kim.bottom_line: Give him a clear ask and back it with outside voices. Pressure has more pull on him than most, so keep the facts ready when the voices arrive.
do: Give him the facts in a short written note first
Let his long answers run, then respond to the strongest point
Match his slower pace and keep your questions short
dont: Assume a warm reception means he will commit
Pile on extra asks when one clear result will do
Andy Kim.warning_sign: He usually gives long answers and talks through a point, with many filler words. If his answers suddenly shrink to a few words, he is on guard. Stop and ask which part of the ask concerns him.
Andy Kim.follow_up: By Friday, put in writing for his staff the request, who backs it, and what happens next.
Andy Kim.personality: Kim brings lively, inquisitive energy to the room, and his short replies arrive in quick runs far more than most peers. He is fairly thorough in his habits, and his language is more emotionally charged than colleagues'. Public remarks from him touch far more subjects than most peers do, and he builds bipartisan coalitions somewhat more often than most. He sees bills through fairly dependably, yet he draws less public attention than most.
Andy Kim.speaks: His tempo runs well slower than most colleagues', and his breaks between phrases are a little shorter. His replies stretch out longer than most colleagues' replies, though he also falls into brisk bursts of short lines more than most. Fillers slip into his talk more often than nearly every colleague, and his tone dips and climbs somewhat more than most. His tone runs warmer than most colleagues'.
Andy Kim.decides: Bipartisan support from across the aisle is what he tests first, because he cooperates with opposing colleagues somewhat more than most. Outside pressure sways him more often than it sways most lawmakers, and he takes charge of talks far less than peers do. So a decision from him sticks when the voices behind the ask are clearly visible to him in every meeting.

archetype.justification: Among the most cooperative members across the aisle, and very reliable at seeing bills through.

Angela Alsobrooks.bottom_line: Bring a shared ask with the detail written out, and ask for one dated commitment. Outside pressure moves her much more than most members, so line up backers early.
do: Lead with the written detail, since she is very agreeable and reliable
Name the partners who share the goal early
Bring voices from outside the building to back the ask
In a hearing, expect a gentle tone and keep answers on the record
dont: Treat a warm first meeting as a firm commitment, since outside voices move her more
Angela Alsobrooks.warning_sign: In a hearing she usually stays gentle, and a sharp question usually gets a softer reply, not a fight. Watch for a change in tone, then lower the stakes and confirm the one point you need.
Angela Alsobrooks.follow_up: Afterward, send a written summary with the ask, the partners named, and one dated step to her office.
Angela Alsobrooks.personality: Alsobrooks stands among the most cooperative members across the aisle, and she is very dependable in carrying bills to the finish. She leans a little toward practical matters. Strong feelings arise much more readily than most, though she is very agreeable. Her wording runs among the least charged in the chamber. Public talk touches a somewhat smaller range of topics than most, and she draws less public notice than nearly any colleague.
Angela Alsobrooks.speaks: Her account of her own work is somewhat more exact and detailed than most. Volume holds much more evenly than most, and her pitch runs much flatter. Her delivery is somewhat quicker than most, with briefer gaps between phrases. Tone stays gentle in ordinary talk, which matches her gentler wording. In a hearing she is among the least confrontational members of the chamber.
Angela Alsobrooks.decides: Before she commits, she checks whether partners from both sides already back it. Very dependable when it comes to bills, a clear, dated step carries real weight with her. Outside pressure moves her much more than most members, so the ask gains weight when local voices join. A deal with her holds best when written down with a named next step.

archetype.justification: Owl fits: she is very curious, fairly careful, and her public words span a broader set of topics than nearly any colleague's.

Angie Craig.bottom_line: Bring a short case on results and facts, and let her reach the conclusion. Outside campaigns move her less, so let the facts do the persuading.
do: Lead with the results the policy delivers and the facts behind them
Let her probe the facts, since her curiosity sits high on the scale
Name a cosponsor from the other party, since she works across the aisle
dont: Stack public pressure on her, since it counts for less with her
Angie Craig.warning_sign: A group session will not reveal whether a point stays open for her after it is raised. Before the session, ask her staff which point she still wants answered, and when she wants it resolved.
Angie Craig.follow_up: Within three days, send her team a single page of results plus a cosponsor list, copying the bill's lead staffer.
Angie Craig.personality: Craig is a curious and organized member who takes in the whole picture. Public words from her range across a wide set of topics, beyond nearly any colleague's, while her bills span many areas. Statements from her are a little more exact and thorough than most. Tough questioning does not throw her much. Her reach across colleagues runs a little ahead of most, as cosponsored bills show.
Angie Craig.speaks: Public talk ranges across more subjects than nearly any colleague's does. Points get framed in somewhat more careful and detailed language than most. She talks faster than most, with much shorter pauses between phrases. Loudness runs more even than most, while her tone pitch rises and drops more than most. Manner is quick and connected, moving between issues without long breaks in the talk.
Angie Craig.decides: Weighing an ask starts with whether the results and facts hold up. Her curiosity opens her to angles the team did not raise, and her cross party ties suit a joint ask. Outside groups register weakly with her compared with most colleagues, so a request leaning on public attention tends to lose ground. Her choices rest on the evidence, so a case that holds up on its facts is what moves her.

archetype.justification: He ranks near the top for curiosity, and his bills reach much wider than most, so he moves across many topics.

Angus King.bottom_line: Bring a question that sparks his curiosity and let him steer the talk, since calls from outside move him more than most.
do: Send him the topic in advance so his curiosity can run
Open with one plain question, since his answers run long
Confirm the next bill step with his staff, since he follows through
dont: Expect him to back down when you challenge him
Angus King.warning_sign: He normally digs in when challenged, so a challenge he lets go unanswered is the sign he has tuned out or is annoyed. Ask him to restate the point in his own words and check whether he still objects.
Angus King.follow_up: When the call wraps, drop him a brief note on the topic he raised, with one question he can answer when ready.
Angus King.personality: King numbers among the most curious senators, and his thinking runs careful and orderly. He is very agreeable and fairly outgoing, yet he is much harder to rattle than most. His bills span many topics, and he holds the floor and digs in when pushed. Views from him carry weight, since he is fairly visible. Put together, he talks at length and answers each point put to him.
Angus King.speaks: He speaks quickly, with short pauses between phrases, and his tone varies more than nearly any colleague's. His answers run long in conversation and in interviews, and their length ranges widely from one to the next. Trails off somewhat less than most, and answers in quick runs somewhat less than most. Under challenge he pushes back far more than most.
Angus King.decides: Any request is judged on whether it sparks his curiosity and fits the areas his bills cover, and pressure from the outside tips him more than most. He follows through on bills more reliably than most, so the next bill step matters to him. Any request has to connect to something he already follows. So his support holds when the ask gives him a question to chase.

archetype.justification: Her careful, detailed talk and wide, reliable bill work fit a diligent and thorough style.

Ann Wagner.bottom_line: Bring a detailed written case, since she is among the most reliable in the House. Outside voices move her a little more than most, so a repeated request has room.
do: Send the detail in writing ahead of time, since she sees bills through
Ask one follow up question in the hearing, since she is combative there
dont: Assume her agreement with a plan means the work is done
Ann Wagner.warning_sign: She usually takes her time with each answer and keeps her points organized. In a hearing, if she suddenly goes quiet and drops a point, she is on guard, so pause and ask what concerns her.
Ann Wagner.follow_up: Send her a short written note with the next step, its owner and its date within two days.
Ann Wagner.personality: Wagner is among the most reserved colleagues and very curious. Her talk covers a wide range of issues, and her bills span a few more issues than most. She speaks about her work with careful, detailed terms rather than broad claims. Visibility sits far lower than most colleagues', which keeps her public profile modest. She serves on House Financial Services and represents a Missouri seat.
Ann Wagner.speaks: Her pace is much slower than most, with pauses that run somewhat longer than most. Her volume rises and falls somewhat more than most, and her pitch stays flatter than most. Words range widely across issues, and her detail on the work is exact. In a hearing she is among the most combative members, so her manner sharpens there. She keeps her points organized and speaks at a deliberate pace.
Ann Wagner.decides: She weighs an ask by how people in the community are helped. Her follow through is among the most dependable in the House, so a written step tends to hold. Commitments hold best when they are written and the next step has a named owner. Her committee seat on House Financial Services keeps her close to the bills in that area. So a decision holds with her when the next step is written down with a date.

archetype.justification: Her issue range ranks among the narrowest in the chamber, and her tone stays combative and skeptical by default.

Anna Luna.bottom_line: Lead with a short case on what the policy delivers, and keep the ask narrow in scope. She is skeptical by default, so keep the facts tight.
do: Lead with the results case, since she is among the most skeptical
Keep the ask narrow and written, since follow-through is among the weakest
Put a named owner and date on every step before you leave
In a hearing, expect sharp questions and answer each one directly
dont: Trade shots with her in a hearing, where she is much more combative
Lean on a warm first meeting as proof of support, since follow-through is weak
Anna Luna.warning_sign: In a hearing she usually turns combative and sharper with each new question. Keep your replies short, stay on the facts, and do not chase a point she has already won.
Anna Luna.follow_up: Afterward, send one short written note with the ask, the facts behind it, and a dated next step to her office.
Anna Luna.personality: Luna is among the most practical in the chamber. She is among the most skeptical members in the chamber, and her detail runs much looser than most. Her issue range is among the narrowest in the chamber, and her replies come across sharp. Strong feelings rise quickly in her, and her wording runs combative in hearings. Her tone reads sharp in most settings.
Anna Luna.speaks: Her range of issues ranks among the narrowest in the chamber. Describing her work, she ranks among the least detailed in the chamber. Tone reads among the sharpest in the chamber. Her wording has a bit more feeling than most. In a hearing, her combative streak runs well above the usual level. Her sharp tone is a constant in how she talks, and her hearing manner is only a stronger form of it.
Anna Luna.decides: She weighs an ask by whether the facts hold up when she tests them. Follow through is among the weakest in the chamber, so she needs a dated owner to act. Her bills reach fewer areas than most, so a narrow ask fits her best. Outside pressure moves her much more than most members do, so a yes needs a named owner.

archetype.justification: Her narrow bills and careful, detailed talk fit a focused, specific worker who lands points precisely.

April McClain Delaney.bottom_line: Bring her one tightly built ask backed by outside voices, since those voices count for more with her than with colleagues.
do: Pair the ask with a shared announcement or joint event
Bring outside groups that publicly back the request to the meeting
dont: Push the ask alone without outside voices behind it
April McClain Delaney.warning_sign: Her pauses are usually long and her volume uneven, so a pause alone tells you nothing certain. If she turns combative in a hearing where she is usually courteous, she has grown wary, so pause, name the concern, and offer a written follow up.
April McClain Delaney.follow_up: Once the session ends, mail her a single page recap of the request naming the outside supporters, and ask who will carry it forward within two days.
April McClain Delaney.personality: McClain Delaney is fairly outgoing but also fairly careful and organized, so she is sociable company with a planner's habits. Her bills span far fewer issues than colleagues. Public talk from her stays on a narrower set of subjects, so she works as a specialist rather than a generalist. Her background as a media lawyer from Maryland shows in a precise, deliberate style. In hearings she runs somewhat softer than colleagues, and her tone stays courteous.
April McClain Delaney.speaks: She talks in phrases split by long gaps, and her voice swells and drops more than colleagues do, so her delivery is uneven rather than loud. Pitch stays flatter than colleagues, so emphasis comes through word choice and pacing. Her talk is careful and detailed, but it stays on a narrower set of issues. Delivery samples come from House floor audio, a format that differs from interviews.
April McClain Delaney.decides: She judges a request by how far outside voices stand behind it, since outside backing lands harder on her than on colleagues. Her bills span fewer issues than colleagues, so she judges a request by whether it sits squarely in her lane, and a broad ask gets less traction. Outgoing by temperament, she responds best to people who will carry the decision alongside her, so every choice needs an owner who follows through.

archetype.justification: Bear fits because her case centers on who is helped, she holds back somewhat in conversation, and she is quicker than most to get worked up.

Ashley Hinson.bottom_line: Lead with who the ask helps, then let her weigh it without pressing for a quick answer. Outside sources carry little weight with her, so pressure will not help.
do: Open with the people the ask would help, in plain terms
Give her time to weigh the ask before asking for a yes
Ask her staff for the next step after the meeting, not in it
Let her finish a point before you respond, since her volume shifts
dont: Assume a warm reception will carry her to a vote
Count on public pressure to move her vote
Ashley Hinson.warning_sign: Casual sessions do not expose how she reacts when a request stalls, since she tends to hold back in conversation. Ask her staff which step she wants written down, then send it after the meeting.
Ashley Hinson.follow_up: Within a week, email her staff one named step and a concise recap of what was asked.
Ashley Hinson.personality: Hinson sits somewhat on the reserved side and tends to be looser with details than most colleagues. She is quicker than most to get worked up, and her words hold a bit more emotional charge than colleagues' do. Her bills reach more issue areas than most, and she is less visible than most for her role. As an Iowa member she takes on a broad agenda without much public exposure.
Ashley Hinson.speaks: She talks at a slightly slower pace than most, with a flatter pitch and a volume that shifts somewhat more than most. Her conversation covers a wider range of topics than the usual colleague, and feeling shows a bit more in her word choice. Delivery reads as clear and deliberate. Volume is the trait to track, since it moves around more than the average talker.
Ashley Hinson.decides: Her view of any request rests on how well it suits the people it reaches and whether it stays within issues she already works on. Because she is reserved, she takes time before committing, and outside sources carry less weight with her. Her bills reach more issues than most, so an ask within that range fits her. A commitment sticks only when someone names the next step.

archetype.justification: Her public profile is lower than almost any senator's, even for her role, and she is quite practical by nature.

Ashley Moody.bottom_line: Put what the policy delivers first, in a few plain lines, and keep the meeting short.
do: Bring the outcomes on a single page before the meeting
Keep the first contact out of the press, since she keeps a low profile
Revisit the ask later, since outside pressure reaches her more than most
Name the one vote you need from her, since she votes fairly reliably
dont: Read her mild hearing tone as a lack of interest
Re-argue a yes once she has given it
Fill the first meeting with a large group
Ashley Moody.warning_sign: In hearings she is usually milder than most members, so a run of pointed questions on one point stands out. When she keeps returning to the same point, she is still weighing it. Answer in one sentence, then let her respond.
Ashley Moody.follow_up: Call her staff within two days to confirm who acts next on the bill and when.
Ashley Moody.personality: Moody keeps a low public profile, even for a senator in her role. She is quite practical by nature and prefers familiar ground. Detail is a weak spot in her public talk, which runs much less careful than most senators'. Her bills stay much narrower than most. Votes and follow-through are fairly dependable, and she has spoken about her husband's career in law enforcement.
Ashley Moody.speaks: Her public words cover only a few issues, and her talk about the work carries much less detail than most. In hearings she comes across milder than most colleagues. On a process question, answer with one plain fact she can act on, then stop. Keep each sentence short and plain, and let her answer before you add the next point. In any formal setting, match her mild tone with your own.
Ashley Moody.decides: Pressure from outside sways her more than most senators do, so have her staff log each contact and the date it came in. Before the next contact, ask her staff which outside voice reached her last, and plan around it. Her public profile is low even for her role, so each new point should reach her staff in writing first. End by asking her staff to name the one point she will weigh next.

archetype.justification: Quick to react, quite skeptical, and warm in wording, he tests claims before he backs them.

August Pfluger.bottom_line: Bring written, technical evidence ahead of time, since he tests each claim and outside voices carry extra pull with him.
do: Send the evidence ahead, so he can check each claim
Name the outside groups that back the numbers
dont: Push a broad ask before the evidence is in hand
Read his warm wording as agreement with the claim
Count on a phone call to settle the matter
August Pfluger.warning_sign: He usually answers in quick bursts and keeps his pitch flat. If he starts asking for the source behind each figure, he is weighing the case seriously. Hand over the source and let him test it.
August Pfluger.follow_up: After the meeting, send a written note with the source for each claim and the date the next check is due.
August Pfluger.personality: Pfluger becomes worked up more readily than most, and his wording runs warmer than nearly all colleagues. He is quite skeptical, and he works on only a handful of issue areas. Conversations seldom bend to him, since he rarely takes the lead. He represents Texas in the House. Upbeat energy shows in his wording, and his style reads as much less forceful than typical colleagues.
August Pfluger.speaks: Gaps between phrases run tighter than most, and his volume barely shifts from one phrase to the next. Pitch barely moves, flatter than nearly any colleague's. Phrasing leans upbeat and action oriented, well beyond the usual range. Even so, his phrasing carries much less force than typical colleagues do, and the tone is gentler. Wording also carries a bit extra feeling. Overall the delivery is clipped and even in tone.
August Pfluger.decides: Testing is how he judges a request, so the evidence behind it has to survive his scrutiny. Pressure from outside carries more pull with him than most colleagues would expect, yet his skepticism means each claim must survive questioning first. He seldom leads a discussion, so the evidence has to carry the argument. A decision holds for him only once the claims behind it have been checked.

archetype.justification: Very careful and organized, with a narrow focus on results, he fits the Bull's direct style.

Austin Scott.bottom_line: Open with the concrete results of the measure in a single clear sentence, then keep to that bill. Evidence and records carry the case, so keep the claims concrete.
do: Open with the result the bill would produce
Show where the bill stands in the process to date
dont: Skip small talk and get to the ask
Open with promises of future gains, since he wants delivered results
Austin Scott.warning_sign: He usually keeps his answers reserved and tied to the record. If his words turn sharp, treat him as guarded, so halt the pitch and reply to his precise question.
Austin Scott.follow_up: Email his legislative aide the bill status and the sources by Thursday, in writing, with one line on each source.
Austin Scott.personality: Scott holds back in public and ranks near the bottom for emotional charge. He works with great care and keeps his material organized, and his talk about policy is much more detailed than most. Bills and words cover a narrow slice of issues, among the least in the chamber. Georgia is his home base, and he is a long standing voice on a narrow set of topics.
Austin Scott.speaks: He speaks in plain, detailed terms and keeps his language low in emotional charge. The range of topics is narrow, among the least in the chamber, and each topic gets a much more detailed treatment than most. He keeps his tone even and keeps the conversation on those subjects. When a point needs support, he returns to the record and rarely wanders into territory outside his few areas.
Austin Scott.decides: Results on the ground and a clearly documented record are the tests he applies to any request. His bills reach among the fewest areas in the chamber, so an ask that stays inside his narrow lane is the one that lands. Support built on facts and documented delivery fits how he reviews a proposal, so an ask survives his review when it rests on the record.

archetype.justification: Her strong public reactions, forceful wording and wide breadth of issues fit a bear who holds the floor and pushes hard.

Ayanna Pressley.bottom_line: Come with one clear ask rooted in the people it helps, since she will take the floor and hold it.
do: Open with the people your ask helps, in plain terms
Keep each question short and let her answer briefly
In a hearing, hold to one bill and name the step it needs next
dont: Answer sharp wording with sharper wording of your own
Count on a commitment holding without a named owner and date
Ayanna Pressley.warning_sign: Usually she talks slowly, with extended pauses between phrases and widely varying answers. If those pauses shrink and her replies come in quick runs, she is on guard and losing patience. Stop, name the point she raised and offer one clear next step.
Ayanna Pressley.follow_up: Name the ask, the bill and the date you need an answer in a written summary for her staff.
Ayanna Pressley.personality: Pressley is outgoing and curious, and her agenda reaches across a wider set of issues than nearly any colleague. Her words carry strong feeling and force, and in talk she leads the room and keeps the floor. Cross-aisle work is rare for her, and she speaks about her own work in much less detailed terms than most. She represents Massachusetts, and her public presence is very high, so she shapes how a conversation runs and you should plan around her lead.
