Ayanna Pressley.speaks: Pace runs slower than most, and the pauses between her phrases stretch well beyond the usual length. Answers swing in length more widely than nearly any colleague's. Wording hits hard and carries a heavy emotional load compared with most. Her agenda spans a broader set of topics than nearly any colleague, so her talk ranges widely even when the question is narrow.
Ayanna Pressley.decides: What she looks at is how closely an ask ties to the people it helps, and a request framed around community impact gets a fairer hearing. Her legislation touches far more topics than most colleagues, so she tends to back an ask that fits her wide agenda. Cross-aisle partnership is rare for her, so backing from across the aisle seldom carries her. Her commitment to votes and bill steps is somewhat weaker than most, so a yes survives only with a named owner attached.

archetype.justification: He is outgoing and among the most curious colleagues, and his phrasing lands with far more force than most, which fits a bold style.

Barry Loudermilk.bottom_line: Let him speak first, then bring a tight case with clear figures. Pressure from outside groups counts for less with him, so the argument has to do the work.
do: Give him the floor first and hear his position
Keep your tone direct, since his phrasing cuts sharp
Name the next step and an owner before leaving
dont: Assume an outside campaign will change his vote
Stack a long list of asks into one sitting
Barry Loudermilk.warning_sign: Usually he answers briskly, and his volume swings up and down more than most. If he trails off mid thought more often and his pauses lengthen, he is losing interest, so stop pitching and ask one direct question.
Barry Loudermilk.follow_up: After the meeting, send him a one page written note with the ask, the people it helps and the dated next step, copied to his legislative director.
Barry Loudermilk.personality: Loudermilk is outgoing and among the most curious members, with a phrasing that carries far more force than most. He takes charge of conversations somewhat more than most, and his longest replies come in shorter than nearly any colleague's. He cooperates across the aisle less than almost anyone, and his legislation spans a broad set of topics. Taken together, he is a bold, wide ranging member who prefers a direct exchange to a long negotiation.
Barry Loudermilk.speaks: His answers are short, and their length varies more than most, with his longest replies coming in shorter than nearly any colleague's. His phrasing cuts sharper than nearly any colleague's, and his public language is far less charged than most. Pauses run a little longer than most between phrases, and his volume swings up and down more than most. In hearings he runs a bit more combative than most members.
Barry Loudermilk.decides: He weighs an ask through his committee interest in financial services, and pressure from outside counts for less with him than with most colleagues. His cross aisle record is among the thinnest in the chamber, so a request across the aisle starts with little credit. Legislation spans a broad set of topics, so an ask lands only when it fits the agenda he already carries.

archetype.justification: His words run much warmer than most, and he commands the floor more firmly than nearly anyone.

Barry Moore.bottom_line: Bring a people focused case, and tie the ask to one clear result. Outside pressure moves him among the least of members, so the case must hold on its own.
do: Lead with who is helped, since people centered stories fit him best
Open with warmth, since his words run much warmer than most
Let him set the tone early, since he commands the floor
Keep your answers short, since his answers run much shorter than most
dont: Rush him to close, since his turns trail off and vary widely
Treat warm rapport as a commitment, since outside pressure moves him among the least
Barry Moore.warning_sign: When a point is challenged, he usually takes the floor and trails off mid thought. Let him finish, then ask one clear question and wait, since he will often keep talking.
Barry Moore.follow_up: Afterward, mail a brief written recap listing the people helped and one dated next step, and copy his office.
Barry Moore.personality: Moore comes across as quite reserved and quite practical, and his detail runs far looser than most. Strong feelings arise somewhat faster for him than for most, and his words run much warmer than most. His bills span a bit wider ground than most, and he holds the floor in conversation more firmly than nearly anyone. His answers run short and uneven, varying among the most in the chamber.
Barry Moore.speaks: Words from him rank among the most forceful in the chamber, and among the most action focused. His wording is among the flattest in the chamber. Answers run far shorter than most, and his answer length varies among the most in the chamber. Even his longest answers run a bit shorter than most, and he trails off among the most in the chamber.
Barry Moore.decides: Before backing a bill he asks if it puts the people it helps at the center of the case. Across the aisle he works somewhat more than most, so a bipartisan partner adds weight. Outside pressure moves him among the least of members, so his own read carries the decision. He takes the floor with force, so any yes needs a dated step to hold.

archetype.justification: Her volume swings more widely than almost anyone's, her language cuts much harder than most, and she builds her case on the community it serves.

Becca Balint.bottom_line: Open the ask with the people it would help, not policy text. She holds the floor and pushes back hard, so a clear human case gives her something to test.
do: Bring two or three short stories about people the ask would help
Ask what she is defending before you answer, and answer that first
Set turn order in formal sessions, since her volume swings and she holds the floor
Have community groups that back the ask call her office, since outside voices sway her
dont: Trade blows over minor points while the main ask waits
Read one short reply as her final word on the ask
Water down the ask to match her sharp words
Becca Balint.warning_sign: She usually defends her main point hard. If she repeats her main defense more often than her usual pattern, she is stuck on that line, not on your ask. Offer the ask in one sentence, then give her room to answer it.
Becca Balint.follow_up: Email her office within two days to confirm the next step she named, with a date.
Becca Balint.personality: Balint is a very outgoing member who steers a conversation, and she holds the floor about as well as anyone in the House. Getting worked up comes much more readily to her than to most, and few match the emotional charge in her words. Her public language is much more cutting than most, and her talk about her job is much less careful and detailed than most. She is fairly curious and open to new ideas, but detail is not her strength.
Becca Balint.speaks: In conversation she takes charge and holds the floor once she has it. Her answers run long there, but in interviews those answers run a little shorter than most. Answer length swings widely from one reply to the next, and she trails off much less than most. Her volume swings far more than almost anyone's on the House floor. After a long answer, ask one follow-up question instead of changing topics.
Becca Balint.decides: She takes the lead in talks and holds the floor, so get your key ask in early, before her turn runs long. She defends positions she has already taken, so tie each new point to a stance she has stated before. Answer length swings widely for her, so plan for both long and clipped replies in one meeting. End each conversation by getting a named next step that she states herself.

archetype.justification: His long pauses, even volume, fairly reliable follow through and written focus fit a tortoise that moves slowly and surely.

Ben Cline.bottom_line: Bring the evidence in writing before you meet, since he moves through each bill step with care.
do: Walk through one bill step by step, not the whole agenda
Pause after each point and let him finish his reply
Lock in one named next step and set its deadline
dont: Fill the silence with extra talk about the agenda
Ben Cline.warning_sign: Usually his wording is gentler than most, and he speaks slowly with long pauses. If his wording turns sharper and his pitch swings wider, he is frustrated with the pace and wants a clear answer now. Give him the direct answer, then stop talking.
Ben Cline.follow_up: Send his staff the agreed next step in writing, with the bill, the owner and the date.
Ben Cline.personality: Cline comes across as quite restrained yet fairly agreeable, and his collaboration crosses the aisle somewhat ahead of most. He has a somewhat wider legislative range than most, and his follow through on bills holds up fairly well. Explanations of bills come out more careful and detailed than most, and he represents Virginia. His public profile is a bit lower than most.
Ben Cline.speaks: Pace runs a notch slower than most, and his pauses run longer than nearly any colleague's. His pitch ranges far wider than most, while his loudness holds much more level than most. Wording is somewhat gentler than most, and his accounts of bills are more careful and detailed than most colleagues. His answers run unhurried and detailed rather than brisk.
Ben Cline.decides: His bar for a request is whether the paper evidence holds and whether every step has a clear owner. Cross-aisle work is somewhat more common for him than for most, so an ask that spans the aisle has fair footing. Pressure from outside registers with him a bit less than with most colleagues, so a yes rests on the case itself. Because his follow through is fairly reliable but not automatic, each step needs a named owner before a yes means much.

archetype.justification: His talk and bills span more areas than nearly anyone, and he is quite reserved in conversation.

Ben Luján.bottom_line: Give him a specific ask in writing, since he rarely takes charge of the room. Outside pressure moves him much more than most members, so bring outside voices.
do: Leave him room to answer without interruption
Line up outside backers for the ask, since external pushes sway him far more
Expect little public airtime, so press the ask in small meetings
dont: Waste time on small talk, since his words are among the least social
Ben Luján.warning_sign: When a conversation turns to contested ground, he usually stops taking charge and lets others speak. Watch for that pull back, then leave room and ask one clear question about his next step.
Ben Luján.follow_up: Afterward, email his office a brief written recap of the request and one dated action, copying his staff.
Ben Luján.personality: Luján covers more ground in his talk and bills than nearly anyone in the chamber, which shapes how he is heard. He is quite reserved in public, and much less visible than most members do. Little rattles him, and his answers rarely come in quick bursts. He is fairly agreeable, and his wording is among the least forceful in the chamber.
Ben Luján.speaks: His talk ranges across a wider set of areas than almost anyone. Words are among the most upbeat in the chamber and among the least forceful. Answer length hardly varies from one turn to the next. He trails off somewhat more than most, so his points can end mid thought. Across his talk, the pattern holds from one exchange to the next.
Ben Luján.decides: Each request gets judged by how widely it stretches over areas he already tracks, and whether it suits his current bills. Outside pressure moves him much more than most members, so local voices can tip a close call. He is much less visible than most, so his backing rarely shows publicly. Any yes from him holds only when a named sponsor owns the next step.

archetype.justification: He takes charge of conversations much more than most and is among the most reliable in seeing bills through.

Bennie Thompson.bottom_line: Bring written technical material early and let him lead the discussion. Pressure will meet a firm defense, so state the ask once and let it stand.
do: Send written technical material ahead, so he can check the numbers
Let him take the floor, then ask one precise question
Confirm each commitment in writing before you leave
dont: Keep pressing the same point once he has answered it
Skip small talk and open with the decision itself
Bennie Thompson.warning_sign: He usually finishes his sentences and holds the floor. If he starts trailing off in the middle of a sentence, he is on guard. Slow down, ask what is worrying him, and let him finish.
Bennie Thompson.follow_up: Send a short email listing each commitment and its owner, the same day, to his office.
Bennie Thompson.personality: Thompson is careful and organized, and he goes into his work in detail across a far greater spread of issues than most colleagues. He is more dependable than nearly any colleague at bringing bills home, and he runs a conversation by taking the floor. In manner he is forceful and far less social than most, so he drives the room rather than mingles in it. He also draws notice, ranking among the most visible of his colleagues.
Bennie Thompson.speaks: He talks in detail across many issues and uses somewhat fewer filler words than most. When challenged he holds his position, and his words grow more forceful under strain. Loudness stays far more level than most, while pitch moves up and down somewhat more. He sticks to substance rather than small talk, and he rarely drifts into social chat. He also gives short, rapid replies somewhat more often than most colleagues.
Bennie Thompson.decides: He tests a request against the written evidence and asks whether it can actually be carried out. Calls and letters from outside move him much less than they move most colleagues. When he has committed to a view, he tends to defend it under challenge. Carefully built plans earn his time, given how reliably he carries bills to passage. He takes charge of the room, so an agreement holds only when someone owns the next step.

archetype.justification: Very outgoing, he leads conversations somewhat more than most, varies his answer length somewhat more than most, and defends his position much more than most.

Bernard Sanders.bottom_line: Lead with the people the policy helps, since stories fit him best, and get a written next step before you leave.
do: Open with one family or community the policy would help
Plan your evidence in advance, since he holds firm when challenged
Count on a mild hearing manner, among the least combative you face
dont: Compete with him for the floor, since he takes charge somewhat more than most
Assume a yes in the room will carry through to the vote
Bernard Sanders.warning_sign: He usually takes charge of the room and leaves somewhat bigger gaps between phrases. If his pauses shorten and his pace climbs, he is digging in, so stop pressing and name the one point you need.
Bernard Sanders.follow_up: By the end of the week, send his office a written list of the people the policy helps and the dates each step is due.
Bernard Sanders.personality: Sanders stands out as very outgoing and somewhat curious, and his public profile outshines nearly any colleague's. Conversations tend to follow his lead somewhat more than most, while his short answers keep the exchange moving. Detail is thin whenever his own work comes up, thinner than almost anyone's, and his record on finishing bills is among the weakest. Among the least combative members in hearings, he still defends his position much more than most when challenged.
Bernard Sanders.speaks: Pace is somewhat quicker than most, with somewhat bigger gaps between phrases, and his pitch is much flatter than most. His answers run short, and their length varies somewhat more than most. He trails off somewhat less than most, and his language is among the least emotionally charged in the chamber. Challenge him and he holds his ground, and that pattern repeats across the shows he appears on.
Bernard Sanders.decides: Whom a request helps is his test, so stories about the people affected earn his attention. Bills that touch several issues can catch his interest, since his bills reach somewhat more areas than most. Among the least dependable on finishing bills, he can give a yes that stalls before the vote. So his yes holds only when someone owns the next step.

archetype.justification: He is quite skeptical, he holds the floor more than most, and his words are as sharp and forceful as anyone's in the Senate.

Bernie Moreno.bottom_line: Lead with the outcome you want and the result the policy will bring, since a brief, plain case fits him best.
do: Bring the figures that show results, stated in plain words
Follow a quick short reply with one pointed question
Put each point as a concrete step someone will take
Ask him to commit to the next vote or step, since his follow-through is strong
dont: Take his sharp wording as hostility toward your cause
Match his forceful wording with yours, because he defends his position
Load the ask with extra points, because his replies run much shorter than most
Bernie Moreno.warning_sign: His words usually run as sharp as any senator's. If the words turn sharper, take that as a sign the ask is not landing. Reduce the ask to one line, and set the sharper wording aside.
Bernie Moreno.follow_up: By Monday, give his staff a short recap of each commitment, with its deadline, in a single email.
Bernie Moreno.personality: Moreno is quite skeptical, and he steers a conversation more firmly than most senators. He is fairly outgoing and fairly curious, and his bills touch somewhat more areas than most. Few Senate members follow bills through as reliably. Cross-party work is much lighter for him than for most senators. His words are among the most forceful in the Senate, and sharper than almost anyone's. He has spoken about immigrating as a child and about fearing for his business in a hard financial crisis. Public attention finds him less than most, even in his role.
Bernie Moreno.speaks: In interviews his answers are one of the shortest in the Senate, and his longest ones stay short too. His replies arrive in fast bunches, far more than most. His pace is slow, and his pitch barely moves. Tone runs warm, and his language is more action-focused than nearly any senator's. He defends his position somewhat more than most when pressed, show after show. Keep your replies to one line and match his pace.
Bernie Moreno.decides: Results the policy can show fit him best. When challenged, he defends his ground across shows, so answer the objection with the result itself. Where it honestly fits, his father-in-law's years raising a family on one paycheck give you common ground. Keep your closing ask tight, since he answers in quick, short runs. End by asking which result he would want to see first and by when.

archetype.justification: Her public tone runs warm, yet her language cuts sharply and she is among the least agreeable colleagues in the chamber.

Beth Van Duyne.bottom_line: Start with what the policy delivers, in a short and direct case. She is blunt, so state each point plainly and leave out vague wording.
do: Bring a short, direct summary of what the policy delivers
Keep your replies brief, since her own answers run longer than almost anyone's
Shape the agenda yourself early, since she seldom takes charge of the talk
Ask which of her past bills reached a vote before you propose this one
dont: Quote her sharpest lines back at her when you reply
Add a second point while her long answer is still running
Mistake her warm tone for an easy yes, though she is hard to win
Beth Van Duyne.warning_sign: She usually leaves the agenda to you, so a sudden push to steer the talk stands out. When she grabs the agenda, she is putting her own point forward. Meet that point first, then return to the ask.
Beth Van Duyne.follow_up: Email her staff within two days to confirm which of her questions is still open.
Beth Van Duyne.personality: Van Duyne is hard to win over, and she is blunt in how she frames a point. She leans toward practical ideas over curious ones, and she leans a little reserved. Detail work is not where she shines, and she trails most members on votes and on follow-through for her bills. She rarely leads a conversation, and her committee seat is on House Small Business.
Beth Van Duyne.speaks: In conversation her answers run longer than those of almost any House member, and she seldom takes charge. On the House floor her loudness varies much more than most, and her pace runs a little quick, with somewhat shorter pauses between phrases. Her public tone is much warmer than most. Hold your reply until a long answer ends, then keep yours brief.
Beth Van Duyne.decides: Results count with her more than abstract ideas, and she is skeptical by default. First impressions do not win her over, and her follow-through falls short of most members. Frame the ask as one concrete result she can accept or refuse on its own, with the vote it needs named plainly. A clear refusal tells you where the case stands, and a soft maybe tells you little.

archetype.justification: She is much more reserved than most and very careful, and she follows bills to a vote very consistently.

Betty McCollum.bottom_line: Bring a shared role for the announcement and a clear written ask. Pressure from outside will not move her much, so the reason has to be on paper.
do: Put the ask in writing with the evidence attached
Offer a role in announcing the result together
Prepare clear answers, since she is far from combative in hearings
dont: Count on outside pressure alone to change her view
Push for a yes on the spot, since she takes time before she commits
Betty McCollum.warning_sign: In a hearing she usually keeps a low edge and does not turn confrontational. If she turns sharp and pointed during a hearing, she has become guarded. Take a short pause, restate the point plainly, and let her answer.
Betty McCollum.follow_up: Mail her office a brief memo with the evidence attached, within two days of the meeting.
Betty McCollum.personality: McCollum is much more reserved than most, and she comes across as very careful and organized. Curious by temperament, she takes in a lot before she speaks. Her bills touch somewhat more areas than most colleagues, and her public talk ranges widely. Her record in carrying bills forward is very strong, and she keeps somewhat lower visibility than most. Within hearings she stays far from combative exchanges.
Betty McCollum.speaks: Across many areas, her public talk ranges somewhat wider than most colleagues. In one conversation she tends to touch several issue areas. Her manner in a hearing is far from combative, and she keeps to the substance. Hearing questions get a plain and civil answer from her, without escalation. Formal settings bring out her plainest manner, more than adversarial exchanges do.
Betty McCollum.decides: She weighs an ask on its fit with her existing record and whether it can be carried through. Pressure from outside groups affects her much less than most, so a request must stand on its own case. Sharing the announcement with a colleague suits her, so the ask gets carried further. Being much more reserved than most, she takes time before she commits. So she needs a named next step before she will move on it.

archetype.justification: He comes across as much more sociable in public than typical, and he works across party lines more than nearly any colleague.

Bill Cassidy.bottom_line: Bring outside voices that back the ask, since they carry real weight with him, and let him defend the position in his own words.
do: Ask for a written commitment on the vote, since his follow through lags
Meet him informally, ideally with a colleague from the other party
Let him hold the floor early, then ask one pointed question
dont: Challenge his position head on, since he defends it harder than nearly any colleague
Rush into his short pauses with extra points
Bill Cassidy.warning_sign: He usually runs conversations and argues his position hard when challenged. If his answers shorten and his sharp edge softens, he is losing interest or has settled his view, so stop arguing and ask for one concrete decision.
Bill Cassidy.follow_up: Send his staff a written note the same day listing each commitment he made and the date each is due.
Bill Cassidy.personality: Cassidy is organized and careful, with a fairly outgoing and curious streak and a temperament that is hard to fluster. Conversations tend to run through him, and he holds the floor and defends his positions harder than most colleagues. Public language is sharp and social at once, cooler in warmth than most, and light on filler. Across the aisle he works more than nearly any colleague, yet carrying bills forward is where he is among the least dependable in the chamber. His visibility runs high for his role.
Bill Cassidy.speaks: In conversation he keeps the floor far more than others do, and his replies run a little shorter than typical. His words are sharp and pointed in tone, much sharper than most, and he defends his position harder than most colleagues when challenged. Gaps between his phrases are somewhat briefer than typical, and his tone runs cooler than most while his language leans clearly toward the social side. Filler is rare in his speech, and his longest replies run somewhat shorter than typical.
Bill Cassidy.decides: Whether an ask lets him steer the discussion and whether he can defend it in public is how he judges it. His work across party lines is wide, but his record on carrying bills through is weak, so a promise from him needs a written trail to hold. When he has settled on a stance, he defends it firmly, and outside voices carry real weight with him. Given how visible his role keeps him, an ask sticks best with outside backing and a written commitment.

archetype.justification: His curiosity is strong, his work is careful and orderly, and few in the chamber cover as many subjects in their public words.

Bill Foster.bottom_line: Keep the case short and direct, built on what the policy delivers. A clear result matters most with him.
do: Bring results in the order the plan delivers them, one step at a time
Open with what the plan does, in one plain sentence
Offer him one figure from the plan to explore
Ask which staff member will carry the plan after the meeting
dont: Take his sharper hearing tone as a rejection of the plan
Hold a press event before the plan is set
Count his cross-party record as a promise to vote your way
Bill Foster.warning_sign: His usual hearing manner is fairly combative, more than most. If that edge fades and his questions go gentle, he has already let your point go. Restate your ask in one plain line, then ask which point he wants to test first.
Bill Foster.follow_up: Send his staff a point-by-point written answer within two days, with an owner and a date for each open item.
Bill Foster.personality: Foster has an open mind, and few members match his curiosity. He is careful and orderly by nature, and thorough in his work. Few House members reach across party lines more than he does, and his bills span much more ground than most. Yet on follow-through he trails most members, and his public profile runs a bit lower than most colleagues'. He is hard to rattle, more so than most. In a hearing he is more pointed than most colleagues. He has spoken about starting a theater lighting company with his brother, now employee-owned.
Bill Foster.speaks: Few members range across more subjects in their public words, and they carry very little emotional charge. Plain, factual words suit him. In hearings he presses a bit harder than most, so when a meeting turns formal, keep your own questions sharp and specific. Give him the same plain, direct tone in every setting, and keep each point to one clear idea.
Bill Foster.decides: His seat on House Financial Services gives a natural link to open with. Results are the frame that fits him, so a plan that shows what it delivers gets the most from him. A one-page statement of that result is a plain move to make before the meeting. Because follow-through trails most members, ask for the yes in writing before you leave.

archetype.justification: He keeps a conversation in his hands, and he is notably loose with details compared with most members.

Bill Hagerty.bottom_line: Keep your ask short and let him set the talk, since he holds the floor. Send written technical evidence ahead, because he takes in cases that way.
do: Put the technical evidence in his hands before the meeting
Let him finish long answers before you reply
Agree a written next step and who owns it
In a hearing, expect a low key exchange
dont: Count on upbeat enthusiasm to carry the ask
Assume he will chase a bill to the finish
Bill Hagerty.warning_sign: His usual pattern is fast, lively delivery at an even volume. When his pace slows and his pitch flattens, he is on guard, so let him set the pace and then restate the single step you want.
Bill Hagerty.follow_up: Send a one page summary within a week naming the next step, the owner, and the date you need it.
Bill Hagerty.personality: Hagerty is one of the most skeptical members around, and he steers conversations firmly. He has a reserved manner and a practical streak, and he is notably less exact about details than most members. Bills span an unusually wide set of issues, and his words are among the least emotionally charged in the chamber. He is much less reliable at seeing bills through, and in hearings he is one of the least confrontational people around.
Bill Hagerty.speaks: He speaks much faster than most, with a pitch that moves a great deal and somewhat longer pauses between phrases. His words are among the most upbeat, forceful, and social in the chamber, and less focused on action than almost anyone's. In conversation he holds the floor and gives longer answers than most, and his replies do not come in quick bursts of brief lines. Answer length shifts widely from one reply to the next, and his interview answers run longer than most.
Bill Hagerty.decides: He weighs an ask by how well it is documented in written, technical form. His bills span many issues, so an ask that touches several of his areas can find a place. Reliability at seeing bills through is weaker than typical, so a commitment from him needs a date and a name attached. Outside voices move him a bit more than most members, so a second voice from outside can tip a close call. His support tends to follow the clearest written case put in front of him.

archetype.justification: He sees bills through more reliably than nearly any colleague and describes his work with much more careful detail than most.

Bill Huizenga.bottom_line: Bring a tight results case and name the next step. He sees bills through, so a dated written commitment will hold him.
do: Build the case around results the policy can show
Ask him to name the vote or markup he takes next
dont: Fill each brief pause with extra background
Open with long setup, since his pace runs quick
Bill Huizenga.warning_sign: In a hearing he usually pushes hard when questions turn to results. If he stops pressing a point and goes quiet, he is pulling back from the detail. Shorten your answer and offer a one page summary.
Bill Huizenga.follow_up: Send a one page written summary of the results, with the next markup and its date, to his staff within two days.
Bill Huizenga.personality: Huizenga ranks among the most curious members and is fairly careful, and few things rattle him. Careful detail marks how he describes his work, more than most colleagues do. His bills span a wider field than nearly any colleague's. Dependability in finishing bills puts him among the top members. Public visibility runs lower than most, and he is from Michigan.
Bill Huizenga.speaks: Pace runs quick, with few pauses and a fairly even volume. His pitch moves up and down more than most, and his descriptions of work carry much more careful detail than most. Coverage runs broader than nearly any colleague's when he speaks. Volume stays fairly even while he presses a point. In hearings he is one of the most combative members.
Bill Huizenga.decides: He weighs an ask by the results it can show and whether the process will hold. He is among the most dependable members about finishing bills, so a dated written commitment is what makes a decision stick. Public campaigns sway him only slightly more than most colleagues, so visible support helps at the margin. Written follow up keeps his support in place.

archetype.justification: His careful, detailed talk and long, unhurried answers fit a watchful, careful observer who weighs each point.

Blake Moore.bottom_line: Lead with bipartisan backers and the technical record, since he joins colleagues across party lines more than almost anyone and follows bills through.
do: Name the colleagues on the other side who back it
Walk through the technical record step by step
Bring a clear agenda and take the lead yourself
dont: Treat a long pause as the end of his point
Assume his friendly tone means he has already agreed
Blake Moore.warning_sign: He usually lets others lead, so a quiet room is normal. If he abruptly takes over the talk and pushes one point hard, read it as guarded, so pause, name the worry, and invite his view.
Blake Moore.follow_up: After the meeting send him the technical summary with the cross aisle backers named, and ask him to confirm his position by a set date.
Blake Moore.personality: Moore reads as very outgoing and very agreeable, with a fairly curious streak and a careful mind. Bills he carries get followed through to a vote more dependably than nearly anyone's. His public account of his work is among the most exact in the chamber, and he builds ties across the aisle to an unusual degree. His public words are warm and action focused, and his tone rarely turns forceful. Utah is the state he serves.
Blake Moore.speaks: Delivery is slow, with some of the longest pauses in the House. Answers run much longer than colleagues' in interviews, and his longest replies stretch well beyond usual length. Sentences rarely trail off, so he tends to finish his thoughts. His talk carries a bit more filler than colleagues'. Words are upbeat and much more action focused, and they carry a warm tone.
Blake Moore.decides: He gives an ask a fair hearing when it reaches across the aisle, since that is where his own ties run. An agreeable streak makes him open to a shared solution. Bills he carries span a slightly narrower set of areas than colleagues', so a proposal should fit the issues he already works on. He ranks among the most dependable in carrying bills to a vote, so a commitment he makes tends to hold.

archetype.justification: Very curious and outgoing, sharp in words, and combative in hearings when formal matters arise.

Bonnie Watson Coleman.bottom_line: Bring one clear ask with its evidence, since outside pressure is among the least able to move her.
do: Bring stories of who is helped, since people and community impact fits her best
Expect sharp questions in hearings, since she ranks with the most combative members
Put the ask in writing so she can test each claim
dont: Trade barbs with her, since her words already cut sharply
Bonnie Watson Coleman.warning_sign: Usually her words are already sharp, so a change in tone is the cue. If her questions sharpen, read it as her guard rising, so take your time and answer each point with its evidence.
Bonnie Watson Coleman.follow_up: Send a short summary by Friday naming the open questions she raised and who answers each.
Bonnie Watson Coleman.personality: Watson Coleman is very curious and outgoing, with a skeptical streak that keeps her testing what she hears. Her words are sharp and carry strong feeling, and she is easily stirred, so an exchange can heat up fast. Her bills cover a wide spread of issues. Formal matters draw out pointed probing, and hearings find her ranked among the most combative members.
Bonnie Watson Coleman.speaks: Her talk is pointed and direct, and her words cut among the sharpest in the chamber. Strong feeling runs through how she puts things, so her delivery carries heat. Questions from her turn pointed in formal settings, and in hearings she stands among the most combative members. She states her views plainly rather than softening them, which keeps exchanges direct.
Bonnie Watson Coleman.decides: Any request gets judged by how it holds up when she checks the evidence herself. Her bills cover a wide spread of issues, so asks inside her areas fit best. Outside pressure carries little weight with her. Because she tests claims closely, an agreement holds only once she has examined the case for herself. She reads each figure closely and pushes for the reasoning behind it.

archetype.justification: Fairly outgoing and curious, and his talk centers on people and community impact, which suits a protective, plainspoken approach.

Brad Finstad.bottom_line: Bring a concrete, plainly stated ask tied to the people it helps, since pressure from outside reaches him clearly more than most colleagues.
do: Tie the ask to the people and community it would help
Line up outside voices who will press the ask with him
Find a colleague across the aisle who shares the goal
dont: Hurry him toward a decision before he has finished
Brad Finstad.warning_sign: A sit down with the group will not reveal his position, because he often lets a point rest before replying. Ask which fact would change his view, then send exactly that fact in writing.
Brad Finstad.follow_up: Directly afterward, email his office the agreed action in writing with a named staff contact and the deadline.
Brad Finstad.personality: Finstad comes across as somewhat sociable and inquisitive, and he holds details more loosely than most colleagues. Public remarks cover a far wider slate of topics than most, though his work is described in much less detailed terms. His legislation covers more ground than most colleagues, and he crosses party lines somewhat more than most. Votes and bill follow through are much weaker than most.
Brad Finstad.speaks: His public talk spans more ground than most colleagues, and he gives much less detail about his work than most. His delivery is much slower than most colleagues', with longer pauses between phrases and a volume that swings more than most. The overall effect is a deliberate delivery in which the big picture comes before the particulars, so he builds his case slowly and in order.
Brad Finstad.decides: A request is weighed on whether it suits the folks back home and whether outside voices stand behind it. Pressure from outside reaches him clearly more than most colleagues, so backing from outside his office carries real weight. His legislation covers more ground than most, so a shared colleague can help. Follow through runs far weaker than most, so a choice holds only with a dated check and a named owner.

archetype.justification: He is reserved to a striking degree, speaks slowly, and keeps a low profile in Congress.

Brad Knott.bottom_line: Bring one narrow, detailed ask and give him time to check it against the facts. Outside voices carry weight with him, so involve them before the decision.
do: Send the facts early so he can check them
Bring voices from outside the room early
In a hearing, expect courteous, low key questioning
Agree a written next step and check the bill's progress
dont: Rush him with fast, multi issue asks
Count on a first refusal holding once outside voices engage
Read his long pauses as a lack of interest
Brad Knott.warning_sign: His usual pattern is low key in hearings and slow to challenge. When he starts to press harder in a hearing than usual, guardedness creeps in, so ease up and restate the single step you want.
Brad Knott.follow_up: After the meeting, send a brief written note listing the action, who owns it, and when the next check on the bill falls.
Brad Knott.personality: Knott stands out as one of the most reserved members around, and he tends to speak in practical terms. He is very practical, and his talk stays on a small set of issues, fewer than most colleagues raise. Details are a bit less of his focus, yet his talk about his own work is one of the most precise in Congress. Bills from him cover fewer issues than most, and he is somewhat dependable at getting bills through. In the chamber he is one of the least visible members, and in hearings he does not turn combative.
Brad Knott.speaks: He speaks at a slow pace, and his tone shifts a great deal from one sentence to the next. Topics stay within a narrow range, and his words come out more precise and detailed than typical. All of his recorded speech comes from floor delivery, so these traits describe that setting. In hearings he does not turn combative, so his manner there stays low key. His pauses between phrases run longer than most.
Brad Knott.decides: A request gets judged on how neatly it fits the few issues his bills cover. Carrying bills forward, he is somewhat dependable, so a commitment he makes tends to hold. In hearings his manner stays low key and he avoids confrontation, so his public stance stays quiet. Outside pressure carries real weight with him, more than with most members, so his position can shift when outside voices pile on.

archetype.justification: He is curious, stands out in his role, and his bills reach across more policy areas than nearly anyone's.

Brad Sherman.bottom_line: Keep your ask to one clear sentence, since his answers run short, even his longest ones.
do: Keep a follow-up question ready after each of his short replies
Name the exact step you want from him before the meeting ends
Let his long pauses run, since he keeps the floor once he has it
Answer sharp hearing questions in one direct sentence each
dont: Count on one fixed reply length for his answers
Take his curiosity or public profile as a sign he backs your ask
Read his hard hearing questions as a verdict on your ask
Brad Sherman.warning_sign: Usually he trails off or gets cut off mid-thought more than most members. If his sentences break off even more often than that, you have lost him. Stop talking, and ask which point he wants to settle first.
Brad Sherman.follow_up: Within a day, send his staff a one-page memo that restates the ask and the next step, with the date each step is due.
Brad Sherman.personality: Sherman is one of the most curious members in the House, and very careful. He is somewhat skeptical by default, yet much less easily rattled than most. His words carry far less emotional heat than nearly anyone's in the House. Bills he sponsors reach into more policy areas than nearly anyone's. Voting and seeing his bills through is a fairly strong suit for him. He serves on House Financial Services, builds across the aisle somewhat more than most, and his profile runs very high for his role. Hearings draw out a much sharper edge in him than in most members.
Brad Sherman.speaks: In interviews his answers run short, and even his longest stay brief. His answer length swings much more than most. Filler words are much less common in his talk than for most members. Talk moves more slowly than almost anyone's in the House. He pauses between phrases longer than almost anyone in the House. His volume varies somewhat less than most.
Brad Sherman.decides: He is somewhat skeptical by default, so expect him to test the ask before he commits. Pressure from outside sways him somewhat more than most colleagues, so keep the ask in front of him through each stage. His follow-through is fairly reliable once he has made up his mind, so a settled yes holds up better than a loose one.

archetype.justification: Community stories fit him best, his words carry more charge than most, and his volume swings widely on the floor.

Bradley Schneider.bottom_line: Lead with the people your bill helps, then secure a written next step, since his curiosity runs ahead of his follow through.
do: Open with one concrete story about who the bill helps
Name the decision date and the person who owns the next step
If he fires quick short answers, keep yours brief and let him finish
In a hearing, expect combative questions and answer each one briefly
dont: Take a run of short turns as an argument
Assume a quick yes will hold without a written follow up
Read his volume swings as temper, when his words are usually gentle
Bradley Schneider.warning_sign: By default his words come out gentler than most, so a sharper edge from him usually means a point has got under his skin. Stop adding material, ask what he needs before you push further, and let him set the pace.
Bradley Schneider.follow_up: Send a short written recap of the ask and the next step within a day, naming the owner and the date.
Bradley Schneider.personality: Schneider is a curious, agreeable member whose public words range across many issues, even though his bills touch slightly fewer subjects than most. He describes his own work with less precision than most, and on bills his follow through is much weaker. In hearings he ranks among the most combative in the chamber. His reach runs wider than his follow through.
Bradley Schneider.speaks: He talks in wide sweeps across issues and keeps the detail light when he describes his work. His language runs somewhat gentler than most and carries a bit more feeling. Delivery comes a bit slower than most, and volume swings widely on the floor. Answers move between long stretches and brisk bursts of short turns, which keeps the rhythm shifting from one exchange to the next.
Bradley Schneider.decides: He sizes up a request by who it helps, since community impact is the framing that fits him best. Agreeable by temperament, he says yes readily, but his bills touch slightly fewer subjects and his follow through lags, so a warm yes does not carry itself. A commitment holds for him only when someone owns it and a deadline is set, so a yes without a next step fades.

archetype.justification: Very reserved, he is far looser with details and concentrates his work on a handful of topics.

Brandon Gill.bottom_line: Keep the ask short and tied to results, since he responds to facts. Outside pressure moves him much less than most, so a clear result carries more.
do: Lead with the facts and the result the policy delivers
Send written detail ahead so he has the specifics he tends to miss
Leave him room to talk since he ranks among the least outgoing
Count on him being somewhat less combative when hearings run than most
dont: Assume outside pressure will move him quickly
Brandon Gill.warning_sign: In hearings he is normally at a somewhat lower level of combat than most, so a sharper tone from him is a change. If he turns pointed, slow down, ask what the concern is, and give him room.
Brandon Gill.follow_up: Pass him a single page listing the request, its next move and the owner by Friday.
Brandon Gill.personality: Gill sits among the most reserved members, and he is very practical. His grasp of fine points runs loose, yet he describes his work somewhat more carefully than most. He is somewhat quicker to get riled than most, and his language carries much less charge than almost anyone's. Public talk and his bill list both stay much narrower than most. Hearings draw somewhat less heat from him than most colleagues. He sees bills through somewhat more reliably than most.
Brandon Gill.speaks: His delivery runs somewhat quicker than most, and his pauses are somewhat shorter than most. Pitch stays much flatter by comparison, while loudness swings somewhat more than the typical speaker. During hearings he is somewhat less confrontational than most colleagues. His remarks stay on a much narrower set of topics than most. When he speaks about his work, the terms are somewhat more exact than most.
Brandon Gill.decides: Whether a request shows a result he can point to is what he weighs, and he holds to his own priorities. His bills cover a narrow set of issues, so asks inside his lane fit him. Outside pressure moves him much less than most, so pressure alone will not carry a decision. A decision tends to hold when it carries a clear next step, since he is somewhat dependable at carrying bills forward.

archetype.justification: Fairly curious, gives long answers, and covers a broad field of topics.

Brendan Boyle.bottom_line: Let him finish his long answers, then fix the coming action in place, since carrying bills to completion is much weaker for him.
do: Send the ask in writing ahead, so he has room to answer fully
Ask who owns each next step, since seeing bills through is his weak point
Expect him to be among the most combative voices in testimony
dont: Cut across his long answers, since they stretch well past what most members give
Count on a verbal yes to carry the bill, since he is much less reliable
Brendan Boyle.warning_sign: Usually he keeps adding points, so a sudden stop stands out. If he drops out of the back and forth and answers in one line, he is losing interest, so ask one direct question.
Brendan Boyle.follow_up: Before Friday, record in writing the agreed actions for him, each paired with an accountable owner and a due date.
Brendan Boyle.personality: Boyle is very outgoing, fairly curious and fairly careful, and his public talk ranges somewhat wider than most. Accounts of his own work come across as less detailed than most colleagues offer, and his record shows he completes bills far less often. He is among the least inclined to lead a discussion, and he gives long answers. Strong emotional charge runs through his words.
Brendan Boyle.speaks: He gives long answers that stay even in length, and his longest replies run well past most. His words run much cooler than most, and his tone shifts more than most. Trailing off comes a little more often than most. Under questioning he is as forceful as almost anyone on the panel. Each reply stays connected to the previous point, so the thread holds across the exchange.
Brendan Boyle.decides: He tests each request on a pair of points: whether the specifics survive scrutiny and whether it can reach a floor vote. Getting bills over the finish line is far harder for him, so a yes should arrive with a designated person for the next action. Public commitments carry weight with him. At hearings he stands among the most combative participants, so a formal setting suits him and he holds his ground.

archetype.justification: Reserved and very practical, he speaks in careful, detailed terms, and his legislation touches a far smaller set of topics.

Brett Guthrie.bottom_line: Lead with what the policy delivers in plain terms, since pressure from outside carries less weight with him.
do: Keep the case short and about outcomes, not process
Confirm the date for each commitment in one line
Match his slower pace and leave room between points
dont: Take his reserve as opposition to the bill
Expect outside voices to move him quickly
Brett Guthrie.warning_sign: By default, in hearings he presses a little harder than most, so a quieter tone there usually means he is losing interest in the answer. Confirm the next step in one line, and let him decide when to continue.
Brett Guthrie.follow_up: Send a brief written note confirming the date for each commitment within two days, naming who owns it.
Brett Guthrie.personality: Guthrie is quite reserved and among the most practical members of the House, and very careful and organized. His public talk is highly careful and detailed, and his legislation touches a far smaller set of topics. His follow through on bills is very dependable, and he keeps a low profile for his role. In hearings he runs a little sharper than colleagues.
Brett Guthrie.speaks: His delivery is a bit slower than most, with longer pauses between phrases, and his volume swings a little. His talk is careful and compact, and it covers a narrow range of issues. Pitch stays a touch flatter than most, so feeling shows more in his words than his voice. Overall he sounds deliberate, and the detail carries most of the point.
Brett Guthrie.decides: He weighs an ask by what it delivers, since his legislation sits in a small number of areas. Once a bill is in motion he is very dependable at seeing it through, so a clear ask fits him. Outside pressure carries less weight with him, so an ask does not gain ground through outside noise. He settles on a yes only after he has the facts, so he commits when the case is complete.

archetype.justification: Slow, long pausing delivery and a very skeptical stance mark a patient Bear.

Brian Babin.bottom_line: Frame the ask as a bipartisan case, then close with one dated step he will own.
do: Let him finish each slow point before you respond
Back each claim with named supporters from across the aisle, since he is quite skeptical
dont: Match his sharp wording with sharper wording of your own
Rush to fill a pause with more arguments
Brian Babin.warning_sign: By default his wording is sharp, and he speaks slowly with long pauses. If his pace quickens and his wording softens, he is pressed or losing interest. Let the pause run and restate your ask in plain words.
Brian Babin.follow_up: Once the meeting ends, send a brief written note listing the agreed step, its date and the member's staff contact.
Brian Babin.personality: Babin is loose with details and quite skeptical in public. He is quicker to get worked up than colleagues generally, and he is less combative in formal hearings than the typical member. He reaches across party lines a bit more than average, and his bills span a few more issue areas. Visibility runs below the typical level. His public voice carries more feeling than most.
Brian Babin.speaks: His pace runs very slow, with pauses longer than nearly any colleague's. Loudness swings somewhat more than most, changing from phrase to phrase. Public wording runs much sharper than most, and it carries a bit more feeling than typical. He describes his work with a looser grip on detail than typical. His manner is deliberate, with long gaps before each point.
Brian Babin.decides: How well an ask crosses party lines matters to him, and outside pressure shifts him somewhat less than most. A push from the room therefore counts for less than the case itself. Because his bills reach a few more issues than most, an ask within those areas fits him better. Nothing is settled with him until the next step is named and the date is set.

archetype.justification: His cross party work, wide issue range, and agreeable manner fit a cooperative legislator who builds broad bills.

Brian Fitzpatrick.bottom_line: Bring a bill with cross party support and a well built ask. A visible push from home can lift a bill, since outside voices carry clear weight with him.
do: Point to the joined bills he already has with the other side
In a hearing, expect a more combative tone than usual
Lead with the concrete steps the bill takes, since his public words favor action
dont: Assume a joined bill guarantees support at every stage
Rely on outside pressure to rescue a weak ask
Brian Fitzpatrick.warning_sign: Usually he talks fast, keeps his volume even, and sounds gentler than most, so a dip in pace is the signal to watch. If he slows and his voice drops, he is weighing the ask, so restate the point and ask what would move it.
Brian Fitzpatrick.follow_up: Mail a single page to his staff listing the joined bills he has with the other side and the vote date within two days.
Brian Fitzpatrick.personality: Fitzpatrick, from Pennsylvania, is very curious and very careful, and few colleagues are more agreeable than he is. Across public talk he spans more ground than nearly any colleague does, and his bills cover a broad field. He is harder to fluster than almost anyone, and his words carry a bit more heat than most. He is very visible in the House, and in hearings he is a bit more pointed than most.
Brian Fitzpatrick.speaks: Delivery runs quick, and pauses between phrases come sooner than most. Public words come across as gentler than most, and they carry a touch more heat. Answers run longer than most in interviews, and the longest ones stretch further too. He trails off somewhat more than most, and filler shows up more than most. Volume stays very even, so the pace carries delivery rather than loudness.
Brian Fitzpatrick.decides: Before backing anything he gauges how far it reaches across the aisle and how broadly the bill covers issues. Pressure from his own district moves him more than most colleagues, so a local ask gets his attention. A bill covering many issues draws his interest, so any choice needs a named partner to hold. Cross party ties already on the bill matter to him, so who has joined the bill matters.

archetype.justification: His votes and bills show a dependable record, and he describes his work with much more precision than most.

Brian Jack.bottom_line: Send written technical evidence ahead, and give him the details in order. His records on votes and bills make a clear written step worth asking for.
do: Send the written technical evidence ahead of the meeting
Begin with the one technical question the plan has to answer
Walk through the details in order, one at a time
Offer to answer any technical question he sends back in writing
dont: Rely on outside voices to move him, since they move him less than most
Treat his gentle tone in hearings as a settled yes
Assume his record on votes settles a question he has not decided
Brian Jack.warning_sign: During hearings he is usually somewhat less combative than most. If he presses one point through several pointed questions in a row, he has moved past that pattern. Give him one open question, and wait for his full answer.
Brian Jack.follow_up: Within a week, send him a written technical summary that names the one next step and who on his staff will take it.
Brian Jack.personality: Jack describes his work in much more detailed terms than most, and he sees his bills through more steadily than most. His bills reach one of the narrowest ranges of issues in the House. Hearings find his tone mild, and he is a bit less combative than most. He has spoken about his grandmother, a long-lived figure in his family, and he is her sole grandchild.
Brian Jack.speaks: His public words describe his work with much more precision than most, so bring the specifics ready. In hearings he is a bit less combative than most, so keep each disagreement to one clear point. Answer each detailed question with the source behind it.
Brian Jack.decides: He is very reliable on votes and bills, so ask early for one named next step, not a general sense of support. Written technical detail gives him time to check the claims, which fits how he works. Set the date you will check back on that step.

archetype.justification: His wording is among the sharpest in the House, and his manner runs a little more forceful than most.

Brian Mast.bottom_line: Keep the case technical and written, and get to the point fast. Outside voices move him much more than most colleagues, so backers he respects matter.
do: Send the technical file ahead, so he can check the numbers
Answer his blunt points directly, without softening them
Keep each point short, since he gives short answers himself
dont: Skip warm small talk, since his manner is among the coolest in the House
Assume a long reply will hold his attention, since his answers run short
Brian Mast.warning_sign: He usually keeps filler close to none, and his answers run short. If filler creeps in and his answers stretch out, he is on guard. Cut to the point, name the concern, and offer one concrete fix.
Brian Mast.follow_up: Send the technical summary and figures in writing to his office, within two days of the vote.
Brian Mast.personality: Mast is somewhat more outgoing than most colleagues, and he likes a direct exchange. He gets worked up far more easily than most colleagues. Public talk covers a narrow set of issues, somewhat narrower than most colleagues. Accounts of his work are much more precise and in depth than most. In hearings he tends to be combative, and his edge carries into adversarial exchanges. He is somewhat more visible than most colleagues.
Brian Mast.speaks: He speaks in a blunt, direct way with sharp wording. Pitch runs somewhat less varied than most, and loudness moves a little more across a sentence. Pauses between phrases run somewhat longer than most. Answers run short, and his replies come back in somewhat fewer words than most. Filler is nearly absent from his delivery, and his answers stay on the point. In hearings he is a combative speaker, and his tone turns sharper in tense exchanges. Warm phrasing is not his habit, and his wording reads as cool.
Brian Mast.decides: His bar is how technical and well documented a request is. Campaigns from outside move him far more than they move most colleagues, so backers he respects outweigh a crowd. A visible shared role suits his temperament, since he is somewhat more visible than most. He is somewhat more outgoing than most, so direct exchanges suit him. Any choice sticks with him only when an owner is named and the record is documented.

archetype.justification: Bear fits because his words run sharp, he gets worked up quicker than most, and bridging with the other camp is rarer than almost anyone's.

Brian Schatz.bottom_line: Bring a plain, specific ask and leave room for long answers. Cross-party ties are thin, so anchor the case in his own coalition.
do: Open with one plain ask, since his answers already run long
Name the members of his own coalition who back the ask
Ask for a firm next step, since he is skeptical of loose promises
dont: Take his sharp wording as personal, since it is his usual manner
Expect a quick yes from one meeting with him
Brian Schatz.warning_sign: He usually answers at length, so a run of short replies is the change to watch. When that happens he is losing interest or getting on guard. Slow down, ask one open question, and wait for the full answer.
Brian Schatz.follow_up: Email him a brief note listing the request and one named action, copied to the aides who will handle it.
Brian Schatz.personality: Schatz is as inquisitive as almost any lawmaker and is fairly outgoing, though a little skeptical. Getting worked up comes easily to him, and his words carry much less emotional charge than nearly any colleague's. Work with the other party ranks at the very bottom of the chamber, yet his bills reach somewhat more topics than most. Control of conversations runs much lower than most, and visibility trails most colleagues for his role. He represents Hawaii.
Brian Schatz.speaks: Talk arrives in long, even answers and trails off less than nearly any colleague. Interview turns run much longer than most, and answer length stays fairly even from one reply to the next. Filler creeps in somewhat more than usual, and words sound flatter than nearly any colleague's. Broad terms dominate over detail when work is discussed, and words run sharp, though they carry little emotional charge.
Brian Schatz.decides: An ask gets sized up by how neatly it sits inside the coalition he already backs, since he crosses over less than almost anyone in the chamber. His long answers show he works a point through rather than trading quick replies. Pressure from outside groups carries less weight with him, so he decides on the case itself. A commitment sticks only when a named step is set.

archetype.justification: Reaching across the aisle, she does so more than almost anyone, and stories of the people a bill reaches move her most.

Brittany Pettersen.bottom_line: Bring a bipartisan partner and a story about the people a bill reaches. Outside pressure moves her far more than most, so keep the ask on those people.
do: Bring a bipartisan partner to the first meeting
Open with the people a bill reaches
In a hearing, expect a low key, civil exchange
Agree a dated next step and who will report back
dont: Count on her to carry a bill to the finish
Lean on outside pressure alone to move her
Assume her cross aisle ties guarantee a joint vote
Brittany Pettersen.warning_sign: Her usual pattern is people centered talk that rarely turns confrontational in hearings. When she grows more pointed than usual and her wording gets heavier, she has turned guarded, so ask whom the change affects and answer that first.
Brittany Pettersen.follow_up: Send a short written note within a week naming the step, who it helps, and the date for the next check.
Brittany Pettersen.personality: Pettersen reaches across the aisle more than nearly anyone, and she is among the least dependable at seeing bills through. She is a bit quicker to get riled than typical members, and her wording carries much less emotional charge. Her descriptions of her work are among the least detailed in the chamber, and her talk ranges wider than most. Bills from her reach a little more ground than typical, and in hearings she does not turn combative. Her profile in the chamber sits a little lower than typical.
Brittany Pettersen.speaks: Her account of her work runs among the least detailed in the chamber. Wording from her is far less emotionally charged than typical. Her talk ranges across a somewhat wider set of topics than typical, with less detail on each. In hearings she is far less confrontational than typical, and her manner there stays courteous. Taken together, her speech is detail light and feeling light, with a wider range of topics than typical.
Brittany Pettersen.decides: She gauges a request by whether it can pick up votes from the other side. Her bills reach across a bit more ground than typical, so an ask that sits inside her areas fits best. Follow through is among the least dependable, so a promise from her needs a date and a named owner. Cases built around the people a bill serves move her, so stories of who gains carry weight. Pressure from outside moves her far more than most members, so outside voices can shift her position.

archetype.justification: Reserved, he is very dependable at carrying bills to the finish and talks about work in careful, detailed terms.

Bruce Westerman.bottom_line: Send written technical material ahead of time, since that is how he weighs a case. Outside pressure reaches him much less than most, so give him time to weigh it.
do: Send written technical detail ahead of any meeting
Expect him to be reserved in the room and plan around that
Confirm each commitment in writing, since he sees bills through
If a hearing gets sharp, expect him to press the detail
dont: Assume outside pressure will carry the decision
Pitch the ask with an upbeat, excited tone
Bruce Westerman.warning_sign: He usually gives full, even answers, so a reply that stops early is a change. If he stops mid thought or trails off, slow down, ask what he is weighing, and give him room to complete it.
Bruce Westerman.follow_up: Send him a single page memo with the request, the written detail and the owner by Friday.
Bruce Westerman.personality: Westerman counts among the most reserved members, and he is very practical. His account of his work is among the most exact in the chamber, and he is very reliable at following bills. His language is much less charged than most. In conversation he takes the lead much less often than most colleagues. Few members touch a narrower set of issues than his bills do. He represents Arkansas's fourth district and once served as House Minority Leader and later as Majority Leader.
Bruce Westerman.speaks: His answers run among the longest in the chamber. His longest replies stretch somewhat beyond most. Bursts of short turns come somewhat more often from him than from most. His pace runs somewhat slower than most, with somewhat longer pauses than most. His pitch hardly rises and falls, flatter than nearly anyone's. In a hearing he turns somewhat more combative than most colleagues.
Bruce Westerman.decides: He gauges a request by how carefully it is built, and he is very dependable once a commitment is set. His bills touch few issue areas, so an ask inside those areas fits him. Pressure from the outside reaches him much less than most members do, so he weighs the facts. He takes the lead much less often, so a decision from him comes after he has tested the facts himself.

archetype.justification: His upbeat words, brisk turns and results focused case fit the Terrier label.

Bryan Steil.bottom_line: Bring a short, results focused ask and let him set the pace. He very reliably follows bills to the finish, so a clear track record carries weight.
do: Frame the ask around what the policy delivers in results
Open with positive energy, since his words run upbeat
Keep answers brief, since he gives short replies
dont: Take over the conversation when he goes quiet
Read his cool tone as opposition to the bill
Assume an ask needing votes across the aisle will move quickly
Bryan Steil.warning_sign: Usually he leads conversations much less than most, so a quiet room is normal. When he suddenly takes charge and presses for an answer, he is losing patience. Stop, summarize the ask in one line, and offer a written follow up.
Bryan Steil.follow_up: Within a week, email him a one line summary of the ask, the evidence on results, and the vote date.
Bryan Steil.personality: Steil comes across as reserved yet curious, and he is very dependable when a bill needs carrying home. His issue range is far broader than almost anyone's, and his accounts of his work are more detailed than almost anyone's. Almost nobody reaches across the aisle less often than he does. Words sound cool yet upbeat, and forcefulness is much lower than most. Answers are shorter than most, filler is nearly absent, and he holds the floor less than most.
Bryan Steil.speaks: He speaks briefly and with an upbeat air, leaving long pauses between phrases. Loudness swings more than almost anyone's does, and the pitch of his voice also shifts somewhat more than most. Many issues come up in conversation, but answers stay short with few filler words. In hearings he runs somewhat more combative than most members, though his tone stays cool overall.
Bryan Steil.decides: He sizes up requests by the results they offer and how brief and clear the case is. Once committed, he is very reliable. Working across the aisle is rare for him, so an ask needing votes across the aisle faces a harder test. Leading conversations is not his habit, so decisions come from the paper, not the room. A commitment sticks only once it is written down, so his support is only as firm as the paper.

archetype.justification: Highly skeptical, much looser with details, and his wording runs sharper than nearly anyone's.

Burgess Owens.bottom_line: Pin down the one ask and get it in writing, since he is skeptical and moved less by outside pressure.
do: Tie each claim to a source, since he tests claims closely
Let him hold the floor, then ask for one written step
Open on common ground, since he speaks with more warmth than most
dont: Mistake his sharp wording for hostility to the whole bill
Count on outside groups to bring him around
Burgess Owens.warning_sign: He usually holds the floor with full, even answers and little filler. When pitch climbs and wording sharpens, he has gone on guard, so halt the pressure and ask what needs settling first.
Burgess Owens.follow_up: Put the one step in writing with a date, and send it to his staff the same day.
Burgess Owens.personality: Owens comes across very outgoing and skeptical, yet warm in his words, and quicker to get agitated than most. His talk covers a far narrower slice of issues than most, and he gives details far looser than most. His bills take in fewer issues than most, and he takes charge of conversations more than most. From Utah, he is a visible figure for his role, and his sharp wording sits beside a warm manner.
Burgess Owens.speaks: He speaks in extended answers with little filler, and he holds the floor in conversation. Wording from him is sharper than nearly anyone's, though his tone runs warm. Pitch swings up and down somewhat more than the usual speaker, and his phrasing lands as less forceful than most. Narrow in range, he covers fewer issues, and his answers stay even in length from turn to turn.
Burgess Owens.decides: Whether a claim survives his own tests is the question he asks, and he is quite skeptical of anything broad. Pressure from outside counts for much less with him than with colleagues, so allies will not carry the vote alone. He holds the floor in a meeting until he has worked through the point, and he draws notice for his role. The ask has to stand on its facts.

archetype.justification: Among the most visible members, he talks across a wide range of issues, holds the floor firmly, and speaks faster than most.

Byron Donalds.bottom_line: Let him run the exchange, then pin him to a written next step. Outside pressure carries clearly less weight with him, so the case has to stand on its own.
do: Let him take the floor first, then keep your reply short
When he digs in, ask for the specific source behind his position
Bring a colleague from across the aisle who shares the goal
Confirm each step in writing, since bills lose momentum with him
dont: Read rapid, brief exchanges as settled agreement
Answer his sharp wording with sharper wording of your own
Expect outside pressure alone to change his mind
Byron Donalds.warning_sign: He normally talks fast and holds the floor, so a slower pace is the change to watch. It usually means he is on guard about the point, so ask what he plans to do with it.
Byron Donalds.follow_up: Once the session ends, put the agreed action into a note for him and name the person on your team who verifies it.
Byron Donalds.personality: Donalds comes across as rather sociable and very doubtful, and gets worked up quickly. Across many issues he offers less careful detail than almost anyone, and his words run sharp and forceful. Working across the aisle is rare for him, and his bills cover more ground than most. Conversations bend to his lead, and he defends his position hard when challenged. He is very visible for his role, and he represents Florida.
Byron Donalds.speaks: He talks fast and pauses only briefly between phrases, with a voice that holds level and little swing. Quick bursts of brief answers come from him, and his longest answers still run longer than most. His words are blunt and forceful, with little warmth and little of the usual filler. When challenged, he holds his position harder than most, and in hearings his tone is less combative than most.
Byron Donalds.decides: He judges a request by whether he can keep control of the discussion. Outside voices count for much less with him, so the case itself has to change his mind. Bills stall on his watch far more often than most, so every agreed action needs an accountable name and a review date. A case he can carry forward moves him, and choices hold only when someone is assigned the next action.

archetype.justification: Outgoing and fairly agreeable, with a much more social public style and weak follow through on bills.

Carlos Gimenez.bottom_line: Open with the results the policy brings in a short direct case, and set a dated next step, since bill follow through is less reliable than most.
do: Show what the policy delivers, with the facts he can carry to a meeting
Ask for a date on the next step before you leave
Let him talk at length, since his longest answers run far past typical
dont: Mistake his agreeable manner for a vote he has promised
Let quick exchanges run without tying them to the one ask
Carlos Gimenez.warning_sign: By default his answers wander with plenty of filler, and he often trails off. If the filler drops and he stops elaborating, he is losing interest or on guard, so ask one direct question about his concern.
Carlos Gimenez.follow_up: Give his staff a brief written note on the results, the one ask, and a date for his answer.
Carlos Gimenez.personality: Gimenez comes across as fairly outgoing, and his public words read as far more social than most colleagues. He is fairly agreeable and a little practical. Bills he files span a bit more ground than most, though he works less with the other side than most. Bill follow through is less reliable than most, and his longest answers stretch well past what most members give. Pressure does not rattle him easily, and once he is pushed he holds to his stance somewhat more than most.
Carlos Gimenez.speaks: He speaks somewhat slowly, with pauses that are somewhat shorter than most and a volume that holds a bit more even than most. His pitch varies somewhat more than most. In interviews his answers run long, the longest stretching well past most, and he trails off somewhat more than most. His public language is much more social and less forceful than the usual member. In hearings he turns a bit sharper than most members, and under challenge he defends his ground more firmly than most.
Carlos Gimenez.decides: Before backing it he gauges what the policy delivers in concrete terms. Outside voices move him a bit more than they move most colleagues, so local backing carries some weight. Bill follow through is less reliable than most, so a decision holds only when a dated next step is in writing with an owner named. Pressure from home counts, but a named owner and a written date are what keep it alive.

archetype.justification: Quite practical, much looser with details, and much narrower in the issues her bills cover.

Carol Miller.bottom_line: Bring a practical case built on who gains, and keep the ask to one issue. A broad ask stalls with her, since she is quite practical.
do: Lead with the people who gain, since that fits her thinking
Keep the ask practical and to one issue she already follows
Confirm the owner and the day before you leave
dont: Open with abstract policy detail rather than who is helped
Carol Miller.warning_sign: You will not see her check out in a general meeting, so look for quiet on the ask itself. When that happens, send the owner and the date in writing that same day.
Carol Miller.follow_up: Send her a single page note with the owner and date, tied to the one issue she already follows.
Carol Miller.personality: Miller is quite practical, and her details come out looser than most. Talk from the member covers a tighter set of topics than most. Her legislation covers as few subjects as almost anyone's in the House. Votes are much less dependable than most. Visibility is much lower than most, including for her role. Public words stay tied to the bills she already follows.
Carol Miller.speaks: Her talk stays inside a small set of issues she already knows. When she explains a bill, she keeps to the issues she knows. Her manner is plain, and she does not spread into topics beyond her own bills. Her speech reads as focused and short on wide ranging detail.
Carol Miller.decides: Who gains from an ask matters to her, as does whether it sits inside her narrow areas. Bills in her portfolio span fewer subjects than almost anyone's, so an ask has to connect to them. A case about who is helped fits her, since people-first framing draws her in. Because she is much less dependable on votes than most, a decision holds only once it has a named owner and a day.

archetype.justification: Among the most agreeable of her colleagues, and her legislation reaches across much more ground than most.

Catherine Cortez Masto.bottom_line: Lead with who your ask helps, since stories about people and communities fit her best.
do: Have local supporters contact her office about the ask
