Tell one story about a family or town the ask would help
Invite a partner from the other side to sign on too
Ask her for a direct yes or no on the next step before you leave
dont: Opening with policy mechanics when stories about people fit her best
Counting on a private yes to hold once outside voices weigh in
Catherine Cortez Masto.warning_sign: By default her public tone is somewhat gentler than most, so agreeable talk in the room is her usual manner. If her replies stop being gentle and she starts answering with general statements, she is holding back, so ask her which part gives her pause.
Catherine Cortez Masto.follow_up: By Friday, send her a short note with one story about a family the ask would help and the partner you invited to sign on.
Catherine Cortez Masto.personality: Cortez Masto represents Nevada and is among the most agreeable of her colleagues, with a somewhat outgoing and curious manner. She is somewhat careful and organized, and somewhat dependable at seeing bills through. Public talk ranges across much more ground than most, and her public tone runs somewhat softer than most colleagues. Her profile sits among the lowest for her post, yet she crosses lines with colleagues somewhat more than most.
Catherine Cortez Masto.speaks: Her talk spreads across a wide set of issues, and her language runs a bit cooler on feeling than most. Her tone is somewhat gentler than most, and her volume varies much less than most. Pauses between phrases run a little short, and her pitch stays a little flatter than most. In hearings she pushes a little less hard than most members.
Catherine Cortez Masto.decides: Her yardstick is who the ask helps, since stories about beneficiaries suit her best. Outside voices shift her stance further than they shift most colleagues, and she reaches over the divide a little more than most. Once a bill is moving she is somewhat dependable at seeing it through, and an ask that arrives with its supporters attached carries the most weight.

archetype.justification: Outwardly she runs quiet, works in a very careful and organized way, keeps her talk narrow and detailed, and draws much less notice than most members.

Celeste Maloy.bottom_line: Send the written technical case ahead of time and lead with it in the room. Outside voices shift her position slightly, so bring credible backers too.
do: Confirm each commitment in writing, since she follows through reliably
Judge her points by content, since her pitch stays flat
In a hearing, send technical questions first, since she is less combative there
dont: Mistake her reserve for indifference to the ask
Assume outside pressure alone will move her, since it moves her only a little
Celeste Maloy.warning_sign: Normally she is quiet in meetings, and in hearings she is less combative than most members. Once she presses a point harder, her guard is up, so stop debating and send the written technical detail.
Celeste Maloy.follow_up: Send a written technical summary of the ask with its sources cited, and ask her to reply in writing by a set date.
Celeste Maloy.personality: Maloy is somewhat guarded and practical, and far harder to rattle than most colleagues. She works in a very careful, orderly way, and her talk stays narrow and highly detailed, more so than nearly anyone in the chamber. Language carries far less emotional charge than typical, and her bills take in a few fewer policy areas than most colleagues. Bill follow through is strong by the standard of the chamber, and she draws much less notice than most members.
Celeste Maloy.speaks: She talks in narrow, detailed terms and keeps her delivery flat, with little rise and fall in pitch. Her talk is precise and carries little emotional weight, and her sentences are built around specifics. In hearings she tends to be less combative than most members. Her flat delivery gives little cue about mood, so the content has to carry the point.
Celeste Maloy.decides: She sizes up a request by how solidly its written detail survives scrutiny, since technical material arriving early suits her best. Outside backers give her ask a modest extra push, since they shift her position only a little. She draws much less notice than most, so the ask will not gain traction through publicity alone. Her bill follow through is strong by the standard of the chamber, so a decision needs a written record to stand.

archetype.justification: Very careful and organized in habit, very dependable on follow through, detailed when describing his work, and hard to fluster.

Charles Fleischmann.bottom_line: Send the written, technical detail ahead so he can check it before the meeting. Arrive with the facts organized and in order.
do: Send the written technical detail a few days ahead of time
Bring a numbered agenda so he can follow the sequence
Give him room to pause, and let silence stand before you reply
dont: Expect a quick answer when a question needs checking
Charles Fleischmann.warning_sign: Usually he is noticeably gentler in hearings and speaks slowly, so a quicker, tighter tone in the room signals he is on guard. Slow down, restate the one fact, and let him check it in writing.
Charles Fleischmann.follow_up: Email his staff the written brief and a numbered list of open questions, with a reply date.
Charles Fleischmann.personality: Fleischmann is careful, organized, and very reliable on votes and bills. Few things fluster him, more so than most. Detail runs through how he talks about his record. His issue range is among the narrowest in the House. He draws a little less attention than most, and in hearings a gentle manner follows. Those traits make him a methodical, dependable member in the room.
Charles Fleischmann.speaks: Pace is unhurried, slower than nearly anyone in the House, with long gaps between phrases. Volume swings noticeably more than nearly anyone's. Work is described in detailed, careful terms, and public phrasing carries a bit more emotional charge than the norm. Long pauses signal thought rather than hesitation, and in hearings he keeps a gentle manner that matches his unhurried, careful way of speaking.
Charles Fleischmann.decides: Careful documentation and numbers that hold up are what he looks for before backing any request. A commitment from him tends to hold, since he follows through dependably on the bills he takes up. Pressure from outside moves him less, so a case built on facts beats a push. A decision needs an owner and a written record, so he can check it later.

archetype.justification: Takes charge of conversations, holds the floor, and stands firm when pressed, with very reliable follow through on bills.

Charles Schumer.bottom_line: Keep the ask short and give him the facts first. He holds firm and public pushes count for less with him than with most colleagues.
do: Lead with the outcome and let him take charge of the discussion
Expect short, forceful answers and match his directness
Build the ask around bills he can carry to a vote
dont: Read his short answers as a sign he is disengaged
Take his rapid, upbeat tone as agreement
Charles Schumer.warning_sign: Usually he pushes back firmly when challenged, so sudden silence where he would normally defend his point means he is weighing you or losing interest. Stop, name what you agree on, and give him room to take the next turn.
Charles Schumer.follow_up: Within two days, send his staff a single page note that lists each bill, its next vote, and who owns it.
Charles Schumer.personality: Schumer appears among the most visible members of the Senate, and he runs the room and holds the floor. He is somewhat outgoing and gets fired up much more readily than most colleagues, and his public talk is upbeat and forceful. Attention to details runs somewhat lower than most colleagues, and his bills touch somewhat fewer topics than the typical member. He reaches across lines somewhat less than most, yet his record on votes and bill follow through is very strong. Those traits make him a member who presses hard, fights for visible wins, and sticks to bills he can carry.
Charles Schumer.speaks: He speaks a little faster than most, leaves long pauses between phrases, and his pitch swings more widely than nearly all colleagues. His answers are brief and direct, and he seldom trails off, so his points land fast and finish cleanly. Filler words are very rare in his speech, so each thought arrives without padding. Hearings find him among the least confrontational voices, and he defends a position firmly when someone pushes back.
Charles Schumer.decides: Requests get weighed by the results they can show, since results and facts fit him best. He is very reliable on votes and bills, so a commitment from him tends to stick once made. Public pressure from outside moves him much less than it moves most colleagues, so a push alone will not change his mind. He defends his line when challenged, so his yes holds once the next step has a date and an owner.

archetype.justification: Her framing fits community impact best, her words read gentler than most, and her talk covers a wide range of issues.

Chellie Pingree.bottom_line: Lead with the people a bill helps, since pressure from outside tends to move her. Bring a clear next step she can take back.
do: Tie each ask to the families or towns it would reach
Ask for a decision she can revisit as outside voices weigh in
dont: Take her gentle tone as proof she is already persuaded
Expect a skeptical first reaction and do not push it
Chellie Pingree.warning_sign: She usually stays reserved and gentle, and she tests ideas before she commits to them. When she goes quiet after you make a point, she is weighing it, not agreeing, so pause and let her speak before adding more facts.
Chellie Pingree.follow_up: After the meeting, send her staff a single page listing the ask, the next step and its owner by Friday.
Chellie Pingree.personality: Pingree is fairly curious and a little reserved, with some skepticism that shows before she gives ground. She is somewhat more easily stirred than most, and her bill portfolio spans more topics than others do. Her words read gentler than most and she stands out a fair amount for her role. The result is an engaged but watchful member who takes her time before committing.
Chellie Pingree.speaks: She speaks across a broad set of issues, and her descriptions of her own work are less exact than most. Her tone is gentler than most, so her points land as considered rather than forceful. In hearings she is less confrontational than most, and her questions tend to probe rather than press. She moves between issues more readily than she digs into any single one.
Chellie Pingree.decides: She weighs an ask by testing it against her own skepticism before she gives ground. Pressure from outside the district tends to weigh on her, so voices from home carry weight in how she decides. Her legislation spans more topics than most, and she is less reliable than most at seeing bills through, so promises need checkpoints. So an agreement only holds when someone is named to carry the next step.

archetype.justification: Among the most outgoing and most skeptical members, with forceful wording and a narrow issue range, which earn the pick.

Chip Roy.bottom_line: Bring a short, bold case and let him take the floor, but bring the details on paper since he will not supply them.
do: Lead with the result the ask delivers in one sentence
If he drifts into broad talk, bring him back to the bill
Put each follow up step in writing with its date
dont: Assume a yes in the room will hold until the vote
Match his sharp wording with sharper wording of your own
Chip Roy.warning_sign: He usually answers in quick runs with wide volume swings, and by default he takes the lead. If he stops breaking up his answers, he has become guarded, so pause and ask which part bothers him.
Chip Roy.follow_up: Within a day, send him a single page covering the ask, the result, and the date each step is due to his office.
Chip Roy.personality: Roy is as outgoing as almost anyone in the House, and just as skeptical, so he arrives in the room ready to test a claim out loud. His words are warm yet forceful, and he talks in broad strokes, staying with a fairly narrow set of issues. He flares up much more readily than most, and in a room he usually leads the conversation. Expect a strong opinion first and the supporting detail later, if at all.
Chip Roy.speaks: He speaks in bold, direct lines, forceful in wording and often sharper than the room expects. Within a narrow lane of policy, he describes his work in broad terms rather than careful detail. Under strain his delivery gets more uneven, with wide swings in volume and long pauses between phrases followed by short quick replies. Emotional charge in his words runs less than most, so he reads as matter of fact even while pressing.
Chip Roy.decides: He screens a request by whether it fits his narrow set of issues and holds up under his skeptical questions. Outside pressure sways him less than nearly all his peers, so a crowd behind a request will not carry it alone. He ranks as one of the least dependable members when it comes to carrying bills, so a yes means little until someone owns the next step. So his support depends on the details holding up under his own questions.

archetype.justification: He reaches across the aisle far more than most colleagues, and his talk covers a broad set of issues.

Chris Pappas.bottom_line: Bring a bipartisan cosponsor list and a plan that names the next step. Pressure does not move him much, so the reason must be solid.
do: Line up a bipartisan cosponsor list before the meeting
Name the next step and who owns it
Prepare for a hearing with the record sent early
Share credit with joint leads, since his public exposure runs far lower
dont: Assume a bipartisan ask will carry itself without a named sponsor
Press for a quick yes, since crowds outside carry less weight with him
Chris Pappas.warning_sign: In a hearing he usually stays somewhat less combative than most members. If he gets sharp or confrontational in testimony, he is on guard. Let him finish, ask one open question, and keep the next point short.
Chris Pappas.follow_up: Send him a one page memo listing each joint sponsor and the next step, within three days.
Chris Pappas.personality: Pappas comes across somewhat reserved, and he is somewhat curious. His talk spans a far broader spread of topics than most lawmakers. Across the aisle, he works far more than most colleagues, and his bills take in somewhat more areas than most colleagues. His record on votes and bills is somewhat stronger than most colleagues, so he backs asks with a track record. Careful detail shows up in how he describes his own work, somewhat more than most. His public exposure runs far lower than most colleagues. In hearings, his manner runs somewhat less combative than most members.
Chris Pappas.speaks: Across his public talk, the issue range runs far wider than most. He describes his work with somewhat more detail than most lawmakers. His answers keep to specifics rather than sweeping claims. Hearing settings bring a somewhat less combative tone than most members. His public framing is broad, and his detail stays on the specifics of each bill. He keeps his remarks organized around the bill itself.
Chris Pappas.decides: Whether he can bring other members across the aisle with it is how he sizes up a request. Outside groups push him far less than most colleagues, so a request resting on its own merits holds up. Shared public credit draws him in, since a joint effort suits how he works. His record on votes and bills is somewhat stronger than most colleagues, so he backs asks with a track record. So a bipartisan ask with a named next step is the one he moves on.

archetype.justification: He often holds the floor and digs in when challenged, a pattern much stronger than most.

Chris Van Hollen.bottom_line: Let him finish, since he holds the floor, and bring outside voices, since they move him more than most.
do: Ask a broad question and let his long answer run
Bring local supporters who can speak to the ask
Open warmly and name the points you share
dont: Interrupt his long answers to move to the next point
Count on quick back and forth to move the point
Read his firm defense as a closed door
Chris Van Hollen.warning_sign: He usually digs in when a view is challenged, so a challenge he lets pass without reply is the sign he is pulling back from the exchange. Stop pushing the point and ask what part still bothers him.
Chris Van Hollen.follow_up: Afterward, email his staff one concrete example of who the ask helps, and name the local supporters who stand behind it.
Chris Van Hollen.personality: Van Hollen is a warm, social member from Maryland who likes to be in the middle of things. He is fairly outgoing and fairly visible, and he holds a little skepticism toward easy answers, and he is fairly careful with his work. His bills reach much more ground than most, and he often commands a conversation, digs in once he is pushed, and holds the floor.
Chris Van Hollen.speaks: He speaks in long, uneven runs and answers in quick back and forth much less than most. Tone swings much more than most, while loudness stays far more level than most peers, and delivery is somewhat quicker than most. Words are forceful and somewhat flatter in tone, and they carry almost no emotional charge. Under pushback he holds his stance and argues at length.
Chris Van Hollen.decides: A request is judged on how neatly it matches the broad portfolio he already carries, and outside advocates press him harder than most. He digs in under challenge and works across the aisle somewhat less than most. Because his bills cover so much ground, every request competes with his other work. So his position firms only after he has talked it through.

archetype.justification: Her wide issue range and very curious, outgoing style show a persistent member who works many fronts at once.

Chrissy Houlahan.bottom_line: Bring her one clear result and allies from both parties, then leave with a named next step.
do: Lead with the result the policy delivers in one sentence
Offer a joined bill that pairs both parties' members
Give her room to finish long answers before you respond
dont: Stake the whole ask on one meeting when she can still be moved later
Mistake her warm tone for a yes on the vote
Assume a bill she backs will reach a vote without follow up
Chrissy Houlahan.warning_sign: She usually talks fast with few pauses and a flat pitch. If she begins steering the talk and grows guarded, pause right away, ask what worries her, and name the next step.
Chrissy Houlahan.follow_up: Send her a one page summary naming a bipartisan cosponsor, with the next step and its date, within two days.
Chrissy Houlahan.personality: Houlahan is outgoing and very curious, and her warm style makes her easy to approach. She covers more issues than nearly anyone in the House, and her bills reach across several areas. She is very visible, yet she leads a conversation much less than others and gives longer answers instead. Taken together, she is a warm, wide-ranging member who prefers to explore a topic rather than dominate it.
Chrissy Houlahan.speaks: She talks fast and in a flat, even pitch, with few pauses between phrases. Her words are warm and upbeat, and they focus on action more than force. In interviews her answers run long and even, and they trail off less than others do. She covers a wide range of issues, and her talk moves across them with a light, friendly tone.
Chrissy Houlahan.decides: Before backing an ask she judges how far it reaches across issues she already follows. Her broad interests mean a bill must connect to several areas to hold her attention. Bills do not always reach the finish line, so follow through matters. Pressure from outside counts for more with her, so a decision sticks only with several sides behind it and a named next step.

archetype.justification: He is curious and agreeable, but on carrying bills to the finish he counts among the least reliable House members and is looser on detail than most.

Christian Menefee.bottom_line: Bring one clear ask, and leave the room with a named owner and a date. You need that date, since his follow-through is among the least reliable in the House.
do: Put the bill details in writing before the meeting, not in the room
Open with a new idea he can test, tied to a role he can front
Take up one bill at a time, and confirm each before moving on
Ask him which point he will check first
dont: Take his agreeable manner as a yes, because follow-through is the weak spot
Count on public attention alone to win him over
Press for a yes now, since outside pressure sways him a little less than most
Christian Menefee.warning_sign: A quiet or general meeting does not show whether the ask will land with him, and talk alone does not settle it. Before the next meeting, ask him to confirm his position on the bill.
Christian Menefee.follow_up: Send his legislative aide a short memo with the ask and the owner the same day.
Christian Menefee.personality: Menefee is a fairly curious, fairly agreeable colleague who is a little reserved in a room. Detail is less of a strength for him than for most. He is quicker to get worked up than most, yet he is less visible than most for his role. Few members follow bills through less reliably than he does. Before taking office, he practiced law at Norton Rose Fulbright and Kirkland & Ellis LLP.
Christian Menefee.speaks: In public clips he is one of the fastest talkers in the House, and his pitch swings up and down more than almost any colleague's. His pauses run a little shorter than most, and his volume stays much more level than most. His public words have little emotional charge, and his talk about work stays loose on detail. Match his quick pace, and keep each question to one line.
Christian Menefee.decides: Outside pressure carries a little less weight with him, so one strong ask outweighs repeated calls. Ask him to put his yes in one sentence, so you can check it against the bill. Make the first ask small enough for him to finish, not a full package. He has spoken publicly about his wife, so family can serve as common ground, used with care.

archetype.justification: Careful and organized more than nearly any colleague, he is very curious and his public talk spans somewhat more topics than most.

Christopher Coons.bottom_line: Open with the concrete gains the policy brings in a concise case, then leave him space to dig into the details.
do: Bring a bipartisan cosponsor to speak to the ask
Ask for a dated yes or no, since he agrees readily in conversation
Bring written detail, since he is very curious about how the policy works
dont: Assume a warm conversation will become a signed commitment
Drop the ask after one early no, since outside pressure can move him
Hurry past his long answers, since he is still working through the case
Christopher Coons.warning_sign: He usually talks fast with short pauses, a flat pitch, and less filler than nearly any colleague. If his pace drops and his pauses lengthen, he is thinking it through, so stop adding points and let him finish before you ask for a decision.
Christopher Coons.follow_up: Send him a short written note that names the cosponsor, the next step, and a date, copied to his legislative director.
Christopher Coons.personality: Coons combines very inquisitive habits with cautious thought beyond nearly any colleague, and he is somewhat outgoing and very agreeable in conversation. Harder to fluster than nearly any colleague, he keeps his words much warmer and more upbeat than most. Reaching across the divide far more than most, his record in moving bills to a vote is somewhat weaker than most. His public profile is very high for his post. He talks about somewhat more topics than most.
Christopher Coons.speaks: Talk comes much quicker than most, with brief gaps between words and a flat pitch, so it sounds brisk and even. His answers are long, and his longest turns go much longer than most colleagues. Challenged, he holds his position somewhat more than most, and his language stays warm even so. He uses less filler than nearly any colleague, so his words come across as clean and direct.
Christopher Coons.decides: Each request is weighed on the results and facts behind it, and a tight pitch with a clear outcome earns his attention. He crosses the aisle readily, so a bipartisan cosponsor on your side can tip him. Outside voices shift him more than most members do, so his support can grow after the first meeting. Getting bills to a vote is a weaker spot for him, so a verbal yes can stall. So his support holds only when someone keeps the next step in front of him.

archetype.justification: Outgoing, cross party in his dealings, gentle in tone, which makes him a natural bridge.

Christopher Deluzio.bottom_line: Lead with the concrete result of the policy, keep the ask short, and let him shape the path to yes.
do: Show the cross party cosponsors on the ask first
Bring local supporters, since pressure from outside counts for more with him
Put each agreed step in writing with a date and owner
In a hearing, expect sharp questions and answer with the facts
dont: Mistake his gentle wording for a weak position
Fill his long pauses with more argument
Christopher Deluzio.warning_sign: He usually keeps a gentle tone and leaves long pauses, so silence is not a no. When his pitch swings more, he is unsettled, so slow down and ask what he needs settled first.
Christopher Deluzio.follow_up: The same day, email a brief recap of the outcome with the agreed action, who owns it, and a check in date.
Christopher Deluzio.personality: Deluzio is outgoing and a little skeptical, and he flares up somewhat more readily than most. He covers a narrower set of issues and describes his efforts in less detail than most, yet his words stay gentle. He works across the aisle far more than colleagues, but he follows bills through less reliably. In the room, his warmth and dealmaking make him easy to work with, and a deal needs checking before it holds.
Christopher Deluzio.speaks: He speaks in gentle, unhurried turns and leaves long gaps before he makes a point. His voice moves through a wider range than most, so emphasis comes through pitch rather than force. Narrow in range, he sticks to a few issues and describes his work in broad terms rather than detail. Even when the point is firm, the wording stays soft, so the force shows in the pauses and tone rather than the words.
Christopher Deluzio.decides: Requests win him over when results are clear and the other side can sign on. Outside voices count for more with him than with most members, so local voices matter. He leans a little skeptical toward claims that only sound good. He follows bills through less reliably than most, so a yes holds only when someone owns the next step.

archetype.justification: His very careful, organized manner, long answers and low dominance in conversation fit an owl that watches closely and speaks at length.

Christopher Murphy.bottom_line: Bring a precise written case and leave room for long answers, since follow through on his bills lags behind most.
do: Send the written case days before the meeting
Let him finish long answers before you respond
Ask one question about the bill's next step
dont: Rush him toward a vote before his reasons are on the table
Assume a promise will carry through without a named owner
Christopher Murphy.warning_sign: Usually he talks very fast, with a volume that stays even and a pitch that swings widely. If his pitch swings wider still and his answers turn briefer, he is building a case. Hear the full case, then restate the one point you need decided.
Christopher Murphy.follow_up: Mail his staff a brief memo listing the bill step, who owns it, and the day a reply is due.
Christopher Murphy.personality: Murphy keeps his work orderly and careful, and he gets rattled less easily than most colleagues. Follow through on bills trails most colleagues by a wide margin, and partnerships across the aisle are somewhat thinner for him than for most. He talks at length, with replies longer than almost anyone's in the chamber. He represents Connecticut, and he is very visible in public.
Christopher Murphy.speaks: Speech runs well quicker than usual, with a volume that stays more even than usual and a pitch that swings widely. Interview answers stretch well past typical lengths, and his longest replies run longer still. His language leans much more toward action than usual, and it is much less social, with less force than nearly any colleague's in the chamber. At hearings his edge stays softer than most members'.
Christopher Murphy.decides: He looks at whether an ask's written case hands him a clear reason to act. Pressure from outside registers with him less than with most colleagues, so a yes rests on his own reading of the case. Bill follow through is far weaker than most, so a yes holds only when a named owner is tied to each step. Partnerships across the aisle are thinner for him than for most, so an ask that depends on crossing the aisle faces a steeper climb.

archetype.justification: Very gentle in wording, with much less emotional heat than most, he speaks plainly and keeps his tone even.

Christopher Smith.bottom_line: Make the ask plainly and stick to one next step, since outside pressure moves him much less than most members.
do: Keep the opening light and reach the ask in a few lines
Bring a short written note that ties the ask to his bills
dont: Mistake his mild manner for a strong commitment
Count on a louder push to change his mind
Christopher Smith.warning_sign: By default his volume stays much more even than most, and his pitch stays a little flatter. If his volume rises and his pitch lifts, that signals he cares about the point, so slow down and ask what he needs.
Christopher Smith.follow_up: Send his office a plain written summary of the ask and its status within two days.
Christopher Smith.personality: Smith is low key and plain in manner, and his wording is very gentle. His language carries much less heat than most. His description of his work carries somewhat less detail, and fewer issues make up his bills, so his focus stays narrow. At seeing bills through, he is somewhat reliable. The impression he gives is of someone who keeps to the point. New Jersey is the state he represents.
Christopher Smith.speaks: He speaks plainly, with a gentle manner and little emotional charge in his words. In his delivery his pauses are somewhat shorter than most, his volume stays much more even than most, and his pitch stays a little flatter. He describes his work with less detail than most. When he presses a point his tone stays even rather than rising. His manner stays low key throughout.
Christopher Smith.decides: On its merits is how he judges an ask, and fewer issues make up his own bills. Commitments from him tend to hold once made, since he is somewhat reliable at seeing bills through. Outside pressure moves him much less than most members, so the case itself carries more weight with him than outside backing. Ties across party lines run somewhat thinner for him than for most.

archetype.justification: He is fairly outgoing and somewhat more combative than most members in hearings, and he builds across party lines more than most.

Chuck Edwards.bottom_line: Confirm the details in writing before you leave. He builds across party lines somewhat more than most.
do: Send a short written note ahead of the meeting, with the ask in one line
Plan a second contact, since outside pressure moves his positions more than most
Greet him warmly, then ask what a cross-party bill needed changed before he backs it
Finish by naming the bill the ask belongs to
dont: Float a new idea in an adversarial exchange before the practical case is set
Argue each point in a formal hearing, where his tone runs firmer than most
Frame the proposal as a fight against the other party
Chuck Edwards.warning_sign: In hearings he is usually somewhat more combative than most members. If he turns polite and stops pressing the point, your ask has lost his attention. Set the point aside for now, and see whether he raises it himself.
Chuck Edwards.follow_up: Send his office a brief note within a week, asking for written answers by a set date.
Chuck Edwards.personality: Edwards, fairly outgoing by nature, reaches across the aisle more than most. His outlook is a little practical, and he is somewhat less curious than most. Detail is not his strongest suit, and he is a bit loose with it. His description of his own work runs in careful, detailed terms, a bit more than most. Getting rattled comes a little slower to him than to most colleagues. His public words carry somewhat more feeling than most speakers do.
Chuck Edwards.speaks: In floor speeches he moves at a far slower pace than most speakers. The gaps between his phrases run somewhat longer than most, leaving more space between points. His volume swings a great deal, more than most speakers. Pitch also moves up and down much more than most speakers do. Emotional weight in his words runs a notch higher than most speakers. Watch one of his floor speeches before you meet to hear how he talks.
Chuck Edwards.decides: He joins other-party bills somewhat more than most, and his cross-party ties run a bit higher than most members'. His outlook leans a bit practical. Across his bills, the issue areas run somewhat wider than most, a fair spread of subjects. Lay the plan out as a short numbered list, one concrete action per line, with the first step at the top.

archetype.justification: He holds the floor more firmly than nearly any colleague does, and he digs in when challenged.

Chuck Grassley.bottom_line: Bring one short ask built on results. When challenged he digs in, so meet his firmness with facts rather than pressure.
do: Point to earlier bills he has carried through to passage
Keep each question short so he has less room to take over
Acknowledge his stated position first, then offer the change as an addition
dont: Count on a long social opener to win him over
Challenge his position head on in the opening exchange
Pad your questions with filler, since he speaks with almost none
Chuck Grassley.warning_sign: He usually keeps almost no filler and defends his position when pressed. When filler creeps into his answers, he is getting irritated or losing interest in the exchange. Pause, restate the one point, and ask him directly whether his position has moved.
Chuck Grassley.follow_up: Once the session wraps, deliver the one change as a written addition to his team, citing a source for each fact before the week closes.
Chuck Grassley.personality: Grassley is a practical, careful legislator who is a bit tougher to rattle than most colleagues and works through the record in an orderly way. From Iowa, he takes firm charge of a room and digs in when challenged, yet his manner is warmer than most without being social. He covers a somewhat narrower set of issues, and his work across the aisle falls well short of most colleagues'. Reliable on the bills he carries through, he is more visible than most, and in the room he is businesslike and far from chatty.
Chuck Grassley.speaks: He speaks in orderly, detailed terms on a fairly narrow set of issues, with a little extra emotional heat. His answers vary in length more than nearly any colleague's, without rapid strings of brief answers. Filler is almost absent from his speech, and his language is flat and forceful rather than lively. When challenged, he restates his position and presses it again. His longest answers still run a little shorter than most.
Chuck Grassley.decides: Testing the facts before committing is how he judges a request, and he holds them to a high standard. Reaching across the aisle is far less usual for him than most, so backing from the other side is not his route to yes. When challenged he restates his stance more firmly, so pressure only hardens him. Because he holds firm once committed, a yes from him usually stays put, and so does a no.

archetype.justification: Community impact fits her best, and in hearings she is more pointed than typical.

Cindy Hyde-Smith.bottom_line: Lead with who a bill helps, and make the ask about what changes for them. Outside pressure pushes her harder than most, so let her own reasoning drive the request.
do: Tell the stories of who gains from the bill
Keep the ask to a clear, practical step
In a hearing, expect a pointed exchange
dont: Lean on outside pressure alone to move her
Count on cross aisle deals to win her over
Stack emotional appeals on top of the facts
Cindy Hyde-Smith.warning_sign: Her usual pattern is emotionally charged talk about who is helped. When she grows more pointed than usual and her wording gets heavier, she is on guard, so acknowledge her concern before you restate the ask.
Cindy Hyde-Smith.follow_up: Send a short written note after the meeting naming the step, the people it helps, and the date you will report back.
Cindy Hyde-Smith.personality: Hyde-Smith is among the most reserved people in Congress and keeps her public profile low. Details are a bit less of her focus than typical, and she is a bit practical. Her own descriptions of her work come across as more precise than typical, and her wording is among the most emotionally charged in the chamber. Joint efforts with the other side are less frequent for her than most, and she completes bills less often than typical. In hearings she is a touch more confrontational than typical.
Cindy Hyde-Smith.speaks: Her wording is among the most emotionally charged in the chamber, and her speech carries real heat. She describes her work in more precise terms than typical, so her speech tends to carry detail as well as feeling. In hearings she is a touch more confrontational than the typical member, and her points come out sharp. Her speech mixes heavy feeling with concrete detail, so both show up in the same breath.
Cindy Hyde-Smith.decides: Real beneficiaries decide her view, so a case built on actual people moves her the most. She works with the other side less than most, so a deal across the aisle is a harder sell. A low profile means few eyes are on her votes, so an ask needs its own visible backers. Outside calls weigh on her more than most, so sustained outside voices can change her position.

archetype.justification: Her public profile is much lower than most, yet in hearings she runs a bit more combative than most.

Claudia Tenney.bottom_line: Plan for a firm stance in hearings, and keep your ask to one clear result that the facts support.
do: Send a short fact sheet of the results a few days ahead
Confirm the meeting length with her office before you arrive
Keep your tone even when the setting turns formal
Skip any public announcement, since she keeps a much lower profile than most
dont: Argue the politics of the policy when she presses you in a hearing
Start with the policy's history instead of its result
Answer her hard questions in a hearing with a long speech
Claudia Tenney.warning_sign: In a hearing she is usually somewhat more combative than most members there. If she turns even sharper, she has stopped weighing the rest of your case. Stop, narrow the ask to a single step.
Claudia Tenney.follow_up: Send her office a short note within a few days, confirming what happens next and when.
Claudia Tenney.personality: Tenney keeps a low public profile, and her role in the House draws much less notice than most. She is quite hard to fluster. Her public talk reaches a somewhat broader set of topics than most. Detail is not her strongest suit, and her work talk is less detailed than most. Her hearing manner runs somewhat more combative than most.
Claudia Tenney.speaks: On the House floor, she talks at a fast clip. Her speech runs faster than nearly any colleague's, with much shorter pauses than most. Her volume and pitch show almost no movement up or down, so the delivery sounds level from start to finish. Have plain, sourced answers ready for hard questions in any formal setting, with the source for each claim on hand.
Claudia Tenney.decides: Outside voices shift her positions more than most, so letting them reach her staff directly can move her. A plain account of results fits her best. Keep the sourcing for her staff to handle with you after the meeting. Agree with her staff on which outside voices reach her, and when. End by asking which claim she would check first.

archetype.justification: His narrow issue focus, flat public wording and low visibility fit a quiet, low-profile member.

Clay Fuller.bottom_line: Offer him a visible shared role to take, since outside voices move him more than most.
do: Name a colleague who would stand beside him at the announcement
Raise the one ask early, since his public profile stays low
Confirm the step in writing after the meeting
dont: Assume a shared role will hold without outside voices
Clay Fuller.warning_sign: A general meeting will not tell you how he reacts when a plan slips, so ask a colleague who has worked with him for that read. Confirm the step in writing so there is a clear trace of what he agreed to.
Clay Fuller.follow_up: Send a short written recap to his office within two days, listing the step and the person who owns it.
Clay Fuller.personality: Fuller is a member whose public talk covers a narrow set of issues and carries far lower emotional charge than most colleagues. He describes his work in less detailed terms than nearly any colleague. Visibility is low for him in general and for his role in particular. He serves on the House Small Business committee. Taken together he is a specialist who keeps to his own issues and rarely draws attention.
Clay Fuller.speaks: His talk stays on a narrow set of issues and rarely strays from them. His words carry far lower emotional charge than most colleagues, so his tone reads flat. Answers from him stay general, with less detail than nearly any colleague offers. He keeps his focus on what he already works on and does not widen the subject. Emotion rarely shows in his words, and his delivery stays matter of fact.
Clay Fuller.decides: A visible shared role suits how he takes on an ask, so pair the request with a colleague. Outside voices move him more than most, so a repeated request has room to land. He is far less visible than most members in the House, so his backing tends to come quietly. So a decision holds when the next step is written and the owner is named.

archetype.justification: His words carry more feeling than nearly every House member, his public tone runs much sharper than most, and he leans less on filler than most.

Clay Higgins.bottom_line: Put results and facts first, and keep your own wording plain. His public words run much sharper than most, so a short, factual case suits him.
do: Send a compact written case with the figures in its opening lines
Be ready to carry the talk, since he seldom takes charge of it
Keep up when he shifts into runs of short replies
Close with the one step you need, stated plainly without filler
dont: Answer his bite with a sharper tone of your own
Stack several questions into one turn when his replies come in short bursts
Pitch the plan with upbeat, excited language
Clay Higgins.warning_sign: He normally carries each thought to its end, and breaks in his answers are uncommon. If his answers start breaking off midway, he has reached a point he will not settle today. Drop it for now and wait until he raises it again.
Clay Higgins.follow_up: By Thursday, email his office the owner and due date for each step, since outside pressure moves him more than most.
Clay Higgins.personality: Higgins is much sharper in his public words than most, and he is more easily worked up than most House members. He runs loose on details, and his bills cover much less ground than most. He builds across party lines somewhat more than most. Fairly outgoing and fairly agreeable, he is also markedly more combative than most members in hearings.
Clay Higgins.speaks: His interview answers run somewhat long, and his longest turns stretch much farther than most. Once talk picks up, he shifts into bursts of brief, rapid answers, so keep pace with him. He finishes his thoughts more cleanly than almost any colleague, so let each point land. He seldom takes charge of the conversation, so you can steer it with a clear first question. Keep the ask short and in writing so it is easy to act on.
Clay Higgins.decides: Results and facts move him, and outside pressure sways him more than most, so a well-sourced ask has real pull. He works across the aisle somewhat more than most, which is part of his record. If his first answer is no, come back later with the same sourced case. Give him a few days with the written case before you ask for an answer.

archetype.justification: Very careful and organized, he speaks in precise, detailed terms and reaches across the aisle more than most.

Cleo Fields.bottom_line: Bring the technical evidence early and show who across the aisle backs it. He moves when outside voices stand behind a clear ask.
do: Send the technical evidence ahead of the meeting itself
Point to the bipartisan bills he has already joined
Bring constituents and outside groups who back the ask
dont: Assume a quiet hearing settles anything
Rely on private pressure alone to move him
Cleo Fields.warning_sign: In a hearing he is normally among the least combative members, so a pointed question from him is the change to watch. Let him finish, then ask which detail he wants to test.
Cleo Fields.follow_up: Soon after the meeting, mail his office a brief technical memo with the evidence and the names of bipartisan cosponsors, and name the staffer who will reply.
Cleo Fields.personality: Fields is outgoing and curious, yet hard to fluster and very careful and organized. He keeps his public talk to a narrow set of issues, and he describes his work with precise detail. Reaching across party lines more than most, he keeps a low public profile for a member in his role. He sits on House Financial Services and represents a Louisiana seat. Together these make him a specialist who engages in substance.
Cleo Fields.speaks: He keeps to a narrow set of issues and talks about them in careful, detailed terms, with a touch more feeling in his words than colleagues show. At hearings he ranks among the least combative members, so his questions come across as civil and specific. He lays out the detail on each point before moving to the next one, which keeps the exchange on the substance.
Cleo Fields.decides: He weighs an ask on the technical detail and on whether the other side already backs it. Backing from outside groups pulls on him more than most, so when constituents back a case it earns his attention. For a member who keeps a low public profile in his role, a choice holds solely when someone owns each step and a next move is named.

archetype.justification: His manner is very reserved, and his approach to work is careful and orderly.

Cliff Bentz.bottom_line: Bring a written plan with dates, then let him reach the decision himself. Public campaigns move him less than most, so the written case must carry the weight.
do: Confirm the bills he has already backed before you raise anything new
Send the written plan ahead so he can review it alone
Give him room to speak first, since he is very reserved
dont: Rely on him to speak up for your ask in public
Lean on public campaigns, since they move him less than most
Cliff Bentz.warning_sign: A quiet meeting will not tell you whether he has read the written terms or accepted them. Before the next call, set a date for his answer in writing.
Cliff Bentz.follow_up: Send the agreed terms in writing, with the owner and due date for each step.
Cliff Bentz.personality: Bentz is very reserved, and few colleagues are more careful and organized. He talks in much more careful and detailed terms than most, though his range of issues is much narrower than most. Legislation from him spans far fewer topics than most colleagues, and few colleagues are more dependable at seeing bills through. He flares somewhat quicker than most colleagues, yet he stays well out of view, both in general and for his role. Oregon is his home base.
Cliff Bentz.speaks: Speech comes somewhat faster than most, and his volume stays somewhat more even than most. Describing his work, he is much more meticulous and granular than most. His public talk covers fewer topic areas than most. He leans on specifics rather than broad claims, so he makes his case with detail. That combination makes his delivery brisk but level, with the detail doing most of the work.
Cliff Bentz.decides: His test is whether the written detail survives a close review. Outside pushes reach him more lightly than they reach most members, so calls and crowds weigh less with him. His follow through is strong, so an ask with a named owner and a due date is the one that moves. A decision needs a written next step to stick.

archetype.justification: Bill follow-through is weaker than almost any senator's, and his detail work is much looser than most senators.

Cory Booker.bottom_line: Open with the people this ask helps, and lock the next step with a date. His follow-through is weaker than almost any senator's, so the dated step carries the weight.
do: Bring two stories of people the ask would help, in plain words
Leave his long pauses unfilled while he holds the floor
Stay on the core point when he pushes back, rather than chasing side issues
Set a dated next step before you leave
dont: Bury the ask under pages of fine print
Take a single brief answer as the end of his position
Assume a casual remark to him will stay private
Cory Booker.warning_sign: His words usually carry somewhat more bite than most. If that bite turns personal, he has moved off your ask. Stop, reduce the ask to one sentence, and name one next step.
Cory Booker.follow_up: Email his staff within two days a short note that answers the point he defends hardest.
Cory Booker.personality: Booker ranks among the most outgoing senators. His public profile is very high as well. Curiosity runs high in him, and he is much looser with detail than most. Few senators match the feeling in his words, and he gets worked up more readily than most. He is chair of his party's Senate communications committee. He sits on Senate Small Business, and his bills reach a somewhat broader set of subjects than most.
Cory Booker.speaks: Answer length swings a lot from reply to reply. His longest replies stretch a bit past most. Pauses between phrases run much longer than most speakers'. Upbeat wording runs through his talk well beyond most colleagues'. Across shows he holds his ground when challenged, a bit more than most. After a long reply, ask one focused question that keeps his attention on the core point.
Cory Booker.decides: Pressure from outside reaches him more than most, so the ask gains weight when it returns. A human case lands with him, since community impact is the frame that fits best. Follow-through is his weak point, so treat any yes as the opening step of the work. His legislative work stays mostly within his own party. End by asking for his position on the core point.

archetype.justification: He leads conversations, holds the floor firmly, and follows bills to passage reliably.

Cory Mills.bottom_line: Lead with a short, direct result and let him push back. He defends positions hard, so a clear result gives him a fact to test.
do: Open with the one result the bill delivers
Put each agreed step in writing before you leave
Answer his challenge on the facts, not on the tone
dont: Mistake his upbeat tone for a yes
Argue the point after he has defended it twice
Cory Mills.warning_sign: He usually defends his position hard when challenged and keeps pressing the same point. If he suddenly asks what you would change, he is open to a narrower version of the ask. Offer that version and let him pick the change.
Cory Mills.follow_up: Email his legislative aide a single sheet recap of the outcome and the follow up step by Friday.
Cory Mills.personality: Mills is very sociable and talks with far more upbeat energy than most. He is a little less practical than most and looser with details than nearly any member. He defends his position with unusual firmness when challenged, and in hearings he is far more confrontational than colleagues. Filler words crop up in his speech more than nearly any colleague's. He is somewhat quicker to bristle than colleagues, and he is fairly visible in the chamber.
Cory Mills.speaks: His pace is among the quickest in the chamber, and his pitch moves through a wider range than nearly any colleague's. Pauses run somewhat shorter than most, and volume varies less than most. Replies tend to be longer than most, and filler creeps in more than almost anyone's. Phrasing cuts somewhat sharper than most colleagues', and public words touch on fewer topics than most. Under challenge he digs in, and in hearings he turns far more confrontational.
Cory Mills.decides: Requests get weighed by whether they yield a clear result, and his stance is easy to read since he is fairly visible. His legislation touches somewhat fewer areas than most, so he presses the ones he already works in. Discussions run on his lead, and his position holds when challenged. So a decision from him comes after a clear case has survived his scrutiny.

archetype.justification: His bill follow-through is fairly dependable, he describes his work in exacting detail, and he keeps a low profile.

Craig Goldman.bottom_line: Bring one clear request and a date. His follow-through is fairly dependable, so a firm date gives him something to hold.
do: Send a written summary of the request and its dates, given his fairly reliable follow-through
Open by stating the request in one sentence and the date you need an answer
Keep the same request at each stage, since outside pressure bends him further
Limit the meeting to the request alone, and leave other topics for another visit
dont: Stage a public event to win him over
Read his fairly reliable follow-through as a sign he already backs your request
Assume a quiet week means he has dropped the bill
Craig Goldman.warning_sign: A general meeting does not show where he will land on the request yet. Ask him which single issue he needs settled before he decides.
Craig Goldman.follow_up: Within two days, send his staff a note on what was agreed, who acts next, and by when, as a short recap.
Craig Goldman.personality: Goldman is a House member who describes his legislative work with much more exacting detail than most colleagues. His public talk ranges over a little fewer issues than most, and his bills reach a somewhat smaller set of issues than most. He is fairly dependable on bills once they are moving. Few members keep a lower profile in the House than he does, and he is seldom in the public eye.
Craig Goldman.speaks: His pace runs a little slower than most, and his gaps between phrases are longer than nearly anyone's. Volume stays among the least variable in the House, and pitch is among the flattest. His public remarks tend to be careful and detailed, down to the specifics of each bill. Leave his long pauses alone, and keep the first meeting unhurried, so each point gets room.
Craig Goldman.decides: Outside pressure carries clear weight with him, so know which voices are already in the room and who else is raising it. His bill follow-through is fairly reliable, so an agreed step tends to get done. Keep the request to one clear sentence, so his staff can answer it quickly. Ask which bill on his list he would move first, and write that date down.

archetype.justification: She is quite reserved and fairly careful, and her public profile is among the lowest in the Senate.

Cynthia Lummis.bottom_line: Bring a short, direct case on what the policy delivers, since outside pushes sway her less than a typical colleague.
do: Lead with the one result the bill delivers, stated plainly
Ask where the bill stands before you pitch anything new
Name the colleagues across the aisle who already back the ask
dont: Read her low public profile as a lack of interest in the issue
Assume a request will land because outside groups back it
Stretch the case with long background material
Cynthia Lummis.warning_sign: In a hearing she usually stays among the least combative members, so a change shows when her questions turn sharp. That usually means she has a concern she has not voiced, so ask which point worries her and let her answer.
Cynthia Lummis.follow_up: Within a day, email her in writing the full figures and sources behind that result.
Cynthia Lummis.personality: Lummis, of Wyoming, is quite reserved and fairly careful, yet her curiosity runs higher than almost anyone's in the Senate. Her bills span a wide set of issues, and she bridges divides far more often than most. Little emotional heat runs through her wording, and she is hard to rattle. Her public profile is about as low as it gets in the chamber, and in the room she comes across as careful and organized rather than showy.
Cynthia Lummis.speaks: Her wording is plain and low in emotional tone. She explains her work with careful, specific detail. Public remarks range across many issues, more than nearly any colleague. At hearings, she sits among the least combative of her peers. Feeling comes through only faintly in her public wording. Her careful remarks sit beside wide topic coverage, so her public voice reads as broad and exact.
Cynthia Lummis.decides: She judges requests by the outcomes they can demonstrate, and outside pushing has less effect on her than on her peers. Her bills span a wider array of issues than nearly any colleague's, so a request has to stand on its own. Because ties across the aisle matter to her, a request that colleagues across the aisle already back gets a fairer hearing.

archetype.justification: His slow pace, careful detail and dependable voting record fit a tortoise closely.

Dale Strong.bottom_line: Bring a careful, detailed case with clear results and give him time to answer. He will not be rushed, and his word tends to hold once he commits.
do: Lay out the results in order, one point at a time
Send the written detail ahead so he can check it
Expect slow answers and let him finish before you respond
dont: Count on press coverage to carry the ask for him
Rush him for a yes in the first meeting
Dale Strong.warning_sign: An open session cannot reveal how he handles a challenge, so watch his written reply. Ask for one concrete step in writing and check whether it arrives when promised.
Dale Strong.follow_up: Send a written summary of the results and the next step within a week, with a named owner.
Dale Strong.personality: Strong is a reserved and practical member whose bills stay in a narrow range of topics. His account of his work is careful and detailed to an unusual degree. Votes and carrying bills through are where he counts among the most dependable members. He keeps a low profile, so people notice his work by what he carries through. In the room he is slow to commit and careful with detail.
Dale Strong.speaks: His pace sits well under most colleagues, and his gaps between phrases run longer. Volume swings more than almost any colleague's. His account of his work is careful and detailed to an unusual degree. Across public appearances he keeps to a few narrow topics. Overall his manner reads as deliberate and exact rather than quick or showy. His remarks follow the same deliberate rhythm throughout.
Dale Strong.decides: He weighs an ask on what it delivers and whether the detail holds up, and he takes his time. Outside voices move him much less than they move most colleagues, so a push from others will not carry him. Because his legislation touches a smaller set of topics than most colleagues, a decision sticks once a clear next step has an owner.

archetype.justification: He is very visible, fairly curious, and quite skeptical, and he holds firm when challenged.

Dan Crenshaw.bottom_line: Lead with results and facts, and expect him to defend his position. Keep the case short, since outside voices shift him a bit more than most.
do: Bring the results you can source, in a short written note
Open with the point you most need him to hold, since he defends his position
Ask your first question early, since few hold a conversation as firmly as he does
Close by asking him to put his position in writing
dont: Plan for a quick agreement, since he is skeptical
Interrupt his opening run before he finishes
Match his forceful words with sharper ones, since his words run more forceful than most
Dan Crenshaw.warning_sign: Usually his answers run thick with filler, more than most colleagues. If the filler drops out and his answers come out clean, he has stopped working the point out loud. Stop, and restate your single point in one sentence.
Dan Crenshaw.follow_up: Send his legislative staff a one-page note within two days, with the one outcome you want him to back.
Dan Crenshaw.personality: Crenshaw is outgoing to a degree few in the House match, and few are more visible for their role. He is fairly curious and quite skeptical by default. He holds firm under challenge harder than nearly any colleague in the chamber, and his public talk covers fewer subjects than most. Bills touch only a small set of issues. He has spoken about his young daughter.
Dan Crenshaw.speaks: In interviews his answers come out a bit longer than most, and their length varies much more than most. Few House members use more filler, and he leaves long pauses between phrases. His pitch swings as widely as anyone's in the House. His words cut a little sharper than most. Give him room in the long pauses, and answer his filler with a clear, short point.
Dan Crenshaw.decides: After he settles on a view, he defends it, so keep the points you raise few and tightly sourced. Outside voices shift him a little more than most, so bring fresh evidence each time. He sees bills through far less often than most colleagues, so keep the next step small and clear. Close by asking him which claim he wants checked first, and when.

archetype.justification: His description of his work is far more exact than most, and his tone reads much gentler than most.

Dan Newhouse.bottom_line: Ask for one clear, detailed step, and give him time to answer. Outside pressure moves him less than almost anyone, so do not expect a quick shift.
do: Give him room to answer, since his answers run somewhat longer than most
Ask for his view early, since he takes the lead much less than most
Keep the language plain and warm, since his words run somewhat warmer than most
dont: Rely on his public role alone to carry the ask
Press him hard after a challenge, since he defends his position somewhat more
Dan Newhouse.warning_sign: When challenged, he usually defends his position harder and his answers come in quick runs. Let him finish, then restate your one ask in a single plain sentence.
Dan Newhouse.follow_up: Afterward, put the next step and a date in a concise note, and copy whoever owns it.
Dan Newhouse.personality: Newhouse carries a public profile somewhat higher than usual for the job, and he leans a little toward the practical. He is very agreeable, and rattles somewhat less easily than most. His wording is much gentler than most in tone, yet among the most emotionally charged in the chamber. Exacting detail marks how he describes his work, and he defends his position more than most when challenged.
Dan Newhouse.speaks: Precision marks his talk about his own work, far beyond most. His wording is among the flattest in the chamber in upbeat feeling, though its emotional charge is among the highest. It is also far less geared to action than most. His answers run a little longer than most. Short, quick runs of replies come from him well above the usual level. Under challenge he holds his ground somewhat more than most. During hearings, his combative streak runs a little below the usual level.
Dan Newhouse.decides: Narrowness of an ask matters to him, since his bills touch somewhat fewer areas than most. Outside pressure moves him less than nearly anyone, so his own read carries the decision. He leads conversations much less than most, so he rarely pushes an ask alone. Once challenged, he defends his view more than most, so any yes needs reasons that hold up.

archetype.justification: He steers talks firmly, holds his ground hard, and is very dependable in carrying bills across the finish line.

Dan Sullivan.bottom_line: Open with the outcome and the facts, since he defends his position hard once challenged.
do: Bring a sponsor from the other side of the aisle
Line up outside groups that already back the case
If he digs in, restate the outcome in one line and wait
dont: Count on him to give up the floor once you press him
Assume his forceful tone means he has already settled the question
Dan Sullivan.warning_sign: He usually fills his answers with filler and defends his position hard, so filler is normal for him. When answers lose their filler and the arguing stops, you are facing a guarded speaker, so ease off and ask what would make the point work.
Dan Sullivan.follow_up: When the session wraps, mail a written recap of the coming action and copy the cosponsor who signs on.
Dan Sullivan.personality: Sullivan is very outgoing, though somewhat less practical than most. Language is very social and forceful, and it carries much more feeling than most. In conversation he takes a firm hold and digs in on his position more firmly than nearly anyone. Votes and legislation show a very dependable record, and he reaches across party lines more than nearly anyone. His bills span far more subjects than most colleagues do. He talks in longer turns, and his speech carries a lot of filler.
Dan Sullivan.speaks: Gaps between phrases run somewhat shorter than most, and loudness shifts more than most do. Tone climbs and dips much more than most. Longest replies run a little past most, and answer length swings more than nearly anyone's. He often trails into unfinished sentences more than nearly anyone in the chamber, and he answers in bursts less than nearly anyone. Under challenge he digs in, and in hearings he presses a little harder than most.
Dan Sullivan.decides: Results and facts come first for him, and he asks whether a colleague across the aisle signs on. Groups outside the chamber move him clearly more than most, so organized outside support can carry real weight. Since he is very reliable on votes and bills, he expects a deal to hold once it is struck, and he works to keep his side.

archetype.justification: Few colleagues hold the room as firmly as he does, and he digs in when someone pushes back.

Daniel Goldman.bottom_line: Let him set the opening, then bring your own agenda and a clear decision to close.
do: Send written technical evidence before the meeting, since it fits how he works
Let him run the first stretch, then steer toward the decision
Expect him to hold his position, and bring the evidence that answers his objection
Work with a partner from the other party before you go public
dont: Cut him off during his long answers, since his replies run long
Assume his first objection ends the discussion, since he defends his position
Count on his follow through without a named owner, since he rarely sees bills through
Daniel Goldman.warning_sign: He usually commands the floor and presses his point, so a moment of quiet from him stands out. If he cuts in quickly and defends his point, he is on guard, so let him finish and then restate your ask.
Daniel Goldman.follow_up: Send him a one page list of agreed steps, each with an owner and a date, by Friday.
Daniel Goldman.personality: Goldman is very outgoing, fairly curious, and a little skeptical. His public wording runs hotter than nearly any colleague's. Cross party work runs a notch ahead of most colleagues. His bill follow through ranks near the bottom of the chamber. He holds the floor in conversation as firmly as nearly anyone, and he digs in when pressed. New York is his seat in the House.
Daniel Goldman.speaks: In conversation he gives longer answers than most, and his longest replies stretch well past typical. He trails off or breaks in mid thought much more than most. His delivery runs a bit quicker than the norm, and pitch shifts more than typical. Volume holds much more level than most, and his pauses run somewhat shorter. Overall, his wording sounds task focused, well short of the typical social register.
Daniel Goldman.decides: Before backing it he asks whether he can lead it, since he tends to set the agenda himself. Pressed, he digs in, so a plan that gives him a stake gains ground. His follow through runs near the bottom of the House, so commitments from him need someone tracking them. Working across the aisle sits a notch ahead of most colleagues, so a bipartisan partner can widen his support.

archetype.justification: Very outgoing, he talks at length and defends his views firmly, which fits the Blue Jay's bold style.

Daniel Meuser.bottom_line: Keep the ask short and hold your ground, since his answers run long. Pressure from outside reaches him more than most, so a visible local backer helps.
do: Give your ask in short form before his long answers begin
If he digs in, bring the record instead of more argument
Turn each step into a task the office can start
dont: In a hearing, expect firm pushback and keep answers on the record
Reopening a point he has already defended wastes the meeting
Skip a gloomy tone, since his public words run upbeat
Daniel Meuser.warning_sign: He usually defends his view at length and keeps talking until the point lands. If he stops defending and lets the point drop, he is weighing the ask, so pause and ask which part concerns him most.
Daniel Meuser.follow_up: Send his staff a written one page summary with the ask and the record, by end of week.
Daniel Meuser.personality: Meuser has a very outgoing style and talks at length with a lot of filler. Public talk spans more subjects than nearly any colleague, and bills carry a broad mix of topics. When challenged, he digs in much more than most colleagues, and his words run somewhat cooler than most. He represents Pennsylvania, and his committee work sits in financial and small business policy.
Daniel Meuser.speaks: He speaks at length, and his answers stay more even in length than most. His talk is padded with filler, much more than most colleagues. Stretches of talk exceed nearly any colleague's in length, and pitch sits a little flatter than most. Loudness changes less than most, so the delivery holds one level even when the subject heats up. That pattern makes each exchange run longer than most expect.
Daniel Meuser.decides: Breadth of support and the record behind a request matter most to him, and once he takes a view, he digs in. His bills cover a broad field, so an ask that fits his interests can find a place. Outside pressure reaches him more than most, so a backer he trusts shifts his view, and he stays firm once he commits.

archetype.justification: Tortoise fits: he ranks near the top for reserve, is carefully methodical, and is among the hardest to fluster.

Daniel Webster.bottom_line: Give him a written, technical case, then ask for one clear step with a date. Crowd pressure moves him less, so the facts have to carry your ask.
do: Send the technical analysis ahead, so he can check it before the meeting
Confirm a dated next step before you leave, since follow through runs behind most
Build a documented record he can study on his own
dont: Count on him to warm up in public, since his reserve runs deep
Lean on a crowd of outside voices, since public pushing counts for less
Daniel Webster.warning_sign: In a hearing, he usually pushes much harder than most colleagues. If he goes quiet after a sharp exchange and his answers shrink, he is withdrawing, so watch that moment.
Daniel Webster.follow_up: Send a technical summary with one dated next step to his staff within three days, copying the bill's sponsor.
Daniel Webster.personality: Webster ranks near the top for reserve, and he is carefully methodical. A little practical, he is among the hardest to fluster. His legislation reaches a narrower set of topics than colleagues', and his public profile stays low, even for his role. His focus stays narrow and his reserve reads as deliberate rather than distant. Those traits make him easy to read.
Daniel Webster.speaks: Pitch swings much more widely than most, while his pace is a bit quicker. Loudness holds more level than the average colleague's. His public topics run narrower than most, and language carries a touch less emotional heat than most. His delivery is brisk and even in volume, with a restrained tone in public. Few topics get wide airtime, so his talk stays on a small set of areas.
Daniel Webster.decides: He weighs an ask on technical grounds and wants the detail laid out before he commits. Public pushing counts for less with him, so a push from groups will not change his view. His follow through runs somewhat behind, and his public exposure stays slight. A decision from him holds only when its next step has a name and a date.

archetype.justification: Interview answers are among the briefest, public visibility is somewhat lower, and finishing bills is far less dependable.

Danny Davis.bottom_line: Bring him a short case about who is helped, and keep the ask clear. Pressure will not move him much, but a clear benefit to people will.
do: Lead with who gains from the bill in one plain paragraph
Keep the ask to one or two sentences and stop
If he trails off partway, let him finish before you reply
Open with the ask itself, since his public tone runs cool
dont: Push harder on the ask when he goes quiet
Stretch the opening with small talk he will not return
Danny Davis.warning_sign: His usual pattern is short answers that trail off before the end, by default. If he stops in the middle of a sentence and gives even less than before, he is losing interest or on guard. Pause, then ask one plain question about who benefits.
Danny Davis.follow_up: Send a single page summary of who benefits to his legislative director within a day.
Danny Davis.personality: Davis is a quiet, low-profile member, and his public visibility is low. Public talk carries strong emotional charge with a focus on action, while he covers a far narrower slice of issues than most. In conversation his answers are briefer than the usual member's, and he often trails off before finishing a thought. Completing bills trails far behind his peers, so his record reads as more sentiment than delivery on bills. Expect energy on one issue, thin detail, and a short exchange rather than a long one.
Danny Davis.speaks: He speaks in short, plain answers and seldom fills a pause with extra words. Emotional charge runs high in his public talk, while the tone stays flat and the focus stays on action. He frames issues around concrete activity and keeps to a narrow range of topics. Interviews show the same brevity, and he often leaves sentences unfinished. Filler is much rarer in his speech than most.
Danny Davis.decides: He judges a request by who benefits, and human stories suit how he frames issues. Outside force grips him far more loosely than it grips most members, so an outside shove barely shifts his stance at all. Across his bills he touches a few more topics than most, so an ask fits best inside those areas. Finishing bills is far weaker for him, so a choice needs a named follow up step to hold.

archetype.justification: His reserved manner and low visibility fit a slow, deliberate operator who keeps a low public profile.

Darin LaHood.bottom_line: Bring written technical evidence ahead of time and a clear ask, since outside pressure has a lighter pull on him than on colleagues.
do: Send the technical evidence before the meeting
Name the one ask and the date it is needed
Keep the room small and let him think it through
dont: Assume a quiet room means he has no concerns
Count on a commitment carrying itself without a date
Darin LaHood.warning_sign: He is usually reserved and quiet, so silence alone is normal and not a warning. If he presses points he would normally let pass, he tenses up, so slow down, restate the one ask, and give him one specific point to check.
Darin LaHood.follow_up: After the meeting send him the technical summary with the one ask and a date for the next step, and confirm the date by message within two days.
Darin LaHood.personality: LaHood has a little reserve and fairly careful habits, a mix that makes him deliberate rather than showy. He is less easily flustered than colleagues, and his bills span a smaller set of issues than colleagues do. He draws much less notice than colleagues, so his public profile stays low. A former prosecutor from Illinois, he tends to weigh a case methodically. The result is a quiet, methodical colleague who builds a case slowly.
Darin LaHood.speaks: His descriptions of his work are somewhat less careful and detailed than colleagues, so his public language stays general rather than technical. His public words carry more emotional charge than colleagues', and that edge shows more clearly in hearings, where he is more combative than colleagues. Framing leans toward the broad point rather than the fine detail.
Darin LaHood.decides: An ask lands best when the evidence is laid out ahead of time, since written technical support fits how he works. Outside pressure has a lighter pull on him than on colleagues, so an outside push carries a little less weight. He is a little less dependable at carrying bills forward, so progress needs an owner named and a deadline fixed.

archetype.justification: His thorough, precise style and his high profile for his role mark him out in the House.

Darrell Issa.bottom_line: Make the technical case the center of the meeting, since written evidence suits him best.
do: Send a short technical brief a week ahead
Open with the one technical question your ask resolves
Ask one question at a time, and let each reply run its natural length
Close with a dated next step, since his commitments tend to hold
dont: Fight him for the floor, since he takes charge of talks much more than most
Launch a loud public campaign, since his role already puts him in view
Stage a sharp exchange in hearings, where he is markedly more combative than most
Darrell Issa.warning_sign: He usually works a point through one full reply at a time, and seldom gets into rapid back-and-forth. If he suddenly begins trading rapid back-and-forth, he is ready to close the point. Stop, send the written detail, and ask which part he wants next.
Darrell Issa.follow_up: Send his staff a technical summary within a few days, then confirm the owner by name.
Darrell Issa.personality: Issa is fairly curious, and he is a very precise, careful person. Few members in the House stand out more for the role he holds. His votes and bill follow-through are much stronger than most, and he builds across party lines much more than most. He takes charge of talks much more than most, and in hearings he is markedly more combative than most members.
Darrell Issa.speaks: In interviews his replies run a bit longer than most, and he trails off much more than most at the end of a point. He almost never breaks a point into quick, clipped exchanges. His public words run much sharper than most. Give his longer replies room, and wait for each point to reach its full length before you respond.
