Darrell Issa.decides: His follow-through is very strong, so a yes from him carries real weight. Outside pressure reaches him clearly less than most colleagues, so repeated campaigns carry less weight. Settle the technical questions before the meeting, so the talk can stay on substance. Keep the written answers in one place, so he can check each point on his own time and then decide.

archetype.justification: His slow, long pauses, wide issue range, and dependable follow through fit a patient, deliberate member.

Darren Soto.bottom_line: Bring a proposal that shows who it helps, since stories about people move him. Pressure from outside counts heavily with him, so back the ask with the people it serves.
do: Tell the story of the people the bill helps
Give him time to finish, since he talks slowly and pauses longer than most
Ask for a named next step, and check it at each stage
dont: Fill his long pauses with your own next point
Assume his low profile will draw press attention to the bill
Darren Soto.warning_sign: Such events cannot reveal how the bill moves through each procedural stage, so the gap is the process itself. Before the meeting, ask staff for the next procedural step and who must act on it.
Darren Soto.follow_up: Within two days, give his staff a single page memo that names the next procedural step and its owner.
Darren Soto.personality: Soto is a fairly curious member who is a little reserved and holds details loosely. His public talk spans issue areas far beyond typical colleagues, and his bills reach a broad set of areas. He crosses the aisle more often than typical colleagues, and he is fairly dependable on bills. Far less notice falls on him than on typical members, so his work runs quietly.
Darren Soto.speaks: Conversation ranges across many areas, well past what typical speakers cover. He describes his work in broad terms rather than detailed ones. Each point gets room to land before he moves on. Threads move on to the next theme, so the talk stays wide and open. Each theme receives a broad treatment, which keeps the overall picture wide. That breadth shows up in each exchange, from the first question to the last.
Darren Soto.decides: He checks whether a request fits the wide set of areas his bills already cover, and a clear account of who gains persuades him. Outside pressure counts for more with him than with most, so organized support from several groups carries weight. He is less visible than most, so a decision from him rests on a named partner who keeps the ask in view.

archetype.justification: His very careful detailed talk, quick reactions, and people focused framing fit an earnest, detail minded member.

Dave Min.bottom_line: Lead with who the bill helps, and bring detailed proof he can check. Outside voices move him clearly more, so line up the groups behind the ask.
do: Bring the people the bill helps, with their own words
Walk him through the detail, since he follows bills through
Pace your turns to match his quick talk
dont: Treat a fast reply as his final answer
Rely on outside voices alone to close the gap
Dave Min.warning_sign: By default he stays a shade less combative in hearings, so a brisk, pointed tone there is a change. When that tone appears, he is on guard, so return to the people the bill helps and ask one question.
Dave Min.follow_up: Within a week, send his staff a short summary of the people the bill helps and a dated next step.
Dave Min.personality: Min is a quite practical member, though fairly outgoing and among the most careful with details. Word choice carries heavy emotional charge, and reactions come fast. Description of work is exact and thorough, well beyond typical colleagues. Votes and bills rank as very dependable across the chamber. Bills cover a narrower set of issues than almost anyone else in the chamber. Notice for the role runs somewhat lower, and hearings bring out less combat than typical.
Dave Min.speaks: Word choice carries heavy emotion from the first point to the last. He uses exact detail rather than broad framing, which sets his talk apart. Remarks stay on a few themes, and each talk sticks within a narrow lane of issues. In hearings, combativeness runs somewhat lower than typical, so the tone stays civil. The feeling in his phrases shows up in the exact detail he supplies.
Dave Min.decides: How an ask affects the people it names is what he weighs most, and stories of who is helped carry real weight. Outside pressure has a strong pull on him, so a coalition behind the ask outweighs a lone push. His visibility runs somewhat low, and his bill list is narrower, so a colleague who speaks for the ask helps him most.

archetype.justification: He is very careful by nature, his role draws a fair amount of attention, and his bills touch a slightly wider range of subjects.

David Joyce.bottom_line: Bring a careful, complete plan, and come back more than once, since pressure from outside sways him more than most.
do: Put the written detail in front of him before the meeting
Open by stating the ask plainly, then name the next step
Line up outside voices who back the ask to weigh in
Return with the same request at a follow-up meeting, since pressure counts with him
dont: Trust that a remark in the room stays off the record
Treat a verbal yes as settled without a written next step, since pressure moves him
Stack several asks into one meeting
David Joyce.warning_sign: A meeting that is quiet or general does not show where he stands, so the meeting alone leaves his position open. Ask what he would want to check before deciding, and note the answer.
David Joyce.follow_up: Email his staff a single page that names the open question and who owns it, within a few days.
David Joyce.personality: Joyce is a careful, agreeable member who is much less easily rattled than most. He is very careful, and few colleagues are as agreeable as he is. His public talk about the work runs more detailed than almost anyone's. Across his bills, a slightly wider set of issues shows up, and his profile sits a bit more visible than most for his role.
David Joyce.speaks: His public words carry a little more feeling than most, and his talk on the work is dense with detail, more so than almost anyone's. Limit each point to a sentence, and keep it concrete. Let him answer in the terms he chose, without you rewording his point at all. Ask one question at a time and let him finish each answer.
David Joyce.decides: Keep what you say in public about the ask the same as what you tell his office, since his role keeps him fairly visible. Outside pressure moves his view more than most members' views, so note which outside voice he cites and when. Close each meeting by asking for his position in one sentence. Keep the question short and plain, so his answer is easy to record.

archetype.justification: His legislation reaches wider ground than nearly every peer, he speaks slowly, and he reaches across party lines somewhat more than most.

David Kustoff.bottom_line: Make the ask short and in writing, and expect outside voices to move him. He works across the aisle somewhat more than most, so a shared ask can land.
do: Put the ask in writing with one clear next step
Bring allies from the other side who back the ask
Give him time to reflect before asking for a yes
dont: Read his slow pace as reluctance
Expect a quick answer on a new question
David Kustoff.warning_sign: In a hearing he usually answers slowly and less combatively than most members. If he goes quiet and takes his time, he is weighing the request. Give that room, then follow up in writing.
David Kustoff.follow_up: Send a short written note restating the ask and one next step with a date to his office within two days.
David Kustoff.personality: Kustoff remains quite reticent, and few things unsettle him. Details come out loosely in his speech, and his work is described with much less careful detail than most. His legislation spans a broader range than almost all colleagues, and bipartisan work comes somewhat more readily to him than most. Visibility runs much lower than typical colleagues. Hearing manner comes across milder than the typical member's, and he is from Tennessee.
David Kustoff.speaks: He speaks slowly, with extended gaps between phrases that run well beyond the usual. His volume moves up and down widely, and his words carry less emotional charge than the typical member's. In hearings his manner is less combative, and he tends to let a question sit before answering. He does not rush to fill the silence. Listeners often wait through those gaps without interrupting.
David Kustoff.decides: He wants proposals that reach bipartisan audiences and that outside voices endorse before he takes them seriously. Visible backing from outside voices sways him more than it sways most colleagues, so a visible ally can tip a close call. He works across the aisle somewhat more than most, so a decision needs a dated next step and a named owner to stick.

archetype.justification: Very outgoing and very agreeable, with much more emotional charge in his words and a fast pace.

David McCormick.bottom_line: Open with the results and a short, direct case for the policy. He holds the floor and defends his view hard, so expect a long argument before he agrees.
do: Let him open the discussion, since he holds the floor
Put the policy's concrete results first in any brief you send
Keep your answers short to match his quick pace
dont: Compete for the floor with him, since he holds it firmly
Answer every challenge with a fresh counterargument
David McCormick.warning_sign: He usually takes charge and talks fast with tight gaps between phrases, so when he stops and lets others hold the floor, he is weighing your point. Let the silence sit, then ask which part he would test first.
David McCormick.follow_up: Within a day of the meeting, give his office a single page recap of the results, with an owner named for the next step.
David McCormick.personality: McCormick strikes people as very outgoing and very agreeable, with language far more emotionally charged than most. He is somewhat less exacting with detail than most. Few things rattle him, and his issue focus stays narrow for a Senate member. He takes the floor, and he sits on Senate Banking from Pennsylvania. He keeps a point alive once he has made it, and he is quick to return to it.
David McCormick.speaks: His replies stretch longer than most members', and his pace is faster than nearly any member's. He talks fast, and his pauses between phrases are much shorter than most. Volume holds more even than nearly anyone's, while pitch climbs and drops more than nearly anyone's. When challenged he digs in harder than nearly anyone. He uses many filler words, and his wording comes across as much more forceful, and somewhat warmer, than most members. His answer length swings widely from one reply to the next.
David McCormick.decides: Results decide how he treats an ask, so a brief case that shows the change is what he needs. Groups outside the chamber move him more than most colleagues, so their backing can change his position. He takes charge of conversations and defends his position hard, so an ask that lets him lead the discussion fits him. Because he is very agreeable in person, a dated commitment made face to face is what keeps him to it.

archetype.justification: His slow, long pausing speech, flat pitch and very reliable follow through fit a slow, deliberate operator who finishes what he starts.

David Rouzer.bottom_line: Bring written technical evidence and a clear next step, since pressure from outside weighs on him more than colleagues and he follows through.
do: Walk him through the technical record in advance
Name the step he has committed to and its date
Hold space for his slow answers before you respond
dont: Mistake a slow reply for a no
Push him into a combative hearing exchange
David Rouzer.warning_sign: He is normally slow, with long pauses and a flat pitch, so a slow reply is normal. If his answers suddenly turn short and clipped, read it as guarded, so pause, name the worry, and give him time before you answer.
David Rouzer.follow_up: After the meeting mail him a technical summary naming each step, who owns it, and when it is due, and request his sign off before that date.
David Rouzer.personality: Rouzer comes across as a little reserved and a little practical, and he is looser on fine print than colleagues. His public talk spans a slightly broader set of subjects than colleagues', and he describes his work with more care and detail. His legislation is a little narrower than colleagues' in the number of areas it touches. Bills he carries tend to reach a vote, and he sees them through with dependable consistency. In hearings he tends to avoid sharp exchanges. He represents North Carolina.
David Rouzer.speaks: Delivery moves slowly, with drawn out gaps between phrases and a flatter pitch than colleagues'. Pace ranks among the lowest in the House. Loudness swings a good deal from one phrase to the next. He describes his work with more care and detail, and his public talk ranges across a slightly broader set of subjects than colleagues'. His hearing manner stays low key.
David Rouzer.decides: Before backing it he tests how well its technical case holds up under review, and technical framing fits how he thinks. His bills span a slightly narrower set of areas, so an ask has to sit inside the issues he already carries. Outside backing carries extra weight with him, so a decision can rest on the people standing behind it. He is very reliable once a commitment is made, so a decision holds when its next step has a clear owner.

archetype.justification: Among the most outgoing and curious colleagues and among the most combative in hearings, which fits a lively, direct style.

David Schweikert.bottom_line: Send a technical case ahead of the meeting, since pressure from outside reaches him clearly less than most colleagues.
do: Share the written evidence before the meeting, with sources
Ask which figure he wants to check first
Agree a dated next step and its owner before leaving
dont: Rely on outside pressure to close the deal
Walk into a hearing expecting him to take the questions gently
David Schweikert.warning_sign: In a hearing a pointed question from him is routine, since he usually ranks among the most combative. If his questions grow shorter and he stops engaging the answer, he is losing patience, so stop and confirm which point he is testing.
David Schweikert.follow_up: By Friday, send his office the agreed next step, its owner, and the evidence due with it.
David Schweikert.personality: Schweikert strikes a very outgoing and very curious note, and he is precise in how he organizes his work. His public talk stays on a much narrower set of issues, and his legislation touches a smaller number of topics than nearly any colleague. For his role he is much less visible than most, and during hearings he ranks among the most combative in the room. Votes and bill follow through run somewhat less dependable than most colleagues.
David Schweikert.speaks: Public remarks stay with a few issues and describe his work in far less detail than most. His pace sits near the bottom of the chamber, with longer pauses between phrases, and his volume swings further than nearly any colleague's. There his manner is sharp, since he ranks with the most combative in the chamber. That mix makes his manner hard to read at first.
David Schweikert.decides: For him a request stands or falls on whether the written evidence survives a close reading. Pressure from outside reaches him clearly less than most colleagues, so lobbying from home will not carry the decision. His legislation touches fewer topics than nearly any colleague, so an ask inside his own areas fits him best. Follow through is somewhat less reliable than most, so a choice needs a named date and an owner to hold.

archetype.justification: Very reliable at seeing bills through, much more detailed in talk about his work, and loose with small details.

David Taylor.bottom_line: Bring the people a bill would help, and the detailed record that shows how it works. He follows through well, but outside force shifts him a little less than most.
do: Lead with the people a bill would help, in plain terms
Walk through how the bill works, step by step
Prepare for hearings in which he is a little less combative than most
dont: Push him to decide before he has the detail in hand
Read his fast, pausing speech as a sign of doubt
Assume outside pressure will do the persuading for you
David Taylor.warning_sign: His usual pattern is a restrained style in hearings, so quiet questioning there is normal for him. Watch for him sharpening his questions in a hearing, which usually means he has a firm objection.
David Taylor.follow_up: Within a day, put the one practical question and the detail behind it into a brief written message.
David Taylor.personality: Taylor carries himself with a little reserve and a little practicality. His public talk about legislation is much more careful and detailed than most, and his legislation spans a far narrower set of issues than the typical member. He is very dependable on the bills he takes up, and in hearings he keeps a lighter touch than most members. A narrow agenda runs through his work, and he finishes what he takes up, so his record rests on follow through.
David Taylor.speaks: His pace is a bit quicker than most, and his pauses run longer between phrases than most. Pitch swings a bit more than most. His public explanations are much more careful and detailed than most, so his talk is full of specifics rather than broad claims. The pitch changes are part of his plain style, not a sign of emotion.
David Taylor.decides: Stories about the people a request reaches carry real weight with him, since he judges it by who benefits. His legislation spans a narrow range of issues, so he is most open to an ask inside the areas he already works on. Bills he takes up tend to get finished, so he follows what he commits to. Outside pressure shifts him only slightly less than most colleagues, so a decision sticks once the record and the people it helps both hold up.

archetype.justification: He is very reserved, and fairly careful and organized, which fits a patient, low key approach.

David Valadao.bottom_line: Pair your ask with a colleague across the aisle and let him announce it. He is very dependable on bills, and pressure from outside gets through to him more readily.
do: Offer a shared announcement that gives a partner a visible part
Confirm each next step in writing, since he follows through on bills
In a hearing, expect firmer questions, since he tends to press points there
dont: Assume his agreement carries the bill without a named next step
Read his reserve as a sign that he has no view on the bill
David Valadao.warning_sign: In formal hearings he is usually more combative than most members, so a firm challenge from him there is a real objection. Ask him what would answer it before you move on.
David Valadao.follow_up: Send his office a short summary of the next vote, naming the owner and the date it is due.
David Valadao.personality: Valadao is very reserved and quite practical in his talk. He is careful and organized in his preparation, and he gives more detailed accounts of his work than most colleagues. His public wording is a notch less emotional than most. Across party lines he works far more often than most, and his bills reach across far more issues than most. Dependable at seeing bills through, his public visibility runs a bit lower than most, and in hearings he presses a little harder than most members. He represents California.
David Valadao.speaks: Work comes up in careful, detailed terms, more than most colleagues bring to it. His public wording sits a notch lower in emotional charge than most, so he sounds more factual than heated. He keeps remarks tied to specifics and does not lean much on broad emotional appeals. In formal hearings he presses a little harder than most members, so his questions tend to carry more edge.
David Valadao.decides: Each ask is tested by whether it can be pushed to completion, and he is very dependable in seeing bills finished. Pressure from outside gets through to him more readily, so a well-timed push from home or from allies can shift him. His bills reach across far more issues than most, so an ask that touches several of his areas can fit. So a decision with him sticks once the next vote is on the calendar.

archetype.justification: Her answers stay short and even, she follows bills through reliably, and her profile stays among the quietest.

Deb Fischer.bottom_line: Lead with a plain request and the policy's results, since she engages with a direct, short case.
do: Give her a short, specific brief on what the policy delivers
Expect short answers, so ask one question at a time
Bring a list of cosponsors from across the aisle
dont: Read her quiet manner as disinterest in the ask
Expect outside pressure to shift her only slightly
Deb Fischer.warning_sign: She usually keeps answers brief and even, and she rarely pads them. If her replies run longer or filler creeps in, she is less comfortable, so slow down and check what she needs.
Deb Fischer.follow_up: After the meeting, send her staff a short written note listing the one ask and the cosponsors who back it, by Friday.
Deb Fischer.personality: Fischer is quieter than nearly everyone in the Senate, and her outlook leans only a little practical. Her work habits are careful and organized, and her legislative focus is narrow compared with most. Following bills through is a strength for her, and she reaches across lines more than most. Filler is almost absent, she rarely trails off, and she seldom draws attention in the chamber.
Deb Fischer.speaks: Her language carries little emotion, and her delivery reads flatter than most in the chamber. When she describes bills she is more exact than most, and she stays with specifics. Her answers are short, and even her longest replies stay brief compared with most. She keeps her answers even in length and seldom starts a rapid run of short replies.
Deb Fischer.decides: She checks if a request sits inside the narrow set of issues she already works on. Outside pressure has some pull on her, but a clear case of results carries the most weight. Her record of seeing work through is strong, so once she agrees she tends to stay with it. So she is the right member to ask when the work needs a patient, dependable partner.

archetype.justification: Few colleagues are as outgoing as she is, and she leads conversations somewhat more than most.

Debbie Dingell.bottom_line: Lead with the results the policy gets, in a brief case, and agree one next step before you leave.
do: Give her a shared role to lead, since she is very outgoing and visible
Confirm each commitment in writing, since her bill follow through trails most colleagues somewhat
Let her take the time she needs, since her answers run well past typical
dont: Cut in to finish her thought, since she often leaves sentences unfinished
Count on a verbal yes alone, since her follow through trails most colleagues somewhat
Expect a harsh tone from her, since her public wording runs softer than most
Debbie Dingell.warning_sign: She usually gives full answers and uses some filler, so a sudden clipped reply from her stands out. If she trails off or cuts her answers short, she is weighing your point, so wait and give her room to complete it.
Debbie Dingell.follow_up: Mail her office a single page note on the agreed step, who owns it, and the due date by Friday.
Debbie Dingell.personality: Dingell is very agreeable and sits among the most outgoing House members. Her detail work trails most colleagues a notch, and she gets worked up a bit easily. Public wording is much gentler than most, and it carries much more emotional charge. Her legislation spans a very wide set of policy areas. Her public exposure runs well ahead of colleagues in her role. Michigan is the seat she holds in the House.
Debbie Dingell.speaks: Her delivery runs somewhat faster than most, with somewhat longer pauses between phrases. Loudness swings somewhat more than most, while her pitch stays somewhat flatter. In interviews her answers run far longer, and her longest replies run well past typical. Her public wording runs noticeably gentler than most, and she trails off more than most. She sounds warm, and she uses a fair amount of filler.
Debbie Dingell.decides: She weighs a request by the way it fits the broad set of issues her bills already cover. Public backing counts for a little less with her, so an ask must stand on its substance. Follow through is somewhat weaker for her than most colleagues, so every decision needs a named owner after the vote. Her visibility runs well ahead of colleagues, so her name carries an ask into view.

archetype.justification: Very outgoing and visible, she takes the floor, defends her position firmly, and keeps her bills to few issues.

Debbie Wasserman Schultz.bottom_line: Bring one clear result and let her make her case first, since she defends her position hard.
do: Open with the one result the policy delivers
Let her finish each answer before you respond
Prepare a tight record before any hearing, since she presses hard there
dont: Match her sharp tone with sharper words of your own
Treat an early objection as her final word
Cede the agenda to her without a clear close
Debbie Wasserman Schultz.warning_sign: She usually defends her position openly when challenged. If she stops contesting a point she had pushed, she has dropped it, so ask her directly what would settle it.
Debbie Wasserman Schultz.follow_up: Within two days, give her office a short summary covering the result and the next step.
Debbie Wasserman Schultz.personality: Wasserman Schultz is very outgoing and highly visible, and she commands the floor more than nearly any colleague. She gets worked up easily, and her language cuts harder than most, so pressure shows quickly. Her bills reach far fewer issues, while her talk about her work lacks detail. In a room she sets the agenda and defends her position openly, so her strength is presence more than detail.
Debbie Wasserman Schultz.speaks: On the House floor her delivery runs somewhat faster than most, with pauses between phrases that are much shorter than most. Her volume rises and falls a little more than most. In interviews her longest replies stretch much longer than most, and her answer length varies much more than most. Her sentences are left unfinished far more often than most, while rapid strings of brief replies show up far less. When challenged she defends ground rather than conceding it.
Debbie Wasserman Schultz.decides: She gives little ground on a position she has defended in public, so an early no can harden. Results and facts fit her best, and pressure from outside shifts her only a little more than most members. Because her bills stay in few areas, an ask counts most when it fits her work, and her yes holds once the result is clear.

archetype.justification: Her public tone is very warm, she builds bridges to the other side more than most, and people-centered cases fit her.

Deborah Ross.bottom_line: Lead with the people your ask helps, and keep the tone warm and plain. She crosses party lines much more than most, so present the plan as shared ground.
do: Phrase the ask in policy terms, not social or group language
Open with a warm, plain thank you before the ask
Watch her floor remarks, noting volume swings, action words and who holds the floor
Ask her which other-party colleagues she has worked with on bills, and name them
dont: Bring a plan with no clear action step in it
Mistake her less social public words for a lack of interest
Let a formal hearing turn into a contest of who is right
Deborah Ross.warning_sign: Her longest answers usually stay shorter than most. If she starts giving long, winding answers, she is talking around your ask. Narrow to one next step and save the detail for a later call.
Deborah Ross.follow_up: Send a one-page summary to her legislative director within two days, restating the ask, who owns each step, and its due day.
Deborah Ross.personality: Ross is very agreeable and easy to work with, and she builds with the other side more than most. Her public talk ranges across far more issues than most members do. Her public tone is very warm. Reliability on votes and bills is fairly strong, and in a room she holds back a little. In formal hearings her edge runs a notch sharper than most members, and getting worked up comes quicker to her than to most.
Deborah Ross.speaks: Her public words are very upbeat, and her talk is action-focused to a degree few House members match. On the House floor her volume swings up and down a lot, more than most members. Her words are among the least social in the House, so keep small talk brief. In interviews her answer lengths vary somewhat less than most, so let each answer finish.
Deborah Ross.decides: Lean on her cross-party record, since she builds across the aisle much more than most. Once she commits she is fairly reliable about seeing it through, so ask what the next vote needs. Keep the ask short, since she takes charge of conversations less than most. Bring the case in plain words, then finish by asking her to decide and to name a date.

archetype.justification: Her outgoing manner and wide curiosity stand out, and she ranks among the most curious members in the House.

Delia Ramirez.bottom_line: Offer her a visible shared role early, one she can lead or announce alongside you, before you get into details.
do: Ask her to shape one new piece of the plan you can front together
Reference the Chicago housing organizer who mentored her, where it fits
Take your time with each answer in a formal hearing, where she is less combative
Close by naming who else already backs the ask
dont: Present the shared role as a favor she could take back
Water down your own points to avoid her sharp edges
Drop the ask after her first answer
Delia Ramirez.warning_sign: In hearings she is usually a bit less combative than most. If she turns sharper than that usual tone, she is no longer weighing your ask. Stop, name the single change you need, and wait for her answer.
Delia Ramirez.follow_up: Before next Friday, mail her team a brief written note that names the shared role you propose and the next step.
Delia Ramirez.personality: Ramirez is outgoing and curious beyond nearly any colleague in the House. She is quite skeptical by default. She is much quicker than most to get worked up, and she runs hot. The bills she carries touch somewhat fewer areas than most, though her public range runs much wider. Careful detail is less of a strength, and her wording cuts much sharper than most. Her visibility is somewhat lower than most for her role. She has spoken warmly of a Chicago housing organizer who mentored her.
Delia Ramirez.speaks: Her volume moves far more than most when she speaks on the House floor, while her pitch lies much flatter than most. On the House floor, pace is a little slower than most. Her speeches are as emotionally charged as anyone's in the House. In hearings she shows a bit less edge than most members do. Answer her sharp wording with plain facts.
Delia Ramirez.decides: Outside pressure sways her positions somewhat more than most, so a second ask has room. She has spoken about her mother's migration to this country. Where it fits naturally, a plan that helps families who made that trip matches what she has said in public. Keep the second ask shorter than the first, since outside voices shift her position a bit more than most. End by asking which claim she would want documented first.

archetype.justification: Among the most reserved colleagues, he is highly careful and orderly, and he works across party lines among the least of any member.

Derek Schmidt.bottom_line: Lead with careful detail and one dated next step, since he is solid on votes and bill follow through.
do: Open plainly with the bill's record, not with a pitch
Give him time to finish each thought before you reply
Name the next step and its owner before the meeting ends
dont: Read his reserve as opposition to the bill
Count on cross-party backing to carry the ask
Rush your points, since he speaks among the slowest in the chamber
Derek Schmidt.warning_sign: By default he is gentler than most in hearings, so a sharper tone there means he has been pushed past his usual limit. Stop the detail, name the decision in one sentence, and let him set when to continue.
Derek Schmidt.follow_up: Send a short written note listing the next step, its owner, and the date to his office within two days.
Derek Schmidt.personality: Schmidt is among the most reserved members, yet he is very curious and very careful. His public talk covers somewhat more topics than most, and his own descriptions of his work are more detailed than most. Legislation spans slightly more subjects than most, and follow through is fairly reliable. He keeps a very low profile for his role, and in hearings he runs a bit gentler than most members.
Derek Schmidt.speaks: He speaks among the slowest in the chamber, with long pauses between phrases. His volume varies among the widest in the chamber, and his pitch moves up and down a bit more than most. Public talk covers a wider mix of topics, and his own descriptions run more detailed than most. Overall his manner is deliberate and precise, with the detail doing the persuading.
Derek Schmidt.decides: He weighs an ask on its own terms, since cross-party backing is rare for him. His bills give him more areas to check a new ask against, and he tests each one against them. Outside pressure sways him a bit more than most, so a request that returns with new facts can move him. He commits only to steps that are named and dated, so a verbal yes stays unsettled.

archetype.justification: He talks about a narrow range of issues, his bills cover few areas, and his follow through on bills is solid.

Derek Tran.bottom_line: Give him a single concrete ask with a visible role and bring voices he trusts. Backing from outside groups matters more for him than most, so line up a coalition.
do: Offer a shared public role he can front with you
Bring the people who back the ask into the room
Get the coming action in writing before you walk out
dont: Push him into a public fight in a hearing
Assume one meeting settles it, since outside voices move him
Derek Tran.warning_sign: He usually stays on the narrow issue at hand. If he turns quiet in a hearing and stops pressing, send the facts in writing rather than pushing him in the room.
Derek Tran.follow_up: Afterward, deliver a concise note to his office listing the agreed action, its owner and a fixed deadline.
Derek Tran.personality: Tran keeps a low profile, and little draws attention to his role. Careful, detailed description marks how he presents his bills, which cover few areas. His talk carries more feeling than most, and he gets worked up fast. His follow through on bills is solid, and in formal rooms he holds back.
Derek Tran.speaks: In hearings he is milder than most, and he keeps close to the narrow point at hand. Feeling runs higher in his talk than most, and when he describes his work he moves into fine detail. His language stays focused rather than broad. Every answer shows his issue focus. He stays on his own area, and that narrow lens shapes what he says.
Derek Tran.decides: Fit with the single topic he already handles determines how he judges a request. Outside voices move him more than most, and he follows through on bills fairly reliably. Visible shared roles fit him, but he keeps a low profile, so a request holds when the people behind it are named and the next step is written. He looks for a fit before committing.

archetype.justification: Sharp, very emotional public words and a combative hearing style mark him as a Ram.

Derrick Van Orden.bottom_line: Give him a visible shared role, and close with one named next step and a date.
do: Pair him with a partner on the public announcement
Prepare for hard pressing in hearings and answer each point
dont: Treat his sharp tone as a rejection of the ask
Derrick Van Orden.warning_sign: By default his words are very sharp and his tone pointed. If his wording turns soft and he stops pressing points, he is losing enthusiasm for the issue. Ask him directly what would make it his priority and let him answer.
Derrick Van Orden.follow_up: Once you leave, put the agreed next step and its date in a brief written summary for him.
Derrick Van Orden.personality: Van Orden is a little reserved and quick to be stirred up, with sharper words than nearly any colleague's. Curiosity runs very high, and skepticism runs quite high as well. In hearings he ranks among the most combative members. Public tone carries far more feeling than most. His follow through is very dependable. He is quite visible in most settings, which keeps his positions in front of colleagues.
Derrick Van Orden.speaks: Sharper than nearly all colleagues, his wording also carries far more feeling than most. Extra precision and detail mark how he frames his issues. He is among the most combative in hearings, and his manner stays pointed when the setting turns formal or adversarial. He presses a point rather than softening it, which makes his public voice easy to read.
Derrick Van Orden.decides: A visible shared role is what he looks for in a request, and pressure from outside shifts him more than it shifts most of his colleagues. Very dependable on follow through, he needs a next step with a name and a date for any decision to stick. Combative in hearings, he will press any ask put to a formal test.

archetype.justification: Her public words are as social as anyone's in the House, and she works with both sides somewhat more than most.

Diana DeGette.bottom_line: Offer her a joint role she can lead in public, and put the partnership in writing. She works across parties more than most, so a joint plan suits her.
do: Prepare a short plan with one named partner she can stand beside
Open with the shared work before the details
Name the colleagues from the other party who already work on the plan
Ask short follow-up questions to draw out her brief answers
dont: Pitch the plan as a high-energy rally
Load the meeting with action items and deadlines
Wait for her to take charge of the agenda
Diana DeGette.warning_sign: She rarely trades quick runs of replies, which is her usual style. If she starts firing fast replies, she has stopped thinking the plan through. Keep the ask narrow, and offer a written answer.
Diana DeGette.follow_up: By Friday, email her office a short summary that lists each shared commitment with its date.
Diana DeGette.personality: DeGette brings a fairly curious and fairly careful mind to her work, and her bills reach somewhat wider than most. Her public talk is social in a way few House members match. Across parties, she builds somewhat more than most. She holds the floor somewhat less than most. Her words about her own work are much less detailed than most, yet they carry a great deal of feeling.
Diana DeGette.speaks: In interviews few House members give shorter answers, and she leaves out filler almost entirely, so leave a beat after each answer. On the House floor her pitch stays a little flatter than most. Hearings bring out a much more pointed side, so keep formal settings firm, set a clear agenda first, and let her finish each point before you weigh in.
Diana DeGette.decides: She is fairly curious, so clear and checkable detail suits her. Give her a few days with the written materials before any call or second meeting. She runs conversations somewhat less than most, and in interviews her longest answers stay short and even. Keep your own remarks as brief as hers, and put any ask after her answer, not before it.

archetype.justification: Her very narrow issue range, few bills, and reserved manner fit a narrowly focused legislator who keeps a low public profile.

Diana Harshbarger.bottom_line: Bring a short, direct case on what the policy delivers, and leave with one named step. Outside pressure pulls on her a little less, so the merits must carry it.
do: Lead with the result the policy produces, in two plain sentences
Confirm the step ahead and who owns it before you leave
dont: Expect a broad audience to amplify the proposal
Take a quiet yes as a settled vote
Diana Harshbarger.warning_sign: Any group setting will not reveal how far her interest goes, since her reserved manner keeps her views close. So before you leave, ask which step comes next and get the date in writing.
Diana Harshbarger.follow_up: Mail her team one page naming the step, who owns it, and the vote date within two days.
Diana Harshbarger.personality: Harshbarger, from Tennessee, is quite reserved and a little less practical than most. Her public focus is among the narrowest in the chamber, and her bills span far fewer areas than most. Details are a bit looser in her talk, and her follow through on bills trails most colleagues. Public attention rarely finds her, even for a role that carries weight.
Diana Harshbarger.speaks: Her public words stay on a narrower set of issues than almost any colleague's, and she rarely ranges beyond them. She describes her work in less careful detail than most, and her talk stays short and plain. Few words go to broader causes, so her speech stays on the specifics of one area. Her public talk gives her work little elaboration, so listeners get the bottom line first.
Diana Harshbarger.decides: Before she takes a stance she asks whether it rests on clear results, and she responds most to what the policy delivers. Pressure from outside reaches her less than it reaches most, so a request must stand on its own. Her follow through is somewhat weak, so any choice needs a named owner plus a firm date to hold. She tends to judge a request by how it reads on paper, so a written case carries weight with her.

archetype.justification: She is very reserved, among the most careful in the chamber, and gives among the shortest interview answers.

Dina Titus.bottom_line: Bring a clear documented ask and let the case carry it, since pressure shifts her much less than most. Expect short answers rather than a long back and forth.
do: Lead with the specific ask and the evidence behind it
Give her time to answer, since her replies run short and slow
dont: Lean on outside supporters to win her over
Cut in before she finishes, since she rarely trails off
Dina Titus.warning_sign: She usually leaves the lead to others, so a quiet room is normal for her by default. If she stops engaging and says less than usual, she is pulling back from the point, so pause and ask one plain question.
Dina Titus.follow_up: Send her office a one page written summary of the ask within two days of the meeting.
Dina Titus.personality: Titus is reserved and curious at once. She ranges across a much broader set of topics than most colleagues, and she is more careful than nearly any member in the chamber. Agreeable in manner, she is difficult to rattle, which keeps pressure from getting to her. Across the aisle she works much less than most, and her bills touch somewhat more issue areas. Put together, she is a thorough legislator who brings wide knowledge to any room.
Dina Titus.speaks: Her talk is slow and unhurried, with short answers, and even her longest replies run briefer than most. She rarely trails off mid sentence. When a conversation speeds up, her replies arrive as rapid bursts of brief answers rather than extended argument. Her words carry little emotional charge, her pitch sounds somewhat flatter than usual, and she frames issues across a broad spread of topics.
Dina Titus.decides: She is agreeable and open to a clear case, but she is not moved by who is backing it. Backers do not carry much weight with her, since outside voices pull on her less than on most members. So a case that leans on backers will not carry her. Her bills reach somewhat more issue areas than usual. Seeing bills through is less reliable for her, so a commitment made in the room needs a date and an owner. In a hearing she is much less combative, so a firm written ask is what gets a yes that sticks.

archetype.justification: His words are warmer and more social than most, and his answers come in brisk bursts that stay on action.

Don Bacon.bottom_line: Bring one clear ask and leave him room to answer, since his replies come in short bursts.
do: Open with the people it helps, and name a shared contact
Frame the ask warmly around what it will get done
If he pauses partway through, let the silence run before you respond
dont: Read his easy agreement as a commitment that will hold
Pile on background detail, since his focus runs to what happens next
Don Bacon.warning_sign: He usually answers in quick bursts and stays agreeable, so his easy manner is the default. If his pauses grow longer and his tone flattens, he is less comfortable with the ask, so slow down and check what is holding him.
Don Bacon.follow_up: Send his staff a short note naming the outcome you agreed and the next step, by Friday.
Don Bacon.personality: Bacon is as conspicuous as almost any figure in the chamber, and his interest runs across an unusually wide set of issues. He is very curious and very agreeable, and his bills span more topics than nearly anyone's. His words are warmer and more social than most, but he is far less forceful in tone. In hearings he is far less confrontational than the typical member. Precision about his work is rarer for him than for nearly every colleague.
Don Bacon.speaks: He speaks across a very wide set of issues and offers less exact detail about his work than nearly every colleague. His language comes across as notably gentle, and his tone carries somewhat more emotion than most. Answers arrive in quick bursts of short replies, shorter than most, and he trails off less than most. Hearings find him much less combative than most members, and his pauses run somewhat longer between phrases.
Don Bacon.decides: Proposals are checked against how well they match the broad spread of topics he already handles. Public pressure has little pull on him, so momentum from outside will not carry an ask alone. Bringing bills across the finish line is less dependable than most, and he leads conversations less than most. So any commitment from him only lasts if someone is tasked with the follow through by a set date.

archetype.justification: He is very curious and very agreeable, and he speaks at a fast clip, faster than most.

Donald Beyer.bottom_line: Bring a short, direct ask, since his words are much less sharp than most. Confirm the next step in writing, since his bill follow through is weak.
do: Keep up his pace in the conversation, since he runs quicker than most
Ask him to join a public announcement, since he is somewhat visible
dont: Count on a verbal promise to carry a bill forward
Cut in on his quick points before he has finished, since his pauses are short
Donald Beyer.warning_sign: He usually talks fast with short pauses, so quick talk is normal for him by default. If he slows down and lets long silences run, he is weighing your point, so pause, let him finish, and then answer briefly.
Donald Beyer.follow_up: Send him a dated written list of the points agreed, within two days, and ask him to confirm it.
Donald Beyer.personality: Beyer is very curious and very agreeable, with a far broader set of topics in his talk than most colleagues. Details come less carefully from him than from most members, and his descriptions of work lack precision. His words are much less sharp than most, yet they carry more emotional weight than nearly any member's. Bills from his office span much more issue areas than most, but follow-through lags. He represents Virginia.
Donald Beyer.speaks: Pace runs quicker than most, with shorter pauses between phrases and a volume that swings somewhat more than most. Pitch swings more than nearly anyone's in the House. Words from him are much less sharp than most and carry more emotional weight than nearly any member's. Coverage spans a far broader set of issues, and descriptions of work come with less careful detail than most.
Donald Beyer.decides: He is very curious and very agreeable, so an ask that opens a new line of thinking will get a fair hearing. His bills span much more issue areas than most. That lets a request span several of them. Follow-through is much weaker than most, so a commitment made in the room needs a dated owner to hold. A written follow up matters more than a verbal promise.

archetype.justification: He crosses party lines more readily than almost every colleague, and he is far less easily flustered than the typical member.

Donald Davis.bottom_line: Bring a colleague from across the aisle into the conversation early, since he already works that way.
do: Start with a friendly exchange before the ask
Give him room to finish his longer pauses before you speak
Ask whether the bill has a vote date and confirm it in writing
dont: Interrupt his long pauses to fill the silence
Read his outgoing manner as a settled yes
Donald Davis.warning_sign: A general meeting will not tell you when his long pauses start to shorten. Usually he weighs each answer in silence, so a change in that rhythm is the signal worth watching. Then name one concrete step to take before the meeting closes.
Donald Davis.follow_up: Email his staff, within two days, the agreed step, the person who owns it, and the due date in writing.
Donald Davis.personality: Davis has a very outgoing manner and is among the hardest members to fluster, and he finds common ground with the other side more than nearly any colleague. His legislation spans a few more issue areas than the average member, and he sees it through with dependable follow up. His public talk about the job is careful and detailed, and his language carries a touch more feeling. Visibility sits lower than his role might suggest, and he represents North Carolina.
Donald Davis.speaks: He moves slowly through his sentences, leaving longer gaps between phrases than nearly any colleague. His volume stays a bit more even than usual, and his tone shifts up and down a little. When he explains the work, his language is careful and detailed, and it covers a bit broader set of topics than most. Pace and pauses together give his answers a patient feel, and he talks through his points without rushing.
Donald Davis.decides: Requests rise or fall on whether the other side will share it and whether it sits inside an area he already works in. A joint ask with a colleague from the other side carries more weight with him. Pressure from home moves him more strongly than it moves many peers, so a visible local voice can shift his view. A decision holds when someone owns the next step, since bills he has carried to passage make follow through matter.

archetype.justification: Very curious and loose with specifics, he ranges somewhat more broadly across public issues than most of his colleagues.

Donald Norcross.bottom_line: Center the case on who it helps, and ask for one trackable step. Outside pressure reaches him a little less, so bring a plan he can hold you to.
do: Name the people the policy helps and the evidence behind them
Ask for a clear answer on the one step he can commit to
dont: Rush the decision, since outside pressure reaches him a little less
Let a pause stretch into a no without a follow up
Donald Norcross.warning_sign: By default he is far more combative than the typical member in hearings, so sharp exchanges are normal for him. If he drops that edge and goes quiet, he is losing interest, so ask one direct question and wait for the answer.
Donald Norcross.follow_up: Send his staff a written list of the agreed step, its date, and its owner.
Donald Norcross.personality: Norcross has a very curious mind, though specifics stay loose. He gets worked up easily, and in hearings he is far more combative than the usual member. Few colleagues are less dependable at following bills through, and he also speaks with somewhat less feeling than most. His visibility is much lower than most members', and he keeps his public profile modest. New Jersey is his state.
Donald Norcross.speaks: His pace runs well slower than the usual member, and his pauses stretch somewhat longer. His volume rises and falls a great deal, while his pitch stays a little flatter than most. When he describes his own work, the terms are less careful and detailed than most members use. In hearings he is far more combative than the typical colleague.
Donald Norcross.decides: He weighs an ask on the people it helps and on whether the next step holds. Keeping bills on track is a weaker point for him, so he is slow to commit until someone checks each step. Since outside pressure reaches him a little less than most members do, a campaign from home carries less weight than a case built on facts. A commitment from him holds only when each dated step gets checked.

archetype.justification: She is somewhat reserved and fairly careful and orderly, talks at a slower pace, and is seldom visible among colleagues.

Doris Matsui.bottom_line: Bring a case built on the people it helps and let her weigh it. Outside pushes carry a little less weight with her, so patience beats urgency.
do: Bring the people your ask helps into the first conversation
Give her time to weigh the facts before you ask for a decision
Expect a much less combative hearing manner from her than from colleagues
Bring a colleague to speak for the ask, since she is seldom visible
dont: Take her reserve as a sign she agrees
Rely on outside pressure to hurry her decision
Doris Matsui.warning_sign: In hearings she is usually much less combative, so a sharper tone is the change to watch. If she turns pointed in a hearing, she is pressing a real objection, so let her finish and answer the specific point.
Doris Matsui.follow_up: Give her staff a brief written recap that names the people the ask helps, plus a reply date.
Doris Matsui.personality: Matsui is fairly curious and fairly careful, and she keeps her work organized. She is somewhat reserved, and her public language is low in emotional charge compared with colleagues. In hearings she stays much less combative than colleagues, and she is seldom visible for her role. She has served in the House for many years and represents California, which gives her long experience in the chamber.
Doris Matsui.speaks: Floor recordings show her at a slower pace than colleagues, with a pitch that stays flat. Emotional charge runs low in her public language, so delivery stays cool even when the topic is charged. Loudness varies somewhat more than usual, which gives sentences a contour even while the pitch stays put. Recorded audio comes from floor sessions only, so these traits describe that setting.
Doris Matsui.decides: Her test of an ask is whether the people it helps stay at the center. Outside voices pushing hard weigh less with her than a clear case does. Being seldom visible for her role, she does not weigh an ask by how much attention it draws. So she commits once the people behind an ask are named and a next step is set.

archetype.justification: Very outgoing and very curious, with upbeat social talk and bills that reach a broader range of issues than most.

Dusty Johnson.bottom_line: Bring the ask with people he knows, and let him talk it through. He holds firm once he has taken a position, so outside pressure moves him less than most.
do: Ask him to talk through the plan out loud before you present
Share the written technical detail before the meeting
When he is challenged, expect him to hold his position
dont: Count on bipartisan cosponsors to carry the ask
Assume his upbeat, social manner means easy agreement
Dusty Johnson.warning_sign: He usually talks in an outgoing, social way and digs in when challenged. If he goes quiet and stops defending his view, he is losing interest, so bring one concrete fact that narrows the ask.
Dusty Johnson.follow_up: Send a short written note after the meeting that names the next step and who in his office owns it.
Dusty Johnson.personality: Johnson comes across as very outgoing and very curious, and he is fairly agreeable. His words are upbeat and social to an unusual degree. He is hard to rattle under questioning. Bills he sponsors span far more issues than most members. Cooperation across the aisle runs far less than most. He stands out for his role in the House. Public exposure for his role is high.
Dusty Johnson.speaks: His work talk is somewhat more precise than most, and his tone sounds upbeat and social. His language carries less feeling than most colleagues. In conversation his answers come in quick bursts more than most, and he uses little filler. His delivery runs slower than most colleagues, with a pitch that stays flatter than most. He digs in when challenged.
Dusty Johnson.decides: He asks of any request whether it suits the wide range of issues his bills already touch. Who will back it in person also counts. He works across the aisle far less than most, so a bipartisan case will not carry him alone. Outside pressure moves him less than most, and he holds a position once he takes it. An ask needs written detail and a clear owner to stick.

archetype.justification: Broad in his talk and his issue list, he works with the other side much less than most and follows bills through less reliably.

Dwight Evans.bottom_line: Bring one short ask with a dated written next step, since pressure moves him less than most members.
do: Send the ask in writing before the meeting
Tie the ask to outside groups already backing it
Look for a partner across the aisle before you ask him
dont: Count on outside pressure to close the deal
Assume a verbal yes will carry through to the vote
Dwight Evans.warning_sign: Public appearances alone will not reveal how he weighs a request. Ask his staff how the last similar item moved and what step came next.
Dwight Evans.follow_up: When the session ends, hand his team one page covering the ask, the step after, and who owns it by a set date.
Dwight Evans.personality: Evans covers more issues in his public talk than nearly anyone in the House. He describes his own work with less care for detail than most, and he works with the other side far less than most colleagues. His bills span more areas than nearly anyone's, and his public presence stays small for the job he holds. Reliability at seeing bills through runs much lower than most, which shapes how far to trust a promise.
Dwight Evans.speaks: His public talk spans more topics than nearly anyone in the House does. He describes his own work in looser, less detailed terms than most colleagues. Listeners tend to get the big picture first, and the specifics come later. His points stay broad rather than fixed to one item, and his manner in the room is open and loose. Listeners hear the wide view before the particulars.
Dwight Evans.decides: Its fit with the wide range of issues he already carries decides how he sees a request. He is slow to back something without a clear path to a vote. Appeals from advocacy groups move him less than they move the typical colleague, so a push counts for less. His follow-through is much less dependable than most. A decision sticks only when a named staffer tracks the next vote.

archetype.justification: His careful, detailed talk and wide-ranging bills set him apart, and his interview answers run longer than most.

Earl Carter.bottom_line: Outside voices sway him far less than most, so the ask itself has to carry the weight. Do not count on repetition to settle the question.
do: Confirm the room, the time, and who will attend
Open with the question itself, then wait for his short reply
Give his longer answers room, since they run longer than most
Confirm the next step and the owner before you leave
dont: Count on a follow-up call to change a firm answer
Read a quiet meeting as a refusal
Ask him for a new bill before the last one has a written plan
Earl Carter.warning_sign: He usually answers in quick bursts, much more than most. If those bursts stop and he speaks in one unbroken stretch, he is working through a point he has not settled. Ask which part is still open, then take that point first.
Earl Carter.follow_up: Send his staff a short note within a few days that restates his answer in your own words.
Earl Carter.personality: Carter is quite reserved and a little practical. Careful detail comes much less naturally to him than to most colleagues. Yet his public talk is much more careful and detailed than most. Follow-through on bills is fairly reliable for him. His legislation spans somewhat more policy areas than most, and his talk ranges across somewhat wider issues than most. Quick bursts of brief replies come more easily to him than to most members.
Earl Carter.speaks: In interviews his replies come in quick bursts more than most, yet his answers run somewhat longer than most. His pace runs somewhat quicker than most, and his pauses are much shorter than most. His volume holds a somewhat more even level than most. Filler turns up somewhat more often than most. Keep your own points brief so the exchange keeps its quick rhythm.
Earl Carter.decides: His follow-through on bills is fairly dependable, so a yes from him is worth securing. Once he agrees, put the bill's next vote on your calendar and check its status before each deadline. Share that calendar entry with his staff, so both offices track the same date. At the end, ask which step of the plan he wants checked again.

archetype.justification: Very curious and very careful, and broad in his talk and bills, he fits the Owl's watchful style.

Ed Case.bottom_line: Bring written technical evidence ahead and let him read at his own pace. Outside voices sway him more than most, so outside support is worth building early.
do: Send the technical brief ahead so he can read it first
Invite questions about the technical detail, since curiosity drives him
dont: Walk out with the vote plan still unsettled
Skip theatrics in a hearing, since he avoids open combat
Ed Case.warning_sign: In a hearing he usually stays off the attack and keeps his points tied to the record. If he turns openly combative, the room has moved against him, so stop adding material and ask which point he disputes.
Ed Case.follow_up: Send his staff a written note with the vote date and each open action within two days.
Ed Case.personality: Case is quite reserved in manner yet very curious, and his work is careful and organized. He covers a much broader set of topics than most, and his talk about the work carries somewhat more detail than most. Bills reach a somewhat wider set of areas than most, and public visibility sits a little lower than most colleagues'. He represents Hawaii.
Ed Case.speaks: He speaks in an unhurried way, with long gaps between phrases, and his loudness swings more widely than nearly any colleague's. Pitch moves a little more than most. He gives the work somewhat more textured, detailed treatment than most, and his public language carries less charge than most. In hearings he stays off the attack much more than most, and he keeps the topics plain even as they widen.
Ed Case.decides: He weighs written evidence closely and moves more when outside voices back him than when asked directly. His interests run across a wide field, so an ask that fits one of them lands. Support that arrives in writing and from outside groups moves him, so a decision follows the evidence he has in hand. Technical material that anticipates his questions helps him reach a yes.

archetype.justification: He is very curious, among the most upbeat in the Senate, and fairly outgoing, so Orca fits best across his traits.

Edward Markey.bottom_line: Offer a shared role he can lead or announce. Outside calls shift him less than most, so the case has to hold on its merits.
do: Match his upbeat energy in the first minute
Let his long answers finish before you respond
Answer his pushback point by point, without raising the stakes
Bring background that backs each point, since he is curious and defends his view
dont: Assume outside calls will shift his position
Treat his gentler public wording as agreement
Edward Markey.warning_sign: He usually talks fast, digs in when challenged, and pauses only fleetingly between phrases. When those pauses vanish and he presses the same point again, he is usually on guard, so stop and ask one direct question about the point at issue.
Edward Markey.follow_up: By Friday, put the shared role and the one question he needs answered into a brief written note, copied to his staff lead.
Edward Markey.personality: Markey brings a very curious mind and fairly outgoing manner, with words among the most upbeat and forceful in the Senate. Skepticism sits deep, and specifics get a little less care from him than most. Public wording comes across gentler than most, yet in conversation he defends views hard. Working across the aisle comes less easily to him than to most, and once he has stated a view he holds it firmly. Turns run long and unbroken, with almost no filler.
Edward Markey.speaks: He talks fast and in a bright, forceful voice, with his pitch rising and falling more than nearly anyone's. Pauses between phrases are short, and his volume rises and falls. His answers run long and vary in length, with little filler. He ranges over a somewhat broader field of topics than most colleagues, and he gives less specific detail about his own work than most. Under challenge he restates his view with more force, not less.
Edward Markey.decides: He weighs an ask on its merits, and outside lobbying shifts his judgment much less than it shifts colleagues. Skepticism runs deep, so he asks for proof before he moves. He takes a stance and holds it when challenged, so pushing him off a position only hardens him. A visible shared role suits how he commits, so his yes holds when he can lead or announce the result.

archetype.justification: Her talk covers more ground than almost anyone, and she is very curious and careful.

Eleanor Norton.bottom_line: Give her a written case with one narrow next step and room for longer answers. Outside pressure moves her less than nearly anyone, so the case must carry itself.
do: Lead with the written case, since she is very curious about the detail
Give her room to finish, since her answers run much longer than most
Ask her to name the one narrow next step, since she takes charge of talk
Expect a gentle tone from her in hearings
dont: Count on a fast answer, since her pace is among the slowest
Lean on warm small talk, since her words run somewhat cooler than most
Eleanor Norton.warning_sign: When a question presses her, she usually lengthens her answers and lets turns trail off. Wait for the end of each turn, then restate the one narrow ask in a single sentence.
Eleanor Norton.follow_up: Afterward, send a written note with the one narrow ask, the evidence behind it, and a dated step.
Eleanor Norton.personality: Norton comes across as quite reserved yet very curious, and her talk covers more ground than almost anyone's. Public wording from her runs somewhat cooler than most, and she is a bit harder to rattle. Her bills span among the widest areas in the chamber. Reaching across the aisle is something she does far less than most colleagues. She has a name for being very careful and organized, yet her account of her own work is much less exact than most. Filler barely appears in her talk, well under what nearly anyone shows, and her answers run much longer than most.
Eleanor Norton.speaks: Her talk ranges across more subjects than nearly anyone around her. She is among the slowest talkers in the chamber, and her pauses run much longer than most. Pitch is much flatter than most, while volume holds somewhat more even than most. Answers run much longer than most, and their length varies among the most in the chamber. In hearings her combative streak runs far below the usual level, and she speaks with little filler.
Eleanor Norton.decides: Narrowness and good documentation decide how she rates an ask. Her bills cover among the broadest sets of issues in the chamber, so a request in those areas fits. Across the aisle, she works much less than most, so a bipartisan push alone will not carry her. Outside pressure moves her among the least of any member, so her own read decides. A commitment from her holds when the next step carries her name and a date.

archetype.justification: He is much sharper than most in hearings, his volume varies more than most, and he is among the most reliable at seeing bills through.

Elijah Crane.bottom_line: Lead with the written technical case, since it is the form that fits him best.
do: Send written technical evidence ahead, with each claim listed once
Open with the technical question you want answered, stated in one line
Keep your tone even in formal settings where his questions run much sharper than most
Close with a named owner and a date for the next written step
dont: Read floor volume swings as a guide to his follow-through, since he sees bills through
Lead with results or stories about families, since neither frame fits him
Raise a brand-new ask for the first time at a formal hearing
Elijah Crane.warning_sign: At hearings, his tone usually runs sharper than most. If his questions turn harder than that usual edge, his patience with the substance is running out. Cut the ask down to a single next step, and ask which point he disputes.
Elijah Crane.follow_up: Send written answers to his legislative staff within a few days, numbered by question, each tied to the written review it answers.
Elijah Crane.personality: Crane runs among the most practical colleagues in the House. He is much looser on detail than most, yet his talk about work is careful and detailed. His talk covers a far narrower set of topics. On votes he is among the most reliable in the House. Few match the feeling in his words, and he is much quicker than most to get heated. He is a notch more visible than most in his role.
Elijah Crane.speaks: His volume swings more than most colleagues' on the House floor, and his pitch sits much flatter than most. His floor pauses between phrases run a little shorter than most. When he describes his work, his words are careful and detailed, well ahead of most colleagues. In hearings he is much more combative than most. Put the detail in writing, since he is exact when he talks about bills.
Elijah Crane.decides: A technical case built around a clear written structure is what moves him. Pressure from outside carries more weight with him than most members do, so keep the written case open to his staff's checks. Few in the House match his follow-through, so his yes can be relied on. Give him time to read the written case before you ask for a view. Ask him to mark the draft wherever he disagrees.

archetype.justification: Her very outgoing, warm word choice and high public visibility fit a sociable, out front member.

Elise Stefanik.bottom_line: Open with the measure's concrete benefits, and expect her to take the floor. Outside pressure moves her far less than typical members, so results do the persuading.
do: Open with the result and the number behind it
Let her take the floor early, then ask for a clear next step
Pitch the ask as a visible win she can announce
dont: Assume her fast pace signals agreement
Lean on outside pressure to move her
Elise Stefanik.warning_sign: By default she takes charge of the conversation and talks fast, so a sudden slowdown is the sign she is on guard. When you see it, stop talking, let her finish, and then ask for the one next step.
Elise Stefanik.follow_up: Within a week, deliver to her office a single page brief on the outcome and the next action, naming an owner.
Elise Stefanik.personality: Stefanik is a warm, outgoing member who likes to lead a conversation and keeps her answers short. She holds details loosely, and her public words lean toward social themes rather than specifics. Visibility ranks near the top, but follow through on bills sits near the bottom of the House. Worked up a little quicker than most, her warmth shows in the room.
Elise Stefanik.speaks: Pace runs among the quickest in the House, and pauses between phrases are brief. Pitch stays nearly flat, and volume varies less than most. Answers run short, and the longest ones are shorter than most. Warm, social word choice sits well apart from action talk, and remarks stay on results. In hearings, combativeness sits below typical, so the tone stays civil.
Elise Stefanik.decides: She weighs an ask by what it delivers, and a case built on results fits her best. Pressure from outside moves her far less than typical members, so a push from others does little on its own. Her follow through on bills sits near the bottom, so a commitment from her needs a named person who checks it. A short ask backed by results gets the most traction with her.

archetype.justification: She is very outgoing and very curious, and few colleagues match how often she joins work across the aisle.

Elissa Slotkin.bottom_line: Bring credible voices from outside her office, since pressure from those voices tends to shift her.
do: Open with what the policy delivers, backed by hard results and facts
Name the colleagues from the other party who already back the ask
Line up outside supporters before the ask reaches her staff
dont: Take her upbeat tone as a yes on substance
Interrupt her answers, which run a little longer than typical
Elissa Slotkin.warning_sign: She usually talks fast and upbeat, with plenty of filler. If she slows and her voice goes flat, she is guarded or losing interest, so lead with your next point and ask what would make it workable.
Elissa Slotkin.follow_up: Mail her staff a single written page of results and facts by the end of the week, naming the step and who owns it.
Elissa Slotkin.personality: Slotkin strikes people as very outgoing and very curious, with a little doubt in her outlook and a quicker than usual readiness to feel stirred up. Her public language is gentle in confrontation but cooler in warmth, and it leans upbeat and focused on action. Descriptions of her own work are less precise and less detailed than most, yet she reaches across party lines more than nearly anyone in her chamber. Her votes and bills are somewhat less dependable than most, and her public presence is somewhat more noticeable than her role alone would suggest.
Elissa Slotkin.speaks: Her delivery runs much faster than most, with unusually short pauses between phrases and a tone that holds much flatter than most. Replies run a little longer in conversation, and she fills gaps with discourse markers much more often than colleagues do. Her words sound upbeat and focused on action, while their warmth runs much cooler than most. When she talks about her own work, her detail is thinner than most colleagues'.
Elissa Slotkin.decides: Before she backs anything, she gauges how much it delivers and whether it can be built across the aisle. Curiosity draws her to new proposals, while skepticism means she wants results and facts before she commits. Her follow through on bills runs somewhat weaker than most, so a record of delivery matters to her. Outside pressure reaches her much more than most, so an ask gains traction when results, facts, and outside voices arrive together.

archetype.justification: She is among the most curious members in her chamber, holds conversations firmly, and gives brief answers.

Elizabeth Warren.bottom_line: Keep the ask short and tight, then answer her challenge head on, since she holds her ground when pushed.
do: Open with one short ask and leave room for her questions
Answer her challenge directly rather than restating your position
Name a written next step and the staffer who owns it
dont: Read her pushback as the end of the discussion
Fill her short answers with extra points
Elizabeth Warren.warning_sign: She usually defends her position hard when challenged, and her words run somewhat sharper than usual. When her rebuttals sharpen and the wording gets harsher, she is on guard, so acknowledge her point before you press further.
Elizabeth Warren.follow_up: Within two days, send her office a short memo that names the agreed step, its owner, and the deadline they set.
Elizabeth Warren.personality: Warren ranks with the most curious members in her chamber, and she holds the floor firmly in a conversation. Across a wide range of issues, she describes her work with less care than many colleagues. Easily stirred, she defends her position hard when challenged. Upbeat and action focused in her wording, she also has a high public profile. Her answers stay brief, so the exchange moves quickly once she has spoken.
Elizabeth Warren.speaks: She gives short answers, and even her longest replies run much shorter than usual. Given the floor, she holds it firmly and keeps pressing her point when challenged. Her words sound upbeat and focused on action, and they come across as much less social than usual. Volume stays somewhat more even than usual, while answer lengths shift from one turn to the next.
Elizabeth Warren.decides: Her measure is how neatly a request matches the broad set of issues she already covers. She is curious and likes to explore a question. Across the aisle she cooperates somewhat less than usual, so an ask that needs support from the other side may struggle. Outside pressure has a little less pull on her than on colleagues. Carrying bills to completion is somewhat weaker for her, so she needs a written next step. Her position hardens once challenged, so an ask has to hold up under pushback before she commits.

archetype.justification: His outgoing, agreeable manner and community focused talk fit an upbeat, sociable operator who speaks for people helped.

Emanuel Cleaver.bottom_line: Open with the people who gain, and keep your tone mild, since his words run gentle and he stays agreeable.
do: Lead with stories about who the program helps
Let him take charge of the discussion
Name the vote and the bill you need him to follow through on
dont: Mistake his long pauses for a lack of interest
Treat a hearing as a debate he must win
Emanuel Cleaver.warning_sign: He is usually slow, with pauses between phrases and a voice that rises and falls, so pauses are normal. If he starts replying in rapid bursts, his guard rises, so pause, restate the one point, and let him take his time.
Emanuel Cleaver.follow_up: Afterward, mail him a concise memo naming the measure, its outside supporters, and the one vote he will stand behind.
Emanuel Cleaver.personality: Cleaver shows very sociable and inquisitive traits, yet he is less easily flustered than his peers, so pressure does not easily knock him off his line. His legislation spans a wide set of issue areas, and his public talk ranges across them too. Beneath that breadth he keeps a careful, organized streak. A Missouri member on the Financial Services committee, his public profile is fairly high for his role.
Emanuel Cleaver.speaks: Delivery is among the slowest in the House, with lengthy lulls between clauses and a voice and pitch that rise and fall often. Answers from him run shorter than colleagues' and vary a good deal in length. He often trails off before finishing a thought. Public words run gentle, yet they carry a lot of emotional charge and a forceful edge.
Emanuel Cleaver.decides: Requests get sorted by who benefits, and the affected people count for more than the mechanics.
