Line up outside backers before the meeting, since pressure moves her
Match her slower pace and leave room between points
Expect a visible presence from her, and plan for firmer questions in hearings
dont: Assume her skepticism will give way after one meeting
Count on a long, detailed answer to win her over
Marsha Blackburn.warning_sign: She usually speaks sharply, so a softer edge in her wording is the signal. When that softening shows, she is weighing the point or growing wary. Ask one direct question and let her finish.
Marsha Blackburn.follow_up: Send her staff a short written summary with the ask, the evidence, and the next step with a date.
Marsha Blackburn.personality: Blackburn shows a fairly outgoing side, rouses a bit sooner than most, and words things more sharply than most. Skepticism runs deep, and her talk stays within a small set of policy areas. Her follow through trails nearly every colleague. Exposure runs fairly high relative to her role, and her public record shows a firm streak. She represents Tennessee. Her manner in the room comes across as direct.
Marsha Blackburn.speaks: She speaks slower than most, with a flatter pitch and volume that stays more even. Her replies come in far shorter than most colleagues'. Phrasing cuts harder than most, and emotional charge runs somewhat higher. Talk stays within a small set of policy areas. Hearings bring out somewhat more combativeness in her than in most members. Pitch stays flatter than most across the answer. Tone holds fairly even across an answer.
Marsha Blackburn.decides: A claim she can check against evidence is what earns an ask her notice. Pressure from outside groups moves her more than most, so visible support can shift her view. Her skepticism means she tests each claim, so a case that holds up under checking earns more weight. Her follow through trails nearly every colleague. A decision holds only when a named step and owner are written down.

archetype.justification: His emotionally charged words, people focused framing, and quick reactions fit a passionate, people focused member.

Martin Heinrich.bottom_line: Lead with the people a bill helps, and make the case personal. Pressure from outside carries real weight with him, so line up a broad base of support first.
do: Describe real families the bill would reach
Expect a sharper exchange in a hearing and prepare for it
Let him set the pace of the discussion, since he is fairly outgoing
dont: Expect a public launch to draw him in on its own
Rely on outside pressure to carry the vote
Martin Heinrich.warning_sign: By default he is fairly outgoing, so a lively tone is normal for him. In hearings, a sharper tone is the sign he is on guard, so acknowledge the people involved and offer one fact.
Martin Heinrich.follow_up: Within a week, write his staff a short note on the families the bill would reach, with the next step and a name.
Martin Heinrich.personality: Heinrich is a highly curious member who is fairly outgoing. He is quick to react when a point hits home, and his word choice carries far more feeling than typical. His follow through on bills is above typical, while he crosses party lines less often. Public talk reaches a broader set of topics than typical colleagues, and the tone leans toward feeling. His visibility runs far below his role, so he is less seen than typical.
Martin Heinrich.speaks: His talk runs across more topics than typical, so his remarks link one issue to the next. His words carry strong feeling, and that shows up in the choice of each phrase. Feeling is visible across topics, not only in one area. In hearings, combativeness runs a bit above typical, so his tone sharpens there. The feeling in his words is easy to hear from the first sentence.
Martin Heinrich.decides: He judges an ask by its human stakes, and a clear account of who gains earns his attention. Outside voices carry heavy weight with him, so a broad base of backers outweighs any single push. His follow through is fairly strong, so a commitment from him holds when the next step is named. His public presence is limited, so a decision from him needs a visible ally to carry it.

archetype.justification: She deals with the other side far more than most, and her public tone runs somewhat hotter than most.

Mary Miller.bottom_line: Bring one bill and its next written step with an owner and date. She works across the aisle much more than most, so a joint ask gets her attention.
do: Name the bill and the step you need from her office
Pair the ask with a colleague from the other side
dont: Leave a bill open without a date, since it will drift
Mary Miller.warning_sign: Brief encounters will not reveal whether she follows through on the bills she backed, so ask staff for each bill status first. Then name the one next step and the date in a line before you leave.
Mary Miller.follow_up: Send a short written note naming the bill, what happens next, and the deadline for her action.
Mary Miller.personality: Miller works with the other side much more than most, while her public words run somewhat hotter in tone than most. She follows bills through much less reliably than most, so commitments need a date. Public profile runs lower than most, and her talk about her work is less careful and detailed than nearly any member in the House. Her bills therefore get less public attention, and a date keeps them moving.
Mary Miller.speaks: Her public words roam a little wider across topics than most, but her accounts of bill steps are less exact than almost any colleague's. Language runs somewhat hotter than most, and her tone reads as more passionate than the bill text itself. She speaks with that heat in public, and the details tend to come second to the point she wants made. That describes how her words sound, not how she votes.
Mary Miller.decides: A joint ask earns her attention, while a bill left without a date drifts for her. Her public profile is lower than most, so a joint request carries more weight than a quiet one. Outside voices reach her more than they reach most, so a visible push can change her mind. An ask without a date or a partner loses its place on her list.

archetype.justification: Her very curious outlook, fairly careful organized habits, and reserved manner fit a deliberate member.

Mary Scanlon.bottom_line: Offer a shared role that gives her something to announce together with you. Pressure from outside moves her less than most, so the role carries the ask.
do: Open with the facts behind the role she can announce with you
Keep your opening short, since her own answers run brief
Ask a direct question, then wait, since she talks quickly
dont: Assume her quick talk settles the point
Lean on outside pressure to change her view
Mary Scanlon.warning_sign: By default she is very curious and talks quickly, so a quick run of questions is her normal style. When she goes quiet and her skepticism shows, she is on guard, so return to the facts and invite her to test them.
Mary Scanlon.follow_up: Within two days, send her office the facts you cited, with the shared role spelled out in one line.
Mary Scanlon.personality: Scanlon is a very curious member with a careful, organized approach, and she is quite skeptical. Her public talk spans topics well beyond typical colleagues, and her bills reach somewhat more issue areas. Teamwork across parties is uncommon for her compared with most colleagues, and her follow through is somewhat less dependable than typical. Public words are among the most social in the House, and her exposure runs a bit above her role.
Mary Scanlon.speaks: She talks a bit faster than most, and her volume stays much more even than typical. Pauses are a little shorter than most, and pitch stays a bit flatter than most. Answers are brief, and the longest ones run among the shortest in the House. Work gets described in broad terms, and the talk does not stay on one topic for long. In hearings she is a bit more combative than most, so her tone sharpens there.
Mary Scanlon.decides: Her attention goes to requests whose facts survive her own probing questions, and to cases that fully resolve her lingering doubts before she commits. Outside pressure carries less weight with her, so a push from others does not settle things on its own. Her ties across the aisle run thin, so a commitment from her needs a named check on the next step.

archetype.justification: Covers broader ground than most colleagues and gives less detail than almost anyone, which fits a busy, loose style.

Matt Van Epps.bottom_line: Lead with results and what the policy delivers, since pressure from outside reaches him a little less than most colleagues.
do: Open with the outcome in your first sentence
Let him finish a long pause before you respond
Name a staff contact who will carry the next step
dont: Rely on outside pressure to carry the decision
Matt Van Epps.warning_sign: A general meeting will not tell you where he stands, since early reactions are hard to read. Ask him which figure would change his view, then send exactly that figure in writing.
Matt Van Epps.follow_up: After the meeting, email his staff the agreed next step with a name and a date, then confirm receipt the same day.
Matt Van Epps.personality: Van Epps covers broader ground than most colleagues, with less detail than most colleagues and a more muted emotional tone than most. He is among the least reliable members at votes and bill follow through, and he is much less visible than most for his role. His style reads as busy and loose, and it covers a lot of ground without much depth.
Matt Van Epps.speaks: His public talk covers broader ground than most colleagues and goes into less detail than almost anyone's. His pace sits near the bottom of the chamber, with longer pauses between phrases and a volume that climbs and drops much more than most. Pitch shifts more than most colleagues', so his delivery has a lot of movement. In short, his delivery is animated and wide reaching.
Matt Van Epps.decides: Before he backs anything he needs clear results and someone to own the next step. Pressure from outside reaches him a little less than most colleagues, so pressure from back home carries less weight with him than the facts do. He is among the least reliable members at votes and bill follow through, so a commitment without a named owner tends to drift. So a decision holds only when a named person carries the next step.

archetype.justification: Among the most skeptical members, with looser details and sharp, emotionally charged wording.

Max Miller.bottom_line: Hold the ask to one line and bring the detail that backs it. He is skeptical, so back the line with facts he can verify.
do: Put the verifiable facts in writing before the meeting
Let him test each fact before he commits
dont: Match his sharp wording with sharper wording of your own
Treat outside pressure as a side issue in your plan
Max Miller.warning_sign: His usual pattern is sharp wording and loose details, so a blunt remark alone means little. Watch for him going quiet on a point he had been pressing, which usually means he is weighing your answer rather than dismissing it.
Max Miller.follow_up: Within a day, hand him the facts behind the ask and the one point he pressed, laid out in a written note.
Max Miller.personality: Miller is fairly outgoing, counts among the most skeptical members in the House, and flares up much faster than most. Phrasing from him cuts sharper than nearly any colleague's, while the emotional weight in his wording is intense. His legislative footprint is somewhat narrower than most, and he follows through on what he takes up. Visibility for his post is noticeable, so he is a dependable operator who keeps to the bills he has taken on.
Max Miller.speaks: His language is cutting, with more emotional charge than most, and he does not soften a point easily. Public explanations go into much more careful detail than most, so sharpness comes with specifics rather than vague complaint. He pushes a case with pointed language and then backs it with careful detail, so his manner is forceful but firmly grounded in detail.
Max Miller.decides: He weighs an ask by testing the facts first, since he is among the most skeptical members in the House and wants proof. After he backs a measure, he sees it through, so a yes from him carries real weight. Pressure from outside pushes him harder than most members, so a decision holds only when the facts still stand after that pressure.

archetype.justification: Fairly outgoing and easily stirred, she stays on a narrow range of issues and keeps a low public profile.

Maxine Dexter.bottom_line: Bring a tight, specific ask she can own publicly, and keep the scope inside a few areas she already works on.
do: Offer a shared public moment she can co-sign
Show how the bill matches her existing record
Set a clear next step with a date so the follow through holds
Open with a warm, friendly exchange before you reach the ask
dont: Lean on a long list of issues rather than one focused case
Maxine Dexter.warning_sign: Usually she is one of the gentlest in hearings and talks at a brisk clip, so a turn toward a harder tone signals she is on guard. Slow down, restate the one ask, and give her room to think.
Maxine Dexter.follow_up: Send her team a brief note naming the one request, its date, and the name of the owner.
Maxine Dexter.personality: Dexter is fairly outgoing, though her public words carry little emotional charge. She works within a narrow set of issues and draws a little less attention than most. She is a touch loose on details, though her votes and bills show fair dependability. In hearings her manner is about as gentle as the chamber gets. Those traits describe a focused legislator who draws modest notice.
Maxine Dexter.speaks: Pace runs a notch quicker than the average member's. Volume swings a bit more than typical. Pitch stays flatter than most, and public language reads lower in emotion than most. She stays on a narrow set of issues, and in hearings she stays low key. Her delivery is brisk in conversation. Plain, specific word choice dominates, with less appeal to large themes.
Maxine Dexter.decides: Her bar is whether a request sits inside the few areas she covers and whether she can present it with colleagues. Pressure from outside has a smaller pull on her, so a single push will not change her answer. Her record on votes is fairly dependable, which means a yes from her usually sticks. An agreement that names an owner and a date tends to hold for her.

archetype.justification: She speaks with more force than most, and she holds the floor more firmly than nearly any colleague.

Maxine Waters.bottom_line: Lead with the people a policy would help, since community impact fits her best, and expect sharp replies if you disagree.
do: Bring people the policy would help and let them speak first
Let her finish her longer answers before you respond
dont: Match her sharpness with sharpness of your own
Interrupt her longer answers before she finishes her point
Expect easy agreement, since she is skeptical by default
Maxine Waters.warning_sign: By default she holds the floor firmly and finishes her sentences. If she stops pressing her point and turns to questions, she is weighing your case or wary of it, so answer with the facts and let her finish.
Maxine Waters.follow_up: Mail her a short page recapping who was helped and the next action, with a date for each.
Maxine Waters.personality: Waters is very curious, and her public words cover many issues, more than nearly any colleague. Tone cuts sharper than nearly any peer, and she is easily stirred, far more than most. Her words carry more feeling than almost anyone's, and she is much warmer than most. Details get looser handling from her than from most, and her bills span many issues. Holding the floor comes easily to her, and she gives shorter answers than most.
Maxine Waters.speaks: In interviews her answers vary in length more than almost anyone's, and her longest ones run longer than most. Her pace is much slower than most, and her pauses run longer than most. Her volume swings more than most, while pitch stays flatter than most. Most of her recorded speech comes from the floor, and feeling shows in her language more than in her delivery.
Maxine Waters.decides: Pressure from outside moves her more than most colleagues, so backing from outside voices carries weight. She weighs an ask by who it helps, since community impact fits her best. Her bills span many issues, so she also weighs how an ask fits the wider areas it touches. A plan that ties the ask to those people gives her a clear reason to act, and a case built on the people affected is what moves her.

archetype.justification: His very outgoing manner, fast pace and long answers fit the Terrier label.

Maxwell Frost.bottom_line: Keep the ask focused and let him talk it through, since he speaks at length. Outside calls carry less force with him, so back the ask with the record.
do: Lead with a tight argument on what the policy actually produces
Let him finish, since he speaks quickly and often trails off
Confirm the next step in writing, since follow through runs a little lower for him
dont: Mistake his outgoing manner for a firm promise
Press hard on a point, since he gets worked up easily
Maxwell Frost.warning_sign: He usually speaks fast and tends to trail off into unfinished thoughts. If he starts finishing every sentence and his words slow, he is weighing the ask, so pause, ask one plain question, and let him finish.
Maxwell Frost.follow_up: Put the agreed next step in writing for his office, naming the staffer who follows up and the due date.
Maxwell Frost.personality: Frost stands among the most outgoing members in the House and is quick to react with heat. His talk covers a far narrower set of issues than most, while his work comes across in less detailed terms than most. Emotional charge runs somewhat lower in his words, and his wording is less social than most colleagues. He answers quickly and often leaves a thought unfinished.
Maxwell Frost.speaks: Turns come quickly, and his pace is among the fastest in the chamber. His longest replies stretch far longer than most, and his answer length keeps a more level shape than most. He trails off much more than usual, and filler creeps in more than most. Volume stays level from start to finish, while pitch swings wider than most, and his words sound pointed when he pushes.
Maxwell Frost.decides: He weighs an ask by results and by how far it fits the narrow set of issues he already works on. His bills cover far fewer topics than most, so an ask inside those areas fits. Outside voices count for less with him, so the record carries the decision. So a decision from him needs a record that holds up under close reading.

archetype.justification: Curious and quite skeptical, she is forceful, pushes back hard when challenged, and talks about a wide range of issues.

Mazie Hirono.bottom_line: Show the backing from the other side behind the ask, and keep your points tight. Her short replies leave little room for a long case.
do: Open with a concrete story about who the policy helps
Name the colleagues across the aisle who already back the bill
Answer each challenge directly, since her wording is sharp and she defends her position hard
dont: Assume she will ignore public pressure, since it moves her more than most
Count on long answers from her, since her replies run short
Mazie Hirono.warning_sign: She usually defends her position hard when challenged, so a firm reply is normal for her. If her tone hardens and she drops a point, she is on guard and irritated. Pause and ask which part of the case she wants checked.
Mazie Hirono.follow_up: Send her a short written summary that names the backers across the aisle and the people the policy helps, within a week.
Mazie Hirono.personality: Hirono is curious and quite skeptical, and she holds her ground hard. Issue coverage is far broader than most, and reaching across the aisle comes much more often to her than to most. Steering conversations and taking the floor come readily to her, and her replies come out short. Her words sound forceful and social, though cool and flat in tone, and she is fairly visible. When challenged, she digs in harder than almost anyone, and she gets worked up a little more than most.
Mazie Hirono.speaks: She talks across a wide set of issues, and her language carries a bit more feeling than most, though her tone stays flat. Replies come short and clipped, and she rarely stops mid thought. She pauses only briefly between phrases, and her volume and pitch hold even. When challenged, she digs in and defends her point firmly. Her longest answers stay brief compared with most.
Mazie Hirono.decides: The people an ask helps count with her, and so does who else already backs it. Pressure from outside can shift her, and support from across the aisle carries real weight with her. Concrete stories about who a bill reaches count for more than figures alone. Once she has stated a position, she defends it hard, so pushing early only hardens her.

archetype.justification: She is fairly outgoing and fairly visible, and she is more visible in her role than most.

Melanie Stansbury.bottom_line: Keep the ask practical and direct, and make the case on what it delivers. Hearings bring out a much more combative side in her, so keep formal settings tight.
do: Propose a joint announcement she can carry, timed to her calendar
Open with the practical result the plan delivers, in one sentence
Keep your reply brief in formal settings when she presses a witness
Close by asking her to name the decision date aloud before you leave
dont: Hand over a long stack of papers before the meeting
Match her edge with an edge of your own
Take a warm welcome as agreement, since outside voices shift her positions more than most
Melanie Stansbury.warning_sign: She usually presses witnesses much harder than most. If she suddenly gives up a point she usually drives hard, she has stopped testing the answer. Leave a one-page summary with her staff, and let the answer stand for now.
Melanie Stansbury.follow_up: Send her chief of staff a brief note within a week, naming the joint role and one next step.
Melanie Stansbury.personality: Stansbury is fairly outgoing, and her role keeps her in view more than most. Skepticism runs deep in her, and few colleagues are as hard to win over. She leans practical, and detail work is less of a strength for her. She runs hot much more readily than most members. Hearings draw out a far sharper side of her than most members show. Her public tone is sharper than most.
Melanie Stansbury.speaks: On the House floor she delivers at a far slower tempo than most speakers. Her pauses are a little shorter than most, and her volume shifts up and down somewhat more than most members. Pitch stays a little flatter than most. Her words carry far less feeling than most, and they land sharper than most. Let her complete each point before you reply.
Melanie Stansbury.decides: Outside groups move her more than most members, so line up outside voices well before the meeting. Ask which doubt she most needs settled, and answer that one first. Put the plan in clear, practical steps she can check. Once the joint role is on the table, answer her doubts with specifics, one at a time. Let her shape the wording of that role before anyone else sees it.

archetype.justification: He is reserved, speaks somewhat slowly, and keeps a low profile in the chamber.

Michael Baumgartner.bottom_line: Bring a short, precise case built on the facts and give him time to digest it. Outside pressure moves him less, so let the facts carry the ask.
do: Send the facts in writing before the meeting
Let him take the time he needs to answer
In a hearing, expect low key questions
Confirm the next step with a date and an owner
dont: Rush him with fast, data heavy talk
Count on outside pressure to move him quickly
Read his long pauses as disinterest
Michael Baumgartner.warning_sign: His usual pattern is slow, quiet talk with long pauses. In a hearing, when he presses harder than usual, he is working through the ask, so give him room and then ask one direct question.
Michael Baumgartner.follow_up: Put a short note in writing within two days naming the step, the owner, and the date for the next check.
Michael Baumgartner.personality: Baumgartner is reserved and very practical, with a narrow focus on the few issues he covers. He is notably less exact about details, and he is far harder to fluster than typical members. His own descriptions of his work are among the most precise in the chamber, and his speech carries less charge than most. Bills from him cover among the fewest issues in the chamber, and he is somewhat reliable at getting bills through. In hearings he is a touch less confrontational, and he keeps a low profile in public.
Michael Baumgartner.speaks: His pace runs a bit slow, and his pauses between phrases stretch much longer than most. Volume rises and falls a great deal, and the pitch shifts more than typical. His wording is somewhat less charged than most, and he goes into precise detail on his own work. In hearings he is a touch less confrontational, and his talk stays within a narrow set of topics. Everything recorded of him comes from floor speech, so these traits describe that setting.
Michael Baumgartner.decides: A request gets judged by how cleanly it fits the narrow issues he already covers. He is somewhat reliable at follow through on bills, so a dated commitment from him tends to hold. In hearings, a firm and courteous ask is the approach, since he is a touch less confrontational. Pressure from outside groups carries less pull on him, so a push from outside does not often change his view.

archetype.justification: His very curious manner, forceful wording and long answers earn the Terrier label.

Michael Bennet.bottom_line: Bring a clear case with a concrete next step, since he takes charge and presses his points. Outside voices move him more than most, so a named ally helps.
do: Lead with results and a plain next step
Let him make his case, since he takes charge of the room
Expect long answers and keep your reply tight
dont: Mistake his forceful wording for a final answer
Let a long exchange end without a named next step
Michael Bennet.warning_sign: He usually takes charge of a conversation and trails off into unfinished thoughts. If he starts completing his own sentences and yields the floor, he has grown guarded, so ease off, ask one plain question, and let him conclude.
Michael Bennet.follow_up: Afterward, mail a short memo covering the agreed next step, naming who follows up and the date due.
Michael Bennet.personality: Bennet tilts somewhat reserved and very curious, with an agreeable streak. Careful and organized, he carries far more feeling in his wording than most. Following through on bills ranks near the bottom in the Senate, and his work across the aisle trails well behind most colleagues. He leads conversations a bit more often than most colleagues, and his points come with forceful, long answers.
Michael Bennet.speaks: In interviews his replies stretch a notch past the usual length. His longest turns run further than usual. Length shifts from turn to turn more than nearly any senator's. He trails off much more than most, and fills gaps with filler somewhat more than most. Volume stays a little more level than most, while his pitch swings widely, and he makes his points with forceful, direct wording.
Michael Bennet.decides: He weighs an ask by results and by whether a cross aisle backer stands behind it. Bills span a little fewer areas than most, so an ask inside his areas fits. Outside voices move him more than most, so a named ally helps the ask. He wants the facts laid out before he commits. So he commits when the next step is named and the record is plain.

archetype.justification: Reserved and low profile, he pauses longer than most and works across party lines much less than most.

Michael Cloud.bottom_line: Bring a single, specific ask and secure a written next step, since he is less reliable at seeing bills through.
do: Name the decision date a week ahead
Let him take his time, since he speaks at a slower pace
dont: Count on him to carry a bill through without a reminder
Read his reserved manner as opposition to the bill
Michael Cloud.warning_sign: By default he presses a bit harder than most in hearings, so a hearing where he asks almost nothing usually means he has checked out. Let the pause run, ask one plain question, and wait for his next step before you push.
Michael Cloud.follow_up: Send a written recap naming the date and the owner of the next step, and copy his legislative staff.
Michael Cloud.personality: Cloud is somewhat reserved and not especially practical. Public talk spans a narrower set of issues, though his own descriptions of what he does run somewhat more careful than most. He rarely works across party lines, and his legislation covers slightly fewer topics. His follow through is somewhat weaker, and he keeps a low profile for his role. In hearings he runs a bit sharper than most members.
Michael Cloud.speaks: He speaks somewhat slowly, with longer pauses between phrases than most, and his volume swings much more than most. His public range is narrower than most, and his descriptions of his work run more detailed than most. Overall he sounds deliberate, and the detail carries most of the point. He pauses before he answers, so exchanges move at his pace rather than the room's.
Michael Cloud.decides: Prior to any support, he asks whether a bloc of his own allies already exists, since he rarely reaches across party lines. Pressure from outside sways him less than most, so a request built on outside voices carries less weight than a direct case. He keeps a low public profile, so a case that needs a public push finds little backing. His follow through is somewhat weaker, so a yes holds only when a dated written step is named.

archetype.justification: Reserved and very agreeable, he is rarely combative in hearings and keeps his commitments well.

Michael Guest.bottom_line: Bring a specific ask and agree a next step with a date. He is among the most reliable with bills, so a dated commitment tends to hold.
do: Bring a specific ask with a named next step and a date
Give him room to talk, since he ranks among the least outgoing
Expect him to stay much less combative than most in hearings
dont: Expect outside pressure to shift him as it shifts most members
Michael Guest.warning_sign: In hearings he is usually much less combative than most, so a sharper, more pointed tone from him is a change. If he gets pointed, slow down, ask what concerns him, and give him room to answer.
Michael Guest.follow_up: Send him a one page note with the ask, the next step and the owner by Friday.
Michael Guest.personality: Guest is very reserved, and he is somewhat practical with a looser grip on detail. He is very agreeable, and he gets ruffled somewhat less often than most. His account of his work is exacting, more than almost anyone's. The legislation he carries spans a much wider set of issues than most, and he is very dependable on bills he carries. Hearings bring out much less combativeness from him than most members.
Michael Guest.speaks: His public words run much gentler than most, and his remarks cover somewhat more issues. His pitch climbs and drops much more than most, while his pauses between phrases are somewhat shorter than most. In hearings his manner stays polite, and combat from him runs much lower than most members. When he discusses his work he is exact, more than almost anyone's in the chamber.
Michael Guest.decides: He first asks whether the work can be finished, and then he backs what he can deliver. His bills span many issue areas, so an ask inside one of those areas fits him. Outside pressure reaches him much less than most members, so he decides on the merits. Being very agreeable, he goes along with a dated commitment, so a decision with a named owner sticks.

archetype.justification: His very wide issue range, detailed talk about his work, and curious nature fit a wide ranging, analytical legislator.

Michael Lawler.bottom_line: Lead with one clear ask tied to a bill he has helped move. Pressure from outside gets a little more traction with him, once the ask is clear.
do: Bring the bill's record of votes and follow through
Point to the bills he has already joined with the other side
If he presses a point, reply with one specific fact
dont: Answer his sharper wording by matching its edge
Trust a quick verbal yes to hold through committee
Michael Lawler.warning_sign: Usually he talks fast and gives full answers, so a fast pace is no signal. If he starts trailing off and repeating his position, he is on guard, so let him finish, then reply with one fact and name who follows up.
Michael Lawler.follow_up: Send his staff a single page note with the one vote you need, the bill's next step, and a named staffer within two days.
Michael Lawler.personality: Lawler, from New York, is fairly curious, and his bills reach across more areas than nearly any colleague's. In his talk about work he is somewhat more careful than most, yet his words carry a bit more emotional charge. He often steers conversations more than most, and in hearings he is a bit more pointed than most. His public manner is sharper than almost anyone's, so his words read as blunt.
Michael Lawler.speaks: He talks much longer than most, and his answers in interviews run long and uneven. His pace is among the fastest, and his pitch swings more widely than nearly any colleague's. Brief back and forth exchanges come somewhat more often than most in his talk. His words lean forceful, with much more force than most, and somewhat more filler in his answers. Challenged points get defended, somewhat more than most.
Michael Lawler.decides: Reach across the aisle and the number of issues a bill touches are what he weighs most. Outside pressure lands on him a little more than on most, so a case with visible local support can move him. Getting bills across the line is a strength for him, so a choice holds once a named vote and a date are fixed. He digs in when challenged, so a decision built on his stated position holds up.

archetype.justification: He is fairly outgoing and one of the most dependable members on votes and bills, and he holds his ground when challenged more than most.

Michael McCaul.bottom_line: Open with the people the plan helps, and plan on him holding the floor once he is in charge. Keep your own turns short.
do: Prepare two short stories about people the plan would help
Open with the military service in his family he has described, where it honestly fits
Use his longer pauses between points to make your next point
Book extra time, since his longest answers run longer than most
dont: Treat an unfinished sentence of his as a finished answer
Argue back the moment he defends his position
Mistake his outgoing, social manner for a promise on a vote
Michael McCaul.warning_sign: He usually thinks out loud, with a lot of filler. If the filler drops away, he has moved to a settled line and has stopped working the point with you. Give him one open question, and let him answer in his own words.
Michael McCaul.follow_up: Give his office a one-page note on the people the plan helps, in writing, before the next vote.
Michael McCaul.personality: McCaul shows a fairly outgoing manner, and his votes and bills record is among the most dependable in the House. He is quite practical, and his bills reach one of the narrowest sets of issues in the House. His public words are gentler than most, and their emotional charge is among the highest in the House. In conversation he takes charge far more readily than most members. He has spoken about his father's service as a bombardier in the Second World War.
Michael McCaul.speaks: In interviews his answers run a bit longer than most. His longest ones run a bit longer too. He thinks out loud with more filler than most. When challenged he holds ground across shows. His volume stays very even. Pauses between his points run longer than most, so let them land. His pitch runs somewhat flatter than most, so listen for the words rather than the tone.
Michael McCaul.decides: A plan that helps people in a concrete way moves him, so keep the people at the center. Once he agrees, he sees bills through more reliably than almost anyone, so get the agreement on record. After he takes a position, he defends it, so bring the written case in early while the position stays open. Finish with one dated step he can say yes to in public.

archetype.justification: Among the least seen House members, with a narrow issue range, long pauses, and emotional charge in his words.

Michael Rulli.bottom_line: Keep the ask narrow and put the next step on paper. Following through is weaker for him than for most, so the written step carries it.
do: Give him the detail in advance, so he can weigh it
Meet one on one, since he is less visible than most
dont: Press for a commitment on the spot, before he has read the detail
Count on him to follow through without a written reminder
Michael Rulli.warning_sign: Sitting in a crowd will not disclose whether he is still weighing the request, since he is less visible than most. Ask him at the end which step he wants written down, then send that step the same day.
Michael Rulli.follow_up: Send a written summary of the detail and the next step within a day, copied to his staff.
Michael Rulli.personality: Rulli ranks among the least seen House members. He keeps his public talk to a narrow set of topics. His words are heavily charged by comparison, which sits oddly with how little he appears in public. Following through on votes is weaker for him than for most. His bills span a narrower set of issues than most colleagues. The result is a quiet specialist whose public voice carries more feeling than his public presence suggests.
Michael Rulli.speaks: His public talk covers a narrow range of issues and is less detailed about his work than most members. His words carry strong emotion when he does speak in public. On the House floor his delivery is slower than most colleagues, with longer pauses between phrases. Volume moves up and down more than most colleagues do. That delivery comes from floor recordings only, so it describes how he sounds there and nowhere else.
Michael Rulli.decides: He tests a request by whether it lines up with the small slate of topics he already handles. His bills span few issues, so an ask tied to one of them fits best. Because he is less visible than most, a public event will not decide it for him. A private meeting with a clear written case works better. Carrying votes through is weaker for him than most, so a commitment needs a named next action and a written record.

archetype.justification: His very organized style and detailed talk about work mark a methodical, quiet member who prefers substance to display.

Michael Simpson.bottom_line: Bring the work details and find bipartisan backers, then ask for one next step with a date.
do: Send the bill's progress record before the meeting
Name bipartisan cosponsors who already support the ask
Line up outside voices, since pressure moves him more
dont: Expect him to speak up first in a crowded room
Mistake his quiet manner for a lack of interest in the bill
Push him for a vote commitment before he has seen the record
Michael Simpson.warning_sign: He usually stays reserved and keeps his detail close, with little talk in a crowd. If he turns combative in a formal setting, the sharp tone is the signal, so stop, ask which part worries him, and offer the record.
Michael Simpson.follow_up: Send a short written note that names bipartisan backers and a next step with a date, within two days.
Michael Simpson.personality: Simpson is very organized and careful, and he is very hard to fluster. He describes his work in detail and reaches across the aisle more than many colleagues. Bills cover a bit fewer issues, and he is much less visible than others in his role. He ranks near the top for combativeness in hearings, so his manner turns sharp when a hearing turns adversarial. Together, he is a reserved specialist who fights for detail when pressed.
Michael Simpson.speaks: He speaks in careful, detailed terms about his work and stays within a narrow range of issues. His words carry a little more emotional charge than many colleagues do. In a formal hearing his manner turns combative, and he ranks near the top for it. He keeps his points plain and focused on the record. Outside a hearing, the same careful style shows up as close attention to the specifics of each bill.
Michael Simpson.decides: Each request is judged by its detail and by whether it fits the issues he already follows. Seeing bills through is one of his habits, and he works across the aisle, so a bipartisan ask gets a fair hearing. Pressure from outside counts for more with him, so a decision sticks when the backing is clear and a named next step is in writing.

archetype.justification: His very social word choice and his place among the most visible members earn the Butterfly label.

Michael Turner.bottom_line: Give him a clear, socially framed ask, since his words are gentle and social. He moves more under outside pressure, so an ally who asks alongside you carries weight.
do: Use gentle, friendly language and keep the tone open
Bring a second person who can speak to the ask publicly
Keep answers short and let him finish his thought
dont: Take a gentle reply as proof he has said yes
Assume his social warmth is a commitment
Michael Turner.warning_sign: Usually he is gentle and social, and he talks fast. When he stops finishing sentences and gives short answers, he is distracted or wants out. Give him one plain question to answer, then close with a short written note.
Michael Turner.follow_up: After the meeting, send him a short written note with the one next step and the staffer who owns it.
Michael Turner.personality: Turner is a gentle, social member who is fairly agreeable and a little reserved. His words carry strong feeling and a very social tone. Among the chamber's narrowest portfolios, his bills touch few topics. His answers run far shorter than most, and he trails off more than most. He fills his speech with more filler than most colleagues, and he is among the most visible members of the chamber.
Michael Turner.speaks: He speaks fast, with a voice that stays even and a pitch that moves up and down more than almost anyone's. His answers are short and often break off, and he rarely runs quick volleys of short replies. In hearings he runs somewhat more combative than most members, though his tone stays gentle. His words carry a social tone and strong feeling.
Michael Turner.decides: He weighs an ask by who else backs it. Outside voices sway him more than most, so a backer who speaks up can change his position. He is fairly agreeable, so an early warm reply can hide a view he has not yet stated. A decision needs a written next step to hold, so his support lasts only when it is put on paper.

archetype.justification: Her very reliable follow through, reserved manner, and low visibility fit a deliberate, low key member.

Michelle Fischbach.bottom_line: Bring an ask with bipartisan backing, since she bridges the aisle more than most. She keeps commitments, so a clear next step will hold.
do: Lead with the bill's cross party cosponsors
Give her time to think and skip filling the silences
Send a short written next step and check that it is done
dont: Read her quiet manner as a lack of interest
Expect a public push alone to win her vote
Michelle Fischbach.warning_sign: By default she is reserved and slow to answer, so a pause is normal. In hearings she is among the least combative, so a sudden sharp tone means she is on guard; ask one plain question and wait.
Michelle Fischbach.follow_up: Within two days, send her staff a short summary of the cross party cosponsors and the one next step, with a date.
Michelle Fischbach.personality: Fischbach keeps a quiet manner and holds details loosely, though her public words carry strong feeling. Her talk covers a broader set of issues, and she reaches over to the other side more often than typical colleagues. Votes and bill follow through are among the most dependable in the House. She is less easily rattled than typical colleagues, and she is among the least visible for her role.
Michelle Fischbach.speaks: Her wording still carries strong feeling even when her manner stays quiet. She describes her work in fairly careful terms, with more detail than typical colleagues. Strong charge runs through each remark, and it shows in the terms she picks. In hearings she is among the least combative, so her tone stays low key. The pattern holds across topics, so listeners hear the same pattern each time.
Michelle Fischbach.decides: She appraises an ask by how many colleagues across the aisle already back it, and a bill that keeps its commitments earns her trust. Public pressure counts for a bit less with her than it does with most colleagues, so an outside push does not settle the matter alone. Her low profile means few people press her in public, and a commitment from her holds best when someone checks the next step with her.

archetype.justification: Very reserved and slow to speak, he sees his bills through more reliably than nearly anyone and talks in careful detail.

Mike Bost.bottom_line: Confirm each step with him before you leave, since he sees bills through more reliably than nearly anyone. In a hearing, expect a firm exchange.
do: Give him time to speak before you add your own point
Match his slow pace in the room and skip rushing him
If he presses you in a hearing, answer with the facts
Ask him to name the steps he will carry out, since he follows through
dont: Read his long pauses as a refusal
Assume a quiet room means agreement
Mike Bost.warning_sign: In a hearing he is usually among the most combative members, so a softer, slower reply from him is the change to notice. That usually means he is weighing the point, so ask which part he can accept.
Mike Bost.follow_up: Afterward, send a written recap covering the agreed steps, naming who will carry each one.
Mike Bost.personality: Bost is very reserved and keeps a low public presence, even for his role. He talks in careful detail, and his words carry strong feeling. His bills cover very few issues, yet he is among the most dependable at following bills through. In hearings he is among the most combative members, and he represents Illinois. He keeps his points tied to the facts and does not wander.
Mike Bost.speaks: He speaks at a slow pace with long pauses between phrases, and his volume swings widely. Careful, detailed sentences carry strong feeling in his words. Answers stick close to the detail. In hearings he is among the most combative, so his replies come back firm and direct. His delivery is deliberate and unhurried, with a pace that stays slow from start to finish.
Mike Bost.decides: Whether the next steps can be carried out is the yardstick he uses, and he reliably sees bills through once committed. A request tied to the areas he already works in fits him better. In a hearing, expect him to hold a firm line, so prepare the facts. A decision needs a named owner for each step to stick, and the record should show who said what.

archetype.justification: Keeps a very low public profile, with a narrow issue range and a practical, careful manner.

Mike Carey.bottom_line: Send a narrow, practical brief early and ask him to confirm the next step in writing, since outside voices move him clearly.
do: Ask him to confirm the next step in writing before you leave
Bring local backers, since outside voices move him clearly
In a hearing, expect him to be much more combative
dont: Count on him to carry your ask publicly, since his profile stays very low
Mistake his practical tone for a commitment he has not made
Mike Carey.warning_sign: By default he keeps a very low public profile and sticks to practical points. If he suddenly presses hard at a hearing, that reads as guardedness, so pause and ask which fact he doubts.
Mike Carey.follow_up: Within two days, email his staff the request, the next action and a date, in a plain memo.
Mike Carey.personality: Carey comes across as very hard to rattle, and quite reserved. He leans practical more than most colleagues. Bills reach far fewer issues than most colleagues, and public talk stays narrow. Public accounts of work come across as broad rather than detailed. In hearings he turns much more combative, and public profile stays very low. His reserve and quiet style make him easy to overlook in a crowded room.
Mike Carey.speaks: He speaks in narrow terms and keeps his public words low in emotional charge. He describes his work in broad strokes rather than detail. In hearings he turns much more combative, so the tone sharpens there. When he speaks he stays inside a small set of topics, and his manner shows up mainly in the few settings where he takes the floor.
Mike Carey.decides: How tightly a request fits the few themes he already covers is his yardstick. Local backers reach him more often than most colleagues, so nearby supporters count. His follow through is somewhat weaker than most, so a decision holds only when it has a dated next step and an owner. Without a named owner and a date, agreements tend to drift.

archetype.justification: His detailed, careful talk about his work and his habit of defending positions when challenged earn the Bull label.

Mike Collins.bottom_line: Come with specific detail and a direct case, and expect short answers. Let him reach the conclusion himself, since he holds his ground once he takes a side.
do: Lead with what the policy delivers, in concrete detail
Keep each ask brief, since his answers run short
Ask for a clear next step with a named owner
dont: Pile on arguments after he has taken a side
Take his sharp wording as a personal attack
Mike Collins.warning_sign: He usually answers briskly and fills replies with filler words. If the filler drops away and he goes quiet, he is on guard, so slow down, ask one plain question, and let him reply.
Mike Collins.follow_up: Send his office a short written note of the agreed step, naming the owner and the date it is due.
Mike Collins.personality: Collins is one of the most outgoing members in the House, yet hard to rattle. He describes his work with exact, granular detail, and his words run warm. His bills are reliable through votes and follow through, and he holds his ground once he has taken a side. Brief answers come easily to him, though his sharper wording can cut when he disagrees.
Mike Collins.speaks: Brisk, brief turns come naturally to him, and he rarely trails off before finishing a point. His volume stays somewhat more even than most, with somewhat longer pauses between phrases than most. He describes his work with exact, granular detail, and his words sound warm when he is friendly. When challenged, he digs in somewhat more than most, and his wording turns sharper.
Mike Collins.decides: He weighs an ask by results and by how well the detail holds up under questions. When challenged, he digs in somewhat more than most, and outside pressure moves him less than it moves nearly any member. A proposal backed by a reliable record and a clear case gets a real hearing. So a decision from him needs a named next step to stick.

archetype.justification: Among the most reserved and most careful members of the chamber, and among the least visible for his post.

Mike Crapo.bottom_line: Offer him a shared role to lead or announce, since that framing fits him best. Pressure alone shifts him less than most, so keep the ask on its merits.
do: Put a shared role in writing before the meeting
Lead with the reasons rather than the pressure
Ask him to name the first step on the bill since he follows bills through
Give him named credit in the release, since his profile is low for his post
dont: Expecting outside voices to close the deal
Pitching a solo announcement, since a shared role fits him best
Mike Crapo.warning_sign: By default his tone is much softer than most, so an easy yes is his usual way and not a commitment. If his agreement turns vague and he stops naming a next step, he is backing off, so ask him for the first step.
Mike Crapo.follow_up: Within two days, send him a note naming the shared role, the first step, and its owner and date.
Mike Crapo.personality: Crapo represents Idaho and is among the most reserved colleagues in his chamber, yet he is very agreeable. He is among the most careful members, and his public descriptions of his work are exact in a way few colleagues match. Across his bills, the range of areas is somewhat wider than most, and his public tone runs much softer than most. He keeps among the lowest profiles in the chamber for his post, and he is somewhat dependable at carrying bills across the finish line.
Mike Crapo.speaks: His talk ranges across somewhat more topics than most, and his public descriptions of his work are exact in a way few colleagues match. His tone stays much softer than most colleagues, and his language carries a little less heat than most. Across his words the range is wide, while the detail on each topic runs high. Public accounts of his work contain few emotional words.
Mike Crapo.decides: He weighs an ask on what it delivers. Outside voices shift him less than most colleagues, so pressure alone will not carry the case. A shared role he can lead or announce with a colleague is the framing that fits him best. He is somewhat dependable at carrying bills across the finish line, so a decision holds only when it has a named first step with an owner.

archetype.justification: He is among the least outwardly expressive members, speaks in precise detail, and is among the most dependable at seeing bills through.

Mike Ezell.bottom_line: Make the ask about people the plan helps, and let him see the detail first. Backers from outside sway him more than they sway most colleagues, so bring them in.
do: Let his volume rise and fall without reading it as heat
Keep your own pitch level, since his voice stays flatter than most
In a hearing, expect fewer pointed questions, since he is less combative there
dont: Assume his follow through alone will carry a bill to the floor
In a hearing, do not read his even tone as agreement
Mike Ezell.warning_sign: Normally he is reserved and speaks with careful detail, and in hearings he is less confrontational than typical. When his manner turns sharper than that in a hearing, he is on guard, so pause, restate the one point, and wait.
Mike Ezell.follow_up: Put the next step in a letter that names its staff owner and a due date.
Mike Ezell.personality: Ezell keeps a very low outward profile, yet his work habits are fairly careful and orderly. His public talk about policy is unusually exact. Crossing party lines happens a little less than with colleagues, and his bills reach a bit broader across policy areas than typical. His follow through on bills is among the strongest in the House, and in hearings he is less confrontational than typical.
Mike Ezell.speaks: He speaks slowly and keeps his tone fairly even, with his volume rising and falling a little more than most. His pitch stays a touch flatter than most, and he describes his work with precise detail. Language is careful and unhurried, with few flourishes of any kind. In hearings he is less confrontational than typical, so his answers stay on the substance.
Mike Ezell.decides: People who stand to gain count most with him, since community impact fits his thinking best. Support from beyond the chamber shifts him more than it shifts most colleagues, so a concrete ask with new backers carries weight. His follow through on bills is among the most dependable in the House, so a decision from him holds once a named next step is attached.

archetype.justification: Few members match his curiosity, his bills span a much broader set of issues than most colleagues, and his longest answers run long.

Mike Flood.bottom_line: Lead the written technical case with the method, since that is the frame that fits him.
do: Get the written technical evidence to him ahead, with the method laid out in steps
Open with the new idea in upbeat, plain words
Limit each follow-up to one question per answer
Close by agreeing the date of the next meeting with his staff
dont: Dig in on the same point when he challenges you
Let a lively tone stand in for the bill's support
Compete with him for the floor once he holds it
Mike Flood.warning_sign: He usually fires off brisk, quick replies one after another. If each reply stands alone with a pause before the next, you have lost him for now. Stop, drop the point for now, and name the one question you still need answered.
Mike Flood.follow_up: Send his office a technical note, one page at most, within a few days, answering each open question in order.
Mike Flood.personality: Flood is curious beyond almost anyone in the chamber, and his bills reach many more issues than most. He is easy to work with, and he tends to run conversations more than most. Answers come in brisk runs more than most, and his longest answers run longer than most. When challenged, he holds his ground somewhat more than most. Few colleagues work across party lines less than he does. His public talk comes across as much gentler than most colleagues. He has spoken about farm bankruptcies he saw while growing up, which shaped his view of ethanol in Nebraska.
Mike Flood.speaks: On the House floor, the volume and pitch of his voice rise and fall more than most, and his pauses run longer than most. His answers in interviews come in brisk runs of replies, and they trail off much more than most. His reply length varies more than nearly any colleague's, so one reply can be brief and the next can run long. In interviews, answer a brisk run of replies with one clear point, not a list.
Mike Flood.decides: Spell out the one test the method must pass before he will weigh it. He holds his ground when challenged, so the case has to hold up under questioning. Outside voices move him somewhat more than most, so a repeat ask has some pull. Clear written detail gives him something to test. Close by asking how much time he needs with the case before the vote.

archetype.justification: Fairly outgoing with action focused wording and among the fewest cross party ties, which earn the pick.

Mike Haridopolos.bottom_line: Lead with a short ask and a clear plan for what happens next. Expect him to hold his own side's line, since he works across the aisle least.
do: Put the next step on paper before you leave the room
Bring a short ask he can act on in one vote
If he starts answering at length, let him finish before you reply
dont: Take his long answers as opposition rather than engagement
Expect him to join across the aisle on your ask
Mike Haridopolos.warning_sign: He usually answers at length and holds his ground when challenged, and by default he trails off mid sentence. If he stops finishing his sentences altogether, he is losing interest, so put the next step in one line rather than another argument.
Mike Haridopolos.follow_up: Within a day, send him one page of next steps with the owner of each one and the date it is due.
Mike Haridopolos.personality: Haridopolos is fairly outgoing and fairly reliable at seeing bills through, but his words run much cooler than most. Action focused terms come from him more than almost anyone in the House, and he bridges the aisle less than almost anyone. He leads a conversation less than most, and he trails off mid sentence much more than most. Those habits describe a fairly outgoing talker who rarely takes the lead.
Mike Haridopolos.speaks: He speaks in action focused terms more than almost anyone in the House, and his wording comes across as somewhat flatter than most. His replies run a bit longer than most, and the longest turns stretch further still. Pauses between phrases run much longer than most, and his volume and pitch rise and fall much more than most. He is much gentler than most in how he phrases disagreement.
Mike Haridopolos.decides: Before any ask he checks whether it fits his action focus and produces a concrete result. Across the aisle he works less than almost anyone, so an ask built on cross party support will not carry him alone. When challenged, he holds his ground somewhat more than most, so a firm reason earns more ground than a warm appeal. So an ask that promises a visible result is the one he takes up.

archetype.justification: Very outgoing and quick to hold the floor and defend his position, he talks faster than nearly any member.

Mike Johnson.bottom_line: Lead with the result before he takes over the room, since he commands the floor much more firmly than most colleagues.
do: Name the one fact that backs the ask in plain terms
Open warmly, since his words run much warmer than most
dont: Interrupt him while he defends a point, since he digs in much more than most
Read his quick yes as a commitment, since follow through is much weaker
Cede the discussion's terms to him without a clear next step
Mike Johnson.warning_sign: By default he defends his position much more than most, and he pushes back at once when challenged. If he stops defending a point and lets it go, he has dropped it, so ask him directly what he needs to see.
Mike Johnson.follow_up: After the meeting, send his office a short written summary with the one step agreed and who will take it, within two days.
Mike Johnson.personality: Johnson is very outgoing and one of the most visible members in the House, and he commands the discussion more than most. Very warm, he is quick to defend his position. His public talk spans fewer subjects than nearly any colleague. He is much less reliable on bills he must see through. Specific detail is loose in his talk, so his strength is presence more than precision.
Mike Johnson.speaks: In delivery he talks among the fastest members, and his pitch rises and falls much more than most. His pauses between phrases are somewhat shorter than most, and his volume stays somewhat more even. In interviews his answers run somewhat shorter than most, and his answer length varies somewhat more than most. He is a little more forceful in tone, and when challenged he defends ground much more than most.
Mike Johnson.decides: Results carry the most weight for him, since results and facts fit him best. Pushing from outside shifts him far less than most members, so harder pressure does not alter his view. He is much less reliable on bills he must see through, so a yes from him holds only when someone tracks the next step. He commands the discussion much more than most, so he tends to set its terms.

archetype.justification: He is outgoing and forceful in word choice, holds the floor more firmly than most, and runs loose on detail.

Mike Kelly.bottom_line: Let him hold the floor early, then ask one clear question at a time. He trails off much more than most, and his bill follow-through is a little weaker.
do: Open warmly, then let him take the floor, since he holds it firmly
Ask early in the meeting, before his long answers take the time
Have him repeat any key point, since he talks fast and often trails off
Confirm which of his staff will attend the meeting beforehand
dont: Count on his bill moving on time, since his follow-through runs a little behind
Keep pressing the same point after he says no
Cram several topics into one sitting
Mike Kelly.warning_sign: He usually talks on for a while, and rarely in quick, back-to-back turns. If he starts answering in rapid, back-and-forth turns, he has stopped working through the plan with you. Put one plain question about his main worry, then listen to the answer.
Mike Kelly.follow_up: Send one page to his chief of staff by week's end, naming the next step and who owns it.
Mike Kelly.personality: Kelly sits among the most outgoing House members. He is also fairly visible in his role. He leans only a little practical, and details run much looser for him than most House colleagues. Quick to get worked up, he runs a bit hotter than most. His tone runs a little softer than most, yet in conversation few colleagues keep the floor as tightly as he does. His words come across as far more forceful than most colleagues do.
Mike Kelly.speaks: In interviews his answers run longer than nearly any colleague's. His longest answers stay long too, and their length varies more than nearly anyone's. Trailing off happens much more than most, and sentences often stay unfinished. His pace is much quicker than most, while his pitch moves a little more than most. His volume stays a bit more even than most. Note your key points before he starts, since his answers run long.
Mike Kelly.decides: His answers run long, and he keeps the floor much more than most, so bring only the one point you need, in plain words. Bill follow-through runs somewhat behind most members, so treat any yes from him as provisional until the bill moves forward. End by asking which step he will take first, so any yes arrives with a clear task attached.

archetype.justification: His public stories about patients sit beside a practical, narrowly focused public style.

Mike Kennedy.bottom_line: Start from the people a plan reaches, and keep the case to what it means at home.
do: Bring stories of the patients and families the plan would reach
Cite a bill of his that he saw through, as evidence of his record
Keep the plan practical, with the steps spelled out
Close by confirming his answer aloud before you leave
dont: Mistake his reserve for disinterest, since he carries bills further than most
Put him at the front of a public event for the plan
Read his reliable follow-through as a promise of quick action
Mike Kennedy.warning_sign: A meeting with no clear ask does not show whether he is ready to act. Stop and ask him to name the one part of the plan he would back.
Mike Kennedy.follow_up: Send his staff a note by Friday listing each agreed point, its owner, and its due date.
Mike Kennedy.personality: Kennedy is strongly practical, and few in the House are more so. He has spoken about his years as a physician caring for mothers and newborns. His public profile sits a little lower than most, both overall and for his role. The bills he backs touch a much smaller set of areas than most. Follow-through is fairly solid, since he sees bills through more than most.
Mike Kennedy.speaks: His words carry a bit more feeling than most, and he describes the work more precisely than nearly any colleague does. His talk stays within a narrower range of topics than almost anyone's. Let him take each point to its end before you add yours. Match his precision: give exact answers in plain words, and say so when you do not know.
Mike Kennedy.decides: He prefers familiar ground, and his bills tend to get finished, so once he agrees, the agreement usually lasts. Before you talk, confirm you both have the same bill number and version in front of you. Then start from the rule already on the books and name the one change the plan makes to it. Stay on that one change until he has answered it.

archetype.justification: Among the narrowest in issue range and among the most forceful in wording, he speaks with precision.

Mike Lee.bottom_line: Bring a narrow, written ask with the technical detail set out, and keep it short. He rarely works across the aisle, so the ask must stand on its own merits.
do: Lead with the technical case in writing, since precise detail suits him
Keep points tight, since he speaks with little filler
Draw him in early, since he takes the lead less than most
In a hearing, expect pointed questions and answer briefly
dont: Match his forceful tone in a hearing, since he gets somewhat more combative there
Assume he will join a bipartisan deal, since he rarely crosses the aisle
Mike Lee.warning_sign: Though forceful, his phrasing toward others usually stays somewhat softer than most. If his words turn sharp and his answers shorten, he is on guard. Stay on your one point, let him answer, and hold any second ask.
Mike Lee.follow_up: Afterward, write up the technical detail, the one narrow ask, and a dated next step in a brief note.
Mike Lee.personality: Lee is very careful and well organized, and fairly outgoing for a member who speaks narrowly. His words rank among the most forceful in the chamber, though they stay far less social than most colleagues. Strong feelings come somewhat less readily to him than to most, and he talks about a narrow range of issues. His bills reach a little wider than most, though his talk stays narrow.
Mike Lee.speaks: His words are among the most forceful in the chamber, and a little less geared to action than most. Delivery runs somewhat quicker than most, while pitch swings far more widely than most. Volume varies somewhat less than is typical. The longest replies are somewhat briefer than most. In a hearing his combative streak runs somewhat above the usual level, and that edge is easy to notice.
Mike Lee.decides: The written detail behind an ask has to hold up before it earns his support. He rarely works across the aisle, so a shared ask needs a strong case of its own. Outside pressure sways him much less than most, so the case must carry itself. He takes the lead somewhat less than most, so any commitment needs a named owner to stick.

archetype.justification: He keeps a low public profile, yet his votes and bill follow-through are much stronger than most.

Mike Levin.bottom_line: Offer him a shared role to front, and ask for one clear commitment you can hold him to.
do: Offer him a visible role to front, once a partner has agreed
Ask him to weigh in on one open question in the plan
Keep your points short and firm if the meeting turns formal
Choose a bill with a clear finish line to start the partnership
dont: Rely on his public profile to draw notice to the plan
Treat a first no as the end of the matter
Hand him a shared title with no work attached
Mike Levin.warning_sign: In hearings he usually presses much harder than most colleagues. Once he turns courteous and moves to scheduling questions, he has stopped weighing the substance. Stop, narrow the talk to one disputed point, and offer a short written answer.
Mike Levin.follow_up: Send his office a short memo by Friday, naming the shared role and the next step.
Mike Levin.personality: Levin is markedly curious and quite reserved. He is much less seen than most, both overall and for his role. His record of votes and bill follow-through is much stronger than most. Cross-party work is a little lighter for him than for most members. The bills he carries span a somewhat wider set of areas, while his public talk reaches far across the agenda, more than nearly any colleague's. In hearings he is markedly more combative than most colleagues. After law school, he worked as a lawyer on energy and environmental issues.
Mike Levin.speaks: In his public talk he covers a range of topics few colleagues match, but he gives less careful detail than most. His language sits a notch lower in emotional heat than most. In a formal setting, have answers ready for hard questions. Bring the specifics yourself, and keep your own tone plain.
Mike Levin.decides: His yes tends to stick, since he sees bills through much more reliably than most. Bring the partner into the drafting early, while the text can still change. Let the partner set the first session's agenda, so he has something concrete to present.

archetype.justification: His public talk ranges across more topics than nearly any colleague's, while he rates very high on visibility in the chamber.

Mike Quigley.bottom_line: Let him run through the issues he cares about, then ask for one concrete step. His words run sharp, so answer with plain facts rather than matching his tone.
do: Send an agenda ahead so the plan stays on track
Give him room to make his case before you narrow it
Keep the next step short and visible in public
dont: Count on his short answers to settle details
Press him to slow down while he is mid thought
Mike Quigley.warning_sign: He usually talks fast with wide pitch swings. If his pace slows and his pauses lengthen, guardedness sets in, so stop, reflect his concern back and ask one clear question.
Mike Quigley.follow_up: Afterward, send a brief written digest covering the plan, its next action, and who owns it.
Mike Quigley.personality: Quigley is highly sociable and very curious, with a wide net of interests. His words are sharp and charged with feeling. In hearings he is sharper than most colleagues. He keeps a wide range of topics in play, and that breadth shows up in his talk. He is very visible, and he tends to be warm and social with colleagues.
Mike Quigley.speaks: Pace is very quick, and pitch moves widely. Volume swings more than most, and answers run short with an even length. Feeling runs much higher in his talk than most, and he sharpens his point when pressed. He trails off somewhat more than most, which shows in how his sentences end. In hearings, he is sharper than most colleagues. Overall his replies come quickly and carry more feeling than most.
Mike Quigley.decides: He judges proposals by how neatly they match his wide curiosity and how visibly they can be displayed. Outside groups sway him somewhat less than most colleagues. He is very visible, so a plan others can watch fits his habits. He tends to follow several threads at once. So a request holds when it fits what he already follows and its next step can be seen in public.

archetype.justification: His careful organized work, long answers and wide bill coverage fit a deliberate, exacting style.

Mike Rogers.bottom_line: Give him the detail in writing before the meeting, since he will hold the floor. He works across the aisle well, so a shared deal can carry his support.
do: Start with the bill's specifics and let him respond at length
Ask for a clear next step while he is still talking
Confirm the step in writing afterward, since he sees bills through
dont: Read a short answer from him as full agreement
Cut off his long answers before he reaches the step
Mike Rogers.warning_sign: He usually gives filler heavy answers and digs in once pressed. If he suddenly goes quiet and stops pressing his point, he is on guard, so ask one open question and wait.
Mike Rogers.follow_up: Send him a written summary with the step, its owner and its date within two days.
Mike Rogers.personality: Rogers is a careful, organized member who is hard to rattle. Working across the aisle well beyond most colleagues is part of his profile, and his bills span many issue areas. Public wording stays far less social than most colleagues do. Among the most visible members in the House for his role, he draws attention. A lot of filler runs through his talk, which shows up in long interview answers.
Mike Rogers.speaks: In interviews, his answers run long, and his longest stretches are longer than nearly any colleague's. Trailing off mid sentence happens more often than nearly any colleague. Volume holds fairly even, though pitch rises and falls with force. Word choice is more forceful than most, and claims come in long stretches. He uses a lot of filler, so his sentences carry extra words.
Mike Rogers.decides: An ask is weighed for fit against the bills he already carries. Outside calls weigh on him more than most, and a repeated ask gains force. He tends to hold the room, so decisions get worked out in the meeting itself. His bills tend to move through, which gives him a record to point to. So a decision holds with him when a named owner carries it through.

archetype.justification: He gives much more careful, detailed accounts of his work, and his bills reach somewhat more issue areas than most.

Mike Rounds.bottom_line: Let outside voices back the ask, since they move him a little more than most, and let him take his time.
do: Budget time for long replies early in the conversation
Confirm the next bill step, since he sees bills through
Keep the warmth up, since his words run somewhat warmer than most
dont: Mistake his gentler wording for an easy yes
Expect a quick concession when you challenge his view
Mike Rounds.warning_sign: He usually pushes back hard when challenged, so a challenge he lets slide without a fight is the sign he has stopped being interested in the point. Ask which part of the case he doubts, and answer that part alone.
Mike Rounds.follow_up: Afterward, put a short note in writing that confirms the bill step you agreed and the detail behind it.
Mike Rounds.personality: Rounds is a fairly curious, very agreeable member from South Dakota and is much harder to rattle than most. He leans somewhat reserved, yet he is very careful in his thinking, and he goes deep on his work and gives long answers when he does. Filler is much rarer for him than for most, and his bills touch somewhat more topics than most. He holds his ground when challenged, more firmly than nearly any colleague.
Mike Rounds.speaks: He speaks at a somewhat slower pace than most, with brief pauses between phrases and a pitch that rises a little. His wording runs warm and leans toward concrete action, with less social energy than most colleagues and flatter excitement. Answers stretch longer than most, and he trails off somewhat less than most. When challenged, he presses his view harder than almost anyone.
Mike Rounds.decides: An ask is weighed by whether it fits his Banking Committee work and whether the bill can actually move. Seeing bills through comes fairly reliably to him, so a credible path to passage counts for a lot. Working across the aisle runs somewhat less than most for him. Defending his view is harder for him than for nearly any colleague, so an early challenge only hardens his stance further.

archetype.justification: He is very careful and a little reserved, and his public profile runs a bit lower than most colleagues'.

Mike Thompson.bottom_line: Send written detail several days ahead. A clear case weighs more with him than repeated calls.
do: Send a written brief that starts with the families the plan reaches
Open by asking which family the plan helps most, and let him name it
Keep public talk about the plan for after the first meeting, given his lower profile
Bring a colleague who can answer detailed questions on the spot
dont: Call back again and again with the same request
Hand him a point with no written source behind it
Lead with a sweeping vision for the plan rather than its steps
Mike Thompson.warning_sign: A mild, general discussion does not show where he stands on the plan. Before you leave, ask for one next step in writing and set its date.
Mike Thompson.follow_up: Within a few days, send his office a short note naming the families the plan helps.
Mike Thompson.personality: Thompson is careful and organized, and he is somewhat reserved. Across issues, his talk covers somewhat less ground than most, while his legislation spans a bit more. He is tough to rattle, more so than most, and his profile sits lower than most. He has talked in public about his son, a police officer. A little practical by nature, he prefers familiar ground.
Mike Thompson.speaks: On recordings his volume holds as level as nearly anyone's in the whole House, with little change from one phrase to the next. His pitch stays on the flat side, so keep your own voice even too. Expect him to speak in an unhurried way, and keep your remarks short and concrete.
