Give him room to finish each thought before you add a word.
Mike Thompson.decides: People-first cases fit him best, and a plain account of who is helped, stated without jargon, suits him well. Pressure from outside sways him somewhat less than most members do, and his bills reach a bit wider than most members. Give each family its own short paragraph, so his staff can find each one quickly and pass it along as written.

archetype.justification: He is quite reserved and quite skeptical, and his answers are among the briefest in the Senate, with long pauses between phrases.

Mitch McConnell.bottom_line: Lead with the result in one short case, and keep your own points brief to fit his short answers.
do: Bring the results in a short written case before the meeting
Keep the meeting short and your points brief, to match his short answers
Give his long pauses room before you add a point
Put the next step and its date in writing before you leave
dont: Argue with his defended position in front of others
Count on his office to carry the next step without a reminder
Press a repeated ask, since pressure reaches him clearly less than most
Mitch McConnell.warning_sign: Usually his turns end cleanly more than almost anyone's in the Senate. If his sentences start trailing off unfinished, he has stopped weighing the ask. Put the ask in a single plain line, then wait for his reply.
Mitch McConnell.follow_up: Send his staff a written results summary within the week, with each figure tied to its source.
Mitch McConnell.personality: McConnell is quite reserved, quite skeptical, and quite practical. Hearings find him among the least combative senators, and he is among the most visible senators for the role he holds. His public talk is much less sociable than most, and he is a bit more difficult to rattle than most. Few senators cover fewer areas in their bills than he does. He ranks among the least dependable on votes and bills in the Senate.
Mitch McConnell.speaks: In interviews his replies are as short as anyone's in the Senate, and even his longest turns are brief. He talks at a pace much slower than most. His pauses between phrases are among the longest in the Senate. Forceful words are much rarer in his talk than in most. Give him time, and do not fill his pauses. Expect short replies, and let the silence sit before you add a point.
Mitch McConnell.decides: A short, direct case on results fits him best. Pressure from outside reaches him clearly less than most members, so the argument has to hold up alone. When challenged, he stands firm, so give him time to answer. Ask his office whether any bill he has backed is still open, and what it needs. Schedule a check-in with his staff before any vote the bill faces.

archetype.justification: Somewhat more outgoing than most, much looser with details, and among the lowest at working across the aisle.

Monica De La Cruz.bottom_line: Keep the ask short and tie it to a written next step, since she is much less reliable at seeing bills through.
do: Offer her a visible role, since she is much less seen than most
Use outside pressure, since it carries a little more weight with her than most
dont: Assume the other side's support will come easily
Treat her past votes as proof a bill will advance
Monica De La Cruz.warning_sign: A general meeting won't show her speaking style as it sounds on the floor, where her recorded speech comes from. Before you meet, watch one of her floor speeches and note whether her style changes from start to finish.
Monica De La Cruz.follow_up: Send her office a one page summary of the ask with one named next step and a date, then check in by Friday.
Monica De La Cruz.personality: De La Cruz is somewhat more outgoing than most and a little less practical, and she is much looser on details. Getting worked up comes somewhat more easily to her than to most, and emotional charge runs much higher in her public wording. Her bills span a much wider set of issues, while she works across the aisle less than almost anyone and is much less reliable at seeing bills through. For her role, she is much less in view than most, and she represents Texas. Together these make her a charged and wide ranging presence whose bills reach further than the ones she sees through.
Monica De La Cruz.speaks: Her speech moves across a somewhat broader set of issues, with somewhat less careful detail about her work than most. Her delivery runs somewhat faster than most, with pauses shorter than nearly anyone's. Pitch is flatter than nearly anyone's in the House, and volume is more even than nearly anyone's. Emotional charge runs much higher than most, so feeling often runs ahead of detail.
Monica De La Cruz.decides: Her bills span a much wider set of issues, so an ask has to earn its place among many competing claims. Outside pressure carries a little extra weight with her than with most members. She works across the aisle less than almost anyone. She is much less reliable at seeing bills through, so a decision needs a named owner and a written date to stick.

archetype.justification: He is very curious and very careful, and his public talk about work runs much more detailed than most.

Morgan Griffith.bottom_line: Bring a detailed written case and let him test every claim. He works across the aisle more than almost anyone, so present the shared gains.
do: Send the detailed technical case ahead, with sources he can check
Bring fresh ideas with written evidence he can test, since he is very curious
Name the colleagues across the aisle who share the goal
dont: Assume a hearing will be quiet, since he presses harder there than most members
Rush him to a conclusion before he has worked the details through
Morgan Griffith.warning_sign: In a hearing he usually presses with more edge than his colleagues. If that edge fades and he goes quiet, he is losing interest, so ask for his answer now.
Morgan Griffith.follow_up: Send him the written case naming the partners across the aisle and a dated next step.
Morgan Griffith.personality: Griffith is very curious and very careful, and he is a bit harder to rattle than most. He works across the aisle more than almost anyone. His legislation spans a slightly narrower set of topics than most. Emotion shows a bit more in his language than in most colleagues. His accounts of his own work are careful and detailed beyond what most colleagues give. He stays well out of view, even for his role. Virginia is his base.
Morgan Griffith.speaks: He takes his time, leaving long gaps between phrases while his volume swings far more than most. Pitch stays a little flatter than most, and his language carries more emotion than most colleagues. In talk he ranges over slightly more issues than most colleagues. The recorded audio all comes from the House floor, so read his delivery as floor delivery only. In hearings he presses harder than most members.
Morgan Griffith.decides: How well the written detail holds up is what he checks in an ask. Since he works across the aisle more than almost anyone, a shared ask carries further with him. Visibility is low for him, so a decision moves on private groundwork rather than public praise. He takes up ideas that come with evidence he can test, and a decision with him needs a named next step and a date to stick.

archetype.justification: He is among the most reliable at seeing bills through and describes his work with exacting attention to detail.

Morgan Luttrell.bottom_line: Bring the full bill record, since he is among the most reliable at seeing bills through. Pressure moves him less than most, so let the record carry the case.
do: Bring the bill's full record and its voting history
In a hearing, keep each reply brief and on the record
dont: Rely on pressure from allies to close the deal
In a hearing, do not match his heat with a sharper tone
Morgan Luttrell.warning_sign: He is usually outgoing in private, but in a hearing he turns much more combative than colleagues. If he drops the friendly tone and presses one point hard, he is in hearing mode. Answer with short, factual replies and do not match his heat.
Morgan Luttrell.follow_up: Email his legislative assistant the bill's full record and each agreed step in writing by Friday.
Morgan Luttrell.personality: Luttrell reads as very outgoing and a little practical, and he ranks among the most reliable at carrying bills forward. He covers a smaller set of topics than nearly anyone, yet his talk about his work is among the most careful and detailed. In hearings he becomes much more combative than most colleagues. He tends to focus on specifics rather than sweeping claims, which makes his positions easy to test.
Morgan Luttrell.speaks: He covers a narrow set of topics. He describes his work with exacting detail, far more than nearly any colleague. In a hearing he becomes much more combative than most colleagues, and he presses each point harder. His answers tend to stick to the specifics of a bill rather than sweeping claims. Few of his points rest on broad themes, so they stay concrete.
Morgan Luttrell.decides: How fully the bill record supports a request is his main measure, since he sees bills through reliably. Being somewhat practical and much more outgoing than most, he responds to a plain account of what the bill does. Pressure from others counts for little with him, so a decision from him sticks only when the record backs it.

archetype.justification: Narrow topics dominate his public talk, and his bills span somewhat fewer areas.

Morgan McGarvey.bottom_line: Keep the request courteous and concrete, since his tone runs much gentler than most. Expect him to talk freely, since he is among the most outgoing members in the House.
do: Frame any disagreement without sharp language
Give him room to finish each thought before you reply
Lead with steps he can act on right away, since he leans practical
dont: Read his long silences as disengagement or hostility
Morgan McGarvey.warning_sign: He usually speaks slowly with long pauses, so silence is normal for him by default. If his words get sharper or he goes curt after a question, he is pulling back, so stop, restate the ask briefly, and give him time.
Morgan McGarvey.follow_up: Send a short written note on the people your plan helps, within two days of the meeting.
Morgan McGarvey.personality: McGarvey is one of the most outgoing members in the House, and he gets worked up faster than nearly anyone. Narrow topics dominate his public talk, and his bills span somewhat fewer areas. Though gentle in wording, he carries more emotional weight than almost anyone's in the House. He leans practical and is a little less careful with details, yet he describes his work in more careful terms than most. His posts are Kentucky and House Small Business.
Morgan McGarvey.speaks: He moves through words at a much slower pace than most and leaves long pauses between phrases. Volume holds somewhat more evenly than most, and pitch sits flatter than nearly anyone's in the House. Words from him carry more emotional weight than almost anyone's, and his talk about work is more careful and detailed than most. In hearings he is much less combative than most.
Morgan McGarvey.decides: He is somewhat agreeable and among the most outgoing members, so a request made in person tends to land. His bills span somewhat fewer issue areas, so a request inside the areas he already legislates on is easier to take up. Serving on House Small Business, he weighs asks against the work that committee covers, so a request outside those areas needs a clear reason to move him.

archetype.justification: Her outgoing manner and very high visibility in the House fit the Butterfly.

Nancy Mace.bottom_line: Bring a concrete ask with a cosponsor from across the aisle, and keep the exchange brisk and direct.
do: Open with the vote date that makes the ask urgent
Give her the public stage for the announcement itself
Bring the cosponsor into the room before the first ask
dont: Argue over her wording in front of colleagues
Leave long gaps in the conversation
Nancy Mace.warning_sign: She usually speaks quickly with sharp wording and leaves few gaps. If she starts trailing off mid sentence and her words turn sharper still, she is getting frustrated, so cut your point to one line.
Nancy Mace.follow_up: Send a one page list of the next votes and their dates to her staff in writing within two days.
Nancy Mace.personality: Mace is outgoing and ranks high in the chamber for visibility, and her language cuts more sharply than nearly any colleague's. Across the aisle, she works more than almost anyone, and her bills reach into many areas. Follow through on bills ranks near the bottom, so her energy often runs ahead of the paperwork. Her manner runs more charged than most, and she often leads the flow of talk.
Nancy Mace.speaks: She talks quickly, with short pauses between phrases and a volume that stays fairly even. Words lean toward action and away from small talk, so she gets to the point. Answer length swings more than most, and sentences sometimes trail off. In a hearing she becomes far more combative than her colleagues, and her public language cuts sharply. Her pace and pauses give her delivery a clipped feel.
Nancy Mace.decides: She first checks the evidence's soundness, then looks for a bipartisan partner who stands behind the request. Her bills reach across a wide spread of issues and she often leads the flow of talk, so an ask inside her areas tends to land. Pressure from outside has less pull on her than on many peers, so a decision holds when she has agreed the next step herself.

archetype.justification: Among the most outgoing and visible members, her words run among the warmest in the chamber.

Nancy Pelosi.bottom_line: Come with a short, direct results case and let her take the floor first. Keep the ask narrow, since her bills touch among the fewest issues.
do: Let her take the floor, then tie your ask to the results it produces
Keep your points short to match her brief answers in conversation
Name the cost of delay in one line, since outside pressure moves her little
Ask her to name the next step before the meeting ends
dont: Compete with her for airtime, since her visibility is among the highest
Count on her to finish each bill, since follow through is much weaker than most
Nancy Pelosi.warning_sign: When a point is challenged she usually defends her position and holds the floor. Let her finish, then restate your one ask in a single sentence and wait for her reply.
Nancy Pelosi.follow_up: Afterward, send a short written summary with one dated next step to her office, tied to the first item you agreed.
Nancy Pelosi.personality: Pelosi counts among the most outgoing members in the chamber, and her words run among the warmest there. She is fairly curious and careful, and much quicker to get worked up than most. Her bills touch among the fewest issues in the chamber, and she is much less reliable than most at seeing bills through. Commanding the floor in talk, she is as firm as nearly anyone, yet her replies are among the briefest.
Nancy Pelosi.speaks: Her description of her own work is somewhat less exact and detailed than most. Much more forceful than most, her words also run somewhat more upbeat in tone. Pauses between her phrases stretch somewhat longer than most, and her pitch holds somewhat flatter than most. Her replies run much briefer than most in interviews, and their length swings much more than most.
Nancy Pelosi.decides: Before backing it she asks whether it delivers results she can point to. Her bills touch among the fewest issues in the chamber, so a narrow ask is the one she can carry. Following bills through is much harder for her than for most, so she needs firm dates to follow. Outside pressure moves her less than almost anyone, so her own read carries the decision.

archetype.justification: Her wide issue range, quick runs of short turns and active public presence fit a persistent, direct style.

Nanette Barragán.bottom_line: Bring one ask with a clear written step, and get it confirmed before you leave. Her follow through is somewhat weaker than most.
do: Keep the ask to one clear step, since her turns come in quick runs
Confirm each step in writing, since follow through is somewhat weaker than most
dont: Read her quick replies as agreement with the ask
Count on her follow through to carry a verbal yes
Nanette Barragán.warning_sign: She usually talks in brisk runs of quick turns. If she suddenly gives one long unbroken answer and stops the back and forth, something has shifted, so pause and ask what changed.
Nanette Barragán.follow_up: Mail her a brief written note within two days that lists the upcoming step plus the owner and the date.
Nanette Barragán.personality: Barragán is fairly outgoing and among the most skeptical colleagues. She gets worked up easily, and her public wording is cooler than most. Talk covers a wide range of issues, wider than nearly any colleague's. Bills span somewhat more issue areas than most, and follow through is somewhat weaker than most. She takes charge of conversations much less than most.
Nanette Barragán.speaks: Her pace runs somewhat faster than most, with pauses somewhat shorter than most. Words run flatter than most, and her wording is far less forceful than most. Her answers run short in interviews, and she leaves fewer sentences unfinished than most. Emotional charge is lower in her wording than most colleagues', and her talk leans toward action. Her turns come in quick runs with more filler than most.
Nanette Barragán.decides: Her standard is whether a request lands within the areas she already works on. Outside pressure moves her less than most members, so a repeated request has less force. Bills slip a bit more often for her, so commitments must have a named owner. She leads a room much less often than most, so decisions get made by colleagues. So a decision holds with her when a named owner and a date are both written.

archetype.justification: Careful and methodical, he keeps his bills to fewer issues and describes his work in detailed terms.

Nathaniel Moran.bottom_line: Name who owns the next step before you leave the room. Seeing bills through is a strength for him, but outside pressure reaches him less than most members.
do: Put each agreed step in writing with a date
Let him take his time, since he talks more slowly than most
dont: Rush him toward a yes in one meeting, since pressure moves him less
Expect him to volunteer much enthusiasm in the room
Nathaniel Moran.warning_sign: A broad session with him will not reveal whether he is still weighing the ask or has set it aside. Ask his staff for the next dated step and write down whatever date they give.
Nathaniel Moran.follow_up: Send his staff a dated list of agreed steps with the owner named for each one.
Nathaniel Moran.personality: Moran is quite reserved and far harder to rattle than the average member. He is careful and methodical, and his own accounts of his work are detailed. His bills span fewer issues, though seeing them through comes fairly easily to him. The emotional charge in his talk runs lower than almost anyone else's in the chamber, and he draws somewhat less notice than most. He represents Texas in Congress.
Nathaniel Moran.speaks: His pace runs somewhat slower than most, and his pitch runs flatter than nearly any colleague's. He talks in careful, detailed terms about a narrow range of issues, with little emotional charge. The detail comes first, and he rarely reaches for charged language to make a case. This delivery read comes from floor speech only, so it describes that setting.
Nathaniel Moran.decides: He weighs an ask on whether the detail holds and whether someone owns the next step. He keeps his bills to fewer issues than most, so an ask outside his areas will not get traction. Seeing bills through comes fairly easily to him, so a step he accepts tends to get done. Outside pressure reaches him a little less than most members, so a campaign from home counts for less. A decision from him holds only when a dated next step is written and owned.

archetype.justification: Hare fits because his talk ranges over more issue areas than nearly any colleague's, while he stays far looser with details.

Neal Dunn.bottom_line: Keep the ask to one clear sentence tied to who it helps. Pressure from outside groups carries clearly less weight with him, so a broad push will not carry him.
do: Name the people the ask helps before any detail
Write down the single next step with a named owner
In a hearing, expect somewhat more combative questions
dont: Count on outside pressure to change his position
Assume he will carry a commitment without a written step
Neal Dunn.warning_sign: In a hearing he usually questions freely, so a drop in that pressure is the signal. When he stops pressing, he is losing interest or on guard. Ask one open question, then let him answer.
Neal Dunn.follow_up: Write him a note naming the one ask, the people it helps, and the next step with an owner.
Neal Dunn.personality: Dunn is fairly curious and touches more issue areas in his public words than nearly any colleague. He is much less careful with details than most, and his bills reach a broader set of issues than most. Follow through is much weaker than most. Few members are less visible for their role. As a Florida member, he presses somewhat harder than most in hearings.
Neal Dunn.speaks: Speech moves loosely across many issue areas rather than staying on one bill. Precise detail on his work is less frequent than in most, so specific questions tend to draw general answers. He describes his bills in loose terms. In hearings he presses somewhat more than most members, and that is the setting where he presses most. Public words range widely, with the broad view taking precedence over the particulars.
Neal Dunn.decides: He looks at whether an ask sits inside issue areas he already speaks to and whether its people are clear. Pressure from outside groups carries clearly less weight with him, so the case has to stand on its own. Follow through is much weaker than most, so a decision sticks only when someone owns the next step. Clear people and a bounded issue make the case easier for him to weigh.

archetype.justification: Her bills stay in few areas, and she reliably sees them through with careful, detailed work.

Nellie Pou.bottom_line: Come with a narrow, carefully documented ask and offer her a shared role to lead. Her record of seeing bills through is what gives the ask its weight.
do: Put the detailed backup in front of her early
Offer a joint announcement she can front
In a hearing, expect combative questions and keep your tone level
dont: Mistake her flat delivery for disinterest, given how reliably she follows bills
In a hearing, meet every challenge with more argument
Nellie Pou.warning_sign: She normally keeps a flat, even manner, so her tone alone is no guide. When she turns combative, she is on guard, and the ask is in trouble. Stop adding points and let her finish.
Nellie Pou.follow_up: Send her office the written ask with its backing by the end of that week, and propose a date for the shared announcement.
Nellie Pou.personality: Pou works a narrow lane and goes deep into it. Her public words stay on a small set of issues and carry careful, detailed work, and her bills cover few areas, yet she reliably sees each one through. Formal settings bring out a sharper side, and she is far more pointed than most members. She represents New Jersey. She is careful with the details of every bill she follows and rarely strays from her own issues.
Nellie Pou.speaks: She speaks in a flat, even pitch with pauses a touch shorter than most. Her wording stays precise and focused on a few topics, and she frames issues in careful, detailed terms. Under hearing pressure her tone turns combative, pressing each point rather than giving ground. Her range of topics is narrow, so she returns to the same few themes. She prefers to discuss the detail she has already mastered.
Nellie Pou.decides: She tests a request on whether it falls within the handful of areas she already works in. Outside voices move her more readily than most members, so the people behind an ask carry real weight. In a formal setting her sharper side grows, and a contest only entrenches her view. So a decision holds only when outside backers stay visible and the ask stays narrow.

archetype.justification: Very reserved and careful to a degree few colleagues match, and he presses somewhat less hard in hearings.

Nicholas Begich.bottom_line: Open with a brief account of what the policy delivers, and let him reach the conclusion himself. Outside voices backing the ask will move him more than most.
do: Arrange for local people who gain to brief him on results
Show him a bill he already backed across the aisle
Agree one dated next step before you leave, since he sees bills through
dont: Piling on arguments when a short, direct case fits him best
Filling every silence before he has finished thinking
Pushing for a vote before outside voices have spoken
Nicholas Begich.warning_sign: By default he presses less hard in hearings than most colleagues, so a sharper tone is the change that counts. If he turns curt in a hearing and stops engaging the facts, he is on guard, so send them in writing and let him finish.
Nicholas Begich.follow_up: Within a day, send him a short note with the facts and the owner and date of the next step.
Nicholas Begich.personality: Begich ranks near the top of his chamber for reserve and for care, and his framing of issues runs a little practical. He describes his work in detailed terms, works across the aisle much more than most, and is fairly dependable at finishing the bills he starts. He represents Alaska and keeps his focus on a narrow set of issues. In hearings he presses somewhat less hard than most colleagues.
Nicholas Begich.speaks: He keeps his talk to a narrow set of issues and describes his work with extra precision. His pauses between phrases run somewhat short, and his volume varies somewhat more than most. In hearings he is a little less forceful than most members. All recorded audio of him comes from the floor, where the format shapes delivery, and private rooms are not captured.
Nicholas Begich.decides: He weighs an ask by the facts it rests on and by what it delivers. He gives serious weight to support from across the aisle because he has joined such bills before. Outside voices tend to shift him further than they shift most members, so an ask backed by people back home carries the most weight. Results and facts suit him best, so a request built on them holds up better in his office.

archetype.justification: Reserved and slow in delivery, with a level pitch and loose handling of details, yet he follows bills through reliably.

Nicholas Langworthy.bottom_line: Bring one clear ask and the written detail behind it, then leave space for his reply. Public pushes land a little softer with him than with most.
do: Send the technical detail in writing before the meeting
Give him room before asking for a commitment
Ask one direct question, then wait through his pauses
dont: Assume a public statement will shift him
Press him for a quick yes at the first meeting
Nicholas Langworthy.warning_sign: In hearings he is usually restrained, so a sudden edge in his questions means he is on guard or losing patience. Stop, restate the point in plain terms, and ask what is missing.
Nicholas Langworthy.follow_up: Within two days of the meeting, email his staff a brief recap of the detail and the one step you agreed, with a reply date.
Nicholas Langworthy.personality: Langworthy is more reserved than nearly any House colleague and keeps a lower public profile than most. He is somewhat curious and somewhat quicker to get fired up than most colleagues. In detail, he is looser than nearly any colleague, yet his public words are broad and heavy with feeling. He follows bills through reliably, though he finds bipartisan work somewhat less natural than most. Those traits add up to a deliberate member whose interest in the big picture shows in public more than in the room, and who is hard to rush.
Nicholas Langworthy.speaks: He speaks slowly and holds a level pitch that few colleagues match, so his delivery sounds unhurried even when the exchange runs long. Pauses run somewhat longer than most, and his volume varies more widely than most colleagues. He frames issues broadly, touching many topics in one exchange, and his public words carry a lot of emotional weight. In a hearing he is a little less combative than most colleagues.
Nicholas Langworthy.decides: He takes time to settle on a view, since written detail fits him better than a conversation in the room. An ask backed only by allies from the other side will not carry him alone, since working across the aisle comes somewhat less easily to him. His bills reach into a few more areas than most, so an ask inside those areas fits his record. A commitment from him holds only once it is written down.

archetype.justification: His careful detailed talk, reliable votes and answers among the shortest in the chamber fit a bull's direct style.

Nick LaLota.bottom_line: Bring a detailed written case and let him read it at his own pace. His answers run among the shortest in the chamber, so the case must do the work.
do: Send the written technical evidence ahead of time so he can check it
Keep your points short, since his answers run among the shortest in the chamber
dont: Fill his quiet pauses with extra argument before he has spoken
Pile new facts onto the ask late, since he follows bills through closely
Nick LaLota.warning_sign: He usually gives replies that run among the shortest in the chamber, with almost no filler. When he goes quiet and his replies stop short of the point, he is on guard, so pause and ask one direct question.
Nick LaLota.follow_up: Send him a short written list of the next steps and the votes they depend on, with a date for each.
Nick LaLota.personality: LaLota is a careful, organized member who is among the most reliable on votes and bills. He is somewhat reserved and fairly agreeable. Words come across as cooler than nearly any colleague's, and talk is short. His wording cuts much sharper than most colleagues', yet he takes charge of talk much less than most. Legislation spans a much smaller field than most colleagues'.
Nick LaLota.speaks: His pace is among the slowest in the chamber, with pauses that run among the longest. Volume varies among the most in the chamber, and his pitch stays among the flattest. Answers stay even in length, and he finishes sentences more reliably than almost anyone. His wording is much sharper than most colleagues'. Filler is nearly absent from his speech, and emotion in his wording runs somewhat higher than most colleagues'.
Nick LaLota.decides: He tests a request by whether the detailed written case holds up and whether it fits his own lines. Pressure counts somewhat more with him than among most members, so backers who matter can change his view. His legislation spans a much smaller field than most colleagues', so an ask must sit inside his lines. He follows through closely, so a decision holds once a named next step is set and kept.

archetype.justification: Somewhat focused on action, she takes charge of conversations somewhat more than most and defends her position much more than most when challenged.

Nicole Malliotakis.bottom_line: Make one short, direct case that shows the policy's results, and back it with facts, because pressure in the room hardens her.
do: Point to bipartisan cosponsors who already back the bill
Answer her doubts with evidence before you ask for support
In a hearing, expect much less combat and answer each question plainly
dont: Assume a verbal yes will carry the bill through votes
Give up on her early no before outside voices weigh in
Compete with her for airtime, since she takes charge somewhat more than most
Nicole Malliotakis.warning_sign: She usually talks quickly and digs in when challenged. If her pace climbs and her sentences trail off, she has grown guarded, so halt, restate your one point in plain words, and let her answer.
Nicole Malliotakis.follow_up: Afterward, mail her office a brief written digest of the results and of the cosponsors who back the bill before the week closes.
Nicole Malliotakis.personality: Malliotakis is a very visible member whose words run much sharper than most, with a little skepticism behind them. Her answers run long, and she leans toward action over social warmth. She reaches across lines somewhat more than most. Yet her record in carrying bills to a vote is somewhat weaker than most, so a yes from her is a start rather than a finish. She defends her position much more than most when challenged, and she takes charge of conversations somewhat more than most.
Nicole Malliotakis.speaks: She talks quickly, and her volume stays a little more even than most while her pitch stays much flatter than most. Her pauses between phrases are short, so the delivery reads as brisk rather than warm. When she gets going she gives long answers, and her longest turn outlasts nearly any member's. She describes her work in broad terms instead of careful detail, and her language carries somewhat less feeling than most. Challenged, she digs in and defends her point, and her sentences trail off much more than most.
Nicole Malliotakis.decides: She weighs an ask on results and facts, so a short, direct case with clear outcomes earns the closest hearing. Pressure from advocates tilts her more than most members, so her support can shift after she hears from them. Bills tend to lose ground after a meeting, so a verbal yes can fade before the vote. So her agreement holds only when someone owns the next step.

archetype.justification: She is among the most outgoing colleagues and fairly curious, and her bills and speeches reach across many issues.

Nikema Williams.bottom_line: Give her room to explore, since she is fairly curious, then close on one ask. Outside pushes carry less weight with her, so the case must earn her yes.
do: Lead with what the bill will do, since her words focus on action
Give her the floor for a long answer before you press the ask
dont: Count on backing from across the aisle to carry the ask
Rely on her to drive the meeting itself
Nikema Williams.warning_sign: In interviews, her answers usually finish cleanly and carry almost no filler. If she starts trailing off in the middle of a sentence, she is pulling back, so stop and ask which point she has not accepted.
Nikema Williams.follow_up: Send her office a short written summary of what the bill will do and who backs it across the aisle, with a date for the next step.
Nikema Williams.personality: Williams is more outgoing than nearly any colleague in the House, and her profile is somewhat above what her post suggests. She is fairly curious and fairly agreeable, and she is open to conversation. Details come less carefully from her, and her public talk ranges across a broad set of issues. Work across the aisle is a smaller part of her record than for most colleagues. Her interview replies run longer than nearly any colleague's.
Nikema Williams.speaks: Public words cover wide ground and stay focused on action. Word choice leans upbeat and is less forceful than colleagues'. Delivery runs somewhat slower than colleagues. Volume rises and falls well beyond the usual range, so delivery has clear variety. In interviews her answers run even in length and seldom trail off. Longest answers run far longer than colleagues, and filler is almost absent.
Nikema Williams.decides: Weighing an ask, she looks at how well it fits the broad set of issues she takes on. Her agreeable nature keeps her open to talk, but she works across the aisle much less, so a deal there does not come easily. Visibility runs a bit above her post, so an ask with a clear public face carries weight. So she stays with an ask only when it fits her own lane.

archetype.justification: Practical and narrow in focus, she talks about fewer issues and keeps her bills to a smaller set of areas, with a quick pace.

Nikki Budzinski.bottom_line: Bring one practical ask with a clear next step, and back it with outside voices, since outside pressure moves her much more than most members.
do: Lead with the practical result, not the background
Confirm the next vote or bill step before you leave
In a hearing, keep one question on the table at a time
dont: Count on outside groups to move her before a vote
Pile several asks into one fast exchange, since she talks quickly
Nikki Budzinski.warning_sign: In hearings she usually stays far less combative than typical colleagues. If she turns sharper there, she is pressed, so restate the one point and stop.
Nikki Budzinski.follow_up: After the meeting, put the ask, the next vote step, and its date in a note to her staff.
Nikki Budzinski.personality: Budzinski is practical and narrowly focused, and her public talk covers a smaller range of issues. She explains her own work in looser terms than others, and her manner is a little reserved. Her bills span fewer areas than typical, and her follow through is a bit less reliable than most. Few outside observers notice her, since her public footprint stays small. In hearings, she is far less combative than typical, which shapes how a hearing goes.
Nikki Budzinski.speaks: Talk runs faster than most, with her volume and pitch rising and falling more than most. Her wording stays narrow, and her accounts of work come across as light on detail. Practical in manner, she gets to the point and keeps points tied to the item on the table. In hearings she is far less combative than typical colleagues, which keeps the tone level.
Nikki Budzinski.decides: A practical result and a next step fixed on the calendar are what she checks in an ask. Outside pressure moves her much more than most members, so a push from groups that already back the ask can change her position. Her follow-through is somewhat less reliable than most, so a yes holds only when a named staffer owns the next step.

archetype.justification: Community minded, very curious, easily stirred, emotionally charged in public words, with wide ranging bills.

Norma Torres.bottom_line: Lead with the people your ask helps, and bring stories about who gains. She is emotionally charged and wide ranging, so a human case lands better than a dry one.
do: Open with the people the ask helps and what changes for them
Offer a clear next step with a named owner
Name the people affected before you raise the numbers
dont: Lead with a dry chart when the room wants a story
Count on a commitment carrying itself after the meeting
Norma Torres.warning_sign: Usually her words run expansive, so a sharper turn in phrasing is the signal. When she gets emotionally charged and presses a point, she is on guard about the issue, so slow down and ask what concern she is protecting.
Norma Torres.follow_up: Send a short written note the same day naming the step, its owner, and the date.
Norma Torres.personality: Torres is a community minded Californian with a very curious mind and an emotionally charged public voice. Her bills span a broader set of areas than typical members, and she covers far more ground in her talk than colleagues do. Emotional charge runs strong in her words, and her phrasing is a touch sharper than most. Her work is described less in detail than most, so she relies on the human picture more than the figures.
Norma Torres.speaks: She talks in broad, emotionally charged strokes and ranges across many issues. Her public words carry far more feeling than most, and her talk about the work is less careful and detailed than typical. Phrasing runs somewhat sharper than most, and she frames issues around the people they touch. Her case tends to rest on lived experience more than on the fine print.
Norma Torres.decides: She weighs an ask by the people it helps and by whether her community will see a result. She follows issues across many areas, so people who know the policy broadly will hold her attention. Follow-through runs somewhat less reliable, so a dated next step and a named owner matter. So a request that shows who gains, and who will check on the promise, is what earns her support.

archetype.justification: Her bills and talk cover more ground than almost anyone's, and her pace runs slow.

Nydia Velázquez.bottom_line: Bring one narrow decision with its cost named, and leave room to answer. Outside pressure moves her less than nearly anyone, so the case must hold up alone.
do: Give each point room, since her pace runs slow and her pauses run long
Ask for a dated owner on each step, since follow through is somewhat less reliable
Name the single decision you need, since outside pressure moves her little
Offer her a visible role, since her public profile sits a bit low
dont: Count on outside pressure to move her, since she is among the least moved
Hurry her through a pause, since her pauses run longer than almost anyone's
Nydia Velázquez.warning_sign: A general meeting will not tell you how she handles a quick back and forth. Put the decision in one sentence before you leave, and ask her for a direct yes or no.
Nydia Velázquez.follow_up: Afterward, deliver to her office a memo stating the choice, its cost, and a dated owner.
Nydia Velázquez.personality: Velázquez ranges across more areas, in talk and in bills, than nearly anyone in the chamber. Her wording runs a bit warmer in feeling than most, with a little more heat. Public attention finds her a little less often than most colleagues, and her talk and bills share that same broad reach. She represents New York and sits on the Financial Services and Small Business committees.
Nydia Velázquez.speaks: Her talk ranges among the widest in the chamber. Her pace runs among the slowest in the chamber, and her pauses run longer than almost anyone's. Loudness swings somewhat more than most, while her tone runs somewhat flatter. Her words carry a bit more feeling than most. Most recordings of her come from the House floor, so this read reflects floor speech only.
Nydia Velázquez.decides: Requests get judged against the broad agenda she already pursues, and the fit decides her view. Outside pressure moves her among the least of members, so her own reading carries the decision. Her bills reach across many areas, so an ask inside those areas fits her best. Following bills through is a bit harder for her than for most, so any commitment from her needs a named, dated owner to hold.

archetype.justification: His talk and bills stay within a much narrower set of areas than most, so a focused ask suits him.

Pablo Hernández Rivera.bottom_line: Keep the ask inside one area he already works in. Pressure from outside pulls on him less than most, so the case has to stand alone.
do: Tie the ask to one area he already works in
Let the case rest on one clear outcome
dont: Lean on outside pressure alone, since it pulls on him less than most
Pablo Hernández Rivera.warning_sign: No group setting will reveal how he handles a request outside his usual areas, so ask a narrow question first. Then take one concrete step: confirm the single area and the next date in writing.
Pablo Hernández Rivera.follow_up: Afterward, send a short written note confirming the one area, the ask, and the next date.
Pablo Hernández Rivera.personality: Hernández Rivera stays within a much narrower set of areas than most colleagues. His talk is somewhat less careful and detailed than most. He represents Puerto Rico in the House. A focus on a few areas shows in how he frames each request.
Pablo Hernández Rivera.speaks: His talk stays within a much narrower set of areas, and his detail runs somewhat thinner than most. He keeps a focused way of speaking and does not range far from his own areas, which keeps each answer on point.
Pablo Hernández Rivera.decides: Before backing anything he judges how narrowly it fits the few areas he already covers. Pressure from outside pulls on him less than most, so the ask has to stand on its own merits. His bills reach much fewer areas than most, so a narrow ask is one he can take up. Any yes he gives needs one named step, since pressure from outside will not carry it.

archetype.justification: His very outgoing manner, much looser detail and warm agreeable wording fit a butterfly that drifts easily from topic to topic.

Pat Fallon.bottom_line: Keep the ask short and tied to one named step, since his answers run long.
do: Let his opening answer run before you narrow the topic
Put the technical evidence in writing a day before
Thank him warmly, then ask one clear question about the next vote
dont: Treat his agreeable tone as a commitment to act
Let his outgoing manner stand in for a stated commitment
Pat Fallon.warning_sign: Usually he speaks in a flat pitch and often trails off in the middle of a point. If his volume climbs and he finishes each thought without trailing off, he has locked onto the point and wants an answer. Ask for that answer directly.
Pat Fallon.follow_up: Forward his office a brief written note that lists the bill's next milestone, who owns it, and when it is due.
Pat Fallon.personality: Fallon shows a very outgoing side and stays very agreeable, while his attention to detail trails well behind most colleagues. His legislation covers a far narrower set of topics than usual, and his follow through is a little below par. In conversation he leads less than most, and he tends to hold the floor longer than most when he does. His public language runs noticeably flat. He represents Texas, and his public presence is above what his post would predict.
Pat Fallon.speaks: Pace runs a notch slower than usual, with a pitch that stays somewhat flatter than most and a volume that swings more than usual. Answers stretch well past the usual length, and the longest replies stretch further still. He often trails off mid point, more than nearly any colleague. Public wording runs flat and less upbeat than most, and it is less forceful than most.
Pat Fallon.decides: A request that fits the narrow set of issues he already takes up gets his support, while one outside that lane gets less traction. Pressure from people he answers to shifts him more than it shifts most colleagues, so backing from them can change his view. Because follow through is somewhat less reliable than most, a yes stays alive only when someone owns the next step.

archetype.justification: He speaks plainly and bluntly, and his longest answers stretch further than most, with more forceful wording than most.

Pat Harrigan.bottom_line: Send a written technical case ahead of the meeting. He speaks bluntly, so the document should carry the detail you need.
do: Put the mechanics in writing and share the document ahead
Close on a clear yes, since his bill follow-through runs better than most
State your main point in firm, plain terms
Ask a single pointed follow-up after a long answer
dont: Take his sharp wording as a final verdict
Judge his view by his longest answer alone, since his length swings widely
Pitch the ask without the concrete steps it sets in motion
Pat Harrigan.warning_sign: He usually ends his points cleanly, so a turn that trails off stands out. When an answer breaks off mid-thought, he is not convinced yet. Ask him to name the point he is still weighing, then pause.
Pat Harrigan.follow_up: Call his staff within two days to confirm the open point and who owns it.
Pat Harrigan.personality: Harrigan is a direct House member whose public language runs warmer than nearly every colleague's. His wording runs much sharper than most, while his words carry a little more feeling than most. Long answers are part of his style. His bills range across a somewhat tighter set of topics than most members. Next to others in his role, he is seen a little less often.
Pat Harrigan.speaks: His answers run long in conversation, more than most, and his longest stretches go on further than most. Interviews show shorter answers from him, so the settings differ. Rapid, clipped replies come more often from him than from most. Filler is light in his talk, and his replies are direct. Keep your own pace even, and let his long answers end before you respond.
Pat Harrigan.decides: A complete written case shared ahead fits him best. Pressure from outside moves him more than most members do, and a sustained campaign can shift his position over time. How long he talks swings more than nearly any colleague's, so read nothing into one short reply. End by asking which point he wants answered first, so the next meeting starts there.

archetype.justification: Her words are among the most forceful in the Senate, and she moves to lead conversations more than most, so a joint role she can announce suits her.

Patty Murray.bottom_line: Offer a joint announcement she can carry, then keep your ask short and direct. She moves to lead conversations, so give her the first word.
do: Bring a joint project to her with a clear part she can announce
Open with a forceful one-line case she can repeat in her own words
Hold your points until she has set the agenda, since she takes charge
Close by asking what the joint role must deliver for her, before you leave
dont: Read her gentle hearing manner, among the mildest in the Senate, as agreement
Lean on warm praise, since her public words run cooler than almost anyone's
Cut her long answers off, since her replies vary a lot in length
Patty Murray.warning_sign: Her sentences usually land complete, since she trails off less than most. If they start trailing off mid-thought, she is losing interest in the point. Pause, then sum up the point in one line and wait for her answer.
Patty Murray.follow_up: Send her staff a written note by Friday, with the joint role and one next step.
Patty Murray.personality: Murray counts among the most forceful speakers in the Senate, and her public words are cooler than nearly anyone's. Her language carries much less heat than most. Getting worked up comes far more easily to her than to most. Careful detail is not where she shines, though she is fairly agreeable. She has spoken about taking shelter in the Capitol while rioters pounded at a door near her. Her public profile runs lower than most members. In hearings she is one of the least combative senators.
Patty Murray.speaks: In interviews her answers tend to stretch somewhat longer than most, and the longest of them do too. Her answer length swings further than almost anyone else's in the Senate. Now and then her replies come in a short string of brief answers, a little more than for most. On the floor, her pitch sits flatter than most, and her pauses run much shorter than most. Let her finish a point before you answer.
Patty Murray.decides: A joint role she can announce fits her best. Persistence pays off with her, so plan a second contact after the meeting. Since outside voices shift her positions more than most, line them up before the meeting. She ranks among the least reliable senators at carrying bills through, so her yes needs a check before it counts. End by naming the staff member who will carry the joint role, so one person owns it.

archetype.justification: He leads conversations more than most, speaks with much more forceful wording than typical, and describes his work with somewhat more careful detail than most.

Paul Gosar.bottom_line: Lead with one clear ask and a short written case. His answers run short, so a tight, verifiable case holds his attention.
do: Share the written evidence well before the meeting
Keep your reply short, since his answers run short
Answer his sharp wording with plain facts, not heat
dont: Open with long background, since his answers run short
Count on public pressure to move him quickly
Paul Gosar.warning_sign: He usually speaks slowly and uses very little filler. If his filler rises and he leaves more silence between phrases, he is weighing the ask. Slow down, confirm the point, and let him reply.
Paul Gosar.follow_up: Within two days, put the facts and one dated next step into a written summary for his office.
Paul Gosar.personality: Gosar sits among the most skeptical members in the chamber, and among the most practical. Feelings rise quicker than nearly any colleague's, and details come out loosely in his speech. Wording is sharper than nearly any colleague's, and manner reads much more social and forceful than most. Crossing the aisle happens less than nearly any colleague manages, and visibility is very high. Arizona is the state he represents.
Paul Gosar.speaks: Slower speech than nearly any colleague marks him, and his pitch runs much flatter than most. Volume swings somewhat more than most, and pauses run somewhat longer than typical. Wording cuts sharper than nearly any colleague's and carries much more force than most. Descriptions of work are somewhat more exact than typical. Answers run shorter than nearly any colleague's. Those habits shape how he sounds in every room.
Paul Gosar.decides: For him, an ask turns on whether the facts hold up when challenged, and he crosses the aisle less than nearly any colleague. Public campaigns sway him less than they sway most colleagues, so a case built on evidence will carry more weight than a campaign. Written facts he can check against his own sources keep his position fixed. A decision needs a dated written next step to stick.

archetype.justification: His replies come in quick runs of brief answers, and few members' longest answers are as short as his.

Paul Tonko.bottom_line: Make the case through the people it would help, and keep your questions short, since he gives brief answers.
do: Bring a few real stories of people the plan would help
Open with a short, plain ask, since his answers run brief
Leave time for his questions on how the plan works, and answer each fully
Close with one clear next step, and confirm the date and owner
dont: Rely on outside calls, since pressure reaches him a bit less than most
Lay on praise to warm him up, since his words run much cooler
Assume he will carry the whole meeting alone, since he rarely holds the floor
Paul Tonko.warning_sign: He usually finishes each point he starts, and his answers end cleanly. If a point starts to trail off mid-sentence, he is not sold on your ask yet. Narrow to one next step, and ask which part he still doubts.
Paul Tonko.follow_up: Send his staff a written summary within a few days, listing who the plan helps and the next step.
Paul Tonko.personality: Tonko is very curious and very careful, and he is fairly agreeable in a room. He is a bit tougher to rattle than most, and his public words are gentler than most. Detail is his strong suit, and he follows through a bit better than most, yet he holds the floor much less than most. In hearings he is a shade less combative than most members, and he keeps a lower profile than most.
Paul Tonko.speaks: In floor speeches his pace runs a little quicker than most, and his volume swells and drops a bit more than most. Even his longest interview answers are among the briefest in the House. His words hold much less feeling, and they come across cooler than most. Far more than most, his replies come in quick runs of brief answers. Let him reach the end of each answer before you respond.
Paul Tonko.decides: He answers in brief turns, so ask his staff for his view on paper before you request a commitment. Outside groups sway him somewhat less than most, so repeated pushes carry less weight. His follow-through is a bit stronger than most, and a commitment he makes usually sticks. Lay out the detail in writing before the meeting, and mark the parts still open.

archetype.justification: He is very careful by nature, and his voting and bill follow-through run much stronger than most members'.

Pete Aguilar.bottom_line: Keep your ask to one clear sentence, since he leads talks somewhat less than most.
do: Put the mechanics in writing and share the document ahead
Open with the single question the document settles
Hold your next point until his long pause has ended
Name the bills he has already moved through the process
dont: Pitch the ask as a deal that depends on other-side votes
Send a second document before the first one is read
Cut the exchange short when his wording turns forceful
Pete Aguilar.warning_sign: He usually answers in quick runs, so one answer that runs on stands out. When he lays out a full position, he is putting a point on the record. Let him finish, then repeat his point back in one line before you reply.
Pete Aguilar.follow_up: Email his staff within two days a written recap of the steps and the one dated next step.
Pete Aguilar.personality: Aguilar serves as chair of his party's House caucus. He is very careful by nature, and he is very much in view for his role. Across his bills, a wide range of issues shows up, and he reaches across party lines much less than most. He leans a little reserved and is somewhat harder to rattle than most. He has talked publicly about his hometown in Redlands.
Pete Aguilar.speaks: His pace runs a bit slower than most. His volume stays even from one phrase to the next, and few House members are as even. In interviews his longest answers run a bit shorter than most. His pauses between phrases run longer than nearly any colleague's. Give each pause room, and do not fill the silence with your own points. Match his unhurried tempo with a slower reply of your own.
Pete Aguilar.decides: A written case shared ahead fits him best. Pressure from outside sways him a bit more than it sways most members, so plan a second contact after the meeting. Lay out the technical detail for each step in its own short section, so the case can be checked line by line. End the meeting by naming the one step he is ready to approve.

archetype.justification: Among the least visible members, and a little reserved, with fast, animated speech across a wide issue range.

Pete Ricketts.bottom_line: Bring a clear written ask with outside voices behind it, because outside pressure moves him much more than most colleagues.
do: Put the ask in writing before you meet him
Bring outside voices who back the ask
Agree dates for each step, since he follows bills through somewhat less than most
Offer a private briefing, since he is among the least seen in public
dont: Drop the follow through once he has agreed to a step
Pete Ricketts.warning_sign: A general meeting won't tell you whether a yes will hold once staff take over the file. Before you leave, get the next step and its date on paper.
Pete Ricketts.follow_up: Within two days, send his legislative staff a one page note restating the ask and the date for each step.
Pete Ricketts.personality: Ricketts is among the least seen members of his chamber, with a little reserve about him. His public talk ranges across a much broader set of issues than colleagues. His language is somewhat more charged than most. Ties across the aisle come somewhat less often for him than for most, and he carries bills through somewhat less reliably than most. A Nebraska member, he mixes a low profile with a wide ranging voice.
Pete Ricketts.speaks: Among the fastest members, he talks with among the shortest pauses between phrases, so his points arrive in quick succession. Volume varies somewhat more than most, and the pitch of his voice swings among the most varied in the chamber. Emotional tone shows up somewhat more than most in his wording. The topics he touches run a much wider span than most.
Pete Ricketts.decides: An ask backed by outside voices gets a real hearing, since he is moved by outside pressure more than most colleagues. Across the aisle he reaches somewhat less than most, so he tends to weigh asks within his own circle. Bills he carries reach passage somewhat less often than most, so a yes needs dates and a named person to check it.

archetype.justification: He takes charge of conversations as firmly as nearly any member, and he stands firm under challenge more than almost anyone.

Pete Sessions.bottom_line: Lead with the results and what the policy delivers, in a short direct case. He holds the floor firmly and works across the aisle much less than most.
do: Put the policy results first and keep the case brief
Let him hold the floor, then ask one pointed question
Expect him to defend the point hard and stay with it
dont: Pile on extra arguments once he has pushed back
Pitch the ask as a deal across the aisle
Pete Sessions.warning_sign: By default he keeps the floor and defends his point, so a firm answer is normal. If he stops defending it and lets others speak, he is weighing a concession, not digging in. Name the next step briefly and let him answer.
Pete Sessions.follow_up: Send a written summary that names the bill, its next move, and the day he agreed to act by, within the week.
Pete Sessions.personality: Sessions is fairly outgoing and commands the floor more firmly than nearly any colleague. He stands firm under challenge more than nearly any colleague, across many shows, and his bills span a wider set of topics than most. Very visible, he speaks in a far cooler and less heated register than most. Working across the floor is far rarer for him than for most, and he sees bills through with fair reliability.
Pete Sessions.speaks: He speaks at a much slower pace than most, with pauses that run longer than most. Answers run long, vary more in length than most, and trail off somewhat more often than most. Volume stays somewhat more even than most, and pitch swings a little more than most. Pressed in hearings, he is as combative as almost any member, and he holds ground across many appearances.
Pete Sessions.decides: Proposals get judged by how firmly they survive his push and whether the policy outcomes are plain. He takes charge of the room, so an ask has to survive his questioning. A wide field of bills means an ask inside his current work gets a fair hearing. He digs in when challenged, so an ask that cannot survive his pushback gets set aside.

archetype.justification: Very reliable at votes and bills, works across the aisle much more than most, and far less conspicuous than most colleagues, which suits a patient, low key approach.

Pete Stauber.bottom_line: Bring a clear story about who is helped and back it with local voices, since pressure from outside reaches him more than most colleagues.
do: Lead with the record across the aisle
Ask the local partners to press the case with him
Put the next step in writing before you leave
dont: Count on public visibility to do the persuading for you
Pete Stauber.warning_sign: Small talk will not show where he stands, since he keeps his view close until the specifics are on the table. Ask him which concrete point would move him, then send that point in writing.
Pete Stauber.follow_up: Send a short follow up letter to his office by Friday naming the agreed step and its owner.
Pete Stauber.personality: Stauber sounds somewhat reserved, and he is quicker to feel pressed than most colleagues. His own description of his work is much more precise and detailed than most, and his public talk spans a broader slate of topics than most. Across the aisle he reaches much more than most colleagues, and his votes and bill follow through are very dependable. His profile sits far lower than most colleagues', given his role.
Pete Stauber.speaks: His public talk is precise and detailed, and it spans a broader slate of topics than most. Emotional heat in his words runs a notch lower than most colleagues'. His pauses between phrases are a little shorter than most, and his pitch holds a little flatter than most colleagues', so his delivery runs even. Taken together, the manner is plain, exact and low in flourish.
Pete Stauber.decides: A proposal rises or falls on whether it can earn backing across the aisle. Pressure from outside reaches him more than most colleagues, so local backing counts for more with him than a polished argument. His votes and bill follow through are very dependable, which means a commitment he makes will hold. So an ask holds for him when local voices and a partner from the other side stand behind it.

archetype.justification: His words run upbeat, and his bills see less follow-through than nearly any colleague's in the Senate.

Peter Welch.bottom_line: Offer him a shared role he can front with a partner, and get every yes in writing, since his follow-through is among the weakest in the Senate.
do: Propose a joint announcement he can help front, once a partner has committed
Set the agenda at the start, since he steers talks less than most
Let his long answers run, then wait for the point at the end
Close by getting a dated commitment in writing, since follow-through is his weak spot
dont: Rush your points to keep up with his quick pace
Treat a sentence he leaves unfinished as his final word
Assume his tone in hearings stays as upbeat as his speeches
Peter Welch.warning_sign: His wording is usually much gentler than most. If it turns sharper than usual, he has stopped weighing the substance. Stop, narrow the disagreement to one point, and offer to take it up in writing.
Peter Welch.follow_up: Send his office a short note on the results by Friday, naming the partners and the next step.
Peter Welch.personality: Welch uses more upbeat words than most, and his wording is a bit more forceful too. He is among the least reliable at voting and bill follow-through in the Senate. The bills he carries span more areas than nearly any colleague's. His wording sounds less social than most, and it leans cooler than most colleagues do. He has spoken about his wife's long illness and the health coverage that came with the family's university job. In hearings he is a touch more combative than most colleagues.
Peter Welch.speaks: In interviews his answers run long, a bit past what most colleagues give, and his filler runs a little heavier than most. Few senators talk faster than he does. His pitch swings more than nearly any colleague's. Volume stays fairly even, and his speech stays quick even across long answers. Plan for long stretches of talk, and let his answers run before you add a point. His filler sits inside those long answers, so listen for the point after it.
Peter Welch.decides: A partner who shares the stage can make a yes easier to get, where the role fits his work. Few senators are less reliable at seeing bills through. Pair the ask with one idea he can explore on his own, since he is curious by temperament. He has spoken about skiing with his wife near home; where it honestly fits, that is shared ground. End by asking which part of the plan he would take to his own staff first.

archetype.justification: She is very outgoing and fairly curious, takes charge of talks, and is seen more often than nearly any colleague.

Pramila Jayapal.bottom_line: Make the case through the people and households the ask would reach, since a case built that way fits her best.
do: Prepare one clear example of a family the ask would help
Open by letting her set the pace, since she takes charge of talks
Keep the greeting brief, since her talk is much less chatty than most
Set a dated follow-up, since she is one of the least reliable on bills
dont: Plan the agenda as if her answers stay short, yet her longest outrun almost anyone's
Read her cooler wording as coldness toward your cause
Count on her visibility alone to carry the ask
Pramila Jayapal.warning_sign: She usually takes the floor and keeps talks moving. If she takes the floor even more firmly than that, the talk is running in her direction. Offer one clear next step, then ask which part she would act on.
Pramila Jayapal.follow_up: By Thursday, give her staff a brief note on the people affected, the next step, and who owns it.
Pramila Jayapal.personality: Jayapal brings a very outgoing style and a fairly curious mind. She is fairly careful, though a little skeptical, and she flares more readily than most. Far more topics come up in her talk than most, and her legislation touches somewhat more areas than most. Her follow-through on bills ranks among the weakest in the House. In hearings her edge sharpens much more than most colleagues. She has spoken about arriving in America alone as a teenager. She is seen more often than nearly any colleague; she is among the most visible for her role.
Pramila Jayapal.speaks: In interviews her answers run much longer than most, while her longest stretches outrun nearly anyone's. Her replies range widely in length, from brief to long stretches. Talk moves at a pace well ahead of most colleagues, with short pauses between phrases. Her volume stays somewhat more even than most, and her pitch changes less than most colleagues'. Her words are gentler than most, and she carries more filler than most colleagues. Match her quick pace and keep your tone even.
Pramila Jayapal.decides: A case built on the people an ask would help fits her best. Few members in the House are less reliable on bills than she is, so treat any yes as the first step, not the finish. Keep the people behind the ask in contact with her office as each step takes shape. Finish by asking which household story she would want to hear first.

archetype.justification: He is curious, his bills span more ground than nearly any colleague, and his visibility for his role puts him among the most visible in the House.

Raja Krishnamoorthi.bottom_line: Let the written technical record do the persuading, since written detail is the case that fits how he works.
do: Put the bill's mechanism on paper step by step before you meet
Open with the action the bill asks the office to take
Ask one open question at a time, since he answers evenly
Close by keeping any public step on hold until the written detail is settled
dont: Argue the same point again once he has defended it
Assume his yes will hold without a written step
Match his sharp tone in a formal hearing with a sharper one of your own
Raja Krishnamoorthi.warning_sign: He usually holds the floor less than most. If he starts holding it well beyond how he usually does, the talk is now running on his point, not yours. Let him finish, then answer the one point he has taken up.
Raja Krishnamoorthi.follow_up: Send his legislative director a numbered list of open technical points, each with a date, within two days.
Raja Krishnamoorthi.personality: Krishnamoorthi is curious and fairly careful, and his bills span more ground than nearly any colleague. He is much weaker than most at seeing his bills through. Few colleagues are more visible for their role than he is. In hearings he presses somewhat harder than most members. His public words carry much less force than most. After graduating from Harvard, he clerked for a federal judge.
Raja Krishnamoorthi.speaks: He moves through his answers much faster than most colleagues, with shorter pauses between phrases. His pitch moves a lot, and his answers come in shorter turns than most. Hearings bring out a sharper side in him. Keep the points few, and let each one land before the next. Bring the written detail so you can follow the thread when he moves quickly.
Raja Krishnamoorthi.decides: Written technical detail fits him best, and a clean page on the mechanism carries more weight than a pitch. Outside pressure counts for very little with him, so the written case has to carry the decision. Confirm the next vote date with his office before any public step, so the written record shows it. End by asking which written detail he wants checked first.

archetype.justification: He answers in short bursts, works across the aisle much less than most, and is loose with detail.

Ralph Norman.bottom_line: Let written, technical evidence carry the case here, since outside pressure will not move him much.
do: Put the hard numbers first and cite the source for each
Ask narrow questions he can answer in a sentence
Anticipate each doubt he has and answer it before he raises it
dont: Rely on warm small talk to win him over
Assume a sponsor from across the aisle will win his support
Take a promised follow up as settled without a check in
Ralph Norman.warning_sign: He usually replies in rapid bursts. When his replies run longer and the filler drops away, he is weighing the point or getting guarded. Stop, name the single point in dispute, and ask which part he wants settled first.
Ralph Norman.follow_up: After the meeting, send his office one page that lists each figure with its source, within three days.
Ralph Norman.personality: Norman is a skeptic who questions claims before he accepts them, and he gets worked up faster than nearly any colleague. His bills reach across many issue areas, yet he talks about them broadly rather than in fine detail. Cool in manner and highly visible, he works across the aisle far less than most, and seeing bills through is among the weakest in the chamber. In the room, that means he pushes his own line rather than building common ground.
Ralph Norman.speaks: He covers many issues in broad strokes rather than fine detail. Heavy emotional charge runs through his wording, more than nearly any colleague in the House. His answers come short and quick, in runs of brief replies with a little filler. Pauses between phrases run a little longer than most, his pitch rises and falls a bit more than most, and his volume stays somewhat more even.
Ralph Norman.decides: He weighs an ask by testing it against his own doubts, so it has to survive his skepticism before he commits. Technical evidence moves him, while outside pressure moves him less than nearly any member. A broad agenda and a seat on Financial Services give him plenty to weigh in on. With few ties across the aisle to lean on, any ask that needs votes from the other side is a hard sell with him.

archetype.justification: Few senators are as hard to persuade as he is, and he defends his position more than most while taking charge of conversations.

Rand Paul.bottom_line: Put the written technical case in his hands before the meeting. When challenged he holds his ground, so the document has to hold up.
do: Send the technical document a few days ahead, not on the day
Keep the ask out of public statements until he has the technical summary
Allow for his slow pace and short pauses before you speak
Confirm the person who acts next and the due date before you go
dont: Pitch the ask as a deal only one bloc can accept
Read his skepticism as a final no
Drop the ask after a single cool meeting
Rand Paul.warning_sign: He usually speaks in unhurried turns, so a run of quick back-and-forth replies stands out. When exchanges turn rapid, he wants to wrap up. Keep the ask to one sentence and slow down.
Rand Paul.follow_up: Call his staff within two days to ask whether he will vote on the bill you need.
Rand Paul.personality: Paul takes charge of conversations more than most, and winning him over is harder than for nearly any senator. Bill follow-through ranks near the bottom in the Senate. He builds more ties across the aisle than nearly any senator, yet his public style reads much cooler than most. He has talked publicly about relatives in the military, and his role makes him among the most visible senators.
Rand Paul.speaks: Pace runs much slower than most colleagues'. Pauses between phrases come quickly, and pitch sits much flatter than most. Volume stays nearly even across a speech. In hearings he comes across as a bit sharper than most. Give each pause a beat, and answer his main point first. Keep your reply to his tempo, since his delivery stays even across the whole speech.
Rand Paul.decides: When challenged he defends his ground much more than most, so the written case has to hold up when it is challenged. Pressure from outside moves him further than most members do, and a return visit with the same ask carries weight. Keep each return visit to one technical point, so the second meeting builds on the first. Close by asking which single point he wants settled.

archetype.justification: His bills stay within a narrower set of issues, and he speaks at a much slower pace.

Randy Feenstra.bottom_line: Build the ask around who it helps, with a plan he can check. Outside pressure moves him among the least of anyone, so let the merits carry it.
do: Frame the request around who gains from it
Give him a plan with clear steps he can verify
Speak at his pace and leave room for pauses
dont: Skip abstract framing, since he puts weight on concrete effects
Assume outside pressure alone will settle his vote
Randy Feenstra.warning_sign: A general meeting will not show how his answers hold up once you ask for specifics. Ask for the same specific example twice and compare the two answers. Note any gap between his summary and the details he gives.
Randy Feenstra.follow_up: Send him a one page note with the plan steps and the evidence behind each, within three days.
Randy Feenstra.personality: Feenstra is a little reserved and keeps a practical focus. Across his bills, the issue range runs somewhat narrower than most colleagues. Follow through on bills is the weaker side of his record, with votes somewhat behind most colleagues. As an Iowa member, he works from a practical base that suits a narrow agenda. His practical streak means he tests each proposal against what it delivers.
Randy Feenstra.speaks: He talks at a much slower pace than most colleagues. Pauses between phrases run somewhat shorter than most. His volume stays as even as almost anyone's in the House. His pitch stays as flat as almost anyone's in the chamber. Those patterns describe his delivery, not his mood. Slower delivery and an even tone give his answers a deliberate rhythm in conversation.
Randy Feenstra.decides: He weighs an ask by its concrete effect on the people it helps. Outside campaigns move him among the least, so a request must stand on its own case. An ask inside the issues he already works on fits better. He values detail over promises, so concrete results matter more than pledges. So a plan with named owners and dates is what sticks with him.

archetype.justification: He speaks with much more edge than most, and his bills span among the narrowest issue ranges in the House.

Randy Fine.bottom_line: Lead with the bottom line and keep the ask simple, since outside crowds sway him less than most.
do: Lead with the bottom line, then give one clear next step
Give him one concrete ask with a named owner
Answer his sharp points directly, without softening them
dont: Argue the point again once he has settled it
Assume a long plan will keep his attention, since his pauses come quickly
Push for a commitment on the spot, since crowds outside sway him less than most
Randy Fine.warning_sign: He usually speaks with much more edge than most, and his wording stays sharp. If the edge drops away and he turns conciliatory, he is on guard. Slow down, name the concern, and offer one concrete fix.
Randy Fine.follow_up: Send him a one page memo with the ask, the named owner, and the date, within three days.
Randy Fine.personality: Fine is somewhat more outgoing than most colleagues, and he likes a lively room. He is quick to flare, far more than most colleagues, and it shows in his tone. Across his public talk, the range of issues is narrow. His bills cover a narrow set of issues. Votes and carrying bills through leave a weak record. He is somewhat more visible than most colleagues, and his temperament is trusting.
Randy Fine.speaks: He speaks with much more edge than most. His phrasing carries much less emotional heat than most colleagues. Across issues, his range is narrow.
