Answers on his own work are thin in detail. In hearings his manner runs somewhat less confrontational than most members. His volume rises and falls somewhat more than most colleagues. His pitch stays much flatter than most speakers. Pauses between phrases run much shorter than most.
Randy Fine.decides: Being somewhat outgoing, he weighs an ask through conversation more than through written detail. Crowds outside sway him less than most, so a request must stand on its own case. An ask inside the issues he already works on fits better. His record on seeing bills through is among the least reliable, so commitments need a named owner. So a promise he makes is only as firm as the owner behind it.

archetype.justification: Outgoing and practical, he talks about a narrow set of issues in careful detail and keeps to them.

Randy Weber.bottom_line: Bring one specific ask and lead with the results and facts, since those are what he responds to.
do: Put the policy change in one short, direct paragraph
Pin down the next step before he leaves the room
In a hearing, answer with facts rather than feeling
dont: Assume his outgoing manner means he will lead the ask in public
Expect outside pressure alone to settle the question
Randy Weber.warning_sign: In a hearing he usually presses a little harder than most, so a sharp question is normal for him. If he presses harder still, he is on guard, so stop, answer in one line, and let him move on.
Randy Weber.follow_up: After the meeting, send a short written note with the results and the next step, then check in within a week.
Randy Weber.personality: Weber is outgoing and practical, and he keeps his talk to a narrow set of issues. He works through those issues in careful, detailed terms, with less heat in his words than most. Visibility runs much lower than his role would suggest, and he sees bills through much less reliably than most. A Texas member, he is a bit more combative than most in hearings.
Randy Weber.speaks: His speech is much slower than most, with somewhat longer pauses between phrases and volume that swings more than most. Pitch stays flatter than most, and his words are somewhat less charged than most. He frames issues in careful, detailed terms, staying inside a narrow range of topics. Under hearing pressure he gets somewhat more combative, and he still speaks slowly.
Randy Weber.decides: He weighs an ask by its results and facts, and by whether it sits inside the issues he already works on. Outside pressure carries a little more weight with him than with most, though it does not replace the case itself. Because he follows bills through much less than most, a yes from him lasts only as long as someone keeps the paperwork moving.

archetype.justification: He works across the aisle far more than most, and his warm words fit an outgoing, visible Orca.

Raphael Warnock.bottom_line: Offer a shared role he can announce, and let the ask ride on his coalition. Outside voices move him more, so bring the people who back him.
do: Offer him a visible shared role he can announce
Bring the people who back the ask in person
Match the energy of the room with upbeat, practical points
dont: Ask for a firm yes before the room has warmed up
Count on his cooperation to carry a bill alone
Raphael Warnock.warning_sign: He usually gives full answers and keeps an unhurried pace. If his pauses lengthen and he stops engaging with the ask, he is losing interest, so stop pressing and offer one concrete next step on his terms.
Raphael Warnock.follow_up: After the meeting, send a short note naming the partners who will join the next step, with a date for each.
Raphael Warnock.personality: Warnock is warm, agreeable and eager to bring others in. Visibility ranks very high for his role, and across the aisle his joint work runs well ahead of most colleagues. His answers stretch longer than usual, and his talk runs warmer than nearly any colleague's. Outgoing and curious, he tends to lean on shared action rather than solo fights, and that suits a room full of partners.
Raphael Warnock.speaks: His pace runs slower than most, with longer pauses between phrases. Replies stretch longer than most, and his words come across as gentler than most. When challenged, he holds his point with some force, and his pitch moves a fair amount. He leads with warmth and keeps his talk tied to what the group can do together. That mix suits a room that wants shared plans.
Raphael Warnock.decides: He checks whether partners split the work and whether it advances something visible. Pressure from outside groups moves him more than most members do, and bipartisan ties make him open to a shared plan. His follow through on bills trails most colleagues a little, so a request lands better when others carry it forward. So a deal sticks with him when partners share the work and stand with him in public.

archetype.justification: Quick to flare, very curious, and centered on community impact, which fits a protective style that defends its position.

Rashida Tlaib.bottom_line: Keep the ask short and tied to who is helped, since she takes the floor and pushes back hard when challenged.
do: Put community impact first and name the people it helps
Let her take the floor first, then answer each challenge directly
Ask one question at a time, since her answers run short
dont: Treat each challenge as a personal attack on your bill
Expect a hearing exchange to stay polite
Rashida Tlaib.warning_sign: Usually she holds the floor, answers briefly, and pushes back when challenged, so a sharp exchange is routine for her. If she stops pushing back and her sentences trail off, she is losing interest, so ask which point still needs testing.
Rashida Tlaib.follow_up: Within two days, put the next step, who owns it, and a date in a memo that her staff receives after the session.
Rashida Tlaib.personality: Tlaib is a very curious, highly outgoing legislator whose speech runs hotter than nearly any colleague's. She gets worked up quickly and gives details looser than almost anyone. Crossing party lines is seldom something she does, and she draws attention on a scale few colleagues match. Her legislation spans a broader set of subjects than nearly any colleague's, while she stands firm when challenged.
Rashida Tlaib.speaks: Her public words carry strong emotion and cover a wide range of issues, and she gives much less detail about her work than most. Even in interviews her answers run short, and she trails off somewhat more than most. Her words are warm and upbeat, and they read as far more sociable than most. When challenged she defends her position much more than most.
Rashida Tlaib.decides: Whether it speaks to the people it would affect is how she judges an ask. When she has taken a stance, she tends to defend it, so a challenge hardens her rather than settling the matter. Across the aisle her record is thin, so an ask that depends on bringing the other side along is a hard sell. So an ask built around her own community base has the best chance.

archetype.justification: Very outgoing and curious, fast paced, quick to take the floor, and hard to dislodge once he defends a point.

Raul Ruiz.bottom_line: Let him make his case, then answer his strongest point with one clear fact. He defends positions hard, and outside force moves him more, so backing matters.
do: Keep your own answers short, since his run longer than most
Offer a shared announcement he can front alongside you
In a hearing, expect hard pushback and a combative tone
dont: Cut off his long answers before he reaches the point
Count on warm words to show he agrees
Push a second time once he has defended his position
Raul Ruiz.warning_sign: His usual pattern is defending a position hard once it is challenged, so that alone is normal for him. Watch for him dropping the defense and conceding a point, which usually means he has lost the argument for now.
Raul Ruiz.follow_up: Send him a one page written summary of the shared announcement, with the next step listed and the names of the people backing it.
Raul Ruiz.personality: Ruiz stays very sociable and very inquisitive, and he is fairly agreeable and careful with details. He takes charge of talks and holds the floor, and he defends his position harder than nearly any colleague in the House. He is strongly combative in hearings. Taken together, he is a forceful operator who sets the terms of the room and holds his ground when challenged.
Raul Ruiz.speaks: His delivery runs well ahead of most in speed, with shorter pauses between phrases than nearly any colleague. Tone shifts more than nearly every colleague does, and loudness varies somewhat more than most. Answers run longer than most, their length stays even, and filler is rarer for him than for most. He trails off less often than nearly every peer, and his phrasing is somewhat sharper than most, with warmth underneath.
Raul Ruiz.decides: Something he can front with allies is what he looks for, and a joint announcement draws him in. Reliability at carrying bills to the finish is lower than most, so he is drawn to the moment more than to the work that follows. Once challenged, he holds firm, and pressure from outside pushes him harder than most, so the decision turns on who backs the request.

archetype.justification: He is very visible in his role and very outgoing, and his bills reach much wider than most.

Richard Blumenthal.bottom_line: Offer a joint role he can stand behind publicly, and send a dated written summary. Pressure from outside counts for less, so the paper does the work.
do: Prepare a joint role he can take, and confirm it with his office
Open by naming the public event where he can front it
Let his long pauses run, since his replies come out short
Close by asking which commitment he will act on first
dont: Bring the same request back in person every week
Take his warm words as a firm yes
Read his short answers as a brush-off
Richard Blumenthal.warning_sign: In hearings he usually asks a little sharper questions than most members do. If he drops a point he had raised, he has let it go, so bring him back with one plain question.
Richard Blumenthal.follow_up: Ahead of the next session, send his office a summary on a single page, with partners named and a date beside each step.
Richard Blumenthal.personality: Blumenthal is outgoing and highly visible in his role. His bills reach across much more ground than most. He is a very careful, organized person. Across party lines he builds somewhat more than most. He is fairly curious and agreeable. In public, his talk gives off less emotional charge than nearly any senator. He has told the story of his father, who escaped Germany with little.
Richard Blumenthal.speaks: In interviews his replies come out much shorter than most, and his longest turns stop a bit sooner. His pauses between phrases stretch longer than nearly any senator's, and his pitch swings widely. His volume swells and fades a bit more than most. Filler is almost absent from his speech, so keep your own points just as tight. His public tone carries much more force than most, so meet its force with a firm, plain case.
Richard Blumenthal.decides: He commits on partnerships he can front publicly, and outside pressure sways him less than most. On votes and bills, his record trails most colleagues in the Senate. Where it fits honestly, mention the family service he has discussed in public, and keep that mention brief. Keep the shared role visible in every written update you send, including the short ones.

archetype.justification: Very careful and organized, a little reserved, and somewhat slower in speech, so he moves through an issue at his own unhurried pace.

Richard Hudson.bottom_line: Put one narrow ask in writing and let him consider it alone before the meeting. Outside voices move his position a little more than pressure in the room.
do: Send the written detail a few days ahead so he can check it
Give him time to decide, since he sees bills through once he commits
Offer a joint announcement that he can front alongside you
dont: Press for a yes at the first meeting
Richard Hudson.warning_sign: He is usually somewhat less combative than most in a formal hearing, so pressing the detail hard means he is contesting the point. Let him finish, then answer the exact question he asked.
Richard Hudson.follow_up: Since he sees bills through somewhat more dependably than most, send his office a written summary within two days with a named next step.
Richard Hudson.personality: Hudson is a careful, organized member who works from detail and speaks with a little reserve. His language is somewhat less charged emotionally than most, and his issue range is narrower than nearly anyone's in the House. Across party lines, he works somewhat less than most, and his bills reach somewhat fewer areas than most. His background includes years in politics, including work as a district director in Congress.
Richard Hudson.speaks: He talks slowly and keeps his sentences specific, and his pauses run a little shorter than most. His volume stays very even, while his pitch moves up and down somewhat more than most, so any shift shows up in his tone rather than his loudness. Across a narrow set of issues, he keeps his language a little less charged than most. Those pitch changes are the clearest sign of a shift in his delivery.
Richard Hudson.decides: Before backing anything he sizes up how neatly it fits detail he can verify, and he waits to commit until he has read the full text. Outside voices carry a little more weight with him than most, so outside support is what changes his mind. An ask inside his own areas fits him, since his bills stay within fewer areas than most. Because he sees bills through somewhat more than most, a written commitment with a date is what keeps him to it.

archetype.justification: He takes charge in conversation, and he holds his ground hard when challenged, with sharper words than most and a very reliable record on votes and bills.

Richard McCormick.bottom_line: Put the result up front, then let him push back, since he will test it. He sees bills through very reliably, so the step after the meeting matters.
do: Bring the specific results in a direct, one-page case
Open by letting him set the first topic, since he takes charge of talk
Let him push each point, and answer each challenge directly
Point to a bill he already saw through, as the model for this ask
dont: Offer a plan with no action step, since his words are among the most action-focused
Assume he is done when a turn trails off, since his turns often end unfinished
Stretch one long pitch, since he replies in quick runs
Richard McCormick.warning_sign: He usually trades quick replies back and forth, much more than most. If those runs stop and he gives one complete reply instead, he is laying out a full case. Note that point and answer it in one line.
Richard McCormick.follow_up: Within two days, send his staff a short written note naming the one dated step he agreed to.
Richard McCormick.personality: McCormick is very reliable on votes and bills, and he is dominant in conversation. His words are among the most action-focused in the House. Careful detail shows up in how he describes his work, somewhat more than most. His bills reach one of the narrowest sets of issues in the House. He is sharper in his words than most, and he holds ground hard when challenged.
Richard McCormick.speaks: His volume swings a lot on the House floor, more than nearly all colleagues. His answers tend to be short and come in quick bursts, and their length varies much more than most. Turns often end unfinished, well beyond most. When challenged he holds ground across shows, so keep your points tight. If his turn ends unfinished, wait a beat before you answer. Keep each point short and plain.
Richard McCormick.decides: A clear result makes the case for him. Once he agrees, he sees bills through very reliably, so get the agreement written down. Outside voices carry a little extra weight with him, so a dated ask from outside helps. His combative streak means each claim will get a challenge, so have the answer ready. Ask which outside voice he would trust to back the ask, and bring that voice in before the vote.

archetype.justification: He is quite reserved, does not seek the lead in conversations, and is careful with detail, which suits a slow and deliberate approach.

Richard Neal.bottom_line: Bring a written case and give him time to weigh it. Pressure from outside has less pull on him, so a careful yes beats a quick one.
do: Send the detailed case in writing before the meeting so he can review it
Ask short questions and leave room for his brief answers
In a hearing, expect polite questions rather than heated exchanges
dont: Push him for an instant decision in front of colleagues
Fill the silences with your own talk, since he does not seek the lead
Richard Neal.warning_sign: He usually answers in a few sentences and does not push a conversation forward. If he suddenly talks at length, he is engaged on the point, so ask him directly what would settle it for him.
Richard Neal.follow_up: After the meeting, give his office a written summary stating by what date, and by whom, the next step gets done.
Richard Neal.personality: Neal is reserved and careful, with more detail in his accounts of his work than most colleagues offer. He is curious and agreeable, and somewhat harder to rattle than most. His public words carry less emotion than nearly anyone's in the House, and his bills span a narrow set of issues. On votes and bills he is very reliable, and in formal hearings he ranks among the least combative members of the House.
Richard Neal.speaks: He gives concise answers in conversation and interviews, and his replies stay close to the same length. He trails off less than nearly any member, and his longest answers are shorter than nearly any member's in the House. Descriptions of his work come in careful, detailed language more than most, and his public wording carries less emotional charge than nearly anyone's. In formal hearings he is among the least combative members of the House.
Richard Neal.decides: Carrying out an ask in practice is his test, and he is very dependable once he has reviewed the case. Pressure from outside has less pull on him, so pushing him works less well. His bills span few issue areas, so an ask inside his areas fits best. He is also fairly agreeable, so an ask framed as a shared step tends to land well. So a yes from him holds only when the next step is on paper.

archetype.justification: His profile stays low even for his role, and his talk about the job is exact.

Rick Allen.bottom_line: Lead with the result and the facts, and keep your ask to one clear decision. Outside pressure sways him more than most, so back the ask with a written case.
do: Prepare the one ask on a single page before you walk in
Open with the result in plain words, and hold any public role for later
Name the members across the aisle who already back the ask
Close by returning to your one ask when outside pressure builds
dont: Sell a brand-new approach before showing it has worked elsewhere
Inflate what the policy delivers beyond what the facts support
Brush off his pointed hearing questions as routine, since he turns combative there
Rick Allen.warning_sign: In hearings he is usually somewhat more combative than most members. If his questions turn sharper than that, he is starting to resist the plan. Bring the talk back to the result, then ask for the next step.
Rick Allen.follow_up: Send his office a short note within a day that confirms the date for the next step.
Rick Allen.personality: Allen leans a little reserved and a little practical, and he is looser with details than most. He is a bit quicker to get worked up than most members. He works with members of the other party more than most. Bills span fewer issue areas than most, and his profile stays much lower than most, even for his role. He has said his parents taught him to respect authority.
Rick Allen.speaks: He runs a bit faster in speech than most, with shorter pauses between phrases and a voice that stays fairly even. His pitch moves a bit more than most. Work talk from him ranks among the most exact in the House, so ask for the specifics. His words carry more charge than most, so keep the tone respectful and the facts plain. Let him lay out the detail before you move on.
Rick Allen.decides: Across party lines he works more than most, and his own cross-party ties show it in his record. His family attends a church, which can be a point of shared ground if it honestly fits the moment, so mention it early. Ask him to name the one part he will carry to his colleagues, and when he will raise it with them.

archetype.justification: Reserved in manner and highly careful and orderly, he is hard to rattle.

Rick Larsen.bottom_line: Send the technical detail first, then ask for one dated next step, since follow through is his weaker side.
do: Send written technical evidence well before the meeting
Name the cross-party cosponsors who already back the bill
Leave room for his longer pauses before you follow up
In a hearing, expect gentle questions and answer each one fully
dont: Assume his agreeable manner means he will commit
Accept a verbal yes without a written next step
Mistake his reserve for disinterest in the bill
Rick Larsen.warning_sign: By default his language is much softer than most, so a sharper edge usually means he has lost confidence in the case. Stop the detail, ask whether he wants the next step in writing, and let him set the pace.
Rick Larsen.follow_up: Within two days, send his team a written summary covering the next move, its owner, and the date.
Rick Larsen.personality: Larsen is counted among the most reserved members, yet very careful and organized, and hard to rattle. Across the aisle he works much more than most, and bills span a far wider set of topics. Seeing bills through lags far behind what his care suggests. During hearings he counts among the least combative in the chamber, and he stays less visible than his role would suggest.
Rick Larsen.speaks: His language is clearly softer than most, with less emotional charge. Public talk covers more topics than most, in somewhat more careful detail, so substance outweighs feeling. He pauses longer between phrases, and his pitch and volume both swing more than most. Feeling stays low while the detail carries the weight. Overall his manner reads as careful and understated, with the substance doing the work.
Rick Larsen.decides: What he weighs first is how well the written technical case holds up, so evidence sent ahead of time fits him best. Pressure from outside shifts him faster than most, and his cross-party work makes him open to a joined ask. His bills span a much wider set of topics, which widens the coalitions he can join. His follow through lags, so commitments need a written owner and date to hold.

archetype.justification: He is practical, much sharper in wording than most, and he digs in hard when challenged, so Bull fits best.

Rick Scott.bottom_line: Lead with results in a short, direct case and back it with voices from outside. Pressure from outside moves him more than most, so the voices carry real weight.
do: Open with what the policy delivers, backed by hard facts
Let him take the floor first, then answer in brief points
If he pushes back, answer with the one fact that settles it
dont: Assume a long, detailed brief will hold his attention
Take his sharp wording as the final word on your bill
Expect an unchecked claim to land with him
Rick Scott.warning_sign: He usually keeps his volume even and holds his position when challenged. When his volume starts swinging up and down, he is usually irritated. Stop and acknowledge the point he disputes before you go on.
Rick Scott.follow_up: Send him a short results memo with the key figures and the agreed next step by Friday.
Rick Scott.personality: Scott is very outgoing and rates among the least abstract senators in the chamber. He is among the most skeptical members, and he works across the aisle less than almost anyone. Emotional charge runs heavy in his words, and they are much sharper than most. He steers conversations and keeps the floor well beyond most colleagues. Under challenge, he digs in harder than almost anyone, and he holds his ground. Reliable on votes and bills, he is a visible, results focused operator.
Rick Scott.speaks: Emotional charge in his words is among the strongest in the Senate, but his tone is a little less forceful than most colleagues. Coverage of issues runs a little narrower than typical colleagues, and detail on his own work comes a little less carefully. Answers come short and direct, with plenty of filler and few trailing sentences. Pace runs a little quicker than most, with an even volume. Under challenge he digs in harder than almost anyone and returns to his point again and again.
Rick Scott.decides: He judges an ask by what it delivers, so a case built on results moves him. Pressure from outside groups moves him more than most colleagues, and a sustained push can carry weight. Once he takes a stance he keeps it, and he digs in harder when challenged, so pushing him off a position only hardens him. He works across the aisle less than almost anyone, so an ask that needs crossover support will struggle. So his support lasts when the results are his to claim.

archetype.justification: His narrow issue focus and detailed, specific talk mark a focused member who works one area at a time.

Riley Moore.bottom_line: Bring one narrow, specific ask with a named next step, since he is reliable at seeing bills through. Outside pressure moves him less, so the case must do the work.
do: Put the bill's record and its one issue up front
Slow your pace and leave gaps, since he speaks slowly
Give him time to reply before you press the next point
dont: Overload the meeting with several asks at a fast pace
Read his slow manner as doubt about the bill
Lead with abstract figures rather than the people your bill helps
Riley Moore.warning_sign: Group sessions will not reveal when he has hit his limit. Watch for the point where he stops adding detail, and if that happens, stop and offer one concrete next step.
Riley Moore.follow_up: Forward a short memo with the request, its owner and a deadline within two days.
Riley Moore.personality: Moore is focused and specific in his work. He talks about a narrow set of issues, in careful, detailed terms, and his bills cover few areas. Seeing bills through is one of his habits. He describes his bills in plain, concrete terms. Visibility runs somewhat lower than others, and emotional charge runs a bit lower too, so he stays quiet in a crowded room.
Riley Moore.speaks: His delivery is plain and unhurried, and he keeps to a narrow set of issues. Careful, detailed terms describe his work, with a bit less emotional charge than many colleagues. When he speaks about his bills, the focus stays on specifics rather than the wider picture. That combination makes his talk easy to follow but slow to reach a point.
Riley Moore.decides: A proposal is weighed by whether it sits inside the small cluster of issues he already follows. Seeing bills through is one of his habits, so a clear, dated plan earns his attention. Outside sway carries little weight with him, so a choice sticks only when the case convinces him and a named next action follows. His visibility for his role runs somewhat lower, so a public role may not suit the ask.

archetype.justification: He ranks very high on curiosity, and he works across a broad set of issues.

Ritchie Torres.bottom_line: Lead with written, technical evidence sent ahead of time, since that is how he takes in a case. Outside pressure moves him less, so keep the case on the facts.
do: Send the written case ahead, with the technical detail
Name a dated step and the person who owns it
Bring a partner from the other side to the table
Ask him a direct question about the facts
dont: Rush him through a long list of asks
Count on outside pressure to settle a question for him
Lean on a loose, filler heavy case
Ritchie Torres.warning_sign: His usual pattern is fast, curious talk with long pauses and a voice that moves a lot. When his pauses grow longer still and his pace slows, he is working through a hard point, so give him room and ask what evidence would settle it.
Ritchie Torres.follow_up: Within a week, send a brief written note naming the next action, who owns it, and when the next check falls.
Ritchie Torres.personality: Torres sits among the most curious members around, and he stands among the most skeptical. He is somewhat careful, and he is somewhat quicker to flare than most. His talk spans more topics than nearly anyone's, yet his descriptions of his own work come across as less exact than typical. Wording runs a bit more emotionally charged than typical, and he is well short of dependable at getting bills through. His bills span an unusually wide set of issues, and he is very visible in the chamber.
Ritchie Torres.speaks: Answers come short, and his longest replies stay brief compared with typical. His interview answers run somewhat shorter than most and trail off much less than typical. He speaks with a lot of filler, well above typical, and his wording is somewhat more social. Gaps between phrases run much longer than most, and his pitch swings somewhat more than most. On the other hand, he speaks somewhat faster than typical and his volume shifts a bit more.
Ritchie Torres.decides: Asks gain traction when they are written and technical enough to test. With bills across many areas, an ask that spans several of them has room. Working with the other side comes more naturally to him than most, so a joint sponsor carries extra weight. His follow through is well short of dependable, so a commitment from him needs a dated next step. Pressure from outside has a smaller pull on him than on most members, so a push does not often decide the question.

archetype.justification: Among the most outgoing, curious, and visible members, he is quick to engage and hard to fluster.

Ro Khanna.bottom_line: Lead with what the policy delivers in a short, direct case, and name the next vote. Outside pressure reaches him less than most, so results have to do the work.
do: Anchor the ask in results and facts, not the story of the fight
Ask for a named vote and the bill's next committee step
Answer his defense with one fact, not a second argument
dont: Treat his agreement in the room as a firm commitment
Assume his fast, upbeat answers settle the question
Ro Khanna.warning_sign: Usually his pace runs quicker than most, and his pitch rises and falls a great deal. If his pace slows and his pitch flattens, he has shifted, so pick up the next step and name who will follow up.
Ro Khanna.follow_up: Send his staff a one page note with the vote date, the bill's next step, and a named owner within two days.
Ro Khanna.personality: Khanna, from California, ranks near the top for outgoing and curious, and he is very careful and well organized. He is hard to unsettle, yet his public words carry little emotional charge. He comes across as gentle, and he joins the other side's bills less often than most. Warmth and upbeat talk mark his style, and his visibility sits among the highest for his position.
Ro Khanna.speaks: He talks slightly faster than most, with much shorter pauses between phrases, and his pitch swings widely. In interviews his answers run somewhat longer than most, and their length stays even. Filler words show up more often in his talk, and he holds his position when challenged. His words are warm and upbeat, and his tone stays social rather than forceful.
Ro Khanna.decides: He weighs an ask on the results it delivers, and a short direct case with facts moves him more than a story does. Campaigns and crowds carry a lighter hold on him than on most members, so a specific request lands harder. Because he defends his position, a bill that holds up under questioning keeps his backing, so a decision needs a vote on the record to stick.

archetype.justification: His fairly careful manner, very reliable follow through and low visibility earn the Tortoise label.

Robert Aderholt.bottom_line: Bring written technical detail and one clear next step. Pressure from outside works on him less than on most, so the evidence has to carry the ask.
do: Send the technical summary in writing before the meeting
Name the bill's next procedural step and its due date
dont: Press him for a fast answer on a complex request
Count on visibility alone to carry the bill
Robert Aderholt.warning_sign: Usually he is among the least combative members in hearings, so gentle questioning is normal for him there. When he starts asking pointed follow up questions, he is testing whether the record holds. Send him the document in writing and let the record answer.
Robert Aderholt.follow_up: Within a week, send him the written technical summary with the next vote date and the staffer who owns the follow up.
Robert Aderholt.personality: Aderholt is a careful, reliable member who goes into more specifics about his work than most colleagues. His issue range is among the narrowest in the chamber. Fewer topics are touched by his bills than by nearly any colleague's, and he is very dependable at finishing them. Among the least visible members in the House, he is also among the least combative in hearings.
Robert Aderholt.speaks: He describes his own work with more care and specifics than most, and he keeps his focus on a narrow set of issues. His manner is plain and low key, with few broad themes. In hearings he is among the least combative members. His talk stays on the particulars rather than sweeping claims, and he keeps each point concrete and specific. Concrete points suit his manner.
Robert Aderholt.decides: Specifics matter to him, as does whether the next step can be put in writing. Outside force gets less traction with him than with most colleagues, so an ask resting on pressure will stall. He follows bills through very reliably. A request he can check against the bill's text is easier for him to weigh, so his backing holds once the next step is on record.

archetype.justification: Practical beyond most, much more careful with details than most, and narrow in the issues he covers.

Robert Bresnahan.bottom_line: Bring the case written and ready, and back it with the outside voices he hears from, since pressure moves him more.
do: Put the policy's results first, since he is practical about outcomes
Point to bills he has carried through, since he is fairly reliable
Keep your answers brief, since his pace runs well ahead of most
dont: Fill his short pauses with extra talk
Rely on outside groups to carry the case for you
Robert Bresnahan.warning_sign: Public settings miss how the detail lands with him, or when he has heard enough. Ask him to name the one figure he needs settled before you move on.
Robert Bresnahan.follow_up: Send the one step in writing the same day, with its owner and date, and copy his staff.
Robert Bresnahan.personality: Bresnahan is quite reserved and one of the most practical colleagues, and he is hard to fluster. He describes his work with far more care and detail than most, and his bills take in a little fewer issues than most. He is fairly reliable on votes and bill follow through, and his wording carries a little more feeling than most. From Pennsylvania, he sits on the Small Business panel and is far less seen than colleagues, even for his role.
Robert Bresnahan.speaks: His pace runs well ahead of most, and his pauses are much shorter than most. Volume moves around more than most, and pitch stays a touch flatter than most. He describes his work with great care and detail, and wording carries somewhat more feeling than most. Narrow in range, he covers a somewhat narrower set of issues, and he moves between points quickly.
Robert Bresnahan.decides: He judges an ask on whether the detail holds and whether the result is clear. Pressure from outside moves him further than most members, so allies and local voices can change his position. He follows bills through with reasonable dependability, so a dated step he owns tends to hold. A practical case carries more weight with him than a broad one.

archetype.justification: He is skeptical by default, and his bills reach one of the narrowest ranges of issues in the House, with long answers and quick, short replies.

Robert Garcia.bottom_line: He is quite skeptical, so send written technical evidence ahead. Outside voices sway him less than most, so let the written case carry the ask.
do: Send the written technical evidence a few days ahead
Open with a plain question about the one step at issue
Let his long answers run out before you add a point, since they run long
Close by stating the single action you want him to take
dont: Cite what outside groups want as his reason to move
Lead with the results you expect, since results are not his frame
Count his long answers as support for the ask
Robert Garcia.warning_sign: He usually talks things through out loud, with plenty of filler. When that filler drops and he answers in set lines, he is working from notes, not from your problem. Stop and ask which part he doubts, then answer that part first.
Robert Garcia.follow_up: Within a week, send his legislative office a written technical note with the exact wording of each claim you made.
Robert Garcia.personality: Garcia is quite skeptical, and among the most practical members in the House. Fairly careful and organized, he gets worked up a bit more easily than most. His bills reach one of the narrowest ranges of issues in the House, while his public language stays on a narrow set of topics more than most. He is as visible for his role as nearly anyone in the House. Very little emotional charge runs through his words.
Robert Garcia.speaks: His pace is among the fastest in the House, with somewhat shorter pauses between phrases. Pitch swings well beyond most. His volume stays much more even than most. His longest answers run well past most, and his words are well beyond most in action-focused talk. Plan for a long run of talk before you get to reply. Keep your turns short and clear.
Robert Garcia.decides: Written technical material sent early fits him best. Outside pressure reaches him less than it reaches most members, which is a lean, not a promise. Keep each part of the case in its own short paragraph, so every point can be read without the rest. Leave out any point the record does not show, since one unsupported claim weakens every other paragraph.

archetype.justification: He is about as reserved as House members get, and he is very practical in outlook.

Robert Latta.bottom_line: Bring a short, specific ask he can check against his record, since outside voices weigh a little heavier with him than with most colleagues.
do: Frame the ask around concrete results he can verify
In a hearing, expect an orderly exchange and prepare the specifics he will probe
Name the next move and who owns it before you leave
dont: Read his brevity as style, since he is about as reserved as members get
Expect a slow decision, since he wants results he can verify first
Walk into a hearing without the exact text he will ask for
Robert Latta.warning_sign: He usually stays among the least combative members in hearings, so any sharper turn stands out. If he sharpens his tone, he turns guarded, so slow down and confirm the facts he cites.
Robert Latta.follow_up: Email his team a single page outlining the next step with the owner named by Friday.
Robert Latta.personality: Latta is about as reserved as House members get, and he is very practical in outlook. He is less easily rattled than most, and he is careful and organized. His bills span very few policy areas compared with nearly every other member. When he describes his own work, he gets into more detail than nearly any colleague. In hearings he is among the least combative members. He also stays low profile in the chamber.
Robert Latta.speaks: His delivery runs at a slower clip than most, with somewhat longer pauses between phrases. His pitch stays flatter than most colleagues, and his voice carries little lift. When he describes his own work, he covers a narrower range of issues and goes deep on details. In hearings his tone stays even, and during formal questioning he seldom presses witnesses hard.
Robert Latta.decides: Whether it sits inside the few areas his bills already cover is how he judges a request. Outside voices sway him a little more than typical, so an ask gains from visible backers. His follow through is very strong, so once he commits, the ask tends to hold. In hearings he is among the least combative members, so formal questioning seldom unsettles him. He stays low profile, so an ask lands on its merits rather than on attention.

archetype.justification: He is a little more social than most, and his wording runs somewhat more charged than most colleagues.

Robert Menendez.bottom_line: Open with the people the bill helps, and let him take the floor early. When he is challenged, he holds his ground, so leave space before you respond.
do: Open with the people the bill helps, and keep the story personal
Let him take the floor early, then ask one precise question
Bring energy and a quick, upbeat tone to the meeting
Make time for personal rapport before the agenda, since he is a little more social
dont: Argue the same point again after he has defended it
Pile on action steps, since his talk leans much less toward doing than most
Robert Menendez.warning_sign: He usually holds his ground when challenged and finishes his thoughts. If he suddenly stops defending his view and turns quiet, he is on guard. Give him a pause, restate the one point, and invite his view.
Robert Menendez.follow_up: Afterward, put in writing for him who was helped, the coming action, and whoever is accountable.
Robert Menendez.personality: Menendez is somewhat more outgoing than most and a little more sharp in wording. He holds the floor at a level few colleagues match. He is among the most visible figures in the chamber, and his public exposure is high for his role. Emotional charge runs somewhat higher in his words than most colleagues. His record on votes and in carrying bills through trails somewhat behind most colleagues. When challenged, he holds his position firmly and keeps talking.
Robert Menendez.speaks: Answers run somewhat shorter than most. Phrasing carries somewhat more feeling than most, with more emotional charge. In conversation his pace runs a little quicker than most, with pitch rising and falling much more than most. When challenged he defends his view much more than most, and his wording runs somewhat sharper than most. His volume holds somewhat more evenly than most colleagues. Tone sounds somewhat brighter than most, with a lively cadence. Cutoffs at the end of a sentence come up somewhat less than most.
Robert Menendez.decides: Benefit to the people reached is the test he applies to any request. He sets the agenda of a decision at a pace few colleagues match. When he has defended a view, he tends to hold it under challenge. His record on votes and bills trails somewhat behind most colleagues, so commitments need owners. Given how visible he is in the chamber, a public commitment carries real weight with him.

archetype.justification: Quiet and reserved, with careful detailed talk and long pauses, he is rarely the loudest voice in the room.

Robert Onder.bottom_line: Send the written case early and keep it to the detail he needs. Pressure from outside moves him less.
do: Send the written case with figures a week before the meeting
If he pauses for a long while, wait rather than filling the silence
dont: Mistake his quiet for disinterest
Treat a hearing as a fight by default
Robert Onder.warning_sign: In hearings he usually holds his edge down and is somewhat less combative than the typical member. If his tone sharpens during a hearing, he is guarded, so pause, ask one direct question, and offer the detail in writing.
Robert Onder.follow_up: After the meeting, send his office a single page covering the detail discussed and your ask, with a date for a reply.
Robert Onder.personality: Onder is reserved and seldom visible, yet he is curious and careful with his work. He talks about policy in detailed terms that few colleagues match, and he sees bills through more reliably than most. His words carry little emotional charge, so he reads as deliberate rather than dramatic. In the room he works from the detail, not the show.
Robert Onder.speaks: He speaks in careful, detailed language about his work, with little charge in his word choice. Delivery is deliberate, and his phrases are separated by gaps much longer than most. Volume and pitch swing up and down more than most. The long pauses are a delivery habit, not hesitation. In hearings he is a little less combative than most members, and he keeps his points tied to specifics.
Robert Onder.decides: He weighs an ask on its detail and on whether the paperwork holds up, not on who pushes hardest. Because he is curious and follows bills through, a clear written case with a named next step earns his attention. Forceful outside campaigns reach him less than most, and in hearings he is somewhat gentler than most members. He is seldom visible, so a quiet case built on the record reaches him where a loud one may not.

archetype.justification: He is quite reserved and very careful and organized, with answers that run long and warm.

Robert Wittman.bottom_line: Come with one specific ask and leave room for his long answers. He follows through less reliably than his talk suggests, so agree the next step before you leave.
do: Give him room to speak first, since he is quite reserved
Let him finish long answers before you reply
Agree on one next step, with an owner and a date
In a hearing, expect him a little less combative than most members
dont: Assume a warm tone means he has agreed to act
Cut in when his answer runs long
Take his long floor pauses as hesitation
Robert Wittman.warning_sign: He usually answers at length. Once a challenge lands and he starts defending his position, he is guarded, so stop pressing and restate the ask with its facts.
Robert Wittman.follow_up: Two days out, hand his staff a single sheet laying out the facts, then have the next step confirmed in writing with a named owner.
Robert Wittman.personality: Wittman is quite reserved yet very agreeable, with a care for details that places him among the most careful in the chamber. His talk is warm and runs long, and he steers conversations a little more than most. When challenged he defends his position a little more than most, so he holds his ground in the room. His follow through trails his words, since he votes and sees bills through much less reliably than most.
Robert Wittman.speaks: He talks in long, full answers and frames his work in careful detail. Warm wording carries forceful points about what he wants. Phrasing stays less social than nearly any colleague and centers on doing things. On the floor his volume swings far more widely than most, while his pitch also varies somewhat more than most. When pressed he holds his line, and his answers stay long and full.
Robert Wittman.decides: He weighs an ask by what the facts show, since results and facts fit how he frames issues. Pressure from outside sways him slightly more than it sways most members. His agreement comes easily, but he is much less reliable at seeing bills through, so his yes is only a start and needs someone to chase it. When he digs in on a point he tends to hold it.

archetype.justification: Her emotionally charged, open style and broader issue range mark a heartfelt speaker who leads with people.

Robin Kelly.bottom_line: Put one clear request in front of her. Outside pressure has little pull on her, so the case has to reach her.
do: Lead with the people your ask helps, since outside pressure does little
Give her space to answer before you add the next point
Keep the ask brief so the first minute carries the point
dont: Chase her with the same request on every follow up
Mistake her low profile for a lack of commitment
Count on outside pressure to settle the question
Robin Kelly.warning_sign: A general meeting will not show when she is ready to decide. Watch for the point where she stops asking questions, then stop and offer one concrete next step.
Robin Kelly.follow_up: Send a single written summary of the ask, the next step and its date within two days.
Robin Kelly.personality: Kelly is heartfelt in her words, which carry strong emotion, and she talks about a broader range of issues than many colleagues. Her bills cover a bit more issues too, and she draws less attention than others in her role. Put together, she is an open member who speaks for the people her issues reach while keeping a quiet presence.
Robin Kelly.speaks: Strong emotion marks the words, and the talk moves across a fairly wide range of issues. Delivery is open rather than sharp, and the feeling comes through in the content. People and their needs come first, before the figures. Scope stays wide, which gives each issue a human frame. The talk stays personal from start to finish, with the people in view.
Robin Kelly.decides: She weighs an ask by the people it affects and by how it fits her broader issue range. Her bills cover a bit more issues too, so an ask inside her areas gets a fair look. Pressure from outside counts for less with her, so a decision sticks only when the case itself persuades her and the next step is written down. Her visibility is low for her role, so a request for a public role may not gain traction.

archetype.justification: He is noticeably warm and cheerful in his public language, and his words are among the warmest in the chamber.

Roger Marshall.bottom_line: Send written technical evidence ahead of time and back it with outside voices, since pressure from those voices tends to shift him.
do: Lead with written, technical detail rather than a broad narrative
Invite a social meeting with outside supporters before you press the ask
Open warmly and point to the bipartisan colleagues already on board
dont: Wait for him to drive the discussion, since he rarely takes charge
Read his brief replies as a full verdict on the ask
Roger Marshall.warning_sign: He usually trails off and keeps answers short, so brevity alone is no sign of trouble. If he cuts replies even shorter, speaks faster, and leaves sentences unfinished, he is losing interest, so leave him a short written summary he can act on.
Roger Marshall.follow_up: Send him a short technical summary in writing before Friday, naming the step and the person who owns it.
Roger Marshall.personality: Marshall is warm, cheerful, and sociable in his public language, though his words come across as less forceful than most. He leans a little practical and a little skeptical, and his talk is looser on specifics than nearly anyone in the chamber. Quicker than most to feel stirred up, he takes charge of conversations much less than typical. His bills range over a little narrower ground than most, though he works across party lines somewhat more than most colleagues do.
Roger Marshall.speaks: His delivery is somewhat faster than most, with much shorter pauses between phrases, a somewhat flatter pitch, and volume that stays level. His answers are brief, and even his longest replies are short by the chamber's standards. Unfinished sentences appear a little more often than typical, and he rarely uses filler. Overall, his manner is quick and even, with little verbal padding and few runs of rapid short replies.
Roger Marshall.decides: Before a yes he tests how well its written detail holds up and whether it fits a narrower set of issues. Bills touch somewhat fewer areas than typical, so a proposal that stays within his lane is easier for him to take on. He reaches across the aisle somewhat more than typical, which makes a bipartisan point worth raising, though he tends to let others lead the room. Outside groups carry clear weight with him, so an ask gains traction when outside support lands before the vote.

archetype.justification: He is exceptionally careful and dependable, describes his work in detail, and speaks with some extra force.

Roger Wicker.bottom_line: Bring a written technical case and a focused ask, then give him time to weigh the detail, since he sees bills through once he backs them.
do: Share the technical evidence early with a short cover note
Let the longer pauses run before you add another point
Offer him a clear path to a yes that holds up
dont: Mistake his reserved manner for disinterest, since he sees bills through
Finish his sentences for him when he trails off
Roger Wicker.warning_sign: He usually keeps his volume very even. If his volume jumps and he drops sentences halfway, he is on guard, so pause, restate the one fact that matters, and let him respond.
Roger Wicker.follow_up: Within two days, send his legislative staff a written note naming the next step, its owner, and the date agreed.
Roger Wicker.personality: Wicker is quite reserved in manner, and he is exceptionally careful, so he works through issues in detail. Heated moments rarely throw him off his footing, and he is somewhat agreeable. When he describes his work, the terms are far more detailed than usual, and his range of issues is somewhat narrow. He is exceptionally dependable when it comes to seeing bills through, and he cooperates across the aisle somewhat less than usual. He is from Mississippi, and his visibility runs somewhat lower than usual for his role.
Roger Wicker.speaks: Loudness holds very level, while his pitch moves somewhat more than usual. Pauses between phrases run a little longer than usual. Answers are short, and the longest replies run much shorter than usual. Trailing off happens somewhat more than usual, and rapid, brief bursts are less common for him. Words read as warm and social, somewhat forceful, and very flat in excitement.
Roger Wicker.decides: Facts must hold up under close reading for him, so he wants the detail in hand before he moves. Across the aisle, his cooperation runs somewhat lower than usual, so an ask that needs the other side carries less pull. A clear path to a yes gives him room to move, since he is somewhat agreeable. He leads conversations somewhat less than usual and answers in short replies, so a question he can answer briefly beats an open invitation. He follows through on what he backs better than nearly anyone, so a clear next step turns his support into action.

archetype.justification: His reserved manner, very little emotional charge and taste for written technical proof fit the Crane.

Roger Williams.bottom_line: Send written technical evidence ahead of the meeting, since outside voices carry less weight with him than most.
do: Lead with the written technical case and its specifics
Find a cross aisle colleague to vouch for the ask first
Invite his input early, since his role keeps him less visible
dont: Mistake his reserved manner for disagreement
Count on outside campaigns to shift him quickly
Roger Williams.warning_sign: A general meeting will not show how he reacts when a deadline or procedure is in question. Ask him one plain procedural question early, then follow up in writing.
Roger Williams.follow_up: Email him a brief memo on the agreed technical points and the date his office should answer by.
Roger Williams.personality: Williams ranks among the most reserved members in the House, yet he is curious and not easily rattled. His talk spans more issue areas than nearly anyone in the House, and he describes his work with exact, granular detail. Emotional charge in his words ranks as low as almost anyone's, and he reaches across less than almost anyone. Put simply, he brings the room facts rather than feelings.
Roger Williams.speaks: His words carry very little emotional charge, and he keeps his answers anchored in facts. He covers a wide spread of issues, and he describes his work with exact, granular detail. A brisk, technical meeting suits his manner, and he stays with the specifics. He rarely reaches for feeling to make a point, so the case has to stand on its own content.
Roger Williams.decides: He weighs an ask on written, technical grounds, and his wide range of bills means he sees many issues. Outside pressure counts for less with him than it does with most colleagues, so the paper itself must carry the decision. He wants the facts laid out clearly before he commits, and a loose pitch will not move him. So a decision from him needs a written case that holds up on its own.

archetype.justification: His reserved, practical manner, narrow bill range, and low visibility fit a deliberate, low key member.

Ron Estes.bottom_line: Bring facts and results in a short case, since they carry most weight with him. Pressure from outside moves him clearly less, so the case must do the persuading.
do: Open with the results and the facts behind them
Show the bill's record of votes and progress
Allow time for a decision, since pressure will not hurry him
dont: Treat his limited public exposure as a sign of disinterest
Rely on pressure to shift him, since it moves him clearly less
Ron Estes.warning_sign: By default he is reserved and practical, so brief, plain answers are normal for him. When he moves from plain answers to a detailed case, he is on guard, so acknowledge the detail and slow the pace.
Ron Estes.follow_up: Within a week, send his office a one page summary of the votes and progress, with the next decision date.
Ron Estes.personality: Estes is a very reserved member who is quite practical. His public talk stays on a few topics, and his bills reach a far smaller set of areas. Details get less care than typical, though he still describes his work in more exact terms. He is among the least visible in the chamber, and in hearings his combativeness stays well under typical levels.
Ron Estes.speaks: He stays on a few topics, so his remarks are narrow and easy to follow. His public words describe his work in fairly careful terms, with more exact detail than typical colleagues. Not one to widen a debate, he keeps the talk on the bill at hand. In hearings he is far less combative than typical, and his tone rarely changes.
Ron Estes.decides: He weighs an ask by its record and results, and a short case built on what it delivers persuades him. Outside pressure moves him clearly less, so an ask lands on its facts alone. His visibility is among the lowest, and his bills show a narrow reach, so a decision sticks only with a named owner who follows the bill.

archetype.justification: He is far from social, and his bills cover among the fewest issues in the chamber.

Ron Johnson.bottom_line: Lead with the concrete effect of the policy in brief, and skip rapport work, since results move him more than warmth.
do: Open with the bill's results and the numbers behind them
Stick to measurable outcomes, not stories about individuals
Answer his sharp questions directly without softening them
dont: Drop the small talk and state the ask first
Assume a long case will hold his attention
Ron Johnson.warning_sign: He usually fills his sentences with extra words and speaks quickly. If the filler drops away, he is concentrating or on guard. Let him finish, then restate the one point plainly.
Ron Johnson.follow_up: Within three days, email his office a single page memo on the bill's results, with sources.
Ron Johnson.personality: Johnson is far from social, and his wording runs much sharper than most. In hearings his manner runs a little more combative than most colleagues. His bills span among the fewest issue areas in the chamber, yet he is among the most dependable in seeing them through. Exposure is very high for a member in his role. His words come across as somewhat flat, with less upbeat energy than most.
Ron Johnson.speaks: He talks at a fast pace, among the quickest in the Senate. Filler words run heavy in his speech, far above the usual level. His pauses between phrases run far briefer than most, and pitch swings much more than most. Volume swings somewhat more than most colleagues. He chooses blunt words, and his phrasing carries much more edge than most.
Ron Johnson.decides: Asks succeed when the results are clear and the bill itself delivers them in practice. Backing from home counts for extra with him, somewhat more than most colleagues. In a room he leads somewhat less than most, so clear steps matter more to him than rapport. His record of seeing bills through is among the strongest, so a practical deal can earn his support. So an ask earns his vote only when the results are concrete and someone credible carries it.

archetype.justification: Bull fits: his wording is sharper and more forceful than others, and he works across the aisle far less.

Ron Wyden.bottom_line: Lead with the concrete result the bill secures, since results and facts land best with him. Outside voices sway him a little, so bring them in early.
do: Open with a short summary of the policy's effect
Let his pauses run, since he trails off less than others
Bring local voices who back the ask into the room
dont: Count on cross-party cosigners to carry the ask
Expect his forceful wording to signal a no
Take his light use of filler as a sign he has lost interest
Ron Wyden.warning_sign: He usually talks slowly with pauses between phrases and finishes his sentences. If he speeds up and sharpens his wording, he is on guard. Stop, restate the one point in plain terms, and ask what would make it workable.
Ron Wyden.follow_up: Mail his staff a one page sheet on the policy result, due within two days, with a reply date named.
Ron Wyden.personality: Wyden is outgoing and forceful, yet careful with facts and somewhat hard to rattle. His public wording is sharp and assertive, and he works across the aisle far less than others. He is fairly curious, his answers run a little briefer than others, and he keeps a narrow set of issues he knows well. In a room he sets the terms, pushes his own case, and rarely fills silences with filler.
Ron Wyden.speaks: He speaks slowly, with long pauses between phrases and a pitch that moves up and down clearly. His public wording is sharp and forceful, yet flat in energy and light on action. Issues stay in a narrow set of topics rather than ranging widely. His answers run a little briefer than others, and he trails off clearly less often than others.
Ron Wyden.decides: A proposal earns his weight by how well it fits results he can show, and short, direct facts move him more than appeals. He works across the aisle far less than others, so a proposal that needs the other side starts with less pull. Outside voices sway him a bit more than they sway others, and his answers stay compact, so each point has to earn its place. He is outgoing but his yes holds only when the ask is tied to results he can point to.

archetype.justification: His sharp wording, loose handling of detail and readiness to get stirred up earn the Badger label.

Ronny Jackson.bottom_line: Keep the ask narrow and factual, since his wording comes across sharp. Outside pressure counts for less with him, so the case itself has to carry the ask.
do: Lead with a tight argument on what the policy actually produces
Let him open the discussion, since taking charge comes naturally to him
dont: Read his sharp wording as personal hostility
Assume outside pressure will win over a skeptic
Ronny Jackson.warning_sign: He usually speaks in loose turns full of filler words. If his wording turns sharper and the filler drops away, he has gone guarded, so back off, use plain facts, and avoid a debate.
Ronny Jackson.follow_up: Afterward, mail the agreed step in a brief written note, naming the staffer who will follow up and the date.
Ronny Jackson.personality: Jackson is fairly outgoing, yet his handling of detail is much looser than most. Quick to react with heat, his wording lands sharper than nearly anyone's. Cooler in tone than nearly anyone, his words still sound more forceful than most. Working across the aisle comes less easily to him than to nearly any colleague, while his public presence is very high for someone in his post.
Ronny Jackson.speaks: Turns vary in length, and his longest replies stretch a bit longer than most. Filler crops up more often than nearly anyone's in the chamber. His wording also lands sharper and more forceful than most, so exchanges with him often feel pointed. Taking charge of a conversation happens somewhat more for him than for most, and his tone is less social than most.
Ronny Jackson.decides: How well it fits the areas his bills already cover shapes his verdict. Crossing the aisle is something he does less than almost anyone, so a cross aisle ask is a hard sell. Outside pushes count for less with him, so the case must carry the ask. Following bills through ranks him among the least reliable members, so a decision from him needs a written next step to stick.

archetype.justification: Her forceful words, firm hold on conversations and visible profile earn the Orca label.

Rosa DeLauro.bottom_line: Let her hold the floor, then ask for one clear decision. She moves less under outside pressure, so the ask must rest on her own reasoning.
do: Let her take the floor early, since she holds conversations firmly
Keep the ask warm and direct from the first sentence
Tie any concession to a date she can check
dont: Count on outside pressure to change her mind
Cut in when she is mid answer, since she runs long
Expect her visibility alone to carry the room
Rosa DeLauro.warning_sign: Usually she talks fast and at length, with heavy filler and trailing sentences. When she goes quiet and drops her pace, she is weighing a concession or disengaging. Let silence sit, then ask one plain question.
Rosa DeLauro.follow_up: Within a week, send her office a one page note with the bill's status, the next vote and the staffer who owns it.
Rosa DeLauro.personality: DeLauro is a warm and forceful member who gets stirred up quickly. She holds the floor more firmly than almost anyone, and her answers run far longer than most colleagues'. Trailing off happens much more than most, and speech carries heavy filler. Tone runs far warmer than most colleagues. Phrasing is unusually forceful, yet she is far less combative in hearings. Follow through runs somewhat behind most, though work is careful and organized.
Rosa DeLauro.speaks: She speaks fast and forcefully, with a warm, social tone and heavy filler. Answers run long, vary in length more than almost anyone's, and often trail off before a clear end. Volume shifts in her voice somewhat more than most. Her pitch stays somewhat flatter than most, and her words carry upbeat energy. In hearings she is far less combative than most members.
Rosa DeLauro.decides: Her own reasoning has to carry a request before she backs it. Outside pressure gets less traction with her than with most members. She holds the floor firmly and is far less combative in hearings, so she tends to test an ask in the room before she commits. Follow through is somewhat weak, so her support lasts only when each concession is tied to a date she can check.

archetype.justification: He sounds much more cutting than most, and his grip on details is loose compared with colleagues, which fits the Badger's combative style.

Ruben Gallego.bottom_line: Lead with who the bill helps and the bills he has joined across the aisle. Pressure shifts him clearly more than most, so pair the ask with those voices.
do: Tell a specific story about who the bill helps
Show the bills you share with his office by subject
dont: Read his long answers as agreement
Expect outside pressure to decide the question for him
Ruben Gallego.warning_sign: He usually talks fast and keeps going, with many filler words. If he slows down and answers in a few words, he is on guard. Ask one plain question about what worries him and wait for the answer.
Ruben Gallego.follow_up: Mail his legislative director a brief note on the agreed step and a date within two days.
Ruben Gallego.personality: Gallego reacts quickly when pressed, more than most colleagues, and details slip past him more readily than they do for others. Phrasing cuts harder than most, and his tone runs cooler and flatter than most. He reaches across to the other side more than nearly any colleague, yet he follows bills through less reliably than nearly anyone. Public talk from him spans many more topics than most, and filler creeps into his speech more than almost anyone's.
Ruben Gallego.speaks: His pace is well quicker than colleagues', and his pauses last somewhat longer than most. His replies stretch further than most, and their lengths barely vary compared with colleagues'. Few of his answers turn to broad themes. Short, rapid exchanges come more often from him than from most. He uses more filler than almost anyone, and his tone is cooler, flatter, and less social than most colleagues'.
Ruben Gallego.decides: Before backing anything he weighs how the people it names gain, and bills he has joined across the aisle carry weight with him. He leads conversations less than nearly any colleague. Pressure from outside has more pull on him than on most members. So a decision from him holds only when the people it helps are part of the case.

archetype.justification: Very careful and organized, and among the most detailed in his public words, the facts that earn the Bee pick.

Rudy Yakym.bottom_line: Bring written, technical material ahead of the meeting and ask him to read it first. Cross party backing will carry little weight with him.
do: Send the written analysis well ahead of the meeting
If he has questions, ask him to put them in writing
Give him time to think before you expect an answer
dont: Expect him to fill silences with a quick answer
Mistake his slower pace for a lack of engagement
Rudy Yakym.warning_sign: He usually speaks at a slower pace with longer pauses between phrases, and in hearings he is less combative than most. If his pauses run longer than usual, he is still weighing the point, so give him the written version and wait.
Rudy Yakym.follow_up: Within a day, send him the written summary with the questions he raised and the name of the staffer who will answer each.
Rudy Yakym.personality: Yakym is very careful in how he works, and his public words are more detailed than almost anyone's in the House. He is fairly outgoing and a little practical, and he reaches across the aisle less than almost anyone. Seeing his bills through is a fairly reliable habit for him. Before Congress he held a sales manager job at a broadband firm.
Rudy Yakym.speaks: He talks at a somewhat slower pace than most, with pauses between phrases that run much longer than most. His pitch stays somewhat flatter than most, and his public descriptions are more careful and detailed than almost anyone's. In hearings his manner runs somewhat less combative than the typical member, so his tone stays even rather than sharp. These habits shape how each exchange with him unfolds.
Rudy Yakym.decides: Weight goes to how much written, technical support sits behind an ask. Pushes from outside register much less on him than on most colleagues, so a push will not carry an ask he has not checked. He is fairly reliable once he commits. Crossing the aisle happens less than almost anyone manages, so an ask needs written evidence before it can move him.

archetype.justification: He follows bills through more reliably than almost anyone, and he is skeptical and practical, with sharper words and narrow issue talk.

Russell Fry.bottom_line: Bring a technical paper ahead, and ask for one dated next step. Few members follow through on bills more reliably than he does.
do: Send his staff one written question about the bill's next vote before the meeting
Answer each formal question with the page of the paper it rests on
Ask how the next step will be followed up, since he finishes bills reliably
Close by restating any doubts he raised, so he can correct your reading of them
dont: Answer his pointed words with a long speech
Treat his doubts as a personal attack, not a question a source can answer
Ask for a decision before his office has had time to read the paper
Russell Fry.warning_sign: His words usually run somewhat sharper than most. If they get sharper still and he stops engaging the paper, he has set it aside for now. Keep to the one point he pressed and come back to the rest in order.
Russell Fry.follow_up: Send his staff written answers by Friday, naming the ask, the owner, and the due date.
Russell Fry.personality: Fry is quite practical and also quite reserved. Few members in the House match his follow-through on bills. His talk is more careful and detailed than almost anyone's. Skepticism runs a little deeper in him than in most colleagues. His words land somewhat sharper than most. His public profile is a bit lower than most, and his issue talk is narrower than nearly anyone's.
Russell Fry.speaks: On the House floor, he moves well quicker than most. His pauses are somewhat shorter than most between phrases. His pitch moves up and down a little more than most. Feeling runs thin in his words, far less than most, so read tone through what he says. Speak plainly and keep each point short, since his words carry so little feeling.
Russell Fry.decides: In hearings he is much more combative than most colleagues, so keep formal exchanges plain and specific. Name the weakest part of the paper yourself, in plain words, before the meeting. Let the written paper carry the detail, not a spoken pitch, so he can check each figure at his own pace. Ask him which section of the paper he would check first, and start there.

archetype.justification: He carries bills to the finish much more than most, paired with a reserved style and a much lower public profile.

Ryan Mackenzie.bottom_line: Get your written technical case to his office ahead of time, and count on a yes from him to hold.
do: Send written technical evidence ahead of time, well before the meeting
Walk through the evidence point by point, in the order you sent it
Come back a second time with the groups that back the plan
Cite bills he has already seen through when you make the case
dont: Ask him to front the plan alone in public
Offer an untested idea with nothing proven behind it
Bury the key figure deep in the written material
Ryan Mackenzie.warning_sign: Usually his wording is much softer than most. If his replies turn curt and pointed, the ask has lost him for now. Send one written answer on the disputed point, then wait for his reply.
Ryan Mackenzie.follow_up: Give his office a brief note with one next step, an owner, and a date within a few days.
Ryan Mackenzie.personality: Mackenzie is quite practical in outlook, and detail is a bit less of a strength. His reserve shows a little, while his record on bills is much stronger than most. By nature he is fairly easy to work with. His public talk about the work is somewhat more careful and detailed than most. Gentle wording marks his public style, more so than most colleagues. For his role, he keeps a much lower profile than most.
Ryan Mackenzie.speaks: His words carry a little less emotional weight than most, so stick to plain points. When he gets into the specifics of a bill, stay with that detail and answer it precisely. Keep your own voice even, and let him finish before you reply.
Ryan Mackenzie.decides: With a fairly agreeable manner, a working session on his objections can suit him. Outside voices shift his positions more than most. His bill record is much stronger than most, so staying with the file is worth it. End by asking which of his objections he would most like answered first.

archetype.justification: He keeps the floor, speaks with forceful word choices, and sees his bills through with very dependable follow-through.

Ryan Zinke.bottom_line: Send written technical detail ahead, and expect him to set the pace early. Outside pressure moves him far less than most, so close on one written next step.
do: Spell out the method step by step, before you reach the conclusion
Open with the question he has to answer, and let him take the floor
Keep each point firm
Ask which staff member will carry the step out
dont: Read a sentence he leaves hanging as his final answer
Answer his upbeat energy with loud, quick enthusiasm
Question him in a formal hearing as if he were hostile
Ryan Zinke.warning_sign: He usually trails off mid-answer without a clean ending. If his turns trail off even more often, leaving nearly every point unfinished, he is losing hold of your case. Pause, and ask which decision he is still weighing.
Ryan Zinke.follow_up: Send his staff a written technical note by Friday, naming the step he agreed to and its due date.
Ryan Zinke.personality: Zinke is an outgoing, forceful member who keeps conversations moving. Public talk from him hits harder than most colleagues, and his tone is more upbeat than almost any colleague's. He describes his work in far more detail than most, and his record on bill follow-through is very dependable. He leans a little toward the practical. In hearings he is less combative than most colleagues.
Ryan Zinke.speaks: His answers in interviews come out fairly long, and his longest turns stretch further still. He trails off more than nearly any colleague does. Answer length varies somewhat more than most. Filler words show up in his talk a bit more than most. Runs of quick short replies come up a little less for him than for most. Give each long answer its full run, then answer the single point that matters most.
Ryan Zinke.decides: Written technical detail is the case that fits him best. Pressure from outside carries less weight for him than it does for most members, so a clear case does much of the work. Once he commits, his yes usually stands, so ask for one. Keep the request to a single dated decision he can confirm. Ask him which point he wants answered in the written note.

archetype.justification: Among the most reserved members, very careful and organized, and much more slowly in speech than most.

Salud Carbajal.bottom_line: Send the ask ahead in writing, let him take his time, and confirm the next step before you leave.
do: Lead with the policy's results and the facts behind them
Bring the bill text with the detail the ask depends on
Offer a small briefing in place of a public event
In a hearing, expect a civil exchange and keep the record tight
dont: Rush his pace or cut his pauses short
Count on outside pressure to carry it for you
Salud Carbajal.warning_sign: He usually speaks slowly and keeps a reserved manner. In hearings, a sharper tone from him signals guardedness, so ease off and give him time to ask his own questions.
Salud Carbajal.follow_up: Send the written detail the day after, with the next step, its owner, and a check in date.
Salud Carbajal.personality: Carbajal ranks among the most reserved colleagues but is very curious, and he is highly careful and organized. He ranges across more issues in his talk than almost anyone, and his bills take in a little more ground than most. He is somewhat less dependable on votes and bill follow through than most. From California, he is a quiet, organized presence who prefers to check the facts before he commits.
Salud Carbajal.speaks: His speech runs far slower than most, with longer gaps between phrases than most.
