His volume moves around more than nearly everyone's, while his pitch stays flatter than most, so emphasis comes through loudness rather than tone. Wide in range, he covers many issues and describes his work with a little less detail than most. In hearings, he is less combative than most members, and he speaks with care.
Salud Carbajal.decides: Requests get weighed on whether the evidence holds, and whether the policy spans the broader slate of topics he works on. A concise, factual case earns his attention. Pressure from outside counts for a bit more with him than with colleagues. Because follow through on bills is weaker than most, his support holds only when someone tracks the next step.

archetype.justification: Few House members are as reserved as he is, and few match his reliability on votes and bills.

Sam Graves.bottom_line: Send a written technical brief ahead, and keep the meeting small. His bills get seen through about as reliably as any in the House.
do: Send the written technical evidence several days before the meeting
Show how the plan would work in practice, step by step
Rest the case on its merits, and give him time before any second push
Close by agreeing on the next step and its due date
dont: Bring a long list of asks, since outside pushing sways him much less
Lead with results or people stories, since neither frame fits his case
Count on a sharp exchange in a formal hearing, since few members are less combative
Sam Graves.warning_sign: He usually keeps his language gentle. If his gentle replies turn sharp on the plan, he has started to test it. Narrow the ask, and give him a written answer to read.
Sam Graves.follow_up: After the meeting, email his office the revised technical evidence within a few days, with each source named.
Sam Graves.personality: Graves is reserved, more than almost any colleague, and his profile sits lower than most. When he describes his work, he goes into much finer detail than most, though his bills span somewhat less ground. His follow-through on bills ranks near the top of the House. His words run a little gentler than most. In formal hearings he is less combative than nearly any House member.
Sam Graves.speaks: On the House floor he runs a little quicker than most, and his volume stays a bit more even. His public talk carries much less heat than most, so keep your tone mild. His pitch sits a little flatter than most as well. In formal hearings he counts among the least combative, so answer him in an even tone if you see him there.
Sam Graves.decides: Technical framing fits how he decides. Outside pressure sways him clearly less than it sways most members, so a case backed by named sources goes further than pressure from others. Before the meeting, look up the bills he has already seen through, and name the closest match as the precedent for your plan. Put it on a single line with its roll-call vote.

archetype.justification: Careful and organized, he is curious and talks in more detail than most, and he rarely pushes hard in hearings.

Sam Liccardo.bottom_line: Bring the technical record and a gentle, specific ask he can agree to. Pressure from outside the room moves him more than most, so line up voices who back it.
do: Send the technical detail before the meeting, so he can check it
Ask him to confirm the next step, since he is fairly reliable
When he pauses at length, wait and let him finish
Bring the next questions he will want to explore
dont: Count his quiet hearing questions as support already given
Expect outside voices alone to carry the decision
Mistake his agreeable manner for a commitment already made
Sam Liccardo.warning_sign: In a hearing he is usually much less combative than most, so a firmer line from him is the change to watch. That usually means he is on guard, so ask what he needs to see.
Sam Liccardo.follow_up: Soon after you meet, send his staff a short written record of the agreed step and its owner.
Sam Liccardo.personality: Liccardo is fairly outgoing and curious, and very careful and organized. He is among the most agreeable members, with gentle words and little emotional charge. His bills cover a bit fewer issues than most, and he follows bills through fairly well. In hearings he keeps a restrained profile, and he sits on House Financial Services for a California seat. Overall the picture is of a careful colleague who works through the record.
Sam Liccardo.speaks: He keeps his focus on fewer issue areas and goes into somewhat more careful detail than most. Words stay gentle and carry little emotional charge. He speaks more slowly than most, pauses for long stretches, and his pitch moves a good deal. In hearings he is less combative than most, so his manner reads as gentle and courteous. He keeps his tone gentle throughout.
Sam Liccardo.decides: He weighs an ask on the technical record and on whether the next step is realistic. Backing from voices outside the room moves him more than most, so it carries weight. Seeing bills through is a fairly dependable habit for him, so asking for a written step he confirms is worthwhile. A decision needs a named next step to stick. Clear facts in writing make the next step easier to hold.

archetype.justification: Few colleagues keep as low a public profile, and he tends to be careful and organized.

Sanford Bishop.bottom_line: Send written technical material early, and agree one next step before you leave, since public pushes carry extra weight with him.
do: Send the technical detail in writing before the meeting
Bring the coalition that backs the ask, since public pressure carries extra weight with him
Plan for quiet press coverage, since his public exposure runs far below his role
dont: Hurry him to a decision before the written detail is in hand
Assume a hearing will feel confrontational, since he ranks with the least combative there
Write off a first objection, since public pressure carries extra weight with him
Sanford Bishop.warning_sign: He usually stays low key in hearings, so a sharper tone stands out. If he presses witnesses hard, he is on guard, so slow down and let the facts carry the exchange.
Sanford Bishop.follow_up: Write his office a brief message with the agreed next step and its date by Friday.
Sanford Bishop.personality: Bishop reads as a little reserved, but fairly curious and fairly careful. When he speaks in public, his topics reach a bit wider than most colleagues. His record on votes and bills is very dependable. His work across party lines runs a notch ahead of most colleagues. Public exposure sits well below his role, and few colleagues keep a lower public profile. He represents Georgia.
Sanford Bishop.speaks: When he talks about his work, his topics reach a bit wider than most colleagues. In hearings he sits among the least combative members, and he seldom presses witnesses. Listeners hear a wide mix of subjects rather than one narrow theme.
Sanford Bishop.decides: He gauges an ask by how well the written record backs it, since technical detail fits him. Public pressure carries extra weight with him, more than with most members, so an ask gains from a visible coalition. His record on bills and votes is very dependable, so a deal stays on track once he signs. Public exposure sits well below his role, so a request needs its backers to speak for it.

archetype.justification: Among the most careful in detailed talk, reliable on bills, and among the most agreeable members.

Sarah Elfreth.bottom_line: Bring her a detailed written case with a shared role she can lead, and close on one named step.
do: Bring a written case, since she follows bills closely
Offer her a shared role, such as announcing the result together
Meet her warm tone before you move to the ask
Confirm the next step and its owner before you leave
dont: Take her agreeable manner as a yes on the whole package
Sarah Elfreth.warning_sign: Her usual pattern is quick bursts of replies, by default. If the bursts stop and her answers grow more even, she is weighing the ask rather than agreeing. Stop, check which part worries her, and address that part before moving on.
Sarah Elfreth.follow_up: Send a brief note two days after you meet, naming the shared role, the step to take next and its owner.
Sarah Elfreth.personality: Elfreth stands among the most agreeable members in the House, with descriptions of her work more detailed than almost anyone's. Her organization runs very careful, while her words land less forcefully than almost anyone's. Bills she carries reach a smaller range of topics than almost anyone's, and she is very reliable at seeing them through. In a room she is one of the members least inclined to take charge, and her role draws somewhat less notice than most.
Sarah Elfreth.speaks: Speech runs faster than almost anyone's in the House, with short pauses and a pitch that sits flatter than almost anyone's. Her words run much warmer than most, and her phrasing is more focused on action than almost anyone's. Answers come in quick bursts, and points are seldom left trailing. Her speech includes a touch more filler than most, and she is far less combative when hearings are held.
Sarah Elfreth.decides: An ask gains her backing through its detail and a clear owner, and a shared role suits the way she works. Pressure from outside gets through to her more than to most members, so a push from others can shift her view. Bills span a narrower set of issues than almost anyone's, so an ask has to sit inside her narrow areas. She follows bills through reliably, so a decision holds once its next step has a named owner.

archetype.justification: She is very outgoing, and her delivery runs among the quickest in the chamber.

Sarah McBride.bottom_line: Bring a clear ask and a visible coalition, and agree a next step before you leave, since public support moves her more.
do: Bring a bipartisan partner early, since public support sways her more than most
Let her open the room, since she is very outgoing and works across party lines
Keep your points short and concrete, since she responds to public support
In a hearing, expect a less combative exchange and prepare the detail she will need
dont: Assume a hearing will feel confrontational, since she is much less combative there
Mistake her outgoing style for a binding yes without written terms
Rush past her quick pace, since she is fairly reliable on votes and bills
Sarah McBride.warning_sign: She usually talks freely in meetings, so a quieter turn from her stands out. If she turns sharp in a hearing, she is on guard, so slow down and confirm the facts she cites.
Sarah McBride.follow_up: Write her office a brief message with the agreed step, its owner, and a date by Friday.
Sarah McBride.personality: McBride tends to be very outgoing and somewhat quick to get worked up. Public talk stays on a tight set of topics, narrower than most colleagues. Work across party lines runs a notch ahead of colleagues, and bills reach across more areas than most. Details get less careful attention than most, and getting worked up comes more easily. Her public profile sits somewhat under her role's usual footprint. Delaware is her home.
Sarah McBride.speaks: Her delivery runs among the quickest in the House, with somewhat shorter pauses between phrases. Volume swings much more than most, while her pitch rises above typical. When she describes her work, she goes into less careful detail than most, and her emotional register runs flatter. In hearings her tone runs milder than most members. Her energy in conversation is high, and she moves through topics at a brisk pace.
Sarah McBride.decides: How well it fits the many issues her bills already touch is what she considers. Public support carries more weight with her than with most members, so a visible coalition helps. Her work across party lines runs a notch ahead of most colleagues, so a bipartisan partner widens her support. Her follow through is fairly reliable, so a commitment from her tends to hold.

archetype.justification: His practical outlook, narrow bill range and reserved manner fit a focused, grounded member.

Scott DesJarlais.bottom_line: Keep the ask short and written, with one step he must take. Outside pressure moves him less than most members, so the ask must stand on its own.
do: Keep to practical facts, which suit his plain, grounded style
Follow up with a short written note, since he rarely sees bills through
Confirm the step by email the same day
dont: Read his reserved manner as agreement with the ask
Scott DesJarlais.warning_sign: He usually keeps his manner plain and his replies to the point. In a hearing, if he suddenly turns combative, he is pressed, so slow down and let him finish.
Scott DesJarlais.follow_up: Send a short written note to his office within two days, listing the step and its owner.
Scott DesJarlais.personality: DesJarlais is a reserved member who is quite practical and holds a narrow issue focus. He is a bit harder to rattle than most, and his talk about work is less detailed than nearly any colleague's. Bills cover among the fewest issues in the House, and he is much less reliable at seeing them through. He represents Tennessee, and his public profile is somewhat lower than most.
Scott DesJarlais.speaks: His pauses between phrases run much longer than most, and he takes his time. Loudness ebbs and flows somewhat more than most. Pitch rises and falls with a bit more range than most colleagues. At hearings he ranks among the fiercest members of the chamber. His answers stay narrow, with less detail than most colleagues offer. He speaks in long pauses that signal care, not hesitation.
Scott DesJarlais.decides: Closeness of a request to the few subjects he already tackles shapes his judgment. Outside pressure moves him less than most members, so a request has to stand on its own. Finishing measures lags far behind for him, so each choice must name its owner. So a decision holds with him when a written step has one clear owner and a date.

archetype.justification: He is more reserved than nearly any colleague, yet he works with the other side more than most.

Scott Fitzgerald.bottom_line: Lead with one direct result and get agreement on a written step. Outside voices sway him somewhat more than most, so the written terms should be settled first.
do: Lead with a short, direct result the policy delivers
Bring a colleague from the other side who backs the ask
Confirm the agreed step in writing within a few days
dont: Assume outside pressure will close the deal
Send a long memo when a short case will do
Scott Fitzgerald.warning_sign: Group settings will not reveal whether he wants the agreement in writing before he commits. Ask early what form he needs, then send it before you leave the room.
Scott Fitzgerald.follow_up: Send his legislative staff a one page memo with the agreed step and its owner by Friday.
Scott Fitzgerald.personality: Fitzgerald is more reserved than nearly any colleague, yet he is fairly curious and fairly careful. Public talk from him covers more topics than nearly anyone's, and his legislation spans more areas than most. His language is far less charged than most colleagues', and he works with the other side somewhat more than most. Few colleagues follow bills through as dependably as he does.
Scott Fitzgerald.speaks: Across many topics in conversation he moves widely, and his work descriptions carry a bit more precision than most colleagues'. Language from him is far less charged than most, so the talk sounds plain and factual. Answers lean on the detail he has rather than broad claims. Throughout, specifics rather than broad themes keep the talk concrete, and the detail he brings keeps his public words grounded.
Scott Fitzgerald.decides: Prior to any yes he checks whether its facts are short, direct, and tied to results. He works with the other side somewhat more than most, so support from across the aisle carries weight with him. Once committed he follows through, so a decision from him sticks once his staff has the terms in writing. Outside pressure has a little more pull on him than on most members, so the written record keeps him anchored.

archetype.justification: He works across the aisle less than almost anyone, and his hearing style is somewhat more combative than most.

Scott Franklin.bottom_line: Bring a specific ask with the next step written down, since he works across the aisle less than almost anyone. Repeated requests have room, since outside voices count.
do: Name a colleague across the aisle who will share the ask
Note the next step in a short written summary
dont: Count on a joint coalition forming without anyone named to lead it
Scott Franklin.warning_sign: He usually works from a settled position and keeps his public talk tight. In a hearing, if he suddenly stops pressing and grows quiet, he is on guard, so pause and ask what concerns him.
Scott Franklin.follow_up: Within two days, mail him a short note covering the step, the owner, and the date.
Scott Franklin.personality: Franklin is a fairly reliable member who works across the aisle less than almost anyone. His public talk covers somewhat narrower ground than most colleagues. In hearings he shows somewhat more combativeness than most colleagues. He represents Florida in the House.
Scott Franklin.speaks: He speaks about a somewhat smaller set of topics than most colleagues. When a hearing gets tense he presses harder than most colleagues do. He stays on the points he already backs, and he does not widen the frame.
Scott Franklin.decides: What he tests first is whether an ask can draw support across the aisle. Outside voices carry some extra weight, so a request is easier to hold when they back it. He is fairly reliable on votes, so a plan with a written step tends to hold. So a decision holds with him when a named owner carries the next step.

archetype.justification: Few colleagues build across party lines less than he does, and detail is seldom where he is strongest.

Scott Perry.bottom_line: Give his long answers room, since he runs long when he has the floor, then ask for one clear commitment.
do: Send written technical evidence ahead, so the detail sits on paper
Open with the one ask, in plain words, before he takes the floor
Keep replies short in a formal exchange, since he answers in brief, quick runs
Hold to the request, since he yields a touch more to outside voices than most
dont: Pitch the ask as a bipartisan effort to win over the other side
Take an unfinished answer on the details as settled agreement
Stage a press event before the details are settled
Scott Perry.warning_sign: Filler is a usual feature of his delivery, so a drop in it stands out. If the filler drops out of his answers, he has heard enough. Stop, and offer a one-line answer to his main objection.
Scott Perry.follow_up: Within two days, send his staff a written outline of the details, each with a clear owner and date.
Scott Perry.personality: Perry is fairly outgoing, but he is quite skeptical by default. Few colleagues work across party lines less than he does, and his public words land with much more force than most. He runs a bit hotter than most members in a room. Detail is seldom his strength, and his public talk about the work is less careful and detailed than most. His bills reach a touch fewer issue areas than most, and he is a very prominent figure for the job he holds. A childhood without electricity or running water is part of his public story. He does not drink alcohol, as he has said publicly.
Scott Perry.speaks: In interviews he moves quickly, and his pitch swings widely, well beyond most colleagues'. His volume runs much more even than most colleagues. His answers run very long, and the longest stretches run longer still. Filler runs thick through his answers, much more than most colleagues'. His public words land harder than most colleagues' do. Keep your own answers brief, and ask about the details when he pauses.
Scott Perry.decides: Technical evidence is what fits him best, since it is what he weighs. A plain, firm case holds its weight, since outside pressure shifts him a bit more than most colleagues. He builds across party lines much less than nearly any colleague, and his bills span a bit narrower field. His family's immigrant story is one he has told in public, so where it honestly fits, it gives you common ground. Close by asking which detail he wants settled first.

archetype.justification: Reserved, careful and organized, he talks in wide, detailed terms and pauses between phrases longer than most.

Scott Peters.bottom_line: Pitch the ask as a broad, careful case, and get a specific next step in writing. Pressure from outside carries less weight with him, so put the one question first.
do: Open with one question you want answered, then invite his detail
Build the ask on the careful, organized detail he already tracks
Give him time to think, since outside pressure will not hurry him
Let pauses run and carry your own case, since his cross party ties are thin
dont: Expect a fast yes from one meeting
Plan a public launch to carry the ask
Scott Peters.warning_sign: Usually his words read gentler than most, and he pauses longer between phrases, so a long silence with a clipped reply signals he is on guard. Let the silence sit, then ask what he needs.
Scott Peters.follow_up: Send a short written note naming the one ask, the next step, and who owns it by the agreed date.
Scott Peters.personality: Peters is reserved in manner but very curious, with a careful, organized streak that shapes how he frames issues. Few colleagues come across as more agreeable, and his words stay gentler than most. His public talk spans a broad set of topics, well wider than the norm, and it carries a lot of emotion. Ties across the aisle are clearly thinner than most, and he draws a little less attention than most.
Scott Peters.speaks: He describes his work with fairly careful detail, a notch above typical. Pace runs somewhat quicker than most, and pauses between phrases run longer than most. Pitch swings far more than most, which gives him a lively sound. Public talk stays wide in its range and emotionally charged, and his delivery reads expressive rather than sharp. Those pauses give him room to think before he answers, which shows in his careful phrasing.
Scott Peters.decides: Fit with his broad agenda and careful organization both decide how he weighs an ask. Pressure from outside carries less weight with him, so a campaign of pushes will not carry a decision. His broad agenda means he will look for how an ask connects to several areas at once. Because his ties across the aisle are clearly thinner, a decision sticks only when the next step has a named owner.

archetype.justification: Among the most outgoing and upbeat colleagues, he speaks quickly and gives long answers.

Sean Casten.bottom_line: Share the technical case in writing ahead of time, since it fits him best, then close on one agreed step.
do: Send the technical evidence in writing before the meeting
Expect fast, long answers and let him finish before you respond
Ask him to put the next step in writing before he leaves
dont: Assume bipartisan ties alone will carry the ask
Read his upbeat tone as agreement on the substance
Sean Casten.warning_sign: By default he talks fast and answers at length, pausing only fleetingly between phrases. If he stops moving quickly between points and starts repeating himself, he is weighing your case or losing patience, so stop and confirm his concern in writing.
Sean Casten.follow_up: Send him a written note the same day with the agreed step, its owner, and the date it is due.
Sean Casten.personality: Casten stands near the top for outgoing and curious traits, and his legislation covers somewhat more topics than most. Fairly careful and organized, his public talk about his work is much less detailed than most. His language is less charged than most yet upbeat beyond nearly all colleagues, and he is easily stirred, much more than most. Crossing the aisle happens somewhat less often for him than for most.
Sean Casten.speaks: Pace is among the fastest in the chamber, with very short pauses between phrases. Volume is more even than nearly anyone's, and his pitch is flatter than nearly all colleagues'. Answers in interviews run longer than nearly any colleague's, and the longest ones are among the longest in the chamber. Words come out upbeat and sociable, and filler shows up somewhat more than most. Most of the recorded speech comes from the floor.
Sean Casten.decides: Written technical support behind an ask matters most to him, so evidence sent ahead of time gets a fair hearing. Pressure from outside lands on him a bit harder than on most members, so a push from outside voices can shift his view. He crosses the aisle somewhat less than most and follows through somewhat less reliably, so a decision sticks only once its next step has a name.

archetype.justification: His talk ranges very widely across issues, he is much less reliable on bills, and he frames cases around who is helped.

Seth Magaziner.bottom_line: Bring the people the bill helps and ask for one clear step, since outside pressure moves him more than nearly any member.
do: Open with who the bill helps, in one sentence
Ask him to commit to one step, since follow through is much weaker
dont: Read his gentle manner as a yes
Treat a drop in his floor volume as the end of talks
Seth Magaziner.warning_sign: By default his pitch moves much more widely than most do, while his wording sounds softer. If his delivery flattens, he has stopped pressing the point, so ask him what he needs to move it forward.
Seth Magaziner.follow_up: Afterward, email his office a brief note naming the one step he agreed to and the date, within two days.
Seth Magaziner.personality: Magaziner talks across a very wide set of issues, while fewer issues fill his bills, so his broad talk runs ahead of his legislative reach. At seeing bills through he is much less reliable than most. Curious and agreeable in manner, he speaks somewhat softer than most. Partnering across party lines comes somewhat more easily to him than to most. Early in his career he taught school in Louisiana.
Seth Magaziner.speaks: He talks somewhat slower than most, with pauses that run somewhat longer, and his volume and pitch rise and fall much more than most. On the House floor those swings are wide and clear, so he sounds energetic when he presses a point. In wording he comes across somewhat softer than most. His description of his work runs somewhat less detailed than most. At a hearing he is much less confrontational than most colleagues.
Seth Magaziner.decides: Community impact fits him best, so he judges an ask by the people it helps. Outside pressure moves him more than nearly any member, so a case backed by people back home carries weight with him. He is much less reliable at seeing bills through, so a yes from him holds only once a follow up is set. That makes his support strong when it comes, but it needs a checkpoint to stay put.

archetype.justification: He is very outgoing and eager but loose with details, and one of the least reliable members at following bills through.

Seth Moulton.bottom_line: Open with the practical result in one short case, and get the ask in writing. He ranks among the least reliable at following bills through.
do: Send a brief note on the practical gains, ahead of the meeting
Put the result first, in the outgoing, social register he uses
Treat every remark as public, since few members get more eyes on them
Confirm the next step by writing, with the owner named
dont: Pile several questions into one long agenda
Interrupt his filler-heavy answers to get to the point
Argue every point in hearings, because he is more combative there than most members
Seth Moulton.warning_sign: He usually gives fuller answers than most. If they turn short and clipped, he has finished with the topic. Narrow to one next step, and leave the rest for a later call.
Seth Moulton.follow_up: Send his staff one written question on the open point, and set the reply date yourself.
Seth Moulton.personality: Moulton is very outgoing and one of the House's most visible figures. He is fairly curious, but close detail does not come easily to him. Carrying votes and bills through ranks among the weakest in the House. He is quicker than most to get worked up. In hearings he is a notch more combative than most, and his tone sharpens. His public words are a bit more upbeat than most.
Seth Moulton.speaks: In interviews his pauses run longer than nearly any other House member. On NPR his pauses run noticeably longer than on Sunday shows. His volume holds more level than most, and his pitch swings far more than most speakers do. Filler words turn up often, well beyond most members. His replies run longer than most, and the longest of them stretch further. Keep your own answers short so he has room to fill the gaps.
Seth Moulton.decides: Ask him which point he would test first, and build your next step around that point. He gives longer answers than most, so wait for the full answer before you reply. He takes charge of conversations somewhat less than most, so leave him room to speak before you sum up. In formal settings he runs somewhat more combative than most, so settle the open point before the hearing.

archetype.justification: Few House members follow through as reliably, and she talks a little more slowly than most.

Sharice Davids.bottom_line: Put a shared role on the table early, since she follows through more reliably than nearly anyone.
do: Point to a bill of hers that she has seen through
Name the colleague who would appear with her, and confirm early
Let her finish a point at her slower pace, then log each commitment
Get outside voices to reach her before the meeting
dont: Water down the ask because her wording runs much gentler than most
Settle for one visit when a return trip could help
Read her reserved style as a lack of interest
Sharice Davids.warning_sign: Her wording is usually much gentler than most. If it turns sharp, she is no longer open to the plan as it stands. Stop, boil the ask down to one line, and offer her time to reply.
Sharice Davids.follow_up: Send her a short written note with the shared role and the next step by Friday.
Sharice Davids.personality: Davids is careful and well organized, and she is very agreeable, with a curious streak. She is among the most dependable members at voting and bill follow-through in the House. The bills she carries touch a broader spread of issues than most, while her public words about the work are much more detailed than most. Her wording runs much softer than most, and it carries a little less emotion than most.
Sharice Davids.speaks: Pace runs a bit slower than most members', with longer pauses between phrases. Her pitch moves somewhat more than most. Her volume varies much more than most. Hearings bring out a somewhat more combative side in her than most members see. Her public talk ranges over many more issues than most. Keep your own tone level, and let her complete each thought.
Sharice Davids.decides: Outside pressure has a slightly larger effect on her than on most. A visible partner can give her a clear reason to commit, since she follows through closely. Let her choose which of you leads the public explanation, so each of you knows the part you own. End by asking which claim she would most like put in writing first, and by when.

archetype.justification: Few senators are as curious, he is quite skeptical, and his public wording is much more forceful and much cooler than most.

Sheldon Whitehouse.bottom_line: Send the written technical case ahead, and keep your own answers direct. A well-built mechanism earns more attention with him than a pitch does.
do: Send a written technical brief a week ahead, with the mechanism in order
Open with the question the mechanism answers, rather than a summary
Let his longer answers finish, since they run longer than most
Confirm each commitment in a dated note, since bill follow-through runs much weaker than most
dont: Treat his skepticism as hostility toward your ask
Lean on action talk in the room, since few senators speak less of action
Chase quick replies with rapid follow-ups, since he gives them much less often than most
Sheldon Whitehouse.warning_sign: He usually gives full replies, and quick bursts come much less often. If he starts firing back one-line answers in quick runs, his attention has moved off your claim. Stop, name the single claim he questions, and send a written note on it.
Sheldon Whitehouse.follow_up: Within two days, call his staff contact to ask when he will answer the one open point.
Sheldon Whitehouse.personality: Whitehouse is one of the most curious senators, and he is quite skeptical by default. He is fairly organized and precise, yet his votes and bill work lag well behind most. Visibility in his role is fairly high, and he is somewhat more easily stirred up than most. Hearings bring out a slightly more combative side in him, and his public language reads much cooler than most.
Sheldon Whitehouse.speaks: His answers in interviews run somewhat longer than most, and their length varies more than most. Pace runs a bit quicker than most, and pitch varies more than most. His volume stays much more even than most. Filler comes up less often than most in his talk. Forcefulness marks his wording more than most, and his words run cooler than most, so keep your replies direct and unhurried.
Sheldon Whitehouse.decides: Name the weakest step yourself before he does, so the case shows its own gaps. Outside pressure counts for a little less with him than most, so the mechanism has to carry the case. He has spoken about his father's service in the Pacific in the war, and where it honestly fits, that is common ground. End by asking which section of the mechanism he wants tested first.

archetype.justification: She crosses party lines somewhat more than most and is very dependable on votes and bills, so a cooperative, reliable approach fits her.

Shelley Capito.bottom_line: Bring a precise written case and a clear next vote to weigh. She is very dependable once she commits, so a clear yes from her will hold.
do: Name the colleagues across the aisle who already support the ask
Ask her to confirm the next vote, since she is very dependable on bills
Expect longer answers in conversation, so leave room to hear her fully
dont: Lean on an upbeat, energetic pitch, since her words run flat and cool
Read her easygoing manner as proof the ask is settled
Shelley Capito.warning_sign: She usually gives longer answers and does not often take charge of the room. If she suddenly goes quiet on a point she normally discusses, she is weighing the ask or has a reservation, so ask her directly which point needs settling.
Shelley Capito.follow_up: Send her a short written note within two days naming the next step, its owner and when it is due.
Shelley Capito.personality: Capito is quite reserved and very careful, and her descriptions of her work come in more detailed terms than nearly anyone in the Senate gives. She crosses party lines a bit more than most, and she is very reliable on votes and bills. Harder to rattle than nearly anyone, she still lets her words run cooler than most. Her earlier career was in education, as a career counselor and as director of an educational information center. Her party's Senate policy committee is one she chairs, and she represents West Virginia.
Shelley Capito.speaks: Her delivery runs quicker than nearly any colleague's, and gaps between her phrases are notably short. Loudness swings far more than most, and pitch shifts more than nearly anyone's. Filler words turn up more than nearly any colleague's, and answers run somewhat longer than most. Wording is gentler than most and cooler than most, with less emotional charge than usual.
Shelley Capito.decides: She sizes up proposals by whether they produce real outcomes locally, and once committed she is very dependable. Pressure from outside has a little more pull on her than most, so a visible push from home can help. Her record of crossing party lines makes a shared deal carry weight with her. So a decision with her holds when the next vote has a date attached.

archetype.justification: Bear fits because her case centers on who is helped, and she describes her work with unusual precision.

Sheri Biggs.bottom_line: Bring one ask tied to the people it helps, and agree a clear next step before leaving. She follows through very reliably, so a written next step will hold.
do: Name the community the ask would help, in concrete terms
Hand over a written summary, since she tracks bills closely
Bring local voices who back the ask and can speak to its people
dont: Leave the meeting without a written next step and an owner
Sheri Biggs.warning_sign: Broad discussion will not reveal how she handles a request that touches a specific group. Before you go in, ask her staff which step she wants written down, and send it after.
Sheri Biggs.follow_up: By a set date, email her staff a brief recap of the ask, the community it helps, and the next step.
Sheri Biggs.personality: Biggs follows bills through to completion very dependably and goes into her work with unusual precision. Bills in her portfolio touch fewer policy areas than nearly any colleague's, and public words stay within a narrow field. She keeps attention on a few areas rather than spreading it. Focus on who is helped runs through her work. Each conversation tends to stay on the matter at hand. Her state is South Carolina.
Sheri Biggs.speaks: She speaks in careful, detailed terms about the policy and keeps talk on a small set of topics. Answers are precise and tend to stay with specifics rather than broad framing. Listeners get the detail of the work rather than the broad picture. Talk is focused rather than expansive, and each answer stays tied to the bill in front of her.
Sheri Biggs.decides: Her approach checks whether the people it helps are clearly named and whether it sits squarely inside her narrow set of issues. Requests outside those areas carry little weight with her, since her bills cover a limited set of policy areas. Her follow through is very strong, so a decision holds only when one named step sits in writing.

archetype.justification: His low profile, narrow issue range and much less combative hearing style fit a quiet member.

Shomari Figures.bottom_line: Ask him for one concrete step, and bring outside voices who back it. Outside pressure moves him more than most, so let those voices carry the case.
do: Name the one concrete step in writing before you meet
Ask a more visible colleague to carry the step with you
dont: Assume his support is settled once outside voices have spoken
Shomari Figures.warning_sign: In hearings he is usually far milder than the typical member. If you see him turn sharp with a witness, he is on guard about the issue, so prepare a plain answer to his objection before you meet.
Shomari Figures.follow_up: Send a short written recap of the step, with its owner and date, within two days.
Shomari Figures.personality: Figures is a member with a narrow issue focus, little emotional charge in his public words, and a low profile in the House. He is hard to ruffle, and when he discusses his work he uses more detailed terms than most colleagues. He is fairly dependable on roll calls and in carrying bills forward, so his commitments tend to last. Taken together, he is a specialist who keeps a low profile while his work goes on.
Shomari Figures.speaks: His talk runs at a fairly quick pace, with much shorter pauses between phrases than most colleagues. His volume holds steadier than most, and his public words carry little emotional charge. Specific bills draw more detailed terms than most colleagues, and his set of topics stays narrow. In hearings he is far less confrontational than most colleagues. Most of his recorded speech comes from the House floor.
Shomari Figures.decides: He weighs an ask by who stands behind it and what step it asks of him. Pressure from outside sways him a bit more than most members, so a request that arrives from several sides carries weight. He keeps far lower visibility than most colleagues, so his support tends to come quietly. So a decision holds with him when the next step is in writing and tied to one clear ask.

archetype.justification: She is very curious and open to new angles, though her record on finishing bills falls short of most colleagues.

Shontel Brown.bottom_line: Offer a joint role she can stand behind, and send a dated written recap. Her curiosity is strong, and outside pressure sways her less than most.
do: Bring a written plan, since her bill follow-through trails most colleagues
Open with the shared role you propose and who else would stand with her
Prepare firm answers in case the plan comes up in a hearing
Close by asking what she needs to see before she commits
dont: Ask hard questions in a formal hearing, since she is much more combative there
Lean on outside calls to move her, since pressure sways her less
Pitch the shared role as routine, with nothing new to explore
Shontel Brown.warning_sign: She usually presses with a firm edge in hearings. If she turns courteous and drops a point fast, she has already settled the matter. Name the single point that would reopen it, and leave a short written answer.
Shontel Brown.follow_up: By tomorrow, send her office a dated recap, with a named person for each step.
Shontel Brown.personality: Brown brings a very curious mind to her work, and her talk covers a bit more ground than most. Her attention to detail is looser than most, and her bills span among the narrowest sets of issues in the House. Her record on bills, votes included, trails most colleagues. Visibility for her role runs lower than most. In formal hearings she is markedly more combative than most members.
Shontel Brown.speaks: Her public tone is somewhat less charged than most. Her account of her own work is somewhat less detailed than most, so ask her for the specifics you need in writing. On the House floor her volume climbs and drops a lot, and her pace runs much slower than most. Her tone in hearings sharpens much more than most members, so keep formal questions short and specific.
Shontel Brown.decides: Her follow-through on bills runs a bit behind most colleagues, so ask for a yes only once the facts are settled. Outside pressure sways her less than most. Her bills span fewer issues than almost any member in the House. She is very curious, so bring one fresh idea she has not heard before, and say plainly what is new in it.

archetype.justification: His details run much looser than most, and his public talk spans somewhat more issue areas, while his bills reach somewhat more topics.

Shri Thanedar.bottom_line: Send the technical detail ahead and ask for one next step. He works across the aisle much more than most, so offer a shared path.
do: Put the written technical case in his hands before any meeting
Offer a shared path that gives both sides a next step
Keep your own tone level even while his volume swings
dont: Count on him to see a bill through without a written follow up
Fill his long pauses with more argument before he has answered
Shri Thanedar.warning_sign: In a hearing he is usually a little more restrained than most colleagues. If his questions drop away and he goes quiet, he is losing interest, so return to the one next step.
Shri Thanedar.follow_up: Send him a short written summary naming the next step, its owner, and the date it is due.
Shri Thanedar.personality: Thanedar is very reserved, and few colleagues are less outgoing. He is fairly curious about the issues in front of him, yet his details run much looser than most. He works across the aisle much more than most, though his follow through on bills lags well behind most. Michigan is his home base, and few colleagues are less visible for their role.
Shri Thanedar.speaks: His volume swings more than nearly anyone's in the House, and pauses between phrases run somewhat longer than most. His public talk spans somewhat more issue areas than most, and his detail on his work is much thinner than most. Breadth leads more than depth, so the written detail has to fill in what speech leaves out. His recorded audio all comes from the House floor, so read his delivery as floor delivery only.
Shri Thanedar.decides: A request that builds a shared path earns his hearing, while one framed as a win for one side stalls with him. He takes written technical detail seriously, since written detail suits how he works and gives him something to test. Because his follow through on bills trails most colleagues, a decision needs a named owner and a written next step to hold.

archetype.justification: His forceful wording, firm hold on conversations and very reliable follow through fit a direct, commanding style.

Steny Hoyer.bottom_line: Come in with one firm ask and a dated plan, since he holds the room. Outside pressure has a clearly weaker pull on him, so commitments need a written step.
do: Name the one step and let him finish his point first
Agree a written step with a named owner before he leaves the room
Expect a direct answer in hearings and prepare a clear follow up question
dont: Read a clipped answer from him as a sign he has agreed
Press a second point after he has closed the discussion
Steny Hoyer.warning_sign: He usually takes the lead in a conversation and keeps his points tight. In a hearing, if he suddenly stops pressing and goes quiet, he is on guard, so pause and ask what concerns him.
Steny Hoyer.follow_up: Send him a short written summary with the step, its owner and its date within two days.
Steny Hoyer.personality: Hoyer is very careful and well organized, and he proves somewhat tougher to rattle than most colleagues in the House. His public words are cooler than most colleagues', and his wording is among the most forceful in the House. His words lean less toward action than most, and he tends to hold the floor. Follow through on bills is among his strengths, though his bills cover among the fewest issues in the House. His public wording carries less emotional charge than nearly any colleague's.
Steny Hoyer.speaks: His pace is among the slowest in the chamber, with pauses longer than nearly any colleague's. Loudness shifts up and down more than nearly any colleague's, and his voice carries weight. He trails off more than nearly any colleague, so his answers can stop before the point lands. His filler and bursts of short turns are much less common than most, and his talk moves with force. In a hearing he turns combative more often than most members, so his manner sharpens. He presses forcefully, and his wording carries more force than most.
Steny Hoyer.decides: Whether the bills reach fits his own areas of work matters most to him. A firm ask gets a hearing from him, since he holds the room well. Commitments hold best when he has signed off on a step in writing, since outside pressure counts for less. He is very reliable, and bills he backs are usually followed through. So a decision holds with him when a written step has an owner and a date.

archetype.justification: Very reserved, less visible than most, and somewhat sharper in hearings than most colleagues.

Stephanie Bice.bottom_line: Get the ask in front of her through people from home, since outside voices shift her further than most.
do: Bring people from home who share the ask and can speak to it
If a hearing follows, prepare for questions that press harder than private talks
dont: Relying on your own pressure alone, when outside voices move her more
Filling her long pauses with your next point before she is done
Mistaking her reserve for a settled view
Stephanie Bice.warning_sign: By default she is a bit sharper in hearings than most colleagues, so a pointed question from her there is normal. If she keeps returning to one challenge after an answer, she is pressing hard, so answer once in writing and let her finish.
Stephanie Bice.follow_up: Before the week ends, write to her with a note that restates the ask and names the people from home who back it.
Stephanie Bice.personality: Bice represents Oklahoma and is very reserved, yet her descriptions of her own work rank among the most exact in the chamber. Public talk ranges across a somewhat broader set of issues, and her bills touch somewhat more areas than most. Feeling runs a bit higher in her public language than most, and she is a little harder to ruffle. Visibility stays lower than most colleagues, and in hearings she is a bit sharper than most colleagues. She works across the aisle a little less than most.
Stephanie Bice.speaks: Her public manner is precise about her own work and wide in what it touches, with her words carrying a bit more feeling than most. Her speech runs somewhat slower than most, with pauses between phrases that run much longer than most, and her volume rises and falls much more than most. All of her recorded audio comes from the floor, where the format shapes delivery. In hearings she is a bit sharper than most colleagues.
Stephanie Bice.decides: She weighs an ask through the voices around it, and outside pressure from home moves her more than most colleagues. She keeps a lower profile than most, so an ask carried by others reaches her more easily than one carried by you alone. Because she works across the aisle a little less than most, a case that leans on partners there needs local voices behind it to land with her.

archetype.justification: Among the most curious members and very careful, he speaks to more subjects than almost anyone.

Stephen Lynch.bottom_line: Bring a careful written case and give him room on each point. Pressure will not carry him, since outside pressure moves him much less than most.
do: Lead with the careful detail and the wider issue context in writing
Keep your replies short so his brief answers can set the pace
Name a colleague across the aisle who can co-sign the ask
In a hearing, expect pointed questions and answer briefly
dont: Rely on his public profile alone to move the vote
Stephen Lynch.warning_sign: When pressed in a hearing, he usually gets more combative, and the shift is easy to see. Give him room to finish, then restate the one ask in a single plain sentence.
Stephen Lynch.follow_up: Afterward, send a short written note with the technical detail and one dated next step to his staff.
Stephen Lynch.personality: Lynch stands among the most curious members in the chamber, and very careful and organized, so he weighs each point closely. He keeps a bit of reserve and is a little less easily rattled than most. Across his talk, a wide spread of subjects appears, and his wording carries a bit more feeling than most. He works with colleagues across the aisle somewhat less than most, though his drafted bills cover a little more ground than most.
Stephen Lynch.speaks: His talk ranges across more subjects than nearly anyone in the chamber. His delivery runs much slower than most, and pitch is among the flattest in the chamber. Pauses are somewhat shorter than most, and his public wording is far less geared to action than most colleagues'. In a hearing, his combative streak runs well above the usual level. Outside hearings, his public wording still runs much sharper than most.
Stephen Lynch.decides: Written specifics that pass his own scrutiny decide whether he backs a request. Across the aisle he works somewhat less than most, so a cross-party push alone will not move him. Outside pressure moves him much less than most, so private argument carries more weight. His own replies come out far briefer than the typical member's, so any commitment needs a named owner and a date.

archetype.justification: He is among the most curious members, and his bills span a wider set of topics than nearly all colleagues.

Steve Cohen.bottom_line: Bring a tight, written technical case and let him run the conversation. He will hold the floor, so a concise close matters more than a long case.
do: Send the technical detail ahead, since his curiosity draws him in
Hold back your reply until he has finished a long answer
Pin down one concrete next step before you leave
In a hearing, expect pointed questions and a fast tempo
dont: Assume a commitment will hold without a written record
Answer his sharp wording with sharper wording of your own
Mistake his high profile for a firm commitment
Steve Cohen.warning_sign: He usually talks fast and breaks off mid thought, so quick bursts are normal. When his pace slows and he finishes each sentence, he has gone on guard. Let him finish his thought, then answer his point.
Steve Cohen.follow_up: Send his office the technical detail and a written summary of the agreed next step and its owner by the end of that day.
Steve Cohen.personality: Cohen is outgoing and very curious, and he is among the most visible figures in the chamber. He leans only slightly toward doubt, heats up more readily than most, and his wording cuts harder than nearly any colleague's. Working with people from the other side comes easily to him, and he often takes charge of conversations. Descriptions of his own work run looser than most, and detail is not his strength.
Steve Cohen.speaks: He talks quickly, and his loudness varies more than nearly any colleague's. Topics range widely, and replies often stretch well beyond the norm, with the longest running far past the rest. Often he leaves sentences hanging. Under the glare of a hearing his wording turns blunt and forceful, and he presses harder still. Pitch swings more widely than almost any colleague's, adding color to every point.
Steve Cohen.decides: Before any ask he tests whether the written case holds up and whether it fits the many issues he already works on. He tests claims before he backs them, and outside voices sway him far less than they sway most colleagues. In formal settings he grows far more combative, yet he still works with people on the other side. So a decision sticks only when the written case is solid and the next step is explicit.

archetype.justification: He follows bills through with fair dependability, takes charge of conversations less than most, and is hard to rattle.

Steve Daines.bottom_line: Ask for one clear step backed by results, since pressure from outside moves him less than most.
do: Open with a concrete result the bill delivers in its first sentence
Show how the ask fits with work he has already done across the aisle
Confirm where the bill stands, since he follows bills through fairly well
In a hearing, expect courteous questions and a polite tone
dont: Count on him to steer the conversation
Assume outside allies will settle his view
Steve Daines.warning_sign: He usually finishes his points cleanly, so a change shows when his sentences start to hang. That usually means he is disengaging or unsure where the ask lands. Stop, ask him what the bill would need to work for him.
Steve Daines.follow_up: Within a day of the meeting, send him a short written summary of the result and the next step.
Steve Daines.personality: Daines, of Montana, is a little reserved and fairly agreeable, and he is hard to rattle. His wording sounds cool and a little less social than most colleagues'. Sentences get finished more reliably than most, and he takes charge of conversations less than most. Bills he sponsors reach a far broader array of issues than most colleagues do, and his bipartisan work runs much more than most. In the room, that combination makes him cooperative and hard to push.
Steve Daines.speaks: He completes his sentences far more often than most and seldom trails off. His wording reads as cool, and it is less focused on action than nearly any colleague's. Runs of quick, short replies show up somewhat less in his talk than in most. Length of his answers stays fairly even across a conversation. Hearings show him among the least combative of his peers. His language is a little more forceful than most. Emotional charge in his words runs lower than in most colleagues' speech.
Steve Daines.decides: He weighs an ask by what it delivers, and pressure from outside does little to change his position. Because he cooperates across the aisle far more than most, he reads an ask for how it bridges sides. Being fairly agreeable, he is open to a case made on the merits. So an ask that colleagues on both sides can back has more pull on him than a plea.

archetype.justification: He takes charge of conversations, stands firm when challenged, and keeps his answers short and practical.

Steve Scalise.bottom_line: Lead with the one ask and keep it short. He takes charge of the conversation and holds firm when pushed, so a long case hands him things to argue.
do: Put your single ask in the first minute
Frame the ask around practical results and bills that can reach a vote
Expect quick pushback and answer it once, plainly
dont: Assume outside voices will change his mind
Spend the meeting on small talk and rapport
Steve Scalise.warning_sign: Usually he digs in when someone challenges him, so a sudden quiet where he would normally push back means he is weighing your point or losing interest. Stop, name the part you can change, and wait for his reply.
Steve Scalise.follow_up: Within two days, send his staff a single page summary of the practical steps, with each owner and date listed.
Steve Scalise.personality: Scalise is highly visible, rivaled by almost no colleague in the House, and one of its most practical. He is somewhat outgoing, somewhat less easily rattled than most colleagues, and a little skeptical of big claims. His public words carry much less feeling than most, and his public talk stays on somewhat fewer issues than most. Bill follow through is reliable, and he takes charge of conversations. Those traits make him a member who keeps a visible role, pushes his case plainly, and does not give way easily when challenged.
Steve Scalise.speaks: His pace runs somewhat quicker than most colleagues, with shorter pauses and an even volume. His pitch stays somewhat flatter than most, and his answers come in short, direct form rather than long stories. On wording, he is less forceful than most, and he answers in quick, clipped bursts much less than most. Under questioning he is about as combative as almost anyone, and he leans toward a firm line when questioned.
Steve Scalise.decides: Requests get weighed on practicality and whether they carry a clear owner. He holds his line when challenged, so a counter needs facts he can check rather than more pressure. Outside voices move him less than most, so his support rests on the work itself. He follows through on bills reliably, so his yes holds once the next step has a name and a date.

archetype.justification: His bills reach somewhat more issue areas than most, and his account of his own work runs somewhat thinner than most.

Steve Womack.bottom_line: Rest the case on its merits and state the ask plainly, since outside calls shift him far less than most.
do: Pin down who on his staff tracks the bill before you leave
Frame the ask around a point his own side already backs
dont: Count on outside voices to carry the ask
Lead with a bipartisan frame, since he crosses the aisle somewhat less than most
Steve Womack.warning_sign: He usually runs somewhat sharper than most, so a jump to much sharper wording is the sign he has stopped being patient with the point. Keep your own tone down and ask which part of the case he rejects.
Steve Womack.follow_up: After the meeting, put the case in a brief written recap for his office, with the bill's status and what comes next so staff can track it.
Steve Womack.personality: Womack is a broad, easygoing member from Arkansas who is much harder to rattle than most. Colleagues find him fairly agreeable, and his stances are easy to find since he is fairly visible. Bills span somewhat more ground than most, while his talk about his own work stays somewhat less detailed, so he runs wide rather than deep. He is somewhat less given to crossing the aisle than most, and follows bills through less reliably than nearly any colleague.
Steve Womack.speaks: He speaks at a slow pace but with short pauses between phrases, so his sentences run together. His volume stays almost level, and his pitch runs somewhat flatter than most. Language carries somewhat more feeling than most, and wording lands with a somewhat sharper edge than most. When he describes his own work, he stays less detailed than most colleagues and does not dwell on the particulars.
Steve Womack.decides: He judges a request on fit with the many areas he already covers, and outside pressure weighs much less with him than with most. Working across the aisle is somewhat less common for him than for most, so a bipartisan push carries less weight. Following bills through ranks him among the weakest in the House, so a yes from him stays a yes only while someone keeps the bill in view.

archetype.justification: Bear fits because his case centers on who is helped, his words run upbeat, and hearings bring out a sharper edge in him.

Steven Horsford.bottom_line: Lead with the people your ask would help, then get a named next step before you leave. Pressure from outside voices tends to carry weight with him, so bring allies.
do: Open with the people the ask would help, in concrete terms
Line up outside supporters before you raise the ask
Let him set the pace, since he rarely takes charge of a conversation
In a hearing, expect firmer questions and answer them plainly
dont: Assume a yes in the room will carry through to a vote
Count on outside pressure alone to settle the question
Steven Horsford.warning_sign: He usually lets others lead the talk and keeps an upbeat tone, so a flat pitch is the signal. When his voice flattens, he is losing interest or on guard. Name the concern, ask what would help, and offer a smaller next step.
Steven Horsford.follow_up: Send a short written summary of the ask, the supporters, and the named next step within a week.
Steven Horsford.personality: Horsford is outgoing and upbeat, and his words carry plenty of enthusiasm. He is a touch looser with details than most colleagues and describes his work in broad strokes, staying focused on the people policy reaches. He is far less forceful than nearly any member and rarely takes charge of a conversation. Follow through trails most colleagues, so enthusiasm does not guarantee delivery. As a Nevada member, he presses somewhat harder in hearings than colleagues do.
Steven Horsford.speaks: Talk comes in upbeat, social runs at a somewhat faster pace than most, with short pauses between phrases. Pitch and volume rise and fall more than most, and answers stretch longer than most. Framing centers on people rather than fine detail. Words come across as gentler than most, yet in hearings the edge sharpens. Overall the delivery is lively and open.
Steven Horsford.decides: He weighs an ask by who it helps and whether outside voices back it. Backing from people he hears from can shift his view, since outside pressure carries more weight with him. A case built on the people affected lands better than a dense memo. His follow through is much weaker than most, so a decision holds only when a named owner carries it.

archetype.justification: His public profile runs high for the job, and his talk turns to who is helped, so community stories fit him.

Suhas Subramanyam.bottom_line: Bring a story about who is helped, with one clear next step tied to it. Keep the ask simple, since follow through on bills is a real strength for him.
do: Back each claim with a fact, since he leans a touch skeptical
Lead with who is helped, since stories about people fit him best
Use a clear next step with a date, since follow through is reliable
In a hearing, expect a civil tone and keep answers on the record
dont: Push him hard in a hearing, since he is much less combative there
Suhas Subramanyam.warning_sign: When pressed in a hearing he usually stays on his point, and his answers stretch somewhat longer. Keep the exchange short, stay on your one fact, and let him finish before you add a second point.
Suhas Subramanyam.follow_up: Afterward, send a short written summary with the people helped and one dated next step to his office.
Suhas Subramanyam.personality: Subramanyam is fairly outgoing, and his public profile runs high for the job. He leans a touch practical and a little skeptical, and runs a bit looser on details than most. Strong feelings come somewhat more easily to him than to most, and his wording reads somewhat cooler than most. He covers somewhat narrower ground in his bills than most, and his wording is among the least forceful in the chamber.
Suhas Subramanyam.speaks: His words lean much more toward action than most, and they run much flatter than most. Pace runs somewhat faster than most, and his pauses between phrases are somewhat longer. Pitch moves somewhat more than most, while his answers run somewhat longer than most. Even his longest answers run a bit shorter, and his answer length is among the most even in the chamber. Under challenge he is much less combative than most in hearings.
Suhas Subramanyam.decides: He asks whether it puts people who are helped at the center. His bill range is somewhat narrower than most, so a focused ask fits him. Outside pressure sways him far more than most members, so local voices weigh heavily. Follow through on bills is fairly dependable for him, so a yes from him sticks once a dated step is set.

archetype.justification: Very outgoing and forceful in her words, she takes charge of conversations and talks fast, fitting the Blue Jay.

Summer Lee.bottom_line: Let her take the floor, then tie your ask to a result she can use. Pressure from outside reaches her more than most, so a visible backer helps.
do: Lead with the result, then pause for her reply
Keep the ask tight and fast, matching her pace
Frame each step as an action she can take
dont: Skip assuming a solid record guarantees every bill moves
Warm openers land poorly with her, since her public tone runs cool
Summer Lee.warning_sign: She usually talks fast with a flat pitch, and she tends to hold the floor. If her pitch lifts, she is weighing your point, so cut the detail and say which choice she has to make.
Summer Lee.follow_up: Send her staff a one page recap of the vote plan and who handles each task by Friday.
Summer Lee.personality: Lee is very outgoing and ranks near the top for getting worked up. Her tone sits near the bottom for warmth, and her words are forceful in a way few colleagues match. Details slip through her talk more than most, and she leads a room in conversation much more than most. Her portfolio touches a narrower set of issues than most colleagues, and she is somewhat more reliable than most at seeing bills through.
Summer Lee.speaks: She speaks at a much quicker clip than most, with much shorter pauses between phrases. Her loudness barely changes, among the least varied in the chamber, and her pitch stays much flatter than most. Trailing off mid thought happens more than most, and filler words turn up much more often than most. Her answer lengths swing more widely than nearly any colleague's.
Summer Lee.decides: She moves when outside pressure builds, since it reaches her more than most. Bills stay in fewer areas than most, so an ask inside a narrow lane gets a hearing. Her record on seeing bills through runs somewhat better than most, and once she agrees, a yes from her tends to hold. Written support that arrives early gives her a reason to commit sooner.

archetype.justification: Among the most reserved and careful, she gives among the shortest answers in the chamber.

Susan Collins.bottom_line: Lead with the outcome and the facts, and pitch it as a case both sides can accept, since she works across party lines more than almost anyone.
do: Name a colleague from the other party who shares the goal
Show how each bill moves from vote to final passage
Ask one question at a time and wait for the answer
dont: Rely on outside pressure alone to move her
Assume a bipartisan label alone will win her over
Susan Collins.warning_sign: She usually keeps her words very gentle, so a sharper tone is a clear change. When her words turn sharp, she is on guard, so stop, let her finish, and answer only what she asked.
Susan Collins.follow_up: After the meeting, send a written note with the next step and a date, within a week.
Susan Collins.personality: Collins is among the most reserved members of the Senate, yet she is very agreeable. She is among the most careful in the chamber and describes her work in far finer detail than most. Her tone runs a little cooler than most, and her language is among the least excited in the chamber. Answers are brief, among the shortest in the chamber, and she trails off somewhat less than most. She works across party lines more than almost anyone, and she sees bills through very reliably.
Susan Collins.speaks: Her volume stays very even, and her pitch stays very flat. Her pauses between phrases come a little shorter than most. In interviews her turns rank among the briefest in the chamber, and her longest turns are briefer still. Her answers vary in length somewhat more than most, and she uses less filler than most. In hearings she presses somewhat harder than most members. She frames issues in careful detail and keeps a gentler tone than most.
Susan Collins.decides: She weighs an ask by its results and facts, and she is willing to work across party lines. Pressure from outside moves her more than most, so organized voices can shift her view. She joins bills across party lines more than almost anyone, so she gives extra weight to bills with support from both sides. A proposal without that support tends to stall in her hands.

archetype.justification: She leans reserved, fairly careful and organized, and few colleagues are less visible, which fits a patient, low key style.

Susie Lee.bottom_line: Lead with support across the aisle and tie it to the people it helps. Outside voices shift her far more than most colleagues, so bring them in.
do: Lead with the people your ask helps
Bring a voice from home who backs the ask
Propose a shared next step across the aisle
dont: Assume a public campaign will move her by itself
Expect quick replies from a reserved member
Susie Lee.warning_sign: Brief sessions will not expose how she tracks a bill once it moves, because her reserved style hides the working calendar. Ask her staff for the vote date and the committee timetable, then confirm the next step in writing.
Susie Lee.follow_up: After the meeting, send her staff a written note with the ask, the people it helps and a dated next step, copied to her chief of staff.
Susie Lee.personality: Lee leans somewhat reserved and fairly careful, with a wider set of topics than most. She reaches across to colleagues in the other party more than nearly anyone, and her legislation spans a wider set of policy areas than most. She is among the least visible members, and her public language is less charged than nearly any colleague's. Together these traits make her a quiet bridge builder who prefers durable coalitions to public fights.
Susie Lee.speaks: Her public language covers somewhat more topics than most, and it reads as matter of fact. It carries far less feeling than nearly any colleague's, so her delivery sounds plain rather than charged. Her public talk leans toward explanation rather than emotional appeal, and a listener hears a plain, even handed argument. Her wording stays on the issues, which keeps the tone informational.
Susie Lee.decides: Whether colleagues across the aisle can share it is how she sizes up an ask. Outside voices move her far more than most colleagues, so outside support counts. Her bills span somewhat more policy areas than most, so an ask needs a clear fit with those areas before it earns her yes. Her coalition habits show a preference for shared credit over public wins.

archetype.justification: Her quick, flat delivery and low emotional charge fit a plain spoken, low key operator who keeps things direct.

Suzan DelBene.bottom_line: Bring outside voices who back a narrow ask and keep it plain, because outside voices carry more weight with her than with colleagues.
do: Lead with the direct ask and the people it helps
Let her press her position, then answer it directly
Bring outside voices who back the ask
dont: Read her gentle wording as easy approval
Go soft in a hearing where she presses
Suzan DelBene.warning_sign: Her pattern is normally quick speech with short pauses and a flat pitch, so flat tone alone is normal. If she slows, leaves sentences hanging, and her pitch rises, she is on guard, so ask one plain question and let her answer.
Suzan DelBene.follow_up: Once the session ends, write her a clear memo on the request, the bill's human effect and its backers, then ask for a reply by a set date.
Suzan DelBene.personality: DelBene is quite reserved, with a skeptical streak and a manner that is hard to fluster. Her bills span a somewhat wider set of issues than colleagues, yet her public talk stays on a narrower set of subjects. In hearings she presses harder than colleagues, so her questioning carries more edge. Her Washington seat frames a plain, direct manner in public.
Suzan DelBene.speaks: Talk from her is fast with very short pauses between phrases, and her pitch stays flat, so delivery sounds brisk and even. Descriptions of her work are somewhat less careful and detailed than colleagues', and her public range of issues is narrow. Words are gentler than colleagues, with little emotional charge, though in hearings she pushes much harder. Volume stays more even than colleagues' speech.
Suzan DelBene.decides: Her view of a request depends on how it touches the several policy areas her bills already reach, since they range across more topics than colleagues do. She is a little less dependable in following bills through, so a decision holds best when a date is attached. External advocates sway her more than peers, so each choice requires supporters who remain active until the vote.

archetype.justification: Her warm, upbeat public wording, gentle tone and wide issue range fit a hummingbird that flits quickly between topics.

Suzanne Bonamici.bottom_line: Bring a specific ask in short form and leave with a dated next step, since her replies are short and her tone gentle.
do: Lead with a short story about who the ask helps
Ask one clear question and wait for her short reply
Agree a dated next step and who owns it
dont: Treat a warm meeting as proof that the vote is secured
Read her upbeat energy as a commitment to the ask
Suzanne Bonamici.warning_sign: Usually she replies in rapid bursts and often leaves sentences unfinished. If she goes quiet and stops mid thought, she is losing patience and wants the exchange to end. Confirm the next step and close.
Suzanne Bonamici.follow_up: Send her staff a short written summary with the ask, the bill and the owner of each step.
Suzanne Bonamici.personality: Bonamici is reserved and fairly careful, and she ranks among the most agreeable colleagues in the chamber. Her legislation touches more topics than nearly anyone's, and her public words carry very little emotional charge. Public tone runs warmer and brighter than nearly any colleague's, and she represents Oregon. She is somewhat less dependable than most at seeing bills through, so her strength is breadth more than follow through.
Suzanne Bonamici.speaks: Her pace runs a bit quicker than usual, with much shorter pauses and a pitch that stays somewhat flatter than most. In interviews her replies come out much briefer than most, their length swings more than nearly any colleague's, and she trails off mid sentence much more than most. Her wording is much gentler than most, and her topics range much wider than most. Her accounts of bill work are thin on fine detail compared with most.
Suzanne Bonamici.decides: Before she backs anything she judges how it fits the wide range of issues she follows, and a request tied to who it helps gets a fairer hearing. Cross-aisle partnering is somewhat thinner for her than for most, so an ask that crosses the aisle needs its own support. Pressure from outside groups registers with her a bit less than with most colleagues, so a yes rests on her own reading of the case. Her follow through lags a little, so a yes needs a named owner and a date to hold.

archetype.justification: Stories about the people a policy serves fit her best, her language cuts sharper than nearly anyone's, and she flares up fast.

Sydney Kamlager-Dove.bottom_line: Lead with the people your ask helps and expect her to test it hard. Her skepticism is strong, so the case has to hold up on its own.
do: Put one real community story at the front of the ask
Pin down who does what, and by when, before you leave
Answer each challenge with a specific fact, not reassurance
dont: Rely on outside pressure to do the persuading for you
Let a heated exchange stand in for a written commitment
Sydney Kamlager-Dove.warning_sign: She usually talks with short pauses between phrases, and her words run sharp. If her voice sharpens further and the pauses vanish, she is getting heated, so slow the exchange and ask what the real objection is.
Sydney Kamlager-Dove.follow_up: Send her a short note listing each commitment, its owner, and the date, within two days.
Sydney Kamlager-Dove.personality: Kamlager-Dove is quite skeptical and flares up fast. Her language cuts sharper than nearly anyone's in the chamber, yet she speaks with far less emotional weight than most. Her talk and bills both stay within a few issue areas. In a hearing she turns a little less combative, which eases her edge. She is a sharp, narrow specialist in the room who presses a few points hard.
Sydney Kamlager-Dove.speaks: Short pauses sit between her phrases, and her volume varies more than most. Her words come across as sharper than nearly anyone's, while her emotional weight is far lighter than most. Range of issues stays narrow, and detail comes out less exact than most. Formal questioning draws a somewhat less combative manner from her than most. Her pace runs slightly slower than most, which lengthens each exchange.
Sydney Kamlager-Dove.decides: Requests that land inside the handful of areas she already covers get her attention, since her bills cover a modest set of subjects. Her skepticism means she tests a case rather than accepting it on trust, and stories about the people a policy serves fit her best. Outside voices carry a little less weight with her than with most, so an ask has to earn her judgment rather than borrow it.

archetype.justification: Her very curious nature and wide issue range fit a watchful observer who ranges widely across subjects.

Sylvia Garcia.bottom_line: Bring a gentle, specific ask built on who it helps, since she ranges across many issues and works across the aisle less than colleagues do.
do: Lead with stories of the people the ask helps
Keep the ask sharp so her curiosity has something to test
Name the members across the aisle who back it
dont: Take her gentle wording as full support for the bill
Sylvia Garcia.warning_sign: She usually trails off mid sentence, so an unfinished thought is normal. If she suddenly finishes every point and her wording turns forceful, she is on guard, so slow down, name her concern, and let her pick the next topic.
Sylvia Garcia.follow_up: After the meeting send her a short note with the people the ask helps and the next topic she chose, and ask her to confirm within two days.
