Sylvia Garcia.personality: Garcia is fairly outgoing and very curious, with a careful streak and a skeptical edge. Her legislation ranges across a wider field than nearly any colleague's. Public talk from her covers many subjects, though she describes her own work less exactly than colleagues. Her public language is notably gentle, with less emotional charge than colleagues'. Across the aisle, she works a bit less than colleagues. She is fairly visible, and she represents Texas.
Sylvia Garcia.speaks: Answers run a bit shorter than colleagues' in interviews, and the longest replies also come up short. Sentences often end unfinished, more so than nearly any colleague's. Talk breaks into brief exchanges somewhat more than colleagues', with few filler words. Language is flat in excitement and less action focused than colleagues'. Tone is gentle, and she becomes somewhat forceful when she presses a point.
Sylvia Garcia.decides: She tends to weigh an ask by the people it helps, so a decision needs proof that those people gain. Her legislation already covers many areas, and an ask that connects to them gets a hearing. The home seat and Financial Services committee role frame the issues she weighs. Moves across the aisle are rarer for her than for most colleagues, so a proposal may need its own backers across the aisle to gain traction.

archetype.justification: She is fairly careful, works across a wide range of issues, and takes much less charge of conversations than most.

Tammy Baldwin.bottom_line: Lead with who the bill helps and ask for one clear step. Pressure from outside reaches her a little more than most, so a trusted local voice helps.
do: Tell the story of who is helped, with one concrete example
Ask her office for the next dated step in writing
If she trails off, let her finish the thought before you reply
In a hearing, expect civil questions rather than a fight
dont: Take her gentle tone as a commitment already made
Expect backing from across the aisle to come on its own
Count on her to take charge of the conversation
Tammy Baldwin.warning_sign: She usually fills her answers with a lot of filler and trails off now and then. If the filler drops out and her answers turn clipped, she is on guard, so ease off and ask what worries her.
Tammy Baldwin.follow_up: Put the agreed points on one written page for her office, with the next dated step and its owner.
Tammy Baldwin.personality: Baldwin is very agreeable and hard to rattle, more so than most. She is fairly curious and fairly careful, and her public talk covers a much broader set of issues than most members. Her wording is gentle and sits at the very bottom of the chamber on feeling. Few people in the Senate take charge of a conversation less, and her bills reach a broader set of issues. Wisconsin is the state she represents.
Tammy Baldwin.speaks: Her words come across cool and gentle, and they carry far less force than the typical member. A broad range of issues comes up in her talk, delivered without much emotional charge. Answers run longer on average, her filler is heavy, and she trails off somewhat more than most. Pace runs somewhat faster than most, with a pitch that swings widely.
Tammy Baldwin.decides: Her view of an ask turns on the people it helps and on whether ties across the aisle are in play. She works across the aisle somewhat less than most, so she is careful about joining a coalition. Pressure from outside reaches her a little more than most members, so a request backed by people at home can change her view. She takes much less charge of conversations, and a commitment from her holds when a written next step names who acts.

archetype.justification: Terrier fits because she is quite skeptical, speaks faster than nearly any colleague does, and public phrasing from her cuts harder than most.

Tammy Duckworth.bottom_line: Lead with one action and its owner, since follow through is her weak point. Pressure from outside carries real weight with her, so bring visible allies.
do: Give her a role she can lead or announce alongside others
Expect fast, skeptical questions and answer each in turn
Bring a detailed answer ready, since her own answers run long
dont: Treat her skepticism as a refusal to engage, since it is her habit
Assume cross-party cover will come easily from her
Tammy Duckworth.warning_sign: She usually speaks sharply, so a softer edge is the signal. When her wording turns gentle, she is losing interest or growing wary. Let her finish, then restate the one action and its owner.
Tammy Duckworth.follow_up: Send her a short written note with the one action, its owner, and a date, since she tracks follow through poorly.
Tammy Duckworth.personality: Duckworth is very curious and fairly outgoing, yet quite skeptical of claims put to her. Getting worked up comes easily to her, ranking high across the chamber, though her words run flatter than nearly any colleague's. Cross-party cooperation is much lower than most, and she trails most colleagues when it comes to finishing bills. As an Illinois member she is fairly visible.
Tammy Duckworth.speaks: Talk comes fast and with fewer pauses than nearly any colleague, and pitch shifts somewhat more than most. Interview answers stretch much longer than most, though their length stays even. Filler arrives much more often than usual, and conversation centers on action rather than broad framing. Words come across as warmer than most, yet less forceful than nearly any colleague's. In hearings the edge is much softer than most members.
Tammy Duckworth.decides: Her test is whether it gives her a visible role and a clear owner. Backing from outside voices shifts her view more than most, since she responds to public support. Her skepticism means she checks claims against the record, so an ask that can be checked holds up better. Her follow through trails nearly every colleague. A decision holds only when a named owner and date are written down.

archetype.justification: Among the most reserved members and among the least visible, so his low profile shapes how to approach him.

Ted Budd.bottom_line: Make an ask built around one community the bill helps. Pressure from outside groups moves him more than most members, so he needs outside weight behind the ask.
do: Open with the community the bill helps, by name
Ask for a one to one meeting, since he keeps a low public profile
Put the next step in writing, since his follow through is much weaker than most
dont: Leave a verbal yes unwritten after the meeting
Read his silence as opposition
Ted Budd.warning_sign: In hearings he is usually less combative than nearly any member, so if he starts pressing a witness hard, the answer has not satisfied him. Slow the exchange, repeat the exact point he raised, and let him move on.
Ted Budd.follow_up: Put the community, the next step and the person who will check it into a written note to his office within a day.
Ted Budd.personality: Budd keeps to himself in public, and his language is a little less charged emotionally than most. He also gets worked up a little more easily than most, and details get somewhat less of his attention than most. Across his public talk, the topic range is wider than most colleagues. He represents North Carolina and sits on Senate Small Business. Taken together, the traits describe a member who keeps a low public presence.
Ted Budd.speaks: He talks fast, so his sentences come quickly, and his pauses between phrases are briefer than nearly any member's. Pitch swings widely from one phrase to the next, and his loudness varies somewhat more than most. He ranges over more topics than most colleagues do, and his language is a little less charged. In hearings he challenges witnesses less than nearly any member.
Ted Budd.decides: A named community standing behind an ask matters to him, so concrete stories about the people affected are what land with him. Pressure from outside groups carries more weight with him than with most members, so outside support can change his position. He is quiet in public and rarely pushes a fight, so a quiet ask with a clear community behind it fits him. Because follow through on bills is much weaker for him than for most, a written next step with a named owner keeps him to a decision.

archetype.justification: He is very outgoing, and his talk stays on a narrow set of topics.

Ted Cruz.bottom_line: Keep the ask short and results focused, and let him take the floor first. He defends his position hard when challenged, so expect the first push to be firm.
do: Put a short, results focused case in front of him
Let him hold the floor, then press your point
In a hearing, expect hard, fast questioning
Acknowledge the pushback before answering it
dont: Count on bipartisan deals to win his support
Read his fast, upbeat talk as a sign he has agreed
Lean on a long, detailed case to win him over
Ted Cruz.warning_sign: His usual pattern is fast, forceful talk with a flow that comes in bursts. When his pauses come more often, he is weighing the ask, and when he defends his position harder, he is digging in, so acknowledge the pushback first.
Ted Cruz.follow_up: Give a brief written summary within a week naming the step, its owner, and the date it is due.
Ted Cruz.personality: Cruz is among the most outgoing people in Congress and among the most visible. He is far less practical than typical, and he carries a mild streak of doubt. His talk stays on a few topics, far fewer than typical, and his descriptions of his work are much less exact. Reaching across the aisle is rare for him, and he is among the least dependable at seeing bills through. His wording runs well above typical in emotional heat, and he is quick to defend his stance.
Ted Cruz.speaks: His pace runs a bit quick, with much shorter pauses between phrases and a pitch that moves a great deal. In conversation he dominates the talk well beyond typical, though his answers stay somewhat shorter than typical. His wording comes across as well warmer than typical, and it reads as among the most upbeat in the chamber. His answer length varies a great deal from one reply to the next, and he answers in bursts more than most. When pressed he digs in well beyond typical, and his stance rarely softens.
Ted Cruz.decides: A request earns his support if results can be shown in a short, direct way. He takes charge in the room, so an ask that lets him lead the talk gets a fairer hearing. Follow through ranks among the lowest for him, so a promise needs a date and a named owner. Cross aisle support is rare for him, so an ask needs its own backers. Pressure from outside groups sways him somewhat more than most colleagues, so an outside push can shift his position.

archetype.justification: He is quite skeptical, defends his position much more than most, and has bills covering more issues than nearly any member.

Ted Lieu.bottom_line: Lead with results and facts in one tight case. He defends his position hard when challenged, so expect him to argue rather than drop the point.
do: Lead with the outcome the policy delivers in plain terms
Set the opposing case beside his, point by point
Expect quick challenges and answer each with one fact
dont: Pile on feelings and appeals in the room
Water down the core claim just to avoid a fight
Ted Lieu.warning_sign: He usually keeps answers short, even, and nearly free of filler. If he starts adding filler and repeating his point, he is digging in, not drifting. Answer with one fact and let him finish.
Ted Lieu.follow_up: Before the next hearing or markup, mail a brief note on the agreed point, with its owner and due date.
Ted Lieu.personality: Lieu is warm and social, and he ranks among the highest for visibility. He is quite skeptical and defends his position much more than most, so debate is part of his style. Bills span a wider set of topics than nearly any colleague's, yet he is much less reliable at seeing each one through than most. Answers stay even in length and rarely trail off, and filler is nearly absent from his speech. He leads conversations a little less often than most, even with that warm manner.
Ted Lieu.speaks: His public words roam across a far wider set of subjects than most, and carry a bit more heat than most. His answers are much shorter than most and stay even in length, with almost no filler. Under challenge he holds firm across shows. His delivery runs a little slower than most, with pauses a little longer between phrases. He is much less forceful than most in how he states a claim.
Ted Lieu.decides: Whether results hold up under challenge is what he tests first, and claims lacking that footing make him quite skeptical. He defends his position much more than most, so a case built on facts holds up better than one built on feeling. Pressure from outside counts for less with him, so the ask has to win on the merits. An ask without a named owner gets argued down.

archetype.justification: Among the most outgoing colleagues, very curious, and much more emotionally charged than most, which suits a lively style built on people.

Teresa Leger Fernandez.bottom_line: Offer a shared role to announce together, since pressure from outside reaches her more than most colleagues.
do: Name a shared role you can both announce in public
Pair her with a colleague from the other party on the ask
Confirm one clear next step before you walk out
dont: Rely on her ties across the aisle to carry the ask
Treat her interest in many issues as a vote for your bill
Teresa Leger Fernandez.warning_sign: In a hearing she usually leans a little more combative than most, so a sharp question is routine and not a warning on its own. If her questions turn personal, she has run out of patience, so slow the exchange and ask what she needs.
Teresa Leger Fernandez.follow_up: After the meeting, email her office the agreed next step by Friday, naming its owner.
Teresa Leger Fernandez.personality: Leger Fernandez is very outgoing and very curious about many issues. Her public talk runs hot, well past most colleagues in emotional intensity, and it spans a broader slate of topics than most colleagues. Across the aisle she is among the least active, and her profile is quieter than most for her role. Her details are somewhat looser than most, and her votes and follow through are somewhat less reliable than most.
Teresa Leger Fernandez.speaks: Her public talk is charged, and she gives somewhat less detail about her work than most. Gaps between her phrases come a little shorter than most, and her loudness shifts somewhat more than most. In hearings she leans a little more combative than most, so her questions can carry edge. Her delivery is energetic rather than formal, and it reads as lively.
Teresa Leger Fernandez.decides: A chance to lead or make an announcement, visibly, is what she looks for first. Pressure from outside reaches her more than most colleagues, so support from beyond her office counts for more with her than the argument alone. Her ties across the aisle are thin, so the ask has to stand on its own. Choices hold only when a partner is named and a date is set.

archetype.justification: Very outgoing, fairly curious, and agreeable, with very short answers and a cool, flat delivery.

Terri Sewell.bottom_line: Keep the ask short and concrete, and expect brief replies rather than a long debate. Outside force shifts her only slightly less than most, so facts must carry it.
do: Put the one ask and its facts on a single page
Show how the bill touches issues she already follows
In a hearing, expect her to be much more combative than most
dont: Take her brief replies as the end of the discussion
Count on a warm tone to win her over
Terri Sewell.warning_sign: Her usual pattern is fast, brief talk that often trails off. Watch for her slowing and giving a fuller answer, which usually means your point landed. Then stop, confirm the one fact she needs, and let her reply.
Terri Sewell.follow_up: Send a short written note that repeats the one fact she needs and the source for it, within a day.
Terri Sewell.personality: Sewell is very outgoing, fairly curious, and agreeable, and she is quicker to get heated than most. Her words carry emotional weight well beyond most, though her warmth runs cooler than nearly any colleague's. She gives very short answers and trails off more than nearly any colleague, and she is strongly combative in hearings. Taken together, she is a sociable, expressive operator whose brief, cool manner keeps conversations moving and leaves some points unfinished.
Terri Sewell.speaks: Delivery runs quicker than most, with tighter gaps between phrases. Her pitch stays somewhat flatter than most, and her volume is more level than most. Wording is somewhat flatter and less forceful than most. Her answers are much shorter than most, and even the longest ones stay brief, with very little variation in length. She trails off more than nearly any colleague, and filler appears a little more often for her than for others.
Terri Sewell.decides: Focus matters most to her here, since her legislation touches a tighter field than most colleagues do. She is fairly curious and agreeable, so she will hear a request out, though seeing bills through is harder for her than most. Pushing from outside shifts her a touch less than most, so a decision sticks only when the ask is narrow and the facts hold up.

archetype.justification: Sharp in wording, ready to defend his position, with much shorter answers, and written technical evidence fits him best.

Thom Tillis.bottom_line: Bring written technical evidence and let it carry the case, not pressure. Outside pressure moves him less than nearly any member, and a challenge in the room hardens him.
do: Send the written, technical case before the meeting
Keep your points short, since his own answers run short
Expect him to push back when challenged, and answer with data
dont: Lean on outside pressure to move him
Assume a warm pitch will win him over
Match his sharp wording with sharper words of your own
Thom Tillis.warning_sign: He usually keeps answers short and level, and he defends a point when pushed. When his answers run longer than usual and he repeats the same point, he is on guard, so stop arguing the point and offer the written evidence instead.
Thom Tillis.follow_up: Within two days of the meeting, send him the written evidence with the ask restated in one line, since follow through is weak.
Thom Tillis.personality: Tillis is somewhat curious and takes a little more to rattle than most, and he is very visible in his role. Talk ranges across a somewhat wider set of issues than most. His language carries much more feeling than most, yet his wording cuts much sharper than most. Among the most social voices, he is still among the least forceful when he asserts a point, so his sharpness lands as jabs rather than arguments. Bills span much broader ground than most, though he is among the least reliable at seeing bills through. Replies come back much briefer than most, and he works across the aisle somewhat less than most.
Thom Tillis.speaks: Answers come in short, direct turns, and he trails off much less than most, with less filler than most. Subjects span a somewhat wider set of issues than most. His language carries much more feeling than most, yet his wording cuts much sharper than most. Pauses run shorter than most, and volume varies less than nearly any colleague's. When pushed, he digs in and repeats his point somewhat more than most. He goes into less detail about his own work than most.
Thom Tillis.decides: He weighs an ask by the written, technical evidence behind it. Outside pressure moves him less than nearly any member, so a push from people back home carries little weight. He is among the least reliable at seeing bills through, so his follow through needs a written record. A direct challenge makes him dig in, so documentation is what sticks with him.

archetype.justification: Among the most reserved members, he talks in much more careful detail than most and works across the aisle more than almost anyone.

Thomas Kean.bottom_line: Bring one specific ask with a clear story about who it helps. Outside voices move him more than nearly any member, so line up support before you ask.
do: Open with one named family the policy would help
Name the members across the aisle who already back the ask
In a hearing, prepare firm answers, since his manner turns somewhat more combative there
Keep your delivery level while his pitch and volume move in bipartisan talks
dont: Assume he will carry a bill to the vote without reminders
Write off a first no, since outside voices can change his answer
Thomas Kean.warning_sign: He usually talks fast with a voice that swings widely, and his wording stays a little gentler than most. If that pattern fades and his delivery turns flat, he is losing interest, so stop adding points and ask what he needs next.
Thomas Kean.follow_up: After the meeting, send him a written list of next steps with a named owner and a date for each.
Thomas Kean.personality: Kean is among the most reserved members, and his work is methodical and orderly. Things fluster him a little less than most, and his public talk covers somewhat fewer topics than most. He works across the aisle more than almost anyone. Yet he ranks among the least dependable when bills need a vote, so his bipartisan work outpaces the bills he finishes.
Thomas Kean.speaks: He talks fast, and his pitch varies further than nearly any member's while his volume rises and falls much more than most. Public wording stays a little gentler than most, and descriptions of his work run in close, exact detail more than most. He covers a somewhat narrower set of topics, and his language is charged with feeling much more than most. In hearings his manner gets somewhat more combative as the setting turns formal.
Thomas Kean.decides: He weighs an ask by who it helps, so a case built on the people who benefit gets his attention. A shared base of support carries real weight with him, and he joins bipartisan bills more readily than nearly any member. He is among the least dependable at seeing bills through, so a yes can stall before the vote. So an ask he has agreed to needs someone tracking it through the vote.

archetype.justification: His very outgoing manner, high visibility and skeptical streak fit a butterfly that moves lightly from one spot to the next.

Thomas Massie.bottom_line: Lead with the one bill step you need, since follow through on his bills is among the weakest in the House.
do: Send the written technical evidence a week ahead
Explain the case in plain steps, one bill at a time
Expect quick, clipped answers and let them stand
dont: Assume a verbal yes will carry through to the vote
Take his sociable wording as a sign he will back the ask
Thomas Massie.warning_sign: Usually he talks very fast, with short pauses and a volume that stays even. If he slows down and his pauses lengthen, he is weighing whether your case will hold up to a test. Give him the one fact he can check, then stop talking.
Thomas Massie.follow_up: Send a short written summary with the bill step, the owner and a date, and ask him to confirm it by return.
Thomas Massie.personality: Massie reads as very outgoing and fairly curious, and he ranks at the very skeptical end of the chamber. Accounts of his own work come across as far less detailed than most. Legislation for him spans a narrower set of topics than most, and bill follow through ranks among the least dependable colleagues. His public presence is very high for a member of this body, and he represents Kentucky.
Thomas Massie.speaks: Pace runs well above the usual range, with much shorter pauses between phrases, and his volume holds more evenly than nearly any colleague's. His pitch moves through a wider range than usual. In conversation his replies come out much briefer than usual, and in interviews even his longest replies run short. Public wording comes across as notably cool, and his talk about his own work is far less detailed than most.
Thomas Massie.decides: On paper, an ask must read clearly to him, and its logic has to hold up to his own test. Follow through on bills ranks near the bottom for him, so a verbal agreement carries little weight until it is written down. Pressure from outside registers with him less than with most lawmakers, so his yes rests on his own reading of the case. His legislation spans a narrower set of topics, so an ask outside his usual lines faces an uphill climb.

archetype.justification: Outgoing and curious, he is also much more combative in hearings than most colleagues.

Thomas Suozzi.bottom_line: Give him a concrete ask to champion, then agree a next step with a date. He moves much more under outside pressure, so backers across the aisle help.
do: Offer him a visible role to lead or announce with you
Bring a fresh question he can explore with his staff
Name a colleague from across the aisle as a cosponsor
If a hearing turns combative, keep your answers brief and factual
dont: Assume his outgoing manner means he will commit on the spot
Thomas Suozzi.warning_sign: He usually keeps quick replies coming and often trails off mid sentence, so a reply that ends cleanly is a change. If he starts to take over the discussion, slow down and ask what he thinks is at stake.
Thomas Suozzi.follow_up: Mail his office a brief sheet of notes on the request, the next action, and who will own it by Friday.
Thomas Suozzi.personality: Suozzi is outgoing, curious, and among the most agreeable members in the chamber. In his public remarks he moves across more issue areas than almost anyone's, and his bills span broader areas than most. He is among the most combative members in hearings, yet his public language is somewhat gentler than most. Visibility runs very high, and his words are very forceful. He is also somewhat warmer than most in public language.
Thomas Suozzi.speaks: In his public remarks he moves across more issue areas than almost anyone's. His words are very forceful, and he talks with a rising and falling pitch much more than most. He answers in quick bursts, and his answer length varies somewhat more than most. Volume rises and falls somewhat more than most, and sentences sometimes drift off before the end.
Thomas Suozzi.decides: A request is judged by whether he can carry colleagues across the aisle with him, so backing from the other camp counts for a lot. External pressure pushes him far more than most colleagues, so a visible backer can shift his view. His follow through is somewhat weaker than most, so an agreed date matters more than a verbal yes. A decision therefore holds when a cross party group stands behind it.

archetype.justification: His wording runs more forceful than most, and follow-through on bills runs fairly well for him.

Thomas Tiffany.bottom_line: He defends his position somewhat more than most, so bring the next step ready. Close with one clear question he can answer yes or no.
do: Ask for a yes once he names the step, since he usually sees bills through
Name the one step he is ready to approve, in one plain line
Let him finish defending a point, then restate the next step
Keep each question single, since his quick runs are rarer than almost anyone's
dont: Read his forceful wording as a refusal of the ask
Treat one clipped answer as his final say
Let a quick run of replies pull you off the agreed step
Thomas Tiffany.warning_sign: He usually answers each question in one unbroken turn, so a run of quick back-and-forth replies stands out. When replies come fast in a row, he is ready to end the meeting. Slow down, name the one point he is weighing, and pause.
Thomas Tiffany.follow_up: Email his staff a brief recap with the next step and a due date within a few days.
Thomas Tiffany.personality: Tiffany gets worked up much more readily than most colleagues, and he leans a little reserved. Detail is not his strongest suit. He reaches across the aisle much less than most, while voting and bill follow-through run fairly well for him. Practicality shapes his ideas more than curiosity does, and he tends to defend his ground. He is somewhat more forceful in his wording than most.
Thomas Tiffany.speaks: In interviews his replies come out shorter than most, and his length swings a lot from one turn to the next. He trails off much less than most, so his turns end complete. Filler words crowd his answers well beyond most speakers'. On the House floor, volume swings a little more than most. Let the first answer stand, then ask one follow-up question.
Thomas Tiffany.decides: Tie the agreed step to a bill he has already moved through the process, since his follow-through runs fairly well. Pressure from outside moves him far less than most, so the next step must carry the ask on its own. He defends his ground across shows, so state the step in terms he can defend when challenged. Before you leave, ask which of his bills he would move next.

archetype.justification: He is outgoing, loose with details, and answers in quick bursts much more than most, so Squirrel fits.

Tim Burchett.bottom_line: Bring one short, concrete ask and leave with a next step in writing. Long explanations lose him, since he trails off before the point lands.
do: Send written technical detail before the meeting, not during it
Pin down a named next step and owner before you leave
If he drifts into detail, bring him back to the one ask
dont: Expect a long detailed case to hold his attention
Assume pressing his position will win him over
Tim Burchett.warning_sign: He usually trails off into filler, so a loose, rambling answer tells you nothing new. When he begins defending a position he has just taken, he is usually on guard, so stop and restate the one point in a sentence.
Tim Burchett.follow_up: Send him a short written summary of the technical points and the agreed next step, with its owner, by the end of the week.
Tim Burchett.personality: Burchett is among the most outgoing members of the House and one of its most visible. He works across the aisle more than almost anyone, and his words are charged with emotion well beyond most. Loose with details, he is quick to act, so the room gets plenty of energy and fewer exact specifics. Sentences usually trail off into filler, and he digs in when challenged. Taken together, he is a dealmaker who runs on momentum and holds his ground when pushed.
Tim Burchett.speaks: He covers a somewhat broader slice of issues than typical colleagues, and he is looser with specifics than nearly any colleague. His words carry strong emotional charge, with a warm tone and a focus on action. In conversation his answers come in quick, short bursts, and he trails off or fills gaps with filler. His delivery rises and falls in pitch with long pauses between phrases. When challenged, he restates his stance rather than refining it.
Tim Burchett.decides: He weighs an ask best when the technical case is in writing and colleagues across the aisle back it. He is a dealmaker, so a backer who crosses lines moves him more than a message alone. Once he has taken a stance, he defends it when challenged and does not give ground easily. Carrying bills to a finish is a little less reliable for him than most, so his yes holds only when someone owns the next step.

archetype.justification: Very outgoing and very curious, and he holds his ground when someone pushes back.

Tim Kaine.bottom_line: Make the ask in one short, direct sentence on what it delivers, and expect him to defend his view if it is challenged.
do: Lead with the result, then the facts, not the story
Answer a challenge with the same facts rather than a new argument
Let each of his quick turns finish before you reply
dont: Mistaking his gentle wording for a soft position
Cutting off a long answer before he reaches his point
Going flat and formal against his upbeat style
Tim Kaine.warning_sign: By default he talks in quick runs and comes back fast, so a lot of talk from him is normal. If he starts repeating his position when challenged, he is digging in, so stop arguing and ask which fact he wants to test.
Tim Kaine.follow_up: Tomorrow, send him a short written summary of what it delivers, with the next step and its owner named.
Tim Kaine.personality: Kaine represents Virginia and is very outgoing and very curious, with a bright, expansive way of talking. He is among the most agreeable members of his chamber, yet much harder to rattle than most. Descriptions of his work are a little less precise than most, and he steers the flow of talk somewhat more than most. He works across the aisle somewhat less than most, and he gives much longer replies than most. In hearings he presses much harder than most, and he keeps a very high profile for his position.
Tim Kaine.speaks: His speech runs much quicker than most, with shorter pauses between phrases and a pitch that varies much more than most. Rapid bursts of short turns come to him more readily than to nearly any colleague, and his longest replies stretch much further than most. Under challenge he holds the line, and in hearings he is sharper than most colleagues. Interviews on public radio show more pitch movement than televised Sunday segments.
Tim Kaine.decides: He weighs an ask by what it delivers and by whether it holds up under pushback, and he tends to defend a position rather than drop it. Once he has settled on a view, he is fairly dependable at getting votes and bills through. Outside voices shift him somewhat more than most colleagues, so an ask carried by people from home carries the most weight with him.

archetype.justification: His votes and bills get through reliably, and he speaks about his own work with somewhat more precision.

Tim Moore.bottom_line: Bring a broad, documented case and close on a concrete next step, since he is more dependable on bills than on working across the aisle.
do: Cite the votes and bill outcomes behind your ask
Expect quick replies and keep a second question ready
Make your case through staff and written materials rather than public events
dont: Assume support from the other side will carry him on its own
Jump into his brief pauses with extra argument
Tim Moore.warning_sign: A panel talk will not show whether his interest is serious or merely polite. Ask his staff for the timeline and what they need before the next vote.
Tim Moore.follow_up: Within the same week, email his office a brief memo listing the next step on the bill and who owns it.
Tim Moore.personality: Moore is reserved and hard to fluster, and his public talk ranges across a wide set of issues. He describes his own work with care, though he is less exacting about small details by nature. His votes are dependable and his bills reach across many issues, yet he works across party lines less than nearly anyone in the chamber. The result is a member who does the groundwork without seeking attention, so his influence builds through his record rather than through the public stage.
Tim Moore.speaks: His delivery is much quicker than most, with brief pauses between phrases and a pitch that swings up and down more than nearly anyone's in the chamber. He moves across many policy areas within one conversation, and when he describes his own work his language is careful and detailed. Put plainly, his manner is quick and wide ranging rather than slow and narrow.
Tim Moore.decides: Each ask is sized up by the ground it covers and whether it can be carried through to a vote. The bills span many issues, so a proposal fitting a wide agenda draws his attention, and once committed he is dependable. He is reserved, so his influence stays out of public view. Because he works across party lines less than almost anyone, backing from the other side tends to carry less weight with him than a plan he can own. The result is that an ask holds his interest when a named owner stands behind a clear plan.

archetype.justification: Very outgoing, more firm in a conversation than nearly any colleague, and quick to push back under challenge.

Tim Scott.bottom_line: Let him keep the floor, and bring facts he cannot wave off. He pushes back harder than nearly any colleague once challenged, so a bare argument will not move him.
do: Open with the result, stated once and plainly
Use his very visible profile to put the ask in public view
Expect pushback, and answer it with the same facts each time
dont: Count on a bipartisan partner to carry the bill
Assume one challenge will soften his position
Tim Scott.warning_sign: By default he holds his ground harder than nearly any colleague when challenged. If he goes quiet and stops answering a challenge, he is losing interest or on guard, so put one fact in front of him and give him room.
Tim Scott.follow_up: Within two days, email his office a one page summary of the result and the facts behind it.
Tim Scott.personality: Scott is very outgoing and warmer in tone than nearly any colleague. His tone runs more upbeat than nearly any colleague's, and he is somewhat curious. A conversation is one he commands with more firmness than nearly any peer. Under challenge, pushing back harder than almost any member is his pattern. He is somewhat less easily rattled than most. Across the aisle, he works less than nearly any member. He is very visible in the chamber.
Tim Scott.speaks: He speaks somewhat quicker than most, with pauses somewhat longer between phrases and a volume more even than nearly any colleague's. His answers vary much more in length than most, and almost no filler sits in his speech, among the least in the chamber. Tone runs warmer than nearly any colleague's, and he presses points with somewhat more force than most. Pitch stays somewhat flatter than most, and the issue range runs somewhat wider than most.
Tim Scott.decides: He weighs an ask by whether a short, direct result can be shown, and once a position is taken he keeps to it. Pushing from outside shifts him somewhat more than most members, so outside backing can move him. He works across the aisle less than nearly any member, and he follows bills through somewhat less reliably than most. An ask that needs the other side therefore has less backing from him.

archetype.justification: He is practical, talks a little sharper than most, and prefers written, technical evidence.

Tim Sheehy.bottom_line: Send written, technical evidence early, then let outside voices carry the ask, since they shift him further than most colleagues.
do: Put the numbers in writing with their sources attached
Line up outside voices who speak to the ask before the meeting
In a hearing, expect a tone a little gentler than most members use
dont: Count on him to publicize the ask on his own
Push him for a quick yes before outside voices are lined up
Soften the ask until it loses its edge
Tim Sheehy.warning_sign: He usually keeps a sharper edge than most, but in hearings he is a little gentler. If his wording turns harsher than that, he is on guard, so stop, name the specific concern, and answer it with the document.
Tim Sheehy.follow_up: Send a written summary by Friday with the figures and their sources, and name who sends the next version.
Tim Sheehy.personality: Sheehy is practical and a little reserved, with a narrow public focus and a low profile. He is far tougher to rattle than most, and he holds details far more loosely than his colleagues do. His words run a little sharper than most, and he is among the least visible in the chamber. Taken together he is a straightforward operator who stays out of the public eye and keeps his talk to a few issues.
Tim Sheehy.speaks: He talks about fewer issues than nearly any colleague, and when he discusses his work he is a little more precise than most. His wording is a little sharper than most and carries a bit less heat, so his tone reads as direct rather than emotional. In hearings he is a little gentler than most members. His manner is matter of fact, leaning on specifics rather than feeling.
Tim Sheehy.decides: He tests an ask against the documents behind it, since written, technical evidence fits him best. His public exposure is among the lowest, so he is seldom the public face of an ask. An ask inside the few issues he already talks about fits him. Outside voices shift his position more than most colleagues, so an ask that others carry tends to move him.

archetype.justification: He is careful, describes his work in detail, speaks slowly with long pauses, and stays a little less visible.

Tim Walberg.bottom_line: Lead with what the policy delivers, keep the case brief, and let him finish each pause before you speak.
do: Open with what the policy delivers, not the debate around it
Let each pause run, since he sees bills through once he commits
Name a specific vote or bill he can follow through on
dont: Pile more facts on top before he has answered
Assume a quieter hearing means he has no concerns
Tim Walberg.warning_sign: In a hearing he is usually somewhat less combative than most, so a more pointed tone is the change to watch. When he turns pointed after a quiet opening, he is on guard, so ask one open question and let him answer.
Tim Walberg.follow_up: Send his legislative aide a short written note of the agreed step within two days, citing the bill and the result it delivers.
Tim Walberg.personality: Walberg is a reserved, practical legislator who works in a narrow lane from Michigan. Careful and organized, he describes his work in close, detailed terms. Hard to fluster, he keeps a tense exchange from knocking him off his point. Bills stay within a few areas, and he sees them through with great reliability. Less visible than many colleagues, his style is deliberate.
Tim Walberg.speaks: He talks slowly, with long pauses between phrases. Volume rises and falls much more than usual, while pitch stays somewhat flatter. Framing is careful and detailed, and it keeps to a narrow set of topics. Answers arrive as specifics rather than sweeping claims, which is how he makes his case. Emotional tone runs somewhat lower than usual, so the substance has to do the work.
Tim Walberg.decides: He weighs an ask by its practical result and by whether it falls within the few areas he already works on. He wants the facts checked before he commits to anything new. Outside voices have a little more pull on him than on colleagues, so backing from people beyond the room can change his view. An ask has to be clear and checkable before it can move him.

archetype.justification: His public language cuts harder than nearly any colleague, and he details his work with unusual precision.

Timothy Kennedy.bottom_line: Bring precise detail and one clear ask, since the bills he carries dependably reach the finish line.
do: Keep your language plain and free of rhetorical flourish
Bring the bill's record and dates in writing
Match his slow delivery and leave room for longer pauses
dont: Read a long pause as a refusal, since pauses are his usual rhythm
Mistake his sharp wording for a personal attack
Timothy Kennedy.warning_sign: By default his language is very sharp, so a softer, slower run usually means he is backing off the point. Stop pressing, restate the one fact that matters, and let him name the next step.
Timothy Kennedy.follow_up: Send him a written summary of the bill's record and the next dated step within two days.
Timothy Kennedy.personality: Kennedy's public language is among the sharpest in the chamber, with intense feeling running through it. He discusses his work in detailed, careful terms more than most, while his public range is somewhat narrow. His legislation touches a far smaller set of topics, yet he is dependable at carrying bills through. Less visible than his role would suggest, he lets the substance do the talking.
Timothy Kennedy.speaks: His delivery runs well slower than most, with longer pauses between phrases and a volume that stays unusually even. His words are sharp and exacting, and they carry strong feeling. Subjects stay within a narrow set, and each one gets deep, careful detail. Pitch rises and falls a little more than most, so emotion shows in tone rather than speed.
Timothy Kennedy.decides: He reads a request by how narrow and specific it is, since his bills stay within a small set of topics. Once the record is clear, he is dependable about carrying a bill through, so a case built on that record gets his attention. His yes holds only when an owner and a date are written down, so a bare request with no date will not hold him.

archetype.justification: Few senators match her curiosity, and her wording runs upbeat, yet she is among the least reliable on votes and bills.

Tina Smith.bottom_line: Offer a visible shared role she can front, and keep the ask to the big idea.
do: Draft a joint statement she can front with a colleague
Start warm and upbeat, then name the ask in one sentence
Keep the talk on your ask, since she is among the least inclined to lead
Ask her to name the one vote she will take before you leave
dont: Read a pleasant reply as a commitment to vote
Press her hard for a yes in the first meeting
Pitch the ask as a bipartisan win
Tina Smith.warning_sign: She usually lets others set the agenda, so a sudden grab of the talk is the cue. When she takes over the agenda, the talk has shifted to her terms. Leave a one-page summary of the ask with her staff.
Tina Smith.follow_up: Send her legislative director a dated list of next steps within a few days, with the owner for each.
Tina Smith.personality: Smith is very warm in her wording and gives people the benefit of the doubt a bit more than most. Few senators are as curious as she is, though her public talk covers one of the widest ranges in the Senate. She is a bit quicker to get worked up than most, and in hearings she is much more combative. Her roll-call and bill follow-through ranks among the least reliable in the Senate, and she works across the aisle a bit less than most.
Tina Smith.speaks: Her pace runs faster than nearly any colleague's, and her pauses run shorter than almost anyone's in the Senate. In interviews her answers run far longer than most, and her answer lengths stay unusually even, more than nearly any colleague's. Short, quick replies come in bursts somewhat more than most, and filler words creep in a shade more than most. When challenged she holds her ground a bit more than most. Keep your own answers brief, and expect quick back-and-forth.
Tina Smith.decides: A bill with her name beside a colleague's would draw her in, since partnership is the frame that fits her. Calls from outside groups count for less with her than they do with most members. The case itself must do the work. Her follow-through is among the weakest in the Senate, so treat a yes as the first step, not the finish. Before you leave, ask her office who will track each step after the vote.

archetype.justification: Warmer than nearly any colleague, very curious, and much harder to rattle than most, which fits the Hummingbird.

Todd Young.bottom_line: Give him room to think, then bring one clear point. Support around your ask tips him more than most, so the backing around it can make the difference.
do: Ask him to finish any point he leaves unfinished
Share the floor early, since he tends to keep it once he starts
Bring outside voices into the conversation before the vote
Open with a warm greeting, since he is more social than nearly anyone
dont: Count on a quick reply, since he talks much slower and holds the floor
Fill his long pauses, which often end unfinished, with your own points
Todd Young.warning_sign: He usually answers slowly, with wide gaps between phrases. When his gaps close up and his replies come in quick runs, he is losing interest, so stop and ask which point still matters to him.
Todd Young.follow_up: Subsequently, write him a short note naming the backers who support the ask and the date the vote will be decided.
Todd Young.personality: Young is warmer than nearly any colleague, and he is much more agreeable than most. He is very careful and very curious, and much harder to rattle than most. His bills cover among the fewest issues in the chamber. Follow through is somewhat more dependable than most. His speech runs flatter than nearly anyone's. Somewhat less notice comes his way than most, and he is more social than nearly anyone's.
Todd Young.speaks: He speaks slowly, with much longer pauses than most and a volume that holds somewhat more evenly than most. Language is warm and social, though its tone is flatter than nearly anyone's. Longest replies run somewhat briefer than most, and answers vary in length more than nearly anyone's. He does not hurry, and his sentences break off much more than most.
Todd Young.decides: How well it fits the few areas he works on is how he sizes it, since his legislation stays inside fewer areas than nearly any colleague. He follows through somewhat more reliably than most, but outside voices carry much more weight with him than with most colleagues. So an ask that stands alone, without people behind it, tends to wait on him.

archetype.justification: Reserved and exacting, he is organized and keeps a lower profile than most.

Tom Barrett.bottom_line: Bring a practical case he can check line by line. Outside pressure moves him more than nearly any member, so build support early.
do: Lead with the practical detail behind each request, one item at a time
Leave a short gap after each point, since his pauses run short
Line up outside voices who back the ask before you press him
dont: Count on a long social opener to build rapport
Read his quiet as disinterest
Tom Barrett.warning_sign: In a hearing he is usually a little less confrontational than most members. If a hearing brings a more confrontational tone from him, he is getting irritated or on guard. Keep the written point short and let him set the pace.
Tom Barrett.follow_up: After the meeting, send his office one written answer to each point he raised, with each source named, within three days.
Tom Barrett.personality: Barrett is a reserved, careful member who works through problems in an orderly way and keeps his public profile low. He is hard to rattle, and his bills stay within a few issue areas rather than spreading out. He follows bills through reliably enough, and he is less visible than most of his colleagues from Michigan. In the room that means he rewards orderly preparation and a narrow focus, and he does not chase attention.
Tom Barrett.speaks: He talks fairly fast and leaves little space between phrases. Volume stays even, and his pitch runs a bit flatter than most across a conversation. His talk about his work is careful and detailed, though it covers a narrow set of issues. Wording carries heavy emotional weight, among the highest in the House. Pauses are short and his delivery stays level from start to finish.
Tom Barrett.decides: He weighs an ask on practical grounds and wants the specifics before he commits. An ask that stays inside the few issue areas he already works in gets a fair hearing. He is moved more than nearly any member by pressure from home, so a no can turn once people he knows speak up. Because he follows bills through reliably, a yes from him tends to hold once given.

archetype.justification: His interview answers are among the longest in the chamber, and his longest stretches outrun nearly every colleague's.

Tom Cole.bottom_line: Send a written technical note ahead of the meeting, since he takes charge and his answers run long. Keep your own replies short so his turns can run.
do: Send a written technical note ahead, with terms defined and steps numbered
Open with the one technical point you need him to answer first
Let his long answers run before you reply
Close by agreeing the timing of the next call, as he is fairly reliable
dont: Answer a formal challenge coolly, since his words run much warmer than most
Plan for a short meeting when his answers run this long
Mistake his forceful wording for a final decision
Tom Cole.warning_sign: In hearings he is usually one of the most combative members of the House. If he turns mild in a hearing and lets a point drop, he has decided the matter is closed. Stop, and name the one open issue before you move on.
Tom Cole.follow_up: Within a few days, send his staff a one-page list of open questions, each with an owner.
Tom Cole.personality: Cole is careful about process, and he is very agreeable. He is much less easily flustered than most. In conversation he steers the talk and keeps the floor much longer than most. His public talk about work is much more detailed than most. His bills cover a narrower set of issues than most. Visibility runs high for the role he holds.
Tom Cole.speaks: In interviews he uses far more filler than nearly any colleague, and his answers stretch in long turns. His tone runs warmer by a wide margin than most, and his language is more forceful than nearly any colleague's. Pace sits somewhat slower than most, while volume sits more even than nearly any colleague's. He answers in short back-and-forth turns much less than most. Pull the point out of his filler, then repeat it back to him.
Tom Cole.decides: He responds to written technical evidence sent ahead of the meeting, which fits him. Pressure from outside sways him more than most members, so a repeated clear ask keeps the item moving. He sets the course of the talk, so agree the order of the points before the meeting starts. Leave room for his long answers, since they stretch further than nearly any colleague's.

archetype.justification: Very visible and somewhat warmer in wording than many, he is much less reliable at seeing bills through.

Tom Cotton.bottom_line: Make the ask short and concrete, and leave with a named next step. He follows through much less reliably than many colleagues, so the step must be written down.
do: Put the one commitment you need on paper before you leave
If he talks quickly, match his pace and keep points brief
Bring the figures that support the ask, since facts fit best
Let him take the public lead on the ask, since he is very visible
dont: Let a vague answer stand as an agreement
Rely on outside pressure to move him
Tom Cotton.warning_sign: His wording is usually much sharper than colleagues'. If his wording softens, he is weighing your ask. Stop, ask which part is giving him pause, and let him answer before you go on.
Tom Cotton.follow_up: Send a written summary the next day listing the commitment and who owns it by name.
Tom Cotton.personality: Cotton is somewhat reserved and somewhat skeptical, and a little harder to fluster than many colleagues. Curiosity runs somewhat higher than many colleagues, and his wording is somewhat warmer. His description of his work is much less detailed than many colleagues', and he is very visible in the chamber. He has represented Arkansas in the Senate for several years, and he is a familiar face there.
Tom Cotton.speaks: His pace is much quicker than many colleagues, with a pitch that swings up and down far more than many. His wording is among the flattest in the chamber and somewhat less forceful than many colleagues. Volume is among the most even in the chamber. Pauses run somewhat longer than many colleagues, and his wording is much sharper than many colleagues. Overall, his delivery reads as quick, flat in feeling, and even in volume.
Tom Cotton.decides: He weighs an ask by its facts and how it fits the few areas his bills cover. Pressure from outside moves him less than many members, so outside appeals carry less weight with him. He values facts that fit the case, so detail sent in advance carries weight. Following bills through is a clear weak spot for him, so a commitment holds only when it is written down with an owner.

archetype.justification: He takes charge of conversations, defends his positions when challenged, and speaks with a forceful, direct manner.

Tom Emmer.bottom_line: Bring a short written case ahead of time and let him test it, since outside pressure will not move him much.
do: Send the written case in advance, with the figures laid out
Let him take the floor early, then hold your questions
Frame the ask around priorities his own side already backs
Match his directness with short, plain sentences
dont: Read his short answers as disinterest
Assume a deal across the aisle will carry him
Count on outside pressure to change his position
Tom Emmer.warning_sign: He usually answers fast and holds the floor, so watch for him cutting his own sentences short. When that happens he is losing interest or getting on guard. Stop, restate the one ask in a sentence, and let him push back.
Tom Emmer.follow_up: Within a day of the meeting, send him a short written recap of the one ask and its evidence.
Tom Emmer.personality: Emmer, a House Majority Whip, is very curious and fairly visible, yet he is looser with specifics than most. His cool, forceful manner means he seldom works across the aisle and digs in once challenged. He is harder to fluster than almost anyone in the chamber, so a challenge tends to sharpen his argument rather than unsettle him. Sitting on House Financial Services, he runs most conversations he joins.
Tom Emmer.speaks: He talks fast and in forceful bursts, and he trails off partway through sentences more often than nearly any colleague. Issues get framed across a wide range of topics, with far less filler than most and less emotional charge. His volume stays much more even than most, while his pitch moves up and down more than almost anyone in the chamber. When challenged, he holds his position rather than softening it.
Tom Emmer.decides: Material handed over before the meeting suits how he weighs an ask best, and pressure from outside has less effect on him than on most members. After he settles a position, he defends it when challenged, and he takes charge of most discussions where it is contested. So a written case he can test himself carries more weight than any push from outside in the room.

archetype.justification: He takes charge of conversations, defends his position hard, and is among the most reliable on votes and bills.

Tom McClintock.bottom_line: Bring written technical evidence early, since he defends his position hard and holds the floor once he has it.
do: Let him finish his point before you answer
Match his quick short turns instead of long speeches
In a hearing, expect the sharpest exchanges and stay on your facts
dont: Compete with him for the floor during the meeting
Expect a dropped point to mean he has accepted it
Assume he will carry a promised vote without a reminder
Tom McClintock.warning_sign: He usually gives rapid replies in bursts and defends his position hard, so a sudden lull is worth noting. If he stops pushing back and lets a point drop, he is losing interest, so slow down and ask what he needs.
Tom McClintock.follow_up: Send the technical evidence in writing ahead of the meeting, then confirm each step by email with a date.
Tom McClintock.personality: McClintock is fairly outgoing, and his curiosity is among the keenest in the chamber. Yet he is also among the most skeptical, and he flares up a little more quickly than most. His language is a little softer in tone, yet it carries more feeling than most. In conversation he takes over the floor much more than most. He is among the most reliable on votes and bills, and his words sound among the least excited in the chamber.
Tom McClintock.speaks: Delivery is slow, yet tone moves up and down much more than most. His volume stays rather level, and his pauses are much shorter than most. Replies often come in fast bursts of brief lines, and his longest answers stay brief. He drifts off partway through thoughts somewhat more than most, and reply length shifts more than almost anyone's. Pressure makes him harden, and in hearings he counts among the most combative voices in the chamber.
Tom McClintock.decides: A written technical brief put before him is what he needs, and he insists on seeing it before committing. Pressure from outside moves him more than most, though it does not replace the written case. Because he is among the most reliable on votes and bills, he expects a stated commitment to be kept, so he holds people to the deadlines they name.

archetype.justification: His words are among the most charged in the Senate, and he answers in quick, short bursts.

Tommy Tuberville.bottom_line: Keep the case short and direct, and expect him to defend his view hard. Outside calls move him among the least of any senator, so the merits must carry it.
do: Send the written technical file and its tables first
Ask him to defend his position in the room, then respond briefly
Work the bipartisan backers into the pitch, since he works across the aisle
dont: Skip the long case, since his answers come in quick, short bursts
Assume his trust settles it, since he is among the least skeptical
Tommy Tuberville.warning_sign: He usually answers in quick bursts and holds the floor. If he slows into full, unhurried sentences, he is on guard. Let him finish, then restate the one point and invite his view.
Tommy Tuberville.follow_up: Send his office a one page memo with the numbers, the bipartisan backers, and the next step, within three days.
Tommy Tuberville.personality: Tuberville is outgoing, and his manner is combative in a room. Worked up quickly, he keeps a trusting temperament. His public talk covers somewhat narrower ground than most. His record on votes and bills is weak, and his detail on work is much less careful than most. Bipartisan ties come easily to him, and he reaches across the aisle a little more than most. His wording carries a good deal of emotional charge. He holds the floor and pushes his position, and he keeps answers short.
Tommy Tuberville.speaks: He answers in quick, short bursts, much more than most. In interviews his answers come out short and clipped. Even his longest replies are much briefer than most. Answer length stays much more even than most. He trails off somewhat less than most. Pauses between phrases run long. Pitch moves up and down with force. Holding the floor comes easily, and words land with heavy emotional weight. Filler runs high, and he speaks with plenty of verbal padding.
Tommy Tuberville.decides: Prior to committing he tests how well the written numbers hold up. Outside groups move him among the least of anyone in the chamber. He defends his view when challenged, and he stays with a position once he takes it. His record on votes and bills is among the least reliable, so commitments need a named owner. Bipartisan backing helps, since he works across the aisle more often than most. So a bipartisan ask with a written plan and a named owner is the one he takes up.

archetype.justification: His public talk about his work is full of specifics, and his bills touch very few issue areas, so his focus is narrow.

Tony Wied.bottom_line: Put one specific ask in writing before you meet, since written technical evidence fits him best. Pressure from outside groups moves him more than most members.
do: Open with the bill's practical specifics before the big picture
Ask him to confirm the details in writing
dont: Rely on argument in the room alone to win him over
Tony Wied.warning_sign: He is usually somewhat less combative than most in a formal hearing, so a sharper challenge from him means the answer did not satisfy him. Stop, restate the figure he asked about, and wait for his next question.
Tony Wied.follow_up: Because he follows through on votes and bills somewhat more than most, send his office a written confirmation of the agreed detail within two days.
Tony Wied.personality: Wied talks about his work with full specifics and keeps his bills to very few issue areas. He is somewhat more dependable than most on votes and bills, so his focus reads as narrow and deliberate. From Wisconsin, he sits on House Small Business. Taken together, the traits make him a member who wants the detail right before he commits to anything. He is not a member who ranges widely, and his talk about his work stays precise.
Tony Wied.speaks: His floor delivery runs somewhat slower than most, with longer pauses between phrases. His volume rises and falls a great deal, while his pitch stays a little flatter than most. Words about his work are exact and specific, and he keeps the range of issues narrow. In hearings, he is a little less combative than most. All of his recorded audio comes from the House floor, so compare it only with other floor speech.
Tony Wied.decides: He weighs an ask by the detail behind it, so a written file with the numbers ready works best. Pressure from outside groups carries more weight with him than with most members, so outside support can change his position. His bills stay within a few areas, so an ask inside those areas fits. Because his record on votes and bills is somewhat stronger than most, a dated written commitment is what holds him to a decision.

archetype.justification: Somewhat wider in his public remarks, his bills touch more issues and he follows bills through, so reliability and range define him.

Tracey Mann.bottom_line: Lead with the result and the facts, then make a clear ask. Pressure from outside lands on him less than most, so a dated next step matters more than urgency.
do: Start with the measurable outcome the policy produces
Bring a clear next step with a date he can keep
dont: Assume outside pressure alone will settle the question
Tracey Mann.warning_sign: A general meeting will not show how he weighs a bill's details once the talk turns technical. Ask a colleague who has worked his committee how he responds when a bill stalls, then plan one concrete step.
Tracey Mann.follow_up: Send his office a one page summary of the ask, the next step and its owner by Friday.
Tracey Mann.personality: Mann talks about somewhat more policy ground than most colleagues, and he describes his work with somewhat more care than most. His legislation touches somewhat more issue areas than most, and he sees bills through somewhat more reliably than colleagues. Across the aisle he joins somewhat fewer efforts than most colleagues. He represents Kansas in a first district seat, and his record is broad.
Tracey Mann.speaks: His pace runs somewhat slower than most, and his volume holds somewhat less variation than most. When he speaks about bills, the terms are more exact than many colleagues'. He covers a broad set of topics in his remarks, spread across more ground than most. In a session, he moves from one topic to the next without narrowing his focus.
Tracey Mann.decides: He weighs an ask by how well it fits the issue areas his bills already cover. A result he can show back home matters, so he backs asks with concrete facts. Pressure from outside lands on him less than most members, so the case must stand on its own merits. He follows through on what he signs onto, so a decision with a dated next step holds.

archetype.justification: His bills take in somewhat more areas than most, and he is among the least visible in the House.

Trent Kelly.bottom_line: Bring written, technical evidence and a clear next step. Outside voices move him much more than most colleagues, so put the reason in print.
do: Put the evidence in writing ahead of the meeting
Line up a bipartisan colleague to sign on first
Credit the affected people and share the stage, since he is among the least visible
Bring the outside voices he listens to, with a clear ask
dont: Skip big public events, since he is somewhat reserved in a crowd
Assume a quick yes from him, since his follow through is somewhat less reliable
Trent Kelly.warning_sign: Written technical evidence sent ahead suits him best, but a general meeting will not show which document he trusts most. Ask him which one would settle the question, and note his answer.
Trent Kelly.follow_up: Send him a one page summary of the written evidence and the outside voices that back the ask, within three days.
Trent Kelly.personality: Kelly is somewhat reserved and somewhat practical in manner. His public talk ranges across somewhat fewer areas than most colleagues. Detail is among the least of his strengths when describing his own work. His bills take in somewhat more areas than most, and he is among the least visible in the House. Across the aisle, he works somewhat less than most, and his record on votes trails somewhat behind. Exposure for his role is among the lowest in the House.
Trent Kelly.speaks: Across his public talk, the range of issues runs somewhat narrower than most. His descriptions of his own work stay general and are among the least detailed of any member. He tends to speak in broad terms about the bills he carries. Those patterns describe his manner, not his motives.
Trent Kelly.decides: He weighs an ask by how well the written evidence holds up. Outside voices move him much more than most, so a request with backers gets a hearing. An ask inside the areas he already knows fits, since his bills take in somewhat more areas than most. Being somewhat reserved, he tends to weigh an argument quietly rather than debate it. So he commits only when someone credible carries the next step.

archetype.justification: His very practical, reserved style and narrow issue focus mark a quiet member who sticks to his lane.

Troy Balderson.bottom_line: Bring a practical, specific case and show the people who back it. Pressure from outside counts for more with him, so lead with local voices.
do: Show how the bill's work reaches local people
Find bipartisan partners on the bill
In a hearing, stay formal and keep the exchange on the record
dont: Press for a quick answer, since he speaks at a slow pace
Lean on outside pressure alone to carry the bill
Treat his bipartisan ties as a promise of his vote
Troy Balderson.warning_sign: He usually keeps to a narrow set of issues. If he turns sharper in a formal setting, he is holding firm on the point, so stop and ask what concerns him before you continue.
Troy Balderson.follow_up: Send a short written summary of the local impact, with a named ally and a date, within two days.
Troy Balderson.personality: Balderson is quite reserved and very practical, and he keeps to a narrow set of issues. He works across the aisle somewhat more than others, and seeing bills through is one of his habits. Details get a bit less of his care than others, and he is much less visible in the chamber. Put together, he is a quiet, practical member who stays in his lane.
Troy Balderson.speaks: He keeps to a narrow range of issues and speaks in plain terms. His words carry a bit less emotional charge, and his delivery stays quiet rather than sharp. In formal hearings his manner is among the least combative. He describes practical results plainly and avoids flourish, so his talk stays focused on what the bill does. Each point is tied to a result people can check.
Troy Balderson.decides: He weighs an ask by whether it serves local people and fits his narrow issues. Seeing bills through is one of his habits, and he works across the aisle, so a bipartisan ask with a clear result gets a hearing. Pressure from outside counts for more with him, so a decision sticks when local backers stand behind the ask and a named next step is written down.

archetype.justification: Gentle public words and a somewhat wide issue range fit a watchful Owl.

Troy Carter.bottom_line: Make the ask easy to say yes to, then get one named next step and its date before you leave.
do: Pitch the ask as work that crosses party lines
Name the staff member who will carry the next step
Ask one question about how the policy would work day to day
dont: Count on outside pressure to close the deal
Troy Carter.warning_sign: By default he speaks in soft, gentle wording and lets arguments pass without heat. If his wording turns sharp, he is growing frustrated or has run out of patience with the point. Ease off and keep the one ask.
Troy Carter.follow_up: After you meet, confirm the next step, its date and the staff member who owns it in a quick note to him.
Troy Carter.personality: Carter is very agreeable and hard to rattle. Public wording is soft, with less emotional charge than nearly any colleague's. He crosses party lines far more than most colleagues, and his bills span a narrower field of issues than most. He describes his work with more careful detail than most colleagues, though his follow through is a little weaker than most.
Troy Carter.speaks: His public words are soft and carry little emotional heat. Ranging across a slightly broader set of issues than colleagues, he frames them with somewhat more careful detail than most. His manner reads as courteous, with no sharp edge in how his words land. Even when a point is contested, the wording stays gentle, with little heat. Overall, the tone stays open and even.
Troy Carter.decides: Because outside pressure sways him less than it sways most members, the case itself has to carry the ask. Follow through is somewhat less reliable than most, so a yes can fade after the meeting. Working across party lines much more than most, he suits a case that crosses those lines. A decision sticks only with a named next step and a set date.

archetype.justification: His much wider issue range, bills across many areas and fairly curious nature earn the Owl label.

Troy Downing.bottom_line: Bring a written, detailed case and a credible outside ally. He moves more under outside pressure than most, so that backing can tip the decision.
do: Send the detailed written case ahead of the meeting
Name the vote date and the staffer who tracks each bill
Bring a local backer to the meeting to speak to the ask
dont: Expect a quick yes on a bill that needs votes across the aisle
Count on curiosity alone to turn him toward the bill
Troy Downing.warning_sign: Usually he is less confrontational in hearings, so a low key tone is normal for him there. When his questions turn sharp and target the record, he has spotted a gap. Send him the written record and let it answer.
Troy Downing.follow_up: Within a week, send him a written summary of the bill's status, the outside backers and the next vote date.
Troy Downing.personality: Downing is a fairly curious and careful member with a much wider issue range than most colleagues. Talk about his own work is among the most specific in the chamber. He works across the aisle much less than most. Bills cover many more issues than most, and he is very reliable at seeing bills through. Hearings find him less confrontational than most members.
Troy Downing.speaks: He speaks with a fairly flat pitch and a voice that rises and falls somewhat more than most. His conversation covers a far broader set of issues than most, and it stays close to specifics. In hearings he tends to be somewhat less confrontational than most members, which keeps the tone even. He keeps to the facts in conversation and avoids sweeping claims.
Troy Downing.decides: The detail behind an ask and the outside support it carries both bear on his view. Outside voices lean on him harder than on most colleagues, so an ask needing votes across the aisle meets a harder test. He works across the aisle much less than most. He is very reliable at seeing bills through, so his backing holds once the plan is written and kept.

archetype.justification: Words that cut harder than nearly any colleague, forceful delivery, and loose handling of detail make the Badger fit.

Troy Nehls.bottom_line: Keep the ask short and concrete, and let him talk before steering back to it. Outside pressure moves him less than most, so the case itself must carry it.
do: Open with proof that the plan works, since he starts from doubt and digs in
Confirm each quick reply with him before you move on
If a hearing turns sharp, answer each point on its facts
dont: Count on a verbal yes carrying through to the vote
Match his sharp wording with sharper words of your own
Troy Nehls.warning_sign: He usually takes the floor and talks a little quicker than most. When he starts defending his position harder, he is on guard, so stop pushing and name the one point he already accepts.
Troy Nehls.follow_up: After the meeting, send him a single page note listing the one vote he agreed to and the date it is due.
Troy Nehls.personality: Nehls is very outgoing and very visible, and he works by force more than by detail. He is much more skeptical than most and much quicker to heat up than most, and he is loose on the specifics, much more so than most. His words are much more charged and forceful than most, while his bills reach much narrower ground than most. In a room he takes charge of the talk and defends his position hard when challenged.
Troy Nehls.speaks: He talks at a pace a little quicker than most. His pitch rises and falls much more than most, while his volume stays much more level than most. Brisk bursts of short lines come from him much more than most. Sharper wording than nearly anyone's in the House marks his talk, and his account of his own work is less detailed than nearly anyone's. When challenged, he defends his position more than most.
Troy Nehls.decides: He weighs an ask by how directly it helps the people a plan would reach. His bills span a much smaller set of issues than most, and his record of getting votes and bills done lags nearly everyone's. Outside pressure has less pull on him than on most members, and when challenged he digs in on his position. So a decision needs a named next step and a date, or it will not stick.

archetype.justification: She leans practical and somewhat careful, and her bills span a slightly narrower set of issues than typical.

Val Hoyle.bottom_line: Bring a specific ask with community stories behind it. Pressure from outside groups weighs on her more, so the ask must hold up to a direct check.
do: Lead with the community stories behind the ask
Agree a dated next step and confirm the owner
In a hearing, expect courteous, low key questions
Bring a clear, practical step she can check
dont: Expect a fierce fight in a hearing
Lean on outside pressure alone to move her
Assume a verbal promise needs no written check
Val Hoyle.warning_sign: Her usual pattern is practical talk with a voice that rises and falls a bit more than typical. When she turns more pointed and her voice swings wider, she is on guard, so lead with the community impact and answer the concern directly.
Val Hoyle.follow_up: Send a short written note within a week naming the step, its owner, and the date for the next check.
Val Hoyle.personality: Hoyle is somewhat outgoing and a little practical, with a careful, organized approach. She is somewhat reliable at seeing bills through, but her bills cover a little less ground than most. She keeps to a narrower set of topics than most colleagues, and her talk stays close to what she already does. In hearings she is far less confrontational than typical colleagues. She represents Oregon in Congress.
Val Hoyle.speaks: Her volume rises and falls somewhat more than typical. All of her recorded audio comes from the floor, so this reading describes that setting. Her talk covers a narrower set of topics than typical, and she stays close to her core subjects. In hearings she is far less confrontational than typical colleagues, and she keeps her manner low key. Taken together, her delivery is a bit more variable in volume than typical, while her topics stay narrow.
Val Hoyle.decides: She weighs an ask by whether its community stories are specific and checkable. Her bills span a narrow set of issues, so an ask that sits inside her areas fits best. Reliable at seeing bills through to a degree, a dated commitment from her tends to hold. In hearings she is far less confrontational, so an ask there can stay courteous and firm.
